title: Cento novelle scelte da più nobili scrittori della lingua volgare, [...] Nelle quali piacevoli et aspri casi d’amore, et altri notabili avvenimenti si contengono. Di nuovo ampliate, reformate, rivedute, et corrette, [...] aggiuntovi di nuovo le figure in principio d’ogni Novella.

authors.name: Sansovino Francesco
authors.biography: Francesco Tatti, generally known as Francesco Sansovino, was born in Rome in 1521 and died in Venice on 28 September 1583. He was the son of the Florentine sculptor and architect Jacopo Tatti, called Sansovino. Baptised in the Roman church of Sant’Eustachio, he had as godfather Giovanni Maria del Monte, the future Pope Julius III. The Sack of Rome in 1527 compelled the family to leave the city, passing through Florence before settling in Venice, where Jacopo entered the service of the Procurators of Saint Mark. Francesco consequently grew up close to the political, artistic, and ceremonial centre of the Republic, although he continued to present himself as Florentine by descent and linguistic allegiance and Venetian by adoption. He also published under the names Anselmo Guisconi and Giovanni Tatti. His education combined humanist letters with the legal studies preferred by his father. Stefano Piazzone da Asola and Giovita Ravizza instructed him in Latin grammar and rhetoric, while Antonio Francini da Montevarchi introduced him to Greek. In 1536 he went to Padua to study law, but also attended the lectures of the classicist Lazzaro Bonamico. His admission to the Accademia degli Infiammati in 1540 placed him within a particularly consequential forum for discussion of rhetoric, philosophy, ethics, and the extension of learned discourse into the vernacular. Among the figures associated with this environment were Sperone Speroni, Alessandro Piccolomini, Benedetto Varchi, Bernardino Tomitano, Marco Mantova Benavides, and Mariano Sozzini. Sansovino became an affiliate of the Accademia Fiorentina in January 1542 and subsequently moved to Bologna, where in 1543 he received a doctorate in civil law. His unpublished Dialogo della pratica della ragione, composed during this formative period, stages an encounter between Bartolus of Sassoferrato and Machiavelli and reveals an early attempt to reconcile juristic tradition with the political language of the Renaissance. Letters exchanged with Pietro Aretino document both Sansovino’s youthful literary ambitions and his gradual resistance to a conventional legal career. By the early 1540s he was already writing poetry, compiling texts, and participating in the editorial culture of Venice. He collaborated with Lodovico Dolce on an edition of Aretino’s verse and published the Lettere sopra le diece giornate del Decamerone in 1542, followed by a short Rhetorica in 1543. His Venetian acquaintances included Dolce, Gaspara Stampa, Giuseppe Betussi, Lodovico Domenichi, Francesca Baffo, and other writers whose careers were closely connected with the presses. He worked as a corrector and editorial assistant, notably in the orbit of the Giolito press, acquiring the practical knowledge of textual preparation, privileges, dedications, typography, and commercial calculation that would later sustain his own publishing activity. A journey to Rome shortly before February 1550, undertaken in the hope that the accession of his godfather Julius III might secure him a curial position, proved unsuccessful, and he returned to Venice. He married Benedetta Musocca, or Misocca, the daughter of the Venetian merchant Vettore Musocca; their children included Iacopo, Fiorenza, and Aurora. In 1554 he definitively abandoned legal practice for the profession of letters.Sansovino’s mature career cannot be adequately described by the modern categories of author, translator, editor, publisher, and bookseller, since he repeatedly combined these functions within a single enterprise. His programme was rooted in the conviction, widely debated among the Infiammati, that the vernacular could make historical, philosophical, technical, and political knowledge available to a readership extending beyond the universities and the learned professions. His publications therefore encompassed medicine and anatomy, rhetoric and oratory, grammar, letter writing, law, history, political institutions, chivalric orders, genealogy, literature, and contemporary warfare. Among the characteristic products of this activity were L’edificio del corpo humano of 1550; his Italian rendering of Aristotle’s De anima in 1551; the juridical dialogue L’avocato, first printed in 1554; collections of vernacular orations; editions and commentaries devoted to Dante, Petrarch, Boccaccio, Ariosto, Bembo, and Sannazaro; and numerous translations or compilations derived from Latin, Italian, Spanish, and other sources. His editorial procedures ranged from translation and abbreviation to compilation, rearrangement, annotation, linguistic revision, and the construction of elaborate paratextual frameworks. Authorship in his books is consequently often collective or stratified rather than unitary, and modern scholarship has shown that the apparently heterogeneous catalogue was governed by recognisable editorial strategies and by close attention to the requirements of the Venetian market.In 1560 Sansovino began publishing and printing on his own account, initially in association with the physician Nicola Tinto. His enterprise employed devices centred upon the crescent moon, including a device accompanied by the motto In Dies, and was accordingly identified with the sign of the Moon. The first years were particularly productive, with imprints appearing under formulas naming Sansovino and his associates; at other times he acted as publisher while employing such printers as Francesco Rampazetto, Stefano Zazzera, the Bonelli, and Daniele Zanetti. He republished established vernacular authors when privileges or commercial circumstances made their texts available, while also issuing medical books, historical compilations, anthologies, and his own works. The undertaking was not uniformly prosperous, and the number of new titles fluctuated considerably, yet the surviving editions demonstrate an unusually sustained passage from service within other workshops to the direction of a recognisable editorial list. Sansovino was enrolled in the Venetian guild of printers and booksellers, although his attempt to obtain a place on its council in 1578 was unsuccessful. His professional identity was expressed with particular clarity in the tripartite classification he gave to his own production: compositions, translations, and collections.Political and historical writing formed one of the most persistent divisions of his work. Del governo dei regni et delle repubbliche, first published in 1561 and subsequently enlarged, assembled descriptions of ancient and modern constitutions in a comparative vernacular repertory. Its sources included Gasparo Contarini, Paolo Giovio, Francesco Guicciardini, Guillaume Postel, Alfonso de Ulloa, Ortensio Lando’s version of Thomas More, and writings by Machiavelli, some of which were incorporated without acknowledgement. Sansovino’s histories of the Ottoman dynasty and Turkish expansion responded to a substantial contemporary demand for information about the Ottoman world, particularly during the wars culminating in the battle of Lepanto. His Concetti politici of 1578 transformed passages from classical and modern historians and political writers into portable maxims intended for governors of republics and principalities. Although Machiavelli was omitted from the declared authorities, a substantial portion of the collection derived from the Discorsi, Il principe, Arte della guerra, and Istorie fiorentine. The collection was repeatedly reprinted and entered English circulation in Robert Hitchcock’s 1590 translation, Quintessence of Wit. Such works are less appropriately judged as claims to philosophical originality than as instruments for reorganising, moderating, and disseminating politically sensitive material among new classes of readers.The most influential of his practical manuals was Del secretario, first issued in four books in 1564 and expanded under his supervision to seven books in 1580. It joined instruction in epistolary composition to formulas of address, model letters, historical documents, and examples drawn from princely and administrative correspondence. In its enlarged form the work also became a carefully managed representation of Sansovino’s own career and patronage, since it incorporated letters sent to him by eminent correspondents and concluded with his autobiographical account to Gianfilippo Magnanini. Its repeated editions, continuing after his death into the seventeenth century, testify to its utility in a period of expanding diplomatic, secretarial, and bureaucratic practice. The manual exemplifies Sansovino’s characteristic ability to convert heterogeneous archival and literary materials into an accessible professional repertory.Sansovino’s enduring reputation rests above all upon Venetia città nobilissima et singolare, published in 1581 in fourteen books. This extensive description developed out of shorter guides to the city, including Tutte le cose notabili e belle che sono in Venetia, issued under the pseudonym Anselmo Guisconi in 1556, and the enlarged Delle cose notabili che sono in Venetia. The mature work integrated topography, ecclesiastical and secular architecture, works of art, magistracies, laws, ceremonies, social customs, princely biographies, writers, patrician families, and the history of the Republic. It drew not only upon printed histories but also upon private family records, monastic erudition, inscriptions, and privileged access to Venetian cultural networks. Although its factual reliability is uneven and its interpretation participates in the political mythology of Venice, it remains an indispensable witness to the city’s monuments, collections, institutions, and self-representation in the later sixteenth century. Its usefulness was recognised by Giovanni Stringa, who corrected and substantially enlarged it in 1604, and by Giustiniano Martinioni, who incorporated Stringa’s material and continued the account to 1663. After Jacopo Sansovino’s death in 1570, Francesco inherited his father’s estate and also contributed to the preservation and reshaping of the architect’s public memory. In 1573 he assumed the title of a knight of the Constantinian Order. Increasing visual impairment afflicted his final years, but he continued to revise, compile, and publish until shortly before his death. He dictated his testament on 24 November 1582 and died in Venice on 28 September 1583 after a fever lasting twelve days; he was buried in the church of San Geminiano. In April 1584 his son Iacopo transferred to Altobello Salicato the printing rights in his father’s privileged and unprivileged works, ensuring their continued circulation. Older criticism frequently treated Sansovino’s dependence upon earlier texts as evidence of haste or deficient originality. More recent scholarship has instead situated him within the material and collaborative conditions of the sixteenth-century book trade: as a mediator between learned culture and the vernacular market, an organiser of textual repertories, and one of the clearest representatives of the writer-publisher whose intellectual labour was inseparable from the production and commerce of printed books.

academic_description: 4to (200x138 mm). [4], 238, [2] leaves. Collation: *4 A-Z4 Aa-Zz4 Aaa-Ooo4. Printer’s device on title page. With 100 woodcuts and numerous large ornamental initials and borders in the text. 20th-century full hazelnut morocco gilt (R. Leuthe Biel-Bienne). Manuscript note on the title page (“Canceris” o “Cancevis”), some occasional minor foxing and staining, a very good copy. First quarto edition, preceded by three octavo editions in 1561, 1562, and 1563 and followed by editions in quarto in 1571, 1578 and 1597. The text was altered from edition to edition. In the prefatory remarks in which Sansovino established the framework of the collection of tales, he states that these stories were related by a company of men and women which had gathered in the house of Francesco Lando at Oriago to escape the plague of 1556. Sansovino’s collection is the first scholarly anthology of the Italian short story, and thus a document of first importance in the history of fiction. It includes tales from Masuccio (ca. 1420-1480), Matteo Bandello (1480-1562), Giovanni Fiorentino (fl. 2nd half of the 14th century), Giovanfrancesco Straparola, (fl. ca. 1500-1527), Girolamo Parabosco, Giovanni Brebia, from the Novelle antiche, Boccaccio, and others.“Di fondamentale importanza per la storia e la fortuna del genere novellistico del Rinascimento è la raccolta di Cento novelle de’ più nobili scrittori della lingua volgare, edita per le cure di Francesco Sansovino” (M. Ciccuto, ed., Novelle italiane. Il Cinquecento, Milan, 1982, p. XXVIII).Each tale is headed by a woodcut, which was expressly made for this edition. They are in the soft, shaded late Venetian style. Furthermore, each story begins with an exquisite woodcut initial formed from plants, wild animals, fishes and reptiles. Of particular interest is the cut on leaf 50: a view of the Piazza San Marco in Venice, looking toward the clock tower. On the left is part of the Biblioteca Marciana, still under construction by Francesco Sansovino’s father Jacopo Tatti Sansovino. Twenty years earlier Jacopo spent some time in prison, because of the collapse of the library’s ceiling in December 1545 (cf. D. Howard, Jacopo Sansovino. Architecture and Patronage in Renaissance Venice, New Haven, CT, 1975, passim).At the end of ‘Giornata IX’ is an interesting passage in which is praised for her outstanding talent the Sienese singer and lutenist Virginia Vagnoli, wife of the well-known musician Alessandro Striggio. She was active for several years at Pesaro at the court of Guidobaldo II della Rovere (cf. I. Fenlon, Music and Patronage in Sixteenth Century Mantua, Cambridge, 1980, pp. 140-141).The printing of the volume was some time attributed to Francesco Rampazzetto, since he used some of the cuts in the same year, but the absence of a Rampazetto’s colophon and Sansovino’s moon device on the title page seem to indicate him as the printer.Francesco Sansovino was born at Rome to the sculptor Jacopo Tatti (Sansovino) by either a wife or an unfaithful concubine. The latter always harbored doubts about Francesco’s paternity. In the aftermath of the Sack of Rome (1527) father and son left Rome for Venice, where he received his early humanistic education in the school of Stefano Piazzone da Asola. Francesco obeying his father, he then studied law in Padua, Florence and Bologna, where he earned a degree in jurisprudence in 1542. Unhappy with law he quarreled with his father and began to write poetry and imaginative vernacular literature in the 1540’s. In 1550 Jacopo, still desirous that his son should travel the road to wealth and position, arranged for an appointment at the papal court of Julius III, who had held Francesco at the baptismal font. But Francesco disliked courtly intrigue and after a brief period returned to Venice. In 1553 he married a Venetian girl of good but non-noble family and settled down to a tranquil life of study and writing. In his career Sansovino wrote, translated, or edited about eighty volumes. He worked on his own initiative and lived on the income of his books. From1560 to 1570 and from 1578 to 1581 he operated his own press. At the same time he continued to compose and edit for other vernacular presses as well. His encyclopedic description of his adopted city, Venetia, cuttà nobilissima et singolare, descritta in XIIII libri (1581), is still a useful source for descriptions of churches, works of art, personalities, famous events and customs of the time. He also wrote a history of the Turks in Europe, Annali Turcheschi (1568), a history of illustrious Italian families Origini e fatti delle famiglie illustri d’Italia (1582), a treatise in seven books on the art of writing letters, Il Secretario (1564), as well as a treatise on the government of kingdoms and republics, Del governo dei regni e delle repubbliche (1561). Sansovino was acquainted with nearly all the popular vernacular authors whose publishing careers centred in Venice: Pietro Aretino, Anton Francesco Doni, Ortensio Lando, Luca Contile, Andrea Calmo, Bernardo Tasso, Lodovico Dolce, and many others. Since he avoided the personal quarrels which flourished in this literary society, he was probably of a calm and peaceable temperament. He enjoyed some recognition with memberships in literary academies, and in 1573 was made a cavalier of the Order of Constantine. Ceaseless literary activity weakened his eyes in the last decade although he continued to write until his death in 1583 (cf. G. Kucinich, Un polygraph venetian del Cinquecento, in: “Paine Istria”, VIII, 1910, pp. 121-130, 145-151; P.F. Grander, Francesco Sansovino and Italian Popular History, 1560-1600, in:“ Studies in the Renaissance”, XVI, 1969, pp. 139-180; E. Bonora, Ricerche su Francesco Sansovino: Imprenditore, librario e letterato, Venice, 1994, passim; and E. Scantanburlo, Nuovi documenti per la biografia di Jacopo Sansovino, in: “Venezia Cinquecento. Studi di storia dell’arte e della cultura”, XI/22, 2001, pp. 17-21).
bibliography: Edit 16, CNCE35523; USTC, 854790; C. Di Filippo Bareggi, Il mestiere di scrivere: lavoro intellettuale e mercato librario a Venezia nel Cinquecento, Rome, 1988, p. 102; B. Gamba, Delle novella italiane in prosa, bibliografia, Florence, 1835, p. 255 (“prima edizione in forma di quarto ed abbellita di nuovi leggiadri intagli in legno”); G. Passano, Novellieri italiani in prosa, Bologna, 1965, I, pp. 541-554 (gives a table listing all the stories appeared in the various printings, their authors, and their order of occurence in each).

title: Ragionamento di Luca Contile sopra la proprietà delle imprese con le particolari de gli Academici Affidati et con le interpretationi et croniche

authors.name: Contile Luca
authors.biography: Luca Contile (1505–1574) occupies a distinctive, if secondary, place in the Italian literary landscape of the sixteenth century. Born in Cetona, near Siena, into a family of comfortable means but diminished noble status, Contile embodied the archetype of the Renaissance cortigiano—peripatetic, ambitious, intellectually versatile, yet perpetually constrained by the demands of patronage. His career unfolded across the courts of Rome, Milan, Naples, and the smaller principalities of northern Italy, mirroring the political and religious upheavals of the era: the splendor and moral ambiguities of Paul III’s Rome, the military campaigns of Charles V and Philip II, the tightening grip of Tridentine orthodoxy, and the gradual shift from the exuberant licentiousness of early Cinquecento humanism toward a more disciplined, often moralistic cultural climate.Origins and FormationContile was born in 1505 to a family whose fortunes had waned not through vice but through the father’s engagement in “mechanical” professions deemed beneath ancestral dignity. In his Ragionamento sopra la proprietà delle Imprese (1574), Contile provides valuable autobiographical details, noting that his paternal grandfather, also named Luca, had married into the Bevignati family of Perugia, which enjoyed ties to the powerful Baglioni. Despite these connections, the family’s social standing had slipped, a fact that appears to have fueled Contile’s lifelong attachment to his kin. Throughout his wanderings, he supported his mother and brothers Guidotto, Camillo, and Ceccante, and showed particular affection for his nephew Giovanni, whom he placed as secretary to Monsignor Michele Della Torre of Ceneda.His early education in Siena exposed him to the major vernacular authors and Latin, skills that enabled correspondence with friends like Federico Orlandini. He dabbled in philosophy, mathematics, and music, but these pursuits remained secondary to the vibrant social life of student brigades—swordplay, wrestling, ball games, and dances—which he later recalled nostalgically from Rome in 1541. The death of his father around 1520 coincided with renewed financial strain, yet Contile was sent to Bologna, where he attended the lectures of the Aristotelian Ludovico Boccadiferro. This period marked a shift from youthful enthusiasm to a more structured engagement with Aristotle’s Ethics and Rhetoric, influences traceable across his oeuvre, from the early Dialogi spirituali to the late Ragionamento. Philosophy, however, remained more an aspiration than a mastered discipline; the practical demands of court life soon prevailed.First Patronage: Agostino Trivulzio and Roman AcademiesIntroduced by Count Giulio Boiardo, Contile entered the service of Cardinal Agostino Trivulzio in Rome. The Eternal City under Paul III (Alessandro Farnese) dazzled the young provincial. In a letter, he painted a vivid, almost Pandoran portrait of a metropolis where virtue and vice coexisted: mercy for the poor, rewards for the learned, honors for soldiers, security from tyranny, and opportunities for merchants—yet also idleness, gambling, and courtesans. This judgment aligned with those of other aspiring literati drawn by Farnese patronage. Contile participated in academies such as the Virtù, Poesia nova, and Sdegno, environments characterized by verbal licentiousness that gradually yielded to Counter-Reformation restraint.His associations included figures like Annibal Caro, with whom he shared cultural preparation, friendships, and genres (epistolography and comedy). Contile mingled with “Berneschi” poets—Gandolfo Porrino, Francesco Bini, Girolamo Ruscelli—sharing their salacious adventures and “sciamannata” discourses, but also their intellectual isolation and parasitic dependence on patrons. Service to Trivulzio was neither onerous nor constant, yet Contile frequently complained of lost autonomy. Notable episodes include accompanying the cardinal to Lucca for Charles V’s entry (1541), where he offered a sharply observed, almost satirical portrait of the emperor’s worn attire, and a wintry halt at Montefiascone, described in letters echoing Caro’s travel miseries. Tensions arose over the delayed marriage of Trivulzio’s nephew Giovanni to Laura Gonzaga, for which Contile had stood guarantor. By 1542–44, he had shifted allegiance toward Alfonso d’Avalos, Marquis del Vasto.Dialogi spirituali and Ideological CommitmentThe Dialogi spirituali (Rome, 1543), elaborated in Milan in 1542 and encouraged by Boiardo and Vittoria Colonna, emerged from this Roman phase. Dedicated to religious conversations among acquaintances from Bologna and Trivulzio’s circle (Pallavicini, Boiardo, Landi, Trivulzio women), the five dialogues address core doctrines: the Trinity, the uniqueness of Christian faith, Jewish obstinacy regarding the Messiah, the afterlife, and the path to heaven. Lacking speculative depth, they articulate a rigid orthodoxy hostile to Reformation currents, vehement against Luther, critical of the Franco-Turkish alliance, and admiring of a strong Catholic defender—whether Charles V or, later, Philip II. Contile’s swift abandonment of lingering reformist sympathies (linked to Colonna) in favor of Tridentine authoritarianism is striking and consistent with his later political sentiments. Tolomei praised their doctrine and spirit while critiquing the grammar.Milan, Naples, and Theatrical ProductionConditions improved markedly at the court of Alfonso d’Avalos in Milan. Educated in chivalric ideals and surrounded by literary influences (Colonna, Costanza d’Avalos), the marquis and his wife Maria d’Aragona fostered a splendid environment. Contile engaged with Pietro Aretino, Paolo Giovio, Girolamo Muzio, and Giulio Camillo. He followed d’Avalos to Germany for the Diet of Worms (1545), expressing curiosity about Luther while handling lesser literary disputes. After d’Avalos’s death in 1546, Contile accompanied Maria d’Aragona to Pavia (where he joined Alciato’s “Chiave d’oro” academy) and Naples/Ischia, before a rupture in 1548 forced his departure.The second Milanese period under Ferrante Gonzaga proved most fruitful literarily. Contile produced La Trinottia (first printed 1542, revised 1550), a Sienese comedy of vices—avarice (Filargiro), lust (Brondio), pride (Icanio)—resolved through intrigue but punished intrinsically by the vices themselves. The prologue personifies human life in its variety. This moral integralism distinguishes Contile’s theater. La Pescara (1550) explores virtuous friendship between Lucio and Curzio amid romantic complications, resolved by anagnorisis; styled a “commedia grave,” it blends pathetic moralism with urban realism, drawing heavily on Plautus. La Cesarea Gonzaga (performed 1549, printed 1550) for a Gonzaga festivity honoring Philip of Austria features cross-dressing and simplified intrigue subordinated to moral acceptability.Subsequent pastorals—Nice (1551) and Argia (1552)—shift toward mythological and encomiastic modes suited to courtly demands, intertwining tragic myths (Adonis, Acis) or Diana’s chastening of sensual love with allegorical representations of Gonzaga figures. The Discorso sopra li cinque sensi del corpo (c. 1552), a commentary on a sonnet by Giuliano Goselini, reveals Contile’s erudition, legitimizing commentary traditions from Pico to Varchi and Savonarolan influences on sensory perception and ideal beauty.Later Wanderings and the RagionamentoService with Cardinal Cristoforo Madruzzo (1552–57) involved travel to the Diet of Augsburg and Milan, alongside pro-Spanish writings like Le sei sorelle di Marte (1556). Subsequent moves—to Ottavio Farnese, Sforza Pallavicino in Venice (where he knew Ruscelli, Dolce, Tasso, Patrizi), and back to Milan and Pavia—reflect chronic economic pressures and restless ambition. In Pavia, as commissioner of the estimo, he enjoyed relative serenity and produced his culminating work, the Ragionamento sopra la proprietà delle Imprese (1574), dedicated to the Accademia degli Affidati. Here Contile distinguishes imprese from related forms (devices, emblems, hieroglyphs), defines the impresa as “componimento di figura e di motto” representing a virtuous design, restricts their use to the magnanimous, and provides biographical notices on academicians, including himself. Though theoretically ambitious, its greatest value lies in these personal and historical details.His Rime (1560, with additions) and Lettere (1564) complete the corpus. The former, including fifty sonnets on Giovanna d’Aragona praised by Francesco Patrizi, remain occasional and encomiastic. The letters lack Aretino’s force or Caro’s brio but offer poignant autobiographical insights into the miseries of courtly servitude: loss of self, friends, family, and ultimately spiritual well-being. Contile died in Pavia on 28 October 1574, active among the Affidati under the academic name “Guidato,” with friends like Giambattista Pico as executor.Additional translations (Istitutioni dell’Imperio, 1558; Origine degli elettori, 1559) and lost works (Virgil translation, duel discourse, academy lectures) attest to ongoing scholarly activity.LegacyLuca Contile exemplifies the challenges facing mid-sixteenth-century Italian intellectuals: the tension between humanistic versatility and courtly dependence, between moral aspiration and practical compromise, and between lingering Renaissance vitality and Counter-Reformation discipline. His theater evolves from balanced moral comedy toward edifying gravity and pastoral encomium, reflecting broader cultural shifts. While lacking the genius of major contemporaries, Contile’s works illuminate the texture of court life, the networks of patronage, and the ideological currents of Tridentine Italy. His Ragionamento and letters remain valuable sources for the history of academies, imprese, and the lived experience of the Renaissance man of letters caught between ambition and necessity. In an age of grand syntheses, Contile offers the instructive portrait of a capable, reflective, and ultimately representative figure.His life and writings repay study not for transcendent originality but for the clarity with which they document the social, literary, and spiritual negotiations of a turbulent century.

academic_description: Folio (349x230 mm). [6], 1-43, [1], 44-161 [recte 162], [1] leaves. Collation: *6 A-Z4 Aa-Pp4 Qq4(-Qq4) Rr8. The final quire was added later, so the previously final leaf Qq4 was excised, and its content (register, errata, and table) was reprinted on the recto and verso of leaves Rr1 and Rr8, respectively. A few other leaves were sometimes cancelled, in this copy leaves S1-2, Aa4, Bb3, Cc1, Hh4 and Mm4 appear to be cancels. Roman type, 54 lines plus headline. Engraved title page, woodcut initials, woodcut printer’s device above colophon on l. Rr8r. Leaf Rr8v is a blank. With 116 engraved illustrations in the text, the first of which is full page and unnumbered, and depicts the device of Philip II of Spain, to whom the work is dedicated; the remaining half-page illustrations show the devices of the Accademia degli Affidati and its members. The illustrations are set within elaborate and elegant borders and bear both the motto and the academic name of the owner of the emblem. Contemporary vellum, modern buckram drop-backed box (traces of ties, binding crinkled and somewhat worn, spine slightly torn with old repairs at ends, front hinge repaired). Old manuscript note at the foot of the text on l. 82r, another note on l. 86r. Title-page somewhat soiled, gutter of the title-page reinforced, occasional staining throughout, a few quires slightly browned, occasional offsetting, repaired tear in Cc1, a few small round wormholes towards end. A very good, tall copy with some deckle edges.Provenance: W.D. Worthington, bookplate; Kerr & Richardson, Glasgow, bookseller’s label at end; T. Kimball Brooker (Bibliotheca Brookeriana, VIII, lot 95). Original edition of this lavishly printed emblem book divided into two parts. The first part (ll. 1-43), after briefly discussing medals and hieroglyphics, deals with devices from a theoretical point of view by raising specific questions. The author, who demonstrates to be well aware of his predecessors’ writings on the subject (citing, among others, Paradin, Giovio, Domenichi, Ruscelli, Ammirato, and Arnigio), distinguishes between crests, coat-of-arms, hieroglyphics, emblems, and devices, seeking to define how the latter differ from the former: the device, which in his opinion is “componimento di figura e di motto rappresentando vertuoso e magnanimo disegno” (‘a composition of figure and motto representing a virtuous and magnanimous design’), is only suitable for virtuous characters and not for “li tinti d’infamia et i professori dell’arti meccaniche, eccettuati gl’ingegneri che stanno a’ servigi de’ principi, i pittori eccellenti e gli statuarii famosi” (‘those tainted with infamy and those practicing mechanical arts, except for engineers who are in the service of princes, excellent painters, and famous sculptors’). The second part, on the other hand, is a veritable tribute to the members of the Accademia degli Affidati, whose devices are extensively commented on and enriched with numerous biographical details. The devices include that of Contile himself (l. 83), in which he provides valuable information about his life, and that of San Carlo Borromeo (l. 86).Towards the end of April 1574, the printing of Contile’s Ragionamento was finally completed, and on August 23, he sent a copy of the newly printed book to the Duke of Parma, informing him that the edition had been ready for four months and, complaining about the quality of the printing, he was hoping for a second edition, which, however, never appeared. The publication had also been delayed by discussions arose among the members of the Accademia degli Affidati regarding its authorship, with some wanting the Ragionamento to be printed in the name of the Accademia, and others wanting it to be published solely under the name of its compiler; the latter party prevailed. Contile’s treatise is considered the most accomplished, and certainly the most useful for the history of the genre. Furthermore, the second part is quite significant as a collection of biographical and genealogical information on the various members of the academy, almost all of which was diligently obtained by Contile through direct or indirect communication with the members themselves or their associates. And so the Ragionamento, as well as being a theoretical and practical book on the genre of devices, can also be considered as a sort of directory to the members of the Pavia academy, with information that we often cannot obtain elsewhere (cf. Abd-el-Kader Salza, Luca Contile. Uomo di lettere e di negozi del secolo XVI, Florence, 1903 (repr. Rome, 2007), pp. 234-239).The Accademia degli Affidati, founded in 1562 on the initiative of Giacomo Berretta, who was its first Prince, and of Counts Galeazzo Beccaria and Ottaviano Langosco, “is undoubtedly a source of pride for the city of Pavia and an irrefutable proof of the favor accorded to scholars of science and literature” (M. Maylender, Storia delle Accademie d’Italia, Bologna, 1926, I, pp. 76-77). The members of the academy used to meet first at the university building, then at the monastery of S. Pietro in Ciel d’Oro in Cittadella, and finally, for many years, they wandered from house to house.Luca Contile, born in Cetona (Val di Chiana), studied at Siena and Bologna, where he attended the lessons of Ludovico Boccadiferro. Afterwards he entered the service of cardinal Agostino Trivulzio at Rome, where he got acquainted among others with Annibal Caro, Francesco Maria Molza, and Gandolfo Porrino. In 1541 he accompanied the cardinal to Lucca for the entry of Emperor Charles V. A year later he moved to Milan to offer his services to Alfonso d'Avalos, marquis of Vasto. At his court Contile became familiar with Pietro Aretino, Paolo Giovio, Girolamo Muzio, and Giulio Camillo. In the summer of 1545 he travelled with his patron through Germany. When Alfonso died in 1546, his widow Maria d'Aragona moved the court to Naples and Contile followed her to Ischia. But, as soon as 1548, he was again in Milan at the service of Ferrante Gonzaga and his wife Isabella di Capua. For them he undertook several missions to Poland and southern Italy. Between 1552 and 1557 Contile served as secretary to Cristoforo Madruzzo, Cardinal of Trent. After a brief employment at Ottavio Farnese’s court, in 1558 he entered the service of Sforza Pallavicino and moved to Venice, where he met Francesco Patrizi, Girolamo Ruscelli, and Ludovico Dolce. After a short period of unemployment he finally found in 1562 a stable place in Pavia, where he spent the rest of life taking part in the literary activity of the Accademia degli Affidati under the nickname of ‘Il Guidato’. He died there in 1574.Contile was a very versatile writer and the author of comedies (Pescara, Cesarea, Trinozia), eclogues (Agia, Nice), poems (Rime, 1560), devotional dialogues (Dialoghi spirituali, 1543), and letters (Delle lettere, 1564) (cf. Abd-el-Kader Salza, Op. cit., pp. 1-102; see also R. Gigliucci, ed., Luca Contile da Cetona all’Europa, Atti del seminario di studi, Cetona 20-21 ottobre 2007, Manziana, 2009, passim).

title: Historia anatomica, Observatioque Medica eviscerati corporis, incliti, qui nuper obijt, Viri Marcelli Sacchetti, Ad Illustrissimos eius familiae viros, & ad doctissimos Medicos Romanos conscripta Neapoli, per Marcum Aurelium Severinum in Regio Gymnasio Chirurgicae, atque Anatomicae rei professorem primum...

authors.name: Severino Marco Aurelio
authors.biography: Marco Aurelio Severino (Tarsia, Calabria, 2 November 1580–Naples, 15 July 1656) was a physician, surgeon, anatomist, natural philosopher, and man of letters whose career joined hospital practice and university teaching to the learned culture of seventeenth-century Naples and the wider European republic of letters. He was born to the jurist Giovan Giacomo Severino and Beatrice Oranges. After his father’s early death, his education was directed by his mother and his uncle Antonio. He studied locally at Tarsia and Roggiano, acquired the classical languages at Cosenza under the Jesuit Orazio Giannino, and was initially intended for the law. On moving to Naples, however, he attended the Jesuit college and then turned decisively to medicine at the Neapolitan Studio. His intellectual formation extended well beyond the statutory medical curriculum. He frequented the private school of the mathematician and natural philosopher Nicola Antonio Stigliola and came into contact with Tommaso Campanella during the latter’s imprisonment in Castel Nuovo. Campanella’s defence of philosophical liberty, together with the naturalism of Bernardino Telesio and the experimental interests associated with Giambattista Della Porta and the Lincean milieu, contributed to Severino’s enduring hostility to an exclusively scholastic Aristotelianism.On 1 February 1606 Severino received the doctorate of philosophy and medicine from the medical college of Salerno. After a brief return to Calabria, he settled permanently in Naples in 1608 and entered the circle of Giulio Jasolino, the Calabrian physician and anatomist whose practice united medicine, surgery, and natural inquiry. Late that year Severino assisted Jasolino at the post-mortem examination of the Theatine Andrea Avellino. He subsequently established himself in private practice and within the extensive hospital system attached to the city’s charitable institutions. By 1612 he belonged to the Accademia degli Oziosi, one of the principal centres of Neapolitan literary and scientific sociability. There he encountered scholars and physicians connected, directly or indirectly, with Federico Cesi’s Accademia dei Lincei, including Mario Schipano and Fabio Colonna. Severino treated Colonna in 1629, but their association was of earlier date; Colonna’s recommendation helped to make Severino known to Johann Faber in Rome. In 1625 Severino was proposed, without success, for admission to the Lincei as a royal physician and anatomist of Naples.In 1622 Severino won appointment as reader in surgery at the Neapolitan Studio. Anatomy was central both to his teaching and to the reputation he acquired through private and hospital practice. His surviving writings record a substantial clinical and pathological casuistry, including the post-mortem examination of Marcello Sacchetti, the Barberini associate and papal treasurer who died at Naples in 1629. Severino’s professional position nevertheless remained complicated by the traditional hierarchy separating learned physic from manual surgery. Modern scholarship has accordingly interpreted his long delay in publishing, and his probable concealment behind the name of his assistant Tiberio Malfi in Il barbiere (1626; recast in 1629 as Nuova prattica della decoratoria manuale et della sagnia), as evidence of the uncertain intellectual status of surgical practice. His mature conception of the surgeon, by contrast, refused the subordination of operative skill to purely textual medicine: surgery was for him a rational and learned discipline grounded in anatomy, observation, accumulated cases, and direct intervention upon the body.Severino first published under his own name in 1632, after a successful operation upon a daughter of Fernando Afán de Ribera, duke of Alcalá and viceroy of Naples. The resulting De recondita abscessuum natura, printed at Naples by Ottavio Beltrano, was a wide-ranging investigation of abscesses, tumours, inflammations, deformities, and other pathological formations, supported by clinical histories and illustrations. It consciously continued the southern Italian tradition represented by Giovanni Filippo Ingrassia, teacher of Jasolino, while giving unusual prominence to visible lesions and operative treatment. An enlarged edition appeared at Frankfurt in 1643. Severino’s advocacy of energetic treatment by iron and cautery brought him into conflict with more conservative practitioners and contributed to his removal from the Hospital of the Incurables in 1635. His reputation abroad was nevertheless firmly established. William Harvey visited him at Naples in 1636, initiating a sustained correspondence in which George Ent also participated. Severino was among the Italian physicians who accepted the circulation of the blood comparatively early, although he sought to connect Harveyan circulation with unresolved questions concerning respiration, the formation of vital spirits, and the relation between air and water.A graver crisis arose in 1640, when former assistants and professional enemies denounced Severino to the diocesan Inquisition. The accusations combined allegations of irreligious conduct with matters of personal life, including the existence of his son Giacinto outside marriage. Severino underwent imprisonment and judicial examination and briefly fled Naples; by the autumn of 1641, however, he had recovered his position and resumed his intellectual and professional activity. At this moment his house became an important destination for northern European medical travellers. Johann Georg Volckamer, a physician from Nuremberg trained at Altdorf and Padua, lived with him in 1641–42 as assistant and secretary. On returning to Germany, Volckamer carried manuscripts and thereafter acted as Severino’s principal editorial intermediary, securing presses, patrons, and readers north of the Alps. Thomas Bartholin and Johann van Horne likewise visited Severino in 1644 during their academic travels. His correspondence extended to Cassiano dal Pozzo, Johann Vesling, John Houghton, Ole Worm, Pietro Castelli, and other physicians and naturalists; among the younger Neapolitans associated with his researches, Tommaso Cornelio was especially important.The principal monument of Severino’s anatomical work was the Zootomia democritaea, issued from the Endter press at Nuremberg in 1645 under Volckamer’s supervision. Based upon decades of dissections and observations of human beings and numerous animal species, it is among the earliest substantial early modern attempts to organize anatomy comparatively. Its title invoked Democritus as the exemplary investigator of animal bodies and as an alternative to Peripatetic authority. Severino treated anatomical comparison not merely as the description of differences but as a means of discerning analogies of structure and function throughout living nature. Human anatomy was consequently to be understood within a larger investigation encompassing quadrupeds, birds, fishes, invertebrates, and even minute organisms. Although his natural philosophy retained teleological, metaphysical, and microcosmic elements, he repeatedly insisted that inherited propositions should be tested against dissection and sensible evidence. The work thus occupies an intermediate position between Renaissance philosophical naturalism, humanist erudition, and the comparative anatomy developed later in the century.After relinquishing his university chair in 1645, Severino continued to publish actively. The De efficaci medicina appeared at Frankfurt in 1646 as an extensive defence and exposition of active surgical therapy; Vipera Pythia, devoted to the viper, venom, and medicinal experiment, followed at Padua in 1650. The Trimembris chirurgia was printed at Frankfurt in 1653, while the Therapeuta Neapolitanus, published at Naples in the same year, included an important catalogue of his printed and projected writings. The Seilo-phlebotome castigata appeared at Hanover in 1654. Other investigations remained unfinished or were published posthumously, notably the Antiperipatias of 1659, which assembled his arguments concerning the respiration of fishes and related zoological questions. The marked geographical dispersion of these editions—Naples, Frankfurt, Nuremberg, Padua, and Hanover—reflects both his European standing and his dependence upon correspondents and former pupils for the material transmission of his texts.Severino’s activities were not confined to medicine. As an Ozioso, under the academic name l’Assettato, he participated in the literary culture of Naples; his Querela della & accorciata appeared in 1644, and his commentary upon the poems of Giovanni Della Casa was printed posthumously by Antonio Bulifon in 1694. His intellectual remains were more extensive than his printed corpus. Roughly seventy volumes of manuscripts associated with him are now preserved in the Biblioteca Lancisiana in Rome, including correspondence, drafts, medical collections, and anatomical drawings. They passed through several hands before their acquisition for Giovanni Maria Lancisi’s library and remain indispensable for reconstructing Severino’s working methods, reading, clinical networks, and editorial projects. During the plague epidemic of 1656 he was summoned by the Neapolitan health authorities to participate in dissections intended to determine the nature of the contagion. He contracted the disease and died on 15 July, receiving an unmarked burial in the church of San Biagio Maggiore in the booksellers’ quarter. His historical importance lies in the conjunction he effected between learned surgery, pathological anatomy, comparative dissection, natural philosophy, and transnational scholarly communication, rather than in any simple claim that he anticipated a single later discipline.

academic_description: 4to (192x139 mm). 15, [1 blank] pp. Collation: A4. Woodcut decorated initial. Modern marbled cardboards. Slighlty browned and foxed, but a good copy. Apparently only copy known. In 1629 Severino was at the height of his fame as a surgeon and anatomist, despite not having published anything yet except a manual on practical surgery (Il barbiere, 1626, reprinted in 1629 under the title Nuova prattica della decoratoria manuale et della sagnia), which came out under the name of his assistant Tiberio Malfi.On 23 August 1629, Severino was called upon to perform an autopsy on the body of Marcello Sacchetti, a powerful Roman merchant and secret treasurer of the Apostolic Chamber who also served the Barberini family as an art connoisseur. He had died in Naples a few days before. The text containing Severino’s anatomical observations on Sacchetti’s body was privately printed in Naples in 1629 and was later included in his main work, De recondita abscessuum natura (pp. 135-143); it also appears in the Severino manuscript (ms. 35 LXXIV.2.13) of the Lancisiana Library in Rome (ll. 70r-83v, 23 August 1629).This edition, of which there is apparently no recorded copy in any library worldwide, was long believed to be lost, and even its existence was doubted. This is how C. B. Schmitt and C. Webster wrote in 1971: “Apparently De recondita abscessuum natura (Naples, 1632) was his first work to appear in print. Various secondary works, including Biographisches Lexikon V, 242; Capparoni II, 67; Tafuri, p. 22; Mercklin, p. 777; Portal, II, 494, list Historia anatomica observatioque medica eviscerati corporis (Neapoli, 1629). Biographisches Lexikon , V, 242 also gives a French translation of the work published by J. Vigier in 2 vols, at Paris in 1629. We have been unable to verify the existence of such editions and there does not seem to be a work of that title among the Severino mss. which we know. Moreover, the early lists of Severino’s writings in Chocolata inda (1644), pp. 69-73 and in Therapeuta Neapolitanus (1653), fols. §§ 2r-§§ 4r do not mention a work of this or of a similar title. It is worth noting that the Fourth Part of Severino’s Zootomia Democritea (1645), p. 286 f. has the title Historia anatomica varii generis animantium describitur, inconibusque certis plurima parte repraesentatur, and the supposed 1629 work might somehow have arisen from a confusion with this” (Harvey and M. A. Severino: A Neglected Medical Relationship, in: “Bulletin of the History of Medicine”, vol. 45, no. 1, January-February 1971, p. 53).Marco Aurelio Severino was a pioneer of comparative anatomy who made major contributions to the advancement of oncology and was highly celebrated in his time.Born at Tarsia in Calabria, he spent the most formative periods of his life in Naples, where he carried out his studies in medicine and began teaching, before obtaining first the chair of surgery and anatomy at the University, then the post of first surgeon at the Ospedale degli Incurabili. In Naples he met and began working with Tommaso Campanella (1568-1639), whom he regarded as a teacher and from whom he took a keen interest in the natural philosophy of Bernardino Telesio (1509-1588).In addition to his influential research and practice in the fields of medicine, anatomy, and animal physiology – and despite threats to his career by the Inquisition, who objected to his allegedly unorthodox beliefs, and others who took issue with his supposedly ‘cruel’ method of healing patients –, Severino forged important international connections with the European intellectual milieu. These relations are well documented by a rich correspondence with figures of international renown and reflect Severino’s eminence and reputation. Among his distinguished correspondents – which include Cassiano dal Pozzo, who assisted Severino in finding skilled illustrators for scientific drawings; John Houghton, who fostered the support of Harvey’s theories; and Johann Georg Volkamer, who became his agent in Nuremberg –, Severino’s relationship with William Harvey (1578-1657) is especially noteworthy. The two physicians met in Naples in 1636 and before his return to England Harvey gave Severino the only known presentation copy of his De motu cordis, now kept at the Houghton Library at Harvard University. The friendship, which peaked in 1645 when Severino dedicated his Phoca illustrates to Harvey, was interrupted by the English Civil War.Severino and Harvey represented two poles in an international network of medical intelligence, they both emphasized the importance of comparative anatomy and of vivisection to the advancement of medicine, and their writings can be read as complementary to one another. Unfortunately, if Harvey’s contributions are properly valued and widely acknowledged, Severino’s full significance remains underrecognized, though studies of his manuscripts – now preserved at the Lancisiana Library – continue to offer scholars much stimulating material for reflection and discussion (cf. O. Trabucco, Severino, Marco Aurelio, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 92, Rome, 2018, s.v.; see also M. Conforti, Surgery, Medicine and Natural Philosophy in the library of Marco Aurelio Severino (1580-1656), in: “Bruniana & Campanelliana”, 10, 2004, pp. 283-298).

title: Ein schönes Büchlin der kunst Chiroma[n]tia deß wolgelerte[n] Magistri Andree corui vo[n] Mira[n]dula

authors.name: Corvus Andreas
authors.biography: Andrea Corvo, also known in Latin as Andreas Corvus, is a fascinating yet elusive figure in the history of Renaissance occult sciences. Active in the late fifteenth and early sixteenth centuries, he stands among the earliest systematic writers on chiromancy (palmistry) in Europe. Despite the considerable influence of his work, biographical details remain frustratingly scarce, and for centuries even his very existence was debated by scholars. His treatise on the reading of hands not only helped establish chiromancy as a respectable intellectual discipline during the Renaissance but also sparked heated polemics among practitioners of the divinatory arts.Life and Historical ContextCorvo was probably born around the middle of the fifteenth century in Carpi, in the territory of Modena. For a long time, his place of origin was uncertain because several early editions of his Chiromantia describe him as “Mirandulensis.” It is now generally accepted that he settled in Mirandola around 1470, likely following the appointment of Antonio de’ Corvi (possibly his brother-in-law) as provost of the city. Beyond this, almost nothing is known of his education, professional activities outside chiromancy, or the date and place of his death.What is clear is that Corvo practiced the art of chiromancy for many years and achieved sufficient renown to dedicate his principal work to Giovanni Francesco Gonzaga, Marquis of Mantua. This dedication served both as a plea for protection against “the bites of slanderers” and as an attempt to lend legitimacy to a divinatory practice often viewed with suspicion by religious and academic authorities.The Chiromantia and Its ControversiesCorvo’s fame rests almost entirely on his Chiromantia, one of the earliest printed treatises devoted exclusively to the reading of hands. Its publication toward the end of the fifteenth century places him at the forefront of a growing European interest in physiognomy and chiromancy, disciplines that sought to interpret the divine signatures inscribed in the human body.The work provoked strong reactions. The Bolognese astrologer and chiromancer Bartolomeo della Rocca, known as Cocles (Cocles), launched a particularly harsh attack in his Anastasis (1504). He repeatedly mocked Corvo, punning on his name by calling him the “black crow” (nero Corvo) or “the blackest crow,” accusing him of plagiarism — dressing himself in peacock feathers while remaining fundamentally a crow. Cocles conceded that Corvo was skilled in the practice of chiromancy but dismissed his theoretical contributions as worthless.Despite these criticisms, Corvo’s text enjoyed remarkable success. Numerous editions appeared under his name, and some of Cocles’s own works were later confused with or attributed to Corvo, creating lasting bibliographical confusion. Other prominent chiromancers, such as Patrizio Tricasso, also criticized him, reflecting the intense rivalries common among practitioners of these arts. The Church placed Corvo’s book on the Index of Forbidden Books, alongside the works of Cocles, Tricasso, Johannes ab Indagine, and Pietro d’Abano. Yet the philosopher Tommaso Campanella later defended chiromancy in his Atheismus triumphatus, arguing that practitioners like Corvo merely observed God’s signs in nature and sinned only when they overstepped their proper bounds.Corvo also received notable praise. Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa of Nettesheim listed him among the leading chiromancers of the age, while the polymath Jean Taisnier highlighted the excellence of his graphical demonstrations of hand-reading.The Printed Editions and Manuscript TraditionThe most important early edition is the extremely rare Excellentissimi et singularis viri in Chiromantia exercitatissimi magistri Andreae Corvi Mirandulensis opus rarissimum de eadem chiromantiae facultate, dedicated to Giovanni Francesco Gonzaga. Printed without typographical indications but dated to the very end of the fifteenth century, this incunable consists of 88 leaves in Gothic characters. It features two full-page woodcuts and 156 smaller illustrations — a remarkable visual apparatus for its time.Subsequent editions and translations testify to the work’s popularity:Picta chyromantia (Venice, 1513)Italian translation Opera Noua de Maestro Andrea Coruo da Carpi (Venice, 1519 and 1530)French translation by Jehan de Verdellay, L’art de chyromance (early 16th century, with later editions in 1611 and 1878)German translation Ein schönes Büchlin der Kunst Chiromantia (Strassburg, 1515)A particularly interesting sixteenth-century manuscript copy survives in the Biblioteca Estense in Modena (Campori collection). This codex contains both physiognomy and chiromancy sections, along with 164 detailed plates illustrating the lines, mounts, and interpretive signs of the hand. A prologue (possibly by Cocles) precedes Corvo’s text, and the author carefully distinguishes between the right and left hands while offering practical reading instructions.Scientific and Cultural SignificanceWhile modern scholarship naturally views Corvo’s chiromantic doctrines as pseudoscientific, his work holds genuine historical importance. It represents an early attempt to systematize and illustrate the reading of hands through empirical observation combined with classical and medieval sources. The rich iconographic apparatus — hands meticulously divided into zones, lines, and “mounts” — made the text accessible and influential beyond learned circles.In the broader context of Renaissance culture, Corvo’s Chiromantia belongs to that fascinating borderland where medicine, natural philosophy, astrology, and divination intersected. Like many of his contemporaries, he believed that the hand was a microcosm reflecting both character and destiny, a visible manifestation of divine order. Though his theoretical framework was criticized even in his own time, the practical and visual dimension of his work ensured its longevity and inspired later generations of chiromancers and physicians.Today, the surviving editions and manuscripts of Andrea Corvo are prized as rare treasures of early printed books and as important documents in the history of Western esotericism. They remind us of a period when the human hand was considered not merely an instrument of labor but a profound text written by nature itself — one that the skilled reader might hope to decipher.

academic_description: 8vo (147x100 mm). [104] leaves. Collation: A-N8. Colophon on l. N8r. Woodcut decorated initials. With overall 168 woodcut illustrations in text including the one on the title page. The woodblocks cover approximately two-thirds of the page. The title woodcut (l. A1r), showing a closed fist surrounded by a floral pattern on a black background, is repeated on l. N7r. At the end of the theoretical section, the illustrated part of the treatise begins on l. C4v with a full-page illustration of a hand, in which the five basic lines, the mountains, and the fingers are named in captions within the image. This is followed on ll. C5r-N7v by 166 woodcuts on a black background depicting hands with various lines and symbols, surrounded by floral patterns. The illustration on l. D4v is the only one not printed on a black background. Next to each woodcut is one or two decorative borders. Below the woodcuts is the letterpress text providing an interpretation of the hand. Right and left hands are shown alternately: on ll. M7v-N4r, two right hands are followed by two left hands. Contemporary half calf over wooden boards, later rebacked, original metal clasp preserved, hardly readable manuscript notes in German and Greek on the front panel. Some light foxing. A very good, genuine copy. Incredibly rare first edition in German, first issue, of which only one copy is recorded at the Bayerische Staatsbibliothek of Munich. A second issue, significantly reset and with the addition of two leaves in quire L, was published by Grüninger in 1515 (cf. VD16, C-5543 and J. Benzing, Bibliographie Strasbourgeoise, Baden-Baden, 1981, no. 424). Of the second issue, only two copies are recorded, one at Bibliothèque nationale et universitaire of Strasbourg and the other at the University of Amsterdam (cf. OCLC, 491221309 and 1262642211). G. Sabbatini (Bio-bibliografia chiromantica, Reggio Emilia, 1946, no. 102) mentions a copy of the 1515 issue sold by the Antiquariat J. Halle of Munich in 1934, but doesn’t seem to be aware of the existence of the 1514 issue. In 1514 Grüninger also issued a Latin edition of this text, of which only one copy is know in Bamberg (cf. VD16, ZV-33904). Finally, he published Corvo’s treatise again in 1524 together with Cocles’ Physiognomie.A French edition of the original Latin text and another edition of the text in the French translation by Jehan de Verdellay, both undated, are usually ascribed to the Lyon presses of Jean Pivard or Jean de Vingle, and variably dated between 1500 and 1515. The Lyon Latin edition, in which the hands are also shown against black backgrounds decorated with floral motifs, may not be the first overall of this text, but is considered to have probably served as a model for Grüninger editions. Debated it is also whether the 1513 Venetian edition by Agostino de Zannis may be the first or, as stated by Th. Musper (Das Original des Titelholzschnittes von Andreas Corvos ‘Chiromantia’, in: “Gutenberg-Jahrbuch”, 1944/49, pp. 126-127), the undated Niccolò & Domenico dal Gesù Venice edition was printed before (cf. ISTC, ic00942500; Edit 16, CNCE14018). The Dal Gesù brothers also printed in 1519 the first edition in Italian of the text.The work is dedicated by the author, of whose life very little is known, to Gianfrancesco II Gonzaga (1466-1519), Marquess of Mantua. Corvo’s seems to be the second printed book in German on palmistry after J. Hartlieb’s Buch von der Hand (Augsburg, ca. 1488-1490).Andrea Corvo was born in Carpi around the middle of the 15th century and settled in Mirandola, probably in 1470 when Antonio de’ Corvi da Carpi, possibly his brother-in-law, was appointed provost of the city. Nothing else is known about Corvo’s education or activities, except that he practised palmistry for many years. Neither the place nor the date of his death are known. He is renowned for the present work on palmistry, which establishes him as one of the earliest writers on the subject in Europe.This also suggests that many later writers drew on his work, which puts the accusations made by Bartolomeo della Rocca (also known as Bartholomaeus Cocles), a famous Bolognese astrologer of the time, into perspective. In his Anastasis (1504), Cocles often plays on the name Corvo (‘Raven’) to undermine his originality and accuses him of drawing on other authors without citing them. Cocles himself acknowledges Corvo’s excellence in the practice of palmistry, but states that he is weak and of no value in theory. Moreover, many editions of Corvo’s Chiromantia were printed under Cocles’s name. This generated misunderstanding and cast doubt on the existence of Corvo, who some believed to be a pseudonym for Cocles; others argued that Corvo used the pseudonym Cocles, but this is unlikely given that, as mentioned, Cocles speaks of Corvo in unfriendly terms. Another famous palm reader, Patrizio Tricasso, also criticised him harshly, but controversies between palm readers and astrologers were well known to be frequent. Corvo’s book was placed on the Index by the Church, alongside the works of Cocles, Tricasso, Giovanni da Indagine and Pietro d’Abano. On the other hand, Corvo was defended by Campanella in his Atheismus triumphatus because, in his opinion, palmists merely observe the signs of God in nature, and therefore only fall into sin if they claim to extend those signs to effects with which they have nothing to do. Also Agrippa of Nettesheim ranks Corvo among the most important palmists of his time, while Taisnier says that he excels above all in the graphic demonstration of palm reading. Corvo’s palmistry was specifically practiced for use in medicine and surgery (cf. De Ferrari, Andrea Corvo, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 29, Rome, 1983, s.v.).

authors.name: Fregoso Antonio
authors.biography: Antonio Fregoso, known variably as Campofregoso, Fulgoso, and later adopting the appellation Fileremo, emerges as a significant yet complex figure within the tapestry of Italian humanism during the transition from the 15th to the 16th century. Born around 1460 in Carrara, he was a scion of the noble Genoese Fregoso family, albeit through an illegitimate line. His life and works provide a window into the intricate interplay of politics, literature, and philosophy during the Italian Renaissance, a period marked by profound cultural and intellectual ferment.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education.Antonio Fregoso's birth into the Fregoso family, a lineage steeped in Genoese nobility, was complicated by his illegitimacy. His mother, Giovanna, remains an elusive figure in historical records, while his father, Spinetta Fregoso, played a pivotal role in his early life. Spinetta's political alliances, particularly with Francesco Sforza, Duke of Milan, positioned young Antonio within a sphere of influence that would shape his future. The irregular legitimization of Antonio by Emperor Frederick III underscores the era's intricate web of political and familial negotiations. Following Spinetta's death in 1467, Antonio came under the tutelage of Cicco Simonetta, a testamentary guardian appointed by his father, which facilitated his integration into Milanese society. The grant of Milanese citizenship by Galeazzo Maria Sforza in 1472 further cemented his status, although subsequent political upheavals, including Simonetta's execution, would challenge his position.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual Networks.Antonio Fregoso's literary output reflects the intellectual currents of his time, blending classical influences with contemporary philosophical discourse. His notable works, 'Riso di Democrito' and 'Pianto di Heraclito,' written in 1505 and 1507, respectively, employ a dantesque structure to explore themes of laughter and sorrow, drawing upon the philosophical dichotomy of Democritus and Heraclitus. These works, alongside the 'Dialogo de Fortuna,' reveal Fregoso's engagement with notions of human fortune and virtue, resonating with the ideas of Erasmus and echoing the allegorical style of Ludovico Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso.' Fregoso's intellectual milieu included figures such as Lancino Curti, Bartolomeo Simonetta, and Gaspare Visconti, with whom he shared literary exchanges that enriched the cultural landscape of Lombardy.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing Circulation.The publication and dissemination of Fregoso's works were facilitated by the vibrant printing culture of Renaissance Italy. The typographical landscape of Milan and Genoa, characterized by the proliferation of humanist texts and the influence of the Aldine Press, provided a fertile ground for Fregoso's ideas. His works were not only circulated within Italy but also translated into French and Spanish, as evidenced by the translations by Michele d'Amboise and Alonso Lobera, respectively. This international reach underscores the broader impact of his writings and their alignment with the humanist ideals that transcended national boundaries.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring Legacy.Antonio Fregoso's legacy is marked by both recognition and obscurity. His mention in Ariosto's 'Orlando Furioso' attests to his contemporaneous relevance, while later literary historians, such as Crescimbeni, acknowledged his philosophical inclinations. The allegorical richness of his works, situated between medieval and Renaissance sensibilities, reflects the transitional nature of his era. Despite the political vicissitudes that marred his life, Fregoso's contributions to Italian literature and philosophy endure, offering insights into the complexities of human fortune and the pursuit of wisdom.

publisher_data: Milan, Pietro Martire Mantegazza & brothers for Francesco Tanzi, 1507
academic_description: 4to (199x135 mm). [10] leaves. Collation: a6 b4. Colophon at l. b4r. The verso of the final leaf features an epigram by Francesco Tanzi. Woodcut decorative initials on a black ground. Early 20th-century half morocco binding, with a gilt title on the spine (Wood, London). On the front pastedown armorial bookplate “Biblioteca di Casate Vecchio”.. Marginal staining and light foxing, pale ink stain to the outer margin of the last five leaves, outer corner of the final leaf repared not affecting the text, old pen scribbles on the last leaf. A wide-margined copy from the libraries of Giuseppe Cavalieri (cf. T. De Marinis, ed., Catalogue des livres compasant la bibliothèque de M. Giuseppe Cavalieri à Ferrara, Florence, 1908, no. 784) and the bookseller Giuseppe Martini (with his typical pencil notes on the flyleaves, cf. E. Barbieri, ed., Da Lucca a New York a Lugano: Giuseppe Martini libraio tra Otto e Novecento, Florence, 2017), who notes that the book also belonged to Charles Fairfax Murray (1849-1919).Exceedingly rare first and only edition of this poem comprising 41 octaves. Contentione di Pluto & Iro (‘The Contention of Pluto and Irus') narrates a dispute between Pluto, the god of wealth, and the beggar Arnaeus, or Irus. The contention concludes without a victor, and the disputants are advised to seek the wise judgement of the President of the Milanese Senate, Iafredo Carlo, to whom the work is dedicated.Unique among Fregoso's oeuvre, this poem is also preserved in a manuscript housed in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan, which, however, presents a more corrupted text than the printed edition; the latter is derived directly from the autograph that Fregoso likely entrusted to his friend Francesco Tanzi, the financier of the edition.Antonio Fregoso (or Campofregoso or Fulgoso) Fileremo (or Filareno, meaning lover of solitude) was likely born in Carrara around 1460, the illegitimate son of Spinetta of the noble Genoese Fregoso family and lord of the city. Lacking male heirs, his father legitimised Antonio by an act later ratified by Emperor Frederick III. Spinetta, allied with the Duke of Milan Francesco Sforza, appointed Cicco Simonetta as the administrator of his estate and guardian of his son in his will. Following Spinetta's death in 1467, Fregoso resided with Simonetta in Milan. In 1472, Galeazzo Maria Sforza officially granted Milanese citizenship to Fregoso, but the following year Simonetta, as ducal minister, deprived him of Carrara and Lunigiana, which were transferred to Federico Malaspina, compensating him with the fief of Sannazzaro in Lomellina. In 1478, upon Gian Galeazzo Sforza's ducal appointment, Fregoso was knighted. After a brief absence, he returned to Milan, where he wed Fiorbellina Visconti di Lodrisio. In 1499, he swore allegiance to Louis XII when the latter conquered the Duchy of Milan, thus retaining his knighthood but losing the fief of Sannazzaro.Fregoso then chose to retire to his villa in Colturano, on the road to Lodi, from where he dispatched his initial works to Iafredo Carlo, president of the Milanese Senate. His retreat from Milan did not preclude him from frequenting the circles of Cecilia Gallerani and Ippolita Sforza Bentivoglio (as evidenced in the Novelle I, 21 and III, 9 by M. Bandello). The impact of the succession in Milan of the Sforzas, French, and Spanish after 1512 on Fregoso's life remains unclear. He likely passed away around 1530. The mention of him among the poets in the 1532 edition of L. Ariosto's Orlando furioso (XLVI, 16, v. 3 ff) does not serve to shift the terminus post quem since many of those mentioned in the poem were already deceased by that date (V. De Matteis, Fregoso, Antonio Fileremo, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 50, Rome, 1998, s.v.).In 1506 and 1507, respectively, Fregoso published two poems, the Riso di Democrito (“Democritus' Laughter”) and the Pianto di Heraclito (“Heraclitus' Weeping”), each in fifteen chapters of tercets. Their translations into French by Michael d'Amboise (1547) and into Spanish by Alonso Lobera (1554) attest to the international renown of these two poems (often published together as I doi filosofi—‘The Two Philosophers').The theme of fortune is explored in the form of a dialogue between the author, Lancino Curti, and Bartolomeo Simonetta in the work Dialogo de Fortuna, first printed in Milan by Pietro Martire Mantegazza in 1507. No longer in tercets but in octaves is Fregoso's most celebrated work, the Cerva bianca (“The White Doe”, Milan, Mantegazza, 1510).In 1521, Fregoso vulgarised Lancino Curti's Silvae, and in 1525, in Milan at the press of Giovanni Giacomo Da Legnano and Bartolomeo da Crema, he published his own ‘silvae', also known as Opera nova, which includes Lamento d'Amore mendicante, Dialogo de musica, Pergoletta de le laudi de Amore, Discorsi cottidiani non vulgari, De lo istinto naturale, De la probità, and De i tre peregrini (cf. A. Dobelli, L'opera letteraria di Antonio Fregoso Fileremo, Modena, 1898).“In definitiva prodotti come quelli del Fregoso stavano a testimoniare, nel primo ventennio del ‘500, la vitalità di una ‘letteratura mista e multiforme, drammatica, narrativa, allegorica, pronta a ogni sorta di esperimenti e però sufficientemente sciolta dall'impaccio delle regole... letteratura tutta moderna, se anche variamente assistita da antichi modelli classici e volgari'. E ne rende fede quel mannello di presenze raccolte intorno al Fileremo, vuoi interlocutori dei suoi dialoghi, vuoi pubblici laudatores delle sue imprese poetiche: editori, poeti nell'una e nell'altra lingua, letterati, oratori, quegli stessi che si ritrovano se si ha la pazienza di seguire certi fili che porge il sistema delle dedicatorie bandelliane: gli esponenti insomma di una cultura legata in fondo ancora alle sue origini cortigiane e destinata nel terzo decennio del ‘500 a frantumarsi per ‘un naturale e mirabile accordo della storia letteraria con quella politica' ” (G. Dilemmi, Un capitolo della cultura settentrionale all'inizio del ‘500, in: A. Fregoso, “Opere”, Bologna, 1976, pp. XXIX-XXX).
