title: Il torneo a piedi, e l’invenzione, ed allegoria, colla quale il Signor Borso Bonacossi comparì a mantenerlo: e l’Alcina maga favola pescatoria fatta rappresentare dal suddetto Signore nella Sala detta de’ Giaganti in Ferrara, alla presenza di tre Altezze Serenissime di Mantova, de i due Eminentissimi Cardinali Sacchetti, e Spada, nel Carnovale dell’Anno 1631. Descritti dall’Aggirato Accademico Fileno. Evvi aggiunto il Tebro Epitalamio, che fu dispensato nella sera, e nel Teatro, in cui si fece il Torneo

authors.name: Berni Francesco
authors.biography: Francesco Berni (Ferrara, 1610–13 October 1673), not to be confused with the celebrated sixteenth-century Tuscan poet of the same name, was a Ferrarese jurist, civic official, professor of eloquence, academician, dramatist, librettist, and author of occasional and historical works. His career belongs to the cultural world of papal Ferrara after the devolution of the duchy in 1598, when municipal institutions, aristocratic households, academies, religious confraternities, and visiting princely courts jointly sustained an active culture of ceremonial oratory and theatrical spectacle. Berni served as secretary to the civic magistracy and was employed as its orator before Pope Innocent X and two of his successors. He also taught eloquence at the University of Ferrara. His position combined legal and rhetorical training with the practical duties of public representation: addresses, commemorations, festival descriptions, academic discourses, and dramatic texts were complementary aspects of a single professional identity.Academies provided one of the principal structures of Berni’s intellectual and social activity. He belonged to the Accademia dei Confusi, before which he delivered L’omicidio amoroso di Radamisto, an academic discourse drawn from the twelfth book of Tacitus’s Annals and printed by the ducal and camerale printer Francesco Suzzi in 1640. He was also prince of the Accademia degli Intrepidi and a founder of the Accademia dei Fileni, in which he bore the name L’Aggirato. These affiliations were not merely titular. His surviving publications show sustained participation in collective exercises that united rhetoric, historical exemplarity, poetry, music, and ceremonial display. L’Accademia raunatasi nel Castello di Ferrara il dì 16 giugno 1645, addressed to Marchese Ercole Trotti, records one such occasion, while the two-volume Dell’Accademia, printed at Ferrara in 1657–1658 by the episcopal printers Alfonso and Giovanni Battista Maresti, assembled a broader body of academic material. The edition was embellished with an engraved frontispiece by Silvestro Maria Curletti, an indication of the visual and bibliographical care accorded to Berni’s learned persona.Berni’s earliest securely documented activity already places him within the culture of the courtly festival. In 1631 he described a foot tournament and its allegorical invention, together with the piscatory fable Alcina maga, represented in the Sala dei Giganti at Ferrara during Carnival. His subsequent writings repeatedly served occasions involving distinguished visitors, marriages, funerals, and civic or dynastic commemoration. Le pretensioni del Tebro e del Po (1642), for which the poetic composition was supplied by Ascanio Pio di Savoia and the description by Berni, commemorated the arrival in Ferrara of Prince Taddeo Barberini. L’esequie trionfali del marchese Guido Villa (1656) documented the elaborate obsequies celebrated in the Ferrarese church of San Francesco. Such publications belong to the bibliographical category of the festival book: they preserved otherwise transient performances by recording their allegorical programmes, scenic actions, ceremonial structures, and political meanings.His historical interests are most conspicuous in De gli eroi della Serenissima Casa d’Este ch’ebbero il dominio in Ferrara, printed by Francesco Suzzi in 1640 and dedicated to Francesco I d’Este, Duke of Modena. Conceived as a sequence of lives commemorating the former rulers of Ferrara, the project remained incomplete: of the twenty-four biographies apparently planned, only five were published, treating Almerico, Tedaldo I, Bonifacio III, Matilda, and Azzo VIII. The volume contained an engraved title and five portrait plates. Contemporary prefatory evidence associated its engravings with Catarino Doino, although the attribution and relationship between these plates and other contemporary series of Este portraits remain bibliographically problematic. Berni’s work participated in a competitive antiquarian and iconographic enterprise through which seventeenth-century authors and engravers reconstructed Este genealogy after the dynasty’s removal from Ferrara. Its combination of historical narrative and portraiture also exemplifies the close collaboration among author, engraver, and printer characteristic of local commemorative publishing.Berni’s most sustained contribution was to musical theatre. In Ferrara he worked within a relatively stable collaborative group comprising the composer Andrea Mattioli, the theatrical engineer Carlo Pasetti, and the patron and organizer Cornelio Bentivoglio. Mattioli set Berni’s La palma d’amore, performed at the theatre of San Lorenzo during Carnival 1650 for the marriage of Francesco Maria Estense Mosti and Caterina Pio di Savoia, and Il ratto di Cefalo, staged on 26 June 1650 in the theatre of the Sala Grande with machinery devised by Pasetti.Il ratto di Cefalo was revived during the following Carnival, when Berni’s L’esiglio d’Amore, composed by Mattioli in collaboration with Filiberto Laurenzi, was likewise performed; the latter was repeated in May 1651 with a new prologue honouring the papal legate Benedetto Odescalchi. The same Ferrarese circle produced Gli sforzi del desiderio, described as a dramatic-musical recreation and mounted in Palazzo Miroglio in 1652 for the passage of the archdukes of Tyrol, and L’Antiopa, performed in the Sala Grande on 23 and 24 February 1653. These works disclose a dramaturgy conceived in conjunction with music, transformations, stage machinery, and the architecture of temporary performance rather than as an autonomous literary text.Berni’s reputation extended beyond Ferrara. He was favourably received by members of the Austrian archducal house and by the ducal courts of Parma and Mantua; in 1658 the Duke of Mantua conferred upon him the title of count. His connection with the Farnese court culminated in the festivities for the marriage of Ranuccio II, Duke of Parma, and Margherita Violante of Savoy in 1660. For the Teatro Farnese he wrote La Filo, overo Giunone rappacificata con Ercole, a musical drama associated with Francesco Manelli, and I sei gigli, a tournament intended for performance on a subsequent evening. Other compositions connected with the same nuptial celebrations included La gara degli elementi and Le ali d’Amore. In these works spoken and sung drama, dance, tournament, allegory, and dynastic compliment formed parts of a coordinated ceremonial programme. The geographical movement of Berni’s texts between Ferrara and Parma demonstrates the mobility of librettists, musicians, engineers, and printed festival descriptions within the courts and aristocratic networks of northern Italy.In 1666 Berni consolidated his dramatic reputation through I drami del signor conte Francesco Berni, da varie impressioni qui raccolti e ristampati, issued at Ferrara by Giulio Bolzoni Giglio and Giuseppe Formentini and dedicated to Ranuccio II. The collection detached a substantial portion of his theatrical writing from the ephemeral circumstances of individual performances and presented it as a coherent authorial corpus. This act of collection is important in the history of the libretto: like several other seventeenth-century dramatists, Berni sought to preserve texts originally printed as occasional performance books by gathering them into an edition intended for continued literary circulation. He nevertheless remained an occasional writer to the end of his life; an ode celebrating the marriage of Hebe and Hercules in honour of Cardinal Sigismondo Chigi, legate of Ferrara, appeared in 1673.Berni died at Ferrara on 13 October 1673, aged sixty-three. His historical significance rests less upon any single work than upon the unusually complete intersection represented by his career: university eloquence, municipal service, academy culture, historical commemoration, dynastic patronage, festival publishing, and opera. His writings document the mechanisms by which seventeenth-century spectacle was conceived, financed, performed, described, and transmitted in print. They also illuminate the professional transformation of the librettist from an occasional supplier of verse into a recognizable author capable of collecting, revising, and presenting his dramatic works under his own name.

academic_description: 4to (198x140 mm). [16], 107, [1] pp. and [6] etched folding plates attributed to Alfonso Chenda (1607-1640). Collation: a-b4 A-M4 N6. 18th-century half vellum, inked title on spine, panels covered by light blue floral paper, red sprinkled edges (slightly worn and rubbed). Private stamp to the title-page verso. Worm track to the lower outer corner of the first ten leaves, which then becomes just a small hole, never affecting the text, other work track to the outer margin of the final leaves with no loss of text, two small holes on l. C2 one of which slightly affects the text, some foxing and staining, more strongly towards the end, all in all a good, genuine copy. Extremely rare first and only edition of the account by Francesco Berni (1610-1673, disguised under the academic name of “Aggirato”) of the first festival held in Ferrara after the War of the Mantua Succession (1628-1631), to celebrate the wedding of Giovanni Francesco Sacchetti (1595-1656) and Beatrice Estense Tassoni (1611-1633), in the presence of the Duke of Mantua, Charles de Nevers -to whom the volume is dedicated- and Cardinal Giulio Sacchetti. The book describes a tournament organised by Borso Bonacossi at Carnival time and accompanied by recited texts (one of which is signed by Ottavio Magnanini), as well as poems, stage designs, and machinery (pp. 6-86). It also contains the Alcina maga, a “favola pescatoria” by Sebastiano Martini (pp. 87-96), a wedding ode by Francesco Berni recited that same evening (Il Tebro, overo la Pittura loquace del pittor muto, pp. 99-107), two sonnets, by Alfonso Fiornovelli and Ippolito Visdomini, and a Latin poem by I. Visdomini. The plates depict the allegorical and historical re-enactments that were performed, including two scenes from the Alcina maga.

authors.name: Bosse Abraham
authors.biography: Introduction & Humanist/Historical Signification. Abraham Bosse, born in 1602 in Tours, France, stands as a pivotal figure in the realm of 17th-century engraving, a period marked by the flourishing of baroque art and the burgeoning influence of scientific inquiry on artistic practices. His works, numbering over 1500 engravings, are not merely artistic expressions but serve as invaluable historical documents that capture the zeitgeist of Louis XIII's France, offering insights into the social customs, fashion, and furniture of the time.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Education. Bosse was born into a family likely engaged in crafts or trade, a common background for many artists of the period, which provided him an early exposure to the intricacies of design and craftsmanship. His formative years in Tours, a city known for its vibrant cultural life and as a hub of artistic production, would have nurtured his artistic inclinations. Bosse's education in perspective under the tutelage of Girard Desargues, a prominent mathematician and engineer, was instrumental in shaping his technical precision and innovative approach to engraving. Desargues was a key figure in the development of projective geometry, and his influence on Bosse is evident in the latter's meticulous attention to spatial composition and depth in his works.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual Networks. Bosse's oeuvre is characterized by a keen observational acuity and a delicate sensibility, which he applied to a wide array of subjects. His series such as 'Le Jardin de la Noblesse Française' (1629) and 'La Noblesse Française en Église' (1630) offer a vivid portrayal of the French aristocracy, while 'Le Mariage à la Ville' and 'Le Mariage à la Campagne' (1633) provide contrasting views of urban and rural nuptial customs. His depiction of everyday scenes, such as 'Les Cris de Paris', echoes the genre scenes popularized by Dutch artists, yet with a distinctly French elegance. Bosse's religious and allegorical works, including 'Les Vierges Sages et les Vierges Folles' and 'Les Quatre Saisons', reflect the period's fascination with moral and philosophical themes, rendered with a baroque theatricality. His intellectual network included associations with the Academy of Painting, where he initially taught before his expulsion in 1661 due to ideological clashes with Charles Le Brun, the Academy's autocratic director. This conflict highlights the tension between individual artistic expression and institutional control during this era.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing Circulation. The publication of Bosse's 'Traité des manières de graver en taille-douce' in 1645 marks a significant contribution to the technical literature on engraving, providing a comprehensive guide to the art of copperplate engraving, a method that would dominate printmaking for centuries. This treatise, reprinted multiple times, underscores the enduring relevance of his technical insights. The typographical context of 17th-century Paris, a city at the forefront of printing and book production, facilitated the wide circulation of Bosse's works, contributing to his reputation across Europe. Parisian printers and publishers, benefiting from the city's status as a cultural and intellectual capital, played a crucial role in disseminating his engravings, which were valued not only for their aesthetic qualities but also as educational tools and collectibles.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring Legacy. Bosse's work was met with critical acclaim during his lifetime, though his career was not without controversy, particularly his exclusion from the Academy of Painting, which reflects broader debates about artistic autonomy and institutional authority. Despite these challenges, his engravings have been celebrated for their technical mastery and nuanced portrayal of contemporary life. His influence extends beyond his immediate period, impacting subsequent generations of artists and engravers. The enduring legacy of Abraham Bosse is evident in the continued scholarly interest in his work, as evidenced by the numerous studies and catalogues dedicated to his oeuvre. His engravings remain a vital resource for historians and art historians alike, offering a window into the social fabric and artistic milieu of 17th-century France.

authors.name: Cirino Andrea
authors.biography: Andrea Cirino (Messina, 1618–Palermo, 6 September 1664) was a Theatine cleric, preacher, antiquarian, and compiler of works encompassing sacred exegesis, classical philology, natural history, and Roman antiquities. Early Theatine biographers describe him as belonging to a noble Messinese family. He entered the Congregation of the Clerics Regular while still an adolescent and made his solemn profession at Messina on 5 July 1634. His intellectual formation joined the scholastic and scriptural disciplines required by his order to an unusually extensive reading of pagan antiquity. Contemporary and near-contemporary accounts repeatedly emphasize his capacious memory, facility in retrieving passages from the Fathers and classical authors, and ability to employ this accumulated learning in preaching. Such testimony is conventionally encomiastic, but it corresponds closely to the conspicuously compilatory structure of his surviving publications.Cirino’s religious career was associated particularly with Messina and with the Theatine house of San Giuseppe in Palermo. He acquired a reputation as a preacher and was remembered for addressing the Palermitan populace during a period of civic disorder, urging the restoration of tranquillity. His earliest identified publication is the funeral oration delivered for Cardinal Giannettino Doria, archbishop of Palermo, printed there by Decio Cirillo in 1643. A devotional discourse for the Messinese feast of the Madonna della Lettera followed at Monteleone in 1649. These works place him firmly within the public culture of the seventeenth-century religious orator, in which sermons and ceremonial addresses served simultaneously as instruments of pastoral instruction, civic representation, and learned display.His most distinctive contribution, however, lay in the immense antiquarian compilations devoted to hunting and animals. The Variarum lectionum, sive De venatione heroum libri duo, printed at Messina by the heirs of Pietro Brea in 1650, examined the origins, practices, and cultural meanings of hunting through an accumulation of testimonia drawn from classical, Christian, historical, and mythographical literature. This enterprise was enlarged in the De venatione et natura animalium libri quinque, issued at Palermo by Giuseppe Bisagni in 1653. The publication is bibliographically complex, comprising separately titled sections, among them the extensive De natura et solertia canum and a book on fishes. Its title advertises the consultation of approximately thirty thousand passages from earlier authors, an assertion characteristic of Cirino’s conception of scholarship as the ordered recovery of an encyclopaedic textual inheritance. The work treats animals not solely as physical creatures but also as scriptural signs, medical substances, political and moral exempla, objects of legal or ritual practice, and witnesses to the customs and migrations of ancient peoples. Its woodcut illustrations and multipart organization also give it a notable place among the scientific and antiquarian books produced by the Palermitan press in the middle decades of the seventeenth century. Although sometimes classified as natural history, its governing method is more accurately described as sacred and classical erudition than as experimental zoology.Cirino’s interests extended beyond animal lore. His Historia delle cause et effetti della peste, published at Genoa in 1656, addressed the epidemic through the medical, historical, providential, and moral categories available to a learned cleric of his age. In 1657 he published at Naples a life of the Theatine Francesco Olimpio. He is also associated with the account of the festivities held in Naples for the birth of Philip Prospero, Prince of Asturias, an example of the richly illustrated festival literature generated within the dominions of the Spanish Habsburgs. His work thus moved between several characteristic forms of Baroque print culture: the occasional oration, devotional biography, civic and dynastic celebration, epidemic history, and large-scale Latin compilation. Modern scholarship has also drawn attention to his connection with the mathematician and natural philosopher Giovanni Alfonso Borelli, describing Cirino as a friend and supporter within the intellectual environment of seventeenth-century Messina and Rome.At his death Cirino left a substantial body of unpublished material. Theatine bibliographers record commentaries on the Apocalypse and other books of Scripture, together with writings on duties, Epictetus and constancy, Platonic philosophy, medicine, prodigies, and apparitions of the Cross. The present whereabouts or survival of all these manuscripts cannot be securely established. His principal posthumous publication was the Variarum lectionum de urbe Roma eiusque conditore Romulo liber singularis, printed at Palermo by Agostino Bossio in 1665 under the supervision of his confrère Francesco Maria Maggio. Devoted to Rome and its founder, it applied Cirino’s characteristic method of cumulative textual comparison to chronology, foundation legends, institutions, religion, and the antiquarian problems surrounding Romulus. The work subsequently entered wider European antiquarian circulation when Albert-Henri de Sallengre included it in the second volume of his Novus thesaurus antiquitatum Romanarum, published at The Hague in 1718.Cirino died in the Theatine house at Palermo after prolonged illness, attributed by early biographers to incessant preaching and study. The best early evidence places his death on 6 September 1664, although some later accounts give 7 September. His posthumous reputation rested less upon an original system of natural or historical explanation than upon the amplitude and organization of his learning. He belongs to the learned ecclesiastical culture of Spanish Sicily in which biblical interpretation, patristics, classical antiquities, civic history, medicine, and natural lore remained mutually permeable fields. His books are consequently important not only for their particular subjects—especially hunting, dogs, fishes, and Roman origins—but also as material witnesses to the compilation, illustration, and printing of encyclopaedic scholarship in seventeenth-century Messina and Palermo.

title: Il Cromuele tragedia del Co: Girolamo Gratiani Segretario, e Consigliere di Stato del Serenissimo Signor Duca di Modona

authors.name: Graziani Girolamo
authors.biography: Girolamo Graziani (1604–1675) stands as one of the most brilliant, politically astute, and representative literary figures of the Italian High Baroque (Seicento). A quintessential courtier-poet, diplomat, and statesman, Graziani operated at the intersection of high political power, courtly panegyric, counter-reformational zeal, and the dazzling stylistic innovations of Marinism. Serving for decades as the Chief State Secretary (Segretario di Stato) to the House of Este in Modena under Duke Francesco I d’Este, Duke Alfonso IV, and the Regent Duchess Laura Martinozzi, Graziani successfully combined the burdens of international diplomacy during the tumultuous decades of the Thirty Years' War and Franco-Spanish rivalry with an extraordinary output of epic poetry, political tragedy, and courtly lyricism. His monumental heroic poem Il Conquisto di Granata (1650) and his pioneering political tragedy Il Cromuele (1671)—one of the earliest European theatrical treatments of Oliver Cromwell and the regicide of King Charles I—ensure his place among the primary architects of seventeenth-century European literary culture.Born in the Marchian town of Pergola around 1604 into a family of respectable provincial standing, Graziani’s early intellectual formation was shaped by the rigorous humanist curricula of the late Renaissance. Trained in classical rhetoric, civil and canon law, Latin literature, and scholastic philosophy, the young Graziani moved early in his youth to the territories of the Duchy of Modena and Reggio. The Este dynasty, having suffered the catastrophic loss of Ferrara to the Papal States in the Devolution of 1598, was actively transforming Modena into a resplendent Baroque capital. To legitimize their dynastic stature and navigate the treacherous diplomatic currents of Western Europe, the Este dukes actively sought brilliant humanists capable of drafting administrative statecraft while crafting immortalizing dynastic propaganda. Graziani entered the service of Duke Cesare d'Este and his successor Alfonso III, but it was under the ambitious, militaristic reign of Duke Francesco I d’Este (1610–1658) that Graziani rose to the pinnacle of state authority.By the 1630s, Graziani was firmly established as Francesco I’s most trusted administrative confidant, officially elevated to State Secretary. His diplomatic duties were vast: he managed the ducal chancery, negotiated complex treaties between the Este court, the Papal See, the Spanish Crown, and the French Kingdom, and orchestrated the grand ceremonial and theatrical pageantry of the Modenese court. Simultaneously, Graziani embedded himself in the primary intellectual networks of the Italian peninsula. He became a prominent member of the prestigious Accademia dei Gelati of Bologna (assuming the academic moniker Il Secondo), maintained close ties with the freethinking libertine circles of the Accademia degli Incogniti in Venice directed by Giovan Francesco Loredan, and spearheaded the activities of the Accademia dei Dissonanti in Modena. These academic connections allowed Graziani to circulate his works among the most influential scholars, bibliophiles, and patrons of his age.Graziani’s literary production reflects the grand aesthetic transition from late Tassean epic classicism to the hyper-metaphorical, conceptist style of Giambattista Marino, tempered by a profound obsession with statecraft (ragion di Stato) and political realism. His early theatrical debut occurred with the tragedy La Cleopatra (1632), which established his reputation as a master of tragic pathos and poetic diction.However, his undisputed masterpiece in the epic genre is Il Conquisto di Granata, published in twenty-six cantos in octava rima in 1650. Set against the backdrop of the fall of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada in 1492 under Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, the poem serves a double purpose: it provides a stunning Baroque display of chivalric warfare, marvelous enchantments, and religious fervor modeled on Torquato Tasso’s Gerusalemme liberata, while simultaneously offering a subtle allegorical encomium for the French Crown and the Este family. Dedicated to the young King Louis XIV of France and his prime minister Cardinal Mazarin, Il Conquisto di Granata secured Graziani a prestigious royal pension from the French court, cementing Modena’s geopolitical alliance with France.In his later years, Graziani achieved an extraordinary breakthrough in political drama with his masterpiece Il Cromuele (1671). In this five-act tragedy, Graziani accomplished the remarkable feat of translating contemporary political events—the English Civil War, the trial and execution of King Charles I Stuart, and the rise of Oliver Cromwell—into a sophisticated Baroque drama. Written while the memory of the English Commonwealth was still fresh across Europe, Il Cromuele explores the dark mechanics of political ambition, Machiavellian deception, royal martyrdom, and divine retribution. Cromwell is depicted not merely as a villain, but as a complex, tortured embodiment of tyrannical ambition and political intellect, reflecting the profound European fascination and anxiety regarding anti-monarchical revolutions. The work stands as a landmark in early modern European political theater, presaging the historical dramas of the Enlightenment.The publishing history of Graziani’s works highlights the meticulous production standards of seventeenth-century printing houses operating under courtly patronage. The first edition of Il Conquisto di Granata was issued in Modena in 1650 by Bartolomeo Soliani, the official printer to the Ducal Court (Stampatore Ducale). Designed as an imperial folio/quarto monument, the edition featured sumptuous typography, elaborate typographic ornaments, and intricate copperplate frontispieces engraved by leading court artists, emphasizing the grandeur of the Este dynasty. The work proved an immediate commercial and critical success, going through multiple reprintings in Venice, Naples, and Paris. Similarly, Il Cromuele was printed in Bologna in 1671 by the press of Emilio Maria and Fratelli Manolessi, printers closely associated with the Accademia dei Gelati. The Manolessi printings were renowned for their crisp Roman and Italic types, architectural woodcut title borders, and clean layout, catering to an elite international audience of academics and political elites.Throughout the latter half of the seventeenth century, Graziani’s works enjoyed immense critical acclaim across Europe. His lyric poetry, compiled in volumes such as Varie poesie e prose (1662), was celebrated for its formal perfection, intellectual wit, and sophisticated use of Baroque conceits (concetti). Intellectuals such as Angelico Aprosio, Lorenzo Magalotti, and Valeriano Castiglione praised Graziani as one of the few poets capable of uniting the poetic splendor of Marino with the structural rigor and moral seriousness of Tasso. In the eighteenth century, during the rationalist reaction against Baroque taste led by the Accademia dell'Arcadia, Graziani’s reputation suffered alongside most Seicento authors. Scholars like Ludovico Antonio Muratori and Girolamo Tiraboschi, while critical of the Baroque hyperbole present in his lyrics, nevertheless acknowledged his extraordinary diplomatic intellect, his monumental mastery of the epic form, and his noble historical erudition.The nineteenth-century romantic and nationalistic historiography, dominated by figures such as Francesco De Sanctis, largely marginalized Baroque literature, dismissing Graziani's courtly panegyrics as products of an era of political servitude. However, twentieth- and twenty-first-century scholarship has brought about a profound rehabilitation of Graziani’s oeuvre. Pioneering studies by Ezio Raimondi, Carmine Jannaco, and Franco Pignatti have recontextualized Graziani as a central architect of Baroque political thought and aesthetic theory. Modern critics now recognize Il Cromuele as a groundbreaking triumph of seventeenth-century drama, praising Graziani's sophisticated engagement with modern history, statecraft, and political tragedy. Today, Graziani is recognized not merely as a court poet, but as a vital intellectual bridge connecting late Renaissance Italian classicism with the complex political and literary realities of early modern Europe.

Woodcut arms of the dedicatee, King Louis XIV, on the title page. Woodcut initials, head- and tail-pieces. Later boards, red sprinkled edges (joints repaired, slightly rubbed and soiled). Upper outer corner of the half title repaired, lower margin of the title page trimmed with loss of a line of text, some foxing, marginal tears to some of the plates skilfully repaired, tiny portion of a plate missing, all in all a good copy. Rare first illustrated edition, also printed in the same here without illustrations in Modena by Soliani and reprinted in Bologna by Manolessi in 1673, of this five-act tragedy by Count Girolamo Graziani, a man of letters from Modena who served as secretary and advisor to the Duke of Modena. The play, conceived in the 1660s during Laura Martinozzi’s regency in Modena, depicts the dramatic events of the English Civil War, pitting the tyrant Oliver Cromwell against the martyr Charles I. Inspired by the typically seventeenth-century tendency to rewrite recent historical events for political purposes, the play paints a hagiographic portrait of the English monarch, whose blood comes to take on a strong symbolic and almost Christ-like significance following his death sentence (cf. P. Di Nepi, Girolamo Graziani e la politica come arte: “Cromuele”, in: “F.M. Annali dell’Istituto di Filologia Moderna dell’Università di Roma”, 2-1979, Rome, 1981, pagg. 113-24).From the very beginning, the tragedy presents itself as a Baroque device in the service of defending the monarchy, through a pseudo-historical - yet theatrical - reconstruction of the events of 1649. It is true that the tragedy makes use of specific historical references, but - as is usually the case in seventeenth-century theater - these are condensed into a single night, that of January 30, 1649 (cf. S. Miglierina, Il sangue di Carlo: apologia e licenza teatrale nel Cromvele di Girolamo Graziani, in: “Krypton”, vol. 1, 2013, p. 47).The first mention of the tragedy’s composition appears in the preface to Girolamo Graziani’s Varie Poesie e Prose (1662). Beginning in 1666, the composition of the Cromuele was accompanied by an extensive correspondence with Jean Chapelain, with whom Graziani - who was on the payroll of Colbert on behalf of the Sun King - corresponded regularly (cf. R. Galli Pellegrini, La Tragédie Italienne à l’école du classicisme Français: le rôle de Chapelain dans la genèse du “Cromuele” de Graziani, in: “Quaderni del Dipartimento di Lingue e Letterature Straniere Moderne, Università di Genova”, 2-1987, pp. 35-57).There is no mention of a performance of Il Cromuele in the preface to the second edition of 1673, nor is there any trace of it in the extensive documentation on theatrical performances in the Este States preserved in the State Archives of Modena. The likely reason for the play’s failure to be staged was the dynastic marriage that took place in 1673 (just two years after the 1671 publication) between Maria Beatrice d’Este and Giacomo Stuart, who had been widowed in the very year of Il Cromuele’s publication by Anna Hyde - the woman with whom he appears to be in love in the tragedy. This was an inconvenient presence for Graziani, who, as secretary of state, had looked after the Este family’s interests in that marriage (cf. M. Fasce, Introduzione e note alle edizioni de Il Cromuele, in: “Storie Inglesi, l’Inghilterra vista dall’Italia tra storia e romanzo XVIII sec.”, C. Carminati-S. Villani, Pisa, 2011, pp. 297-330).Girolamo Graziani, who earned a degree in law and humanities in Bologna, served as an advisor and secretary to the princes, that is, to the sons of Alfonso III of Modena. After several legal disputes, he traveled in 1648 on a diplomatic mission to Paris, where he witnessed the Fronde, before returning to Modena in 1649, where he continued his diplomatic and literary career. Graziani was in Paris, at the French court, at the time of the execution of the King of England, and this suggests that he was a direct witness of the scandal that the event could have caused at the court of the nephew of the murdered king. Graziani decided to recount those events in a dramatized version twenty-two years after Charles’s death, thirteen after Cromwell’s, and eleven after the restoration of the monarchy in England (cf. F. Tarzia, Graziani, Girolamo, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 58, Rome, 2002, s.v.).

authors.name: Moniglia Giovanni Andrea
authors.biography: Giovanni Andrea Moniglia (1624–1700) stands as one of the most multifaceted and influential cultural figures of the Tuscan High Baroque, occupying a singular position at the intersection of medical science, courtly diplomacy, and the historical evolution of Italian dramatic and operatic literature. Serving for decades as chief court physician (medico primario) to the House of Medici while simultaneously operating as the principal playwright and librettist for Cardinal Giovan Carlo de' Medici and the Accademia degli Immobili, Moniglia embodied the early modern ideal of the polymathic humanist-physician. His dramatic works, set to music by preeminent composers such as Francesco Cavalli and Jacopo Melani, bridged the transitional zone between the grand heroic-mythological traditions of Venetian opera and the emerging vernacular realism of Tuscan comedy. In the realm of musicology, Moniglia is universally recognized as a foundational architect of proto-buffo operatic forms, while in the history of medicine, his contentious clinical treatises and high-profile debates with figures like Francesco Redi and Lorenzo Bellini reflect the stormy transition from traditional Galenic humoralism to Galilean empirical observation and iatromechanical theory in late seventeenth-century Florence.Born in Florence on March 22, 1624, into an established family of Ligurian descent, Moniglia was the son of Silvestro Moniglia and Maddalena. From an early age, he demonstrated an extraordinary aptitude for classical letters, rhetoric, and natural philosophy. His formal academic trajectory commenced at the prestigious Studio Pisano (University of Pisa), where he matriculated to study medicine and philosophy during a period of profound intellectual fermentation. Under the influence of the Galilean scientific revolution that continued to permeate the Tuscan university network, Moniglia absorbed both the classic Galenic-Hippocratic corpus and the modern mechanical and anatomical innovations championed by contemporaries such as Giovanni Alfonso Borelli and Marcello Malpighi. Upon receiving his doctorate in medicine around 1648, Moniglia returned to Florence, where his sophisticated command of Latin humanities, combined with a sharp clinical acumen, rapidly earned him entry into the aristocratic salons of the ruling dynasty.Moniglia's ascent within the Medici court hierarchy was swift and decisive. He secured the patronage of Cardinal Giovan Carlo de' Medici, a key cultural manager of the state who recognized Moniglia's dual talents in medicine and dramatic poetry. Appointed as the Cardinal's personal Archiater, Moniglia subsequently expanded his medical duties across the grand-ducal household, eventually serving Grand Duke Ferdinand II, Grand Duchess Vittoria della Rovere, and Grand Duke Cosimo III de' Medici. Despite his demanding responsibilities at court, Moniglia became embroiled in the intense medical polemics that divided late seventeenth-century European science. Positioned somewhat conservatively between empirical observation and scholastic doctrine, Moniglia engaged in fierce public pamphlets against the celebrated naturalist Francesco Redi and the brilliant iatromechanist Lorenzo Bellini. His controversies regarding the nature and treatment of fevers (De ortu et natura febrium), the therapeutic use of cinchona bark (quinine), and the administration of purgatives showcased a combative intellectual disposition, earning him both fierce detractors and staunch defenders within the Accademia della Crusca and the broader European Republic of Letters.Parallel to his scientific career, Moniglia achieved monumental stature as the chief dramatist for the Accademia degli Immobili, the prestigious theatrical academy founded under Cardinal Giovan Carlo's direct protection. Operating within the newly constructed Teatro della Pergola—designed by court architect Ferdinando Tacca and inaugurated in 1657—Moniglia established a new paradigm for Florentine theatrical spectacle. His libretto for Il podestà di Colognole (1657, set to music by Jacopo Melani and often performed under the title La Tancia), is widely regarded by theater historians as a seminal precursor to eighteenth-century opera buffa. By introducing rustic Tuscan characters, dialectal humor, domestic intrigue, and sharp social satire into the lyric stage, Moniglia disrupted the rigid hegemony of noble court pageantry, creating a vibrant musical comedy format that achieved widespread popularity across the Italian peninsula.Moniglia's theatrical versatility was equally evident in his grand heroic operas and courtly pageants. In 1658, he authored the libretto for Iperpermestra, featuring music by the undisputed giant of Venetian opera, Francesco Cavalli. Commissioned by Cardinal Giovan Carlo to celebrate the birth of the Spanish Infante Philip Prospero, Iperpermestra was a monumental production that combined complex psychological characterization, dramatic tension, and astonishing stage machinery engineered by Tacca. This was followed in 1661 by Ercole in Tebe (music by Jacopo Melani), an extravagant dynastic opera mounted for the lavish wedding of Prince Cosimo (later Grand Duke Cosimo III) to Marguerite Louise d'Orléans. Moniglia's ability to seamlessly weave dynastic allegory, mythological grandeur, and intricate stage mechanics ensured his position as the supreme theatrical arbiter of the Medici court for over three decades.The dissemination of Moniglia's literary output was facilitated by the vibrant print culture of Baroque Florence. His individual libretti were published as elegant quarto and octavo pamphlets by court printers such as the Stamperia di S.A.S. (directed by Amador Massi and Lorenzo Vigna), Cosimo Matassi, and Vincenzio Vangelisti, complete with detailed descriptions of the stage machinery, scenic transformations, and balletic interludes. Recognizing the enduring value of his dramatic corpus, Moniglia supervised a definitive three-volume collected edition of his theatrical works titled Poesie drammatiche del dottor Gio. Andrea Moniglia stampate d'ordine dell'Altezza Serenissima di Toscana, published in Florence by Cesare Bindi between 1689 and 1690. This monumental typographical project preserved his vast output—including comedies, musical dramas, and moral plays such as Il Taciturno, Il schiavo di sua moglie, and Hipermestra—for future generations, solidifying his literary reputation outside the immediate ephemerality of theatrical performance.In his final years, Moniglia remained an esteemed and formidable presence in Florentine intellectual life, maintaining his medical consultations and academic standing until his death on September 21, 1700. Historiographical assessments of Moniglia have undergone significant evolution. Eighteenth-century literary historians such as Giovanni Mario Crescimbeni and Francesco Saverio Quadrio praised his metric elegance and comedic invention, while nineteenth-century musicologists occasionally dismissed his libretti in favor of later Metastasian ideals. However, modern scholarly reevaluations—led by musicologists and theater historians such as Robert Lamar Weaver, Lorenzo Bianconi, Sara Mamone, and Teresa Megale—have reinstated Moniglia as a pivotal, revolutionary figure. His sophisticated integration of Tuscan comedic traditions into lyric drama laid the structural and stylistic foundations for the rise of European comic opera, securing his legacy as a central titan of seventeenth-century Italian court culture.

Rare original edition of this festival book published to commemorate the equestrian ballet that was performed for the wedding of Cosimo III de Medici (1642-1723) and Marguerite Louise d Orléans (1645-1721) on 20 June, 1661. This elaborate theatrical and mechanical spectacle was performed in the amphitheater behind the Palazzo Pitti, now known as the Boboli Gardens. Alessandro Carducci, the court choreographer, designed the elaborate ballet and wrote the account, Giovanni Andrea Moniglia wrote the celebratory poems, Domenico Anglesi (ca. 1610-1674) composed the music, and Ferdinando Tacca (1619-1686) designed the complex machinery of the performance. Stefano della Bella (1610-1664) engraved the plates, which depict the grand cavalcade of Hercules, accompanied by the chariots of the Sun and the Moon and followed by knights representing Europe, Asia, Africa, and America; the knights’ teams and the goddesses’ carriages around Mount Atlas; and the plan of the tournament and equestrian ballet, with detailed diagrams of the maneuvers. In the center of plate 1 is the colossal figure of Atlas, an imposing machine that not only dominated the arena but also sang, opening to reveal four female singers within the celestial sphere he supported. Prince Cosimo himself appeared as Hercules, identifiable in the engraving by his club and lion skin.

title: Delle fortificationi di Giovan[n]i Scala mathematico. Nuovamente ristampate con agiunta d’diverse piante e fortezze

authors.name: Scala Giovanni
authors.biography: Giovanni Scala (flourished late 16th – early 17th century) stands as a pivotal figure in the dissemination of practical mathematics, architectural geometry, and surveying techniques during the Italian Counter-Reformation. Functioning at the crucial juncture where Renaissance humanist theory intersected with empirical workshop craftsmanship, Scala performed a monumental service to early modern science by editing, structuring, illustrating, and expanding the mathematical papers of the Venetian engineer and architect Giovanni Pomodoro. Published under the title Geometria prattica tratto degl'scritti di Giovanni Pomodoro (first issued in Rome in 1599), Scala’s work transformed complex geometrical principles into accessible, highly visual, and operational methodologies for architects, military engineers, land surveyors (agrimensori), and artillery officers. In an era when European states were increasingly reliant upon precise territorial mapping, fortificational design, and urban planning, Scala bridged the divide between abstract Euclidean theory and the concrete mechanical needs of late Renaissance society. His career reflects the rising status of the mathematical practitioner (matematico pratico) in early modern Europe—an intellectual profile distinct from university-bound natural philosophers, dedicated instead to the mastery of instruments, visual representation, and applied spatial computation.The biographical specifics regarding Scala’s early life and geographic origins remain sparse, a common feature among sixteenth-century mathematical practitioners who operated outside academic faculties of theology or law. Active primarily in Rome during the pontificates of Clement VIII (Ippolito Aldobrandini) and Paul V (Camillo Borghese), Scala belonged to a vibrant network of topographers, engravers, instrument makers, and architectural draftsmen who converged upon the Papal capital. Rome at the turn of the seventeenth century was experiencing an intense phase of architectural renewal, infrastructural expansion, and hydraulic engineering, creating a high demand for skilled geometricians capable of calculating land boundaries, structural loads, and perspective projections. Scala’s formal education was rooted in the traditions of practical geometry (geometria practica), a discipline traced back to medieval treatises such as Hugh of Saint Victor’s Practica geometriae and Leonardo Fibonacci’s Practica geometriae, but radically transformed during the sixteenth century by the introduction of copperplate printing and advanced surveying instruments. Scala’s close collaboration with the works of Giovanni Pomodoro suggests a direct apprenticeship or intellectual affinity with Venetian engineering circles, where practical geometry was heavily utilized in naval construction, hydraulic management in the Venetian Lagoon, and military bastion fortifications.Scala’s masterwork, the Geometria prattica tratto degl'scritti di Giovanni Pomodoro, represents a landmark synthesis of spatial theory and instrumental application. Divided into structured books or sections, the treatise systematically leads the reader from basic plane geometry—such as the construction of lines, angles, polygons, and circles—to advanced applications in altimetry (measuring heights), bathymetry and planimetry (measuring surface areas), and stereometry (calculating volumes). A defining characteristic of Scala’s methodological approach is his reliance on visual pedagogy. Rather than presenting abstract, text-heavy Euclidean proofs, Scala paired concise explanatory text with full-page copperplate engravings that demonstrated how geometrical problems were solved in the field using specialized surveying instruments. These instruments included the surveying compass, the quadrant (quadrante), the sight-vane or alidade, the squadra zoppa (adjustable square), and early variants of the graphometer. Scala meticulously illustrated how a surveyor could determine the height of an inaccessible tower, calculate the distance across a river, or lay out the perimeter of a pentagonal fortress without direct physical measurement, relying instead on the principles of similar triangles, optical sightlines, and proportional computation. Furthermore, Scala’s commentary contextualized these techniques within contemporary architectural design, showing how planar geometry governed the proportions of classical columns, facades, and vaulting systems.The publishing history and typographical evolution of Scala’s treatise provide crucial insights into the seventeenth-century market for technical literature. The editio princeps was printed in Rome in 1599 by the printer Stefano Paolini at the expense of Giovanni Martinelli, formatted as a grand folio to accommodate the lavish copperplate engravings. The visual clarity of these plates, engraved with fine line work and sharp calligraphic lettering, set a new benchmark for Italian mathematical publishing. The commercial success of the 1599 edition prompted numerous reissues and expanded printings across Italy throughout the seventeenth century. Notable Roman reissues appeared in 1603 and 1624 (printed by Carlo Vinti and Giovanni Martinelli), while Venetian pressmen quickly recognized the text's lucrative appeal, issuing reprints in 1667, 1691, and 1704 under the imprints of publishers like Stefano Curti. The physical composition of these volumes—utilizing high-quality rag paper, clear Roman and Italic types for the main commentary, and separate plate pressings—demonstrates the sophisticated production logistics required for technical treatises in early modern printing shops. The work circulated widely across European borders, finding its way into the libraries of military academies, noble patrons, and practicing architects in France, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Low Countries, where it was frequently consulted during the siege warfare and territorial re-mappings of the Thirty Years' War.The reception and enduring legacy of Giovanni Scala within the historiography of science and architecture highlight his role as a master popularizer and systematizer of technical knowledge. In the decades following its initial appearance, the Scala-Pomodoro treatise was cited as an authoritative manual alongside the works of prominent contemporaries such as Guidobaldo del Monte, Federico Commandino, Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola, and Galileo Galilei. Architectural historians, including Luigi Vagnetti and Mario Docci, have underscored Scala’s contribution to the formalization of architectural drawing conventions and perspective science, noting how his clear geometric diagrams helped codify the language of graphical representation used by Baroque master-builders. While nineteenth-century historians of mathematics occasionally dismissed practical treatises in favor of pure theoretical breakthroughs, modern scholarship has re-evaluated Scala’s monumental effort, recognizing that the proliferation of operational geometry was indispensable to the Scientific Revolution and the modernization of early modern European infrastructure. By converting abstract mathematical principles into reproducible visual instructions and instrumental procedures, Giovanni Scala ensured that practical geometry became a foundational pillar of early modern engineering, architecture, and spatial science.

authors.name: Vitruvius Pollio
authors.biography: Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, more commonly known as Vitruvius, stands as a monumental figure in the annals of architectural history. His comprehensive treatise, 'De Architectura', composed in the late 1st century BC, is the oldest surviving work on architecture and has profoundly influenced architectural theory and practice through the ages, particularly during the Renaissance. Vitruvius's work is not merely a technical manual but a profound synthesis of architectural knowledge, reflecting the cultural and intellectual milieu of Augustan Rome. His treatise covers a wide array of topics, from the principles of building design to the theoretical underpinnings of architecture, and serves as a bridge connecting ancient Greek architectural traditions with Roman innovations.Vitruvius's early life remains shrouded in mystery, with scant biographical details available. His full name, Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, suggests a connection to the Roman gens Vitruvia, though the precise details of his lineage are uncertain. The nomenclature 'Pollio' may indicate his association with the Pollia tribe, particularly in the region of Fanum Fortunae, modern-day Fano. His education likely encompassed a broad spectrum of disciplines, typical of Roman intellectuals of his time, including studies in mathematics, engineering, and the liberal arts. Vitruvius himself mentions his role as a scriba armamentarius, overseeing the construction of war machines, which underscores his technical expertise and the practical experience that informed his writings.'De Architectura', dedicated to Emperor Augustus, is Vitruvius's magnum opus, comprising ten books that systematically address the principles of architecture. The treatise begins with a dedication to Augustus, highlighting Vitruvius's gratitude for the patronage and pension he received. The work covers a wide range of topics, including the selection of building sites, materials, and the design of various structures, from temples to private homes. Vitruvius's emphasis on symmetry, proportion, and the triadic principles of firmitas (strength), utilitas (utility), and venustas (beauty) reflects his philosophical grounding in Pythagorean and Stoic thought. His work also engages with the broader intellectual currents of his time, drawing on the writings of Greek architects and philosophers, thereby positioning him within a network of Roman and Hellenistic scholarship.The transmission of Vitruvius's text through the centuries is a testament to its enduring significance. The first printed edition appeared in Rome in 1486, edited by Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli and Pomponio Leto. This incunable marks the beginning of Vitruvius's Renaissance revival, as architects and humanists sought to reconnect with the classical past. Subsequent editions, such as the 1511 Venetian edition by Fra Giocondo, expanded the treatise's reach, incorporating illustrations to compensate for the lost original diagrams. The Italian translation by Cesare Cesariano in 1521 further facilitated its dissemination, making Vitruvian principles accessible to a broader audience. The typographical landscape of the 15th and 16th centuries, characterized by the burgeoning of print culture, played a crucial role in cementing Vitruvius's legacy in architectural theory and practice.Vitruvius's treatise, while not immediately influential in antiquity, gained prominence during the Renaissance, becoming a cornerstone of architectural education and practice. Figures like Leon Battista Alberti, Andrea Palladio, and Leonardo da Vinci drew extensively from Vitruvian principles, integrating them into their own works and treatises. The 'Vitruvian Man' by Leonardo, for instance, exemplifies the application of Vitruvian concepts of human proportion to artistic and architectural design. Despite debates regarding the precise dating and authorship of the treatise, its impact is undeniable. The 'De Architectura' continues to be a foundational text in the study of architecture, reflecting the rich interplay of technical, aesthetic, and philosophical ideas that have shaped the built environment from antiquity to the modern era.

academic_description: Folio (308x208 mm). [12], CX leaves. Collation: AA-BB6 A-N8 O6. Title page printed in red and black within a woodcut border featuring a figure of Cicero in a medallion at the head and other figures in battle array, among them Augustus Caesar, Julius Caesar, and Alexander the Great, and trophies of war. With 136 woodcuts in text. Register and colophon on l. BB6r. Contemporary or slightly later vellum over boards, spine reinforced, panels partially covered with two manuscript fragments (worn and rubbed, worm tracks on spine). Outer margin of the title page frayed, some marginal pale staining, overall a good, genuine copy with wide margins. Second Durantino edition of Vitruvius’ treatise, after the first published in Venice in 1524 by the Nicolini da Sabbio brothers. Comparison with the Como edition shows the text to have been fully reviewed, since much of the vocabulary differs.“Francesco Lutio Durantino’s edition of Vitruvius (Venice, 1524) is in fact only a slightly transformed copy of Cesariano’s treatise. Durantino made spelling corrections and used Fra Giocondo’s illustrations. He published the first five books of Cesariano’s Vitruvius in smaller format with spelling changes, incorporating a few pictures based on Fra Giocondo; he also translated Cesariano’s Latin captions into Italian and added several references to central Italian places and people for his own provincial audience” (Millard, p. 499).The woodcuts are close copies of the full set of blocks from the Giocondo edition of 1511 printed at Venice by Giovanni Tacuino. The copies were made for the first Durantino edition. Zoppino secured all of the 1524 blocks except one, that on leaf N1r, which is a recutting with the heads of the figures strangely enlarged.

academic_description: 16mo (135x78 mm). She then established her own publishing house under the name “Madame Cavanagh”, specializing in plays.

authors.name: Montreux Nicolas de
authors.biography: Nicolas de Montreux (c. 1561–1608), widely known under his precise anagrammatic humanist pseudonym Ollenix du Mont-Sacré, stands as one of the most prolific, versatile, and historically decisive literary figures of the late French Renaissance. Positioned at the tumultuous intersection of the French Wars of Religion, the Catholic League’s political ascendancy in Brittany, and the aesthetic transition from Pléiade poetic idealism to early Baroque drama and pastoral prose, Montreux authored a monumental corpus spanning pastoral novels, tragic and pastoral theater, epic poetry, pious treatises, and chivalric continuations. Despite experiencing periods of critical neglect following the seventeenth-century consolidation of French Neoclassicism, modern scholarship recognizes Montreux as an indispensable precursor to Honoré d'Urfé’s L'Astrée and a central architect of French courtly entertainment during the reign of Henri III and the Catholic League hegemony under Philippe-Emmanuel de Lorraine, Duke of Mercœur.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationBorn around 1561 in the province of Maine (or possibly Touraine, within the cultural orbit of the Loire Valley), Nicolas de Montreux emerged from a family of modest provincial nobility or upper-bourgeois legal administrators. Details regarding his earliest years remain shrouded in the archival casualties of the Wars of Religion; however, his earliest published compositions demonstrate a sophisticated humanist education steeped in classical Latinity, vernacular Italian scholarship, and rhetoric. Montreux was thoroughly trained in the legal traditions of the late Valois realm, likely pursuing jurisprudence alongside classical letters—a Dual curriculum typical of late sixteenth-century French men of letters. By the early 1580s, Montreux had aligned his personal and intellectual trajectory with the aristocratic houses of western France. His formative literary endeavors were marked by an intense engagement with Italian models, particularly the pastoral works of Jacopo Sannazaro, Torquato Tasso, and Giovanni Battista Guarini, whose courtly and arcadian topoi Montreux successfully transplanted into French prose and verse.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksMontreux’s literary career gained spectacular momentum with the publication of Le Premier Livre des bergeries de Joliette (Paris: Jean Richer, 1585). Dedicated to Marguerite de Lorraine, Duchess of Joyeuse, this work served as a fundamental milestone in the development of the French pastoral novel. Blending interpolated verse, Neoplatonic discourses on divine and earthly love, and allegorical depictions of contemporary courtly figures, the Bergeries de Joliette provided a stylized refuge from the sectarian violence consuming France, while simultaneously functioning as a platform for moral and philosophical meditation. Montreux expanded this pastoral arc through subsequent volumes, cementing his reputation under the persona Ollenix du Mont-Sacré.Parallel to his narrative prose, Montreux established himself as a pioneering dramatist. His early pastoral play, Athlette (1585), adapted Italian dramatic structures for the French stage, integrating chorus movements, complex amorous entanglements, and rhymed alexandrines. As the Wars of Religion reached their zenith in the late 1580s, Montreux migrated to Brittany, entering the immediate personal service of Philippe-Emmanuel de Lorraine, Duke of Mercœur—the fiercely independent governor of Brittany and uncompromising leader of the Sainte Ligue. Serving as court poet, librarian, and political secretary to Mercœur in Nantes, Montreux composed works that seamlessly blended Catholic counter-reformational zeal with courtly panegyric. His dramatic production during this period was extraordinary: he authored the tragedies Sophonisbe (1592) and Isabelle (1594), which drew heavily upon Seneca and Italian humanist tragedy to explore the tragic collisions of statecraft, personal honor, and divine providence. His pastoral plays performed before the ultra-Catholic court at Nantes—most notably Diane (1594) and L'Arimène, ou l'Art de regner (1597)—were sophisticated theatrical spectacles designed to legitimize Mercœur’s princely ambitions and project an image of courtly order amidst regional conflict.Montreux’s intellectual ambition extended into epic and chivalric domains. He published a continuation of the famous romance cycle, Le Seizième Livre d'Amadis de Gaule (1577/1581), and composed the sweeping hexametric/alexandrine epic L'Espagne conquise (1597–1598), which celebrated the legendary crusading exploits of the Christian monarchies against Islamic power in the Iberian peninsula—a transparent allegory for the Catholic League’s ideological struggle against Protestantism. Following the submission of Mercœur to King Henri IV in 1598 and the pacification of France under the Edict of Nantes, Montreux relocated to Paris. In his final decade, his literary tone shifted markedly toward religious devotion, stoic moral philosophy, and spiritual prose, exemplified by works such as L'Œuvre de la Chasteté and various translations of late classical Greek romances, including Heliodorus’s Aethiopica (adapted as Les Chastes et Loyales Amours de Chariclea et Theagene).Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationThe publication history of Nicolas de Montreux’s works provides a vivid window into the material culture of printing during the late Valois and early Bourbon eras. Montreux collaborated with several of the most prominent printing houses in Paris and Nantes, reflecting the geographic and political shifts of his career. His earliest Parisian imprints were issued from the workshops of Jean Richer and Jamet Mettayer, printers renowned for their high typographical standards, elegant italic founts, and meticulous woodcut ornaments. Richer’s release of the Bergeries de Joliette in 1585 showcased an sophisticated octavo layout tailored for noble domestic readers, complete with delicate criblé initials and elaborate printer’s devices.During his tenure in Nantes under the Duke of Mercœur, Montreux was central to the operation of the provincial League presses. His primary typographical collaborator in Brittany was Julien Mercier, the official printer to the Catholic League in Nantes. Mercier’s press was responsible for generating both official political manifestos for Mercœur and the luxurious First editions of Montreux’s dramatic and epic works, including Sophonisbe, Isabelle, and L'Arimène (1597). These Nantes imprints, often produced on heavy linen paper with distinctive regional woodblock borders, represent crucial artifacts of League propaganda and regional court culture. Upon his return to Paris under the amnesty of Henri IV, Montreux’s late works were produced by major Parisian publishers such as Guillaume de La Noyre and Toussaint Du Bray, illustrating his reintegration into the capital’s commercial print market. The widespread circulation and multiple pirated or reprinted editions of his pastoral works across Lyons, Rouen, and Paris testify to his commercial success and broad readerly appeal across the turn of the seventeenth century.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyDuring his lifetime, Nicolas de Montreux was lauded by contemporaries as a master of vernacular eloquence and a supreme innovator in pastoral and dramatic forms. His mastery of complex anagrams, ornate rhetorical figures, and multi-generic structures earned him a revered position within courtly circles. However, the rapidly changing aesthetic standards of the seventeenth century—marked by Malherbe’s linguistic reforms, the rise of French Classicism, and the monumental success of Honoré d'Urfé’s L'Astrée (1607–1627)—led to a swift decline in Montreux’s critical standing. XVIIth-century critics often castigated late Renaissance writers associated with the League or the late Valois mannerist style for over-ornamentation, stylistic hybridity, and archaic syntax.For nearly two centuries, Montreux remained largely consigned to the footnotes of literary history, dismissed as a mere footnote or a provincial imitator. The systematic rehabilitation of Montreux began in the mid-twentieth century, spearheaded by the seminal biographical and bibliographical monograph of Rose-Marie Daele (1946). Subsequent scholarship in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries—led by scholars such as Daniela Dalla Valle, Angela Evain, Jean Vignes, and Roland Béhar—has completely re-evaluated Montreux’s historical importance. Modern academic consensus views Montreux not as a passive imitator, but as an energetic aesthetic pioneer who successfully mediated between Italian Renaissance genres and the specific political imperatives of late sixteenth-century France. His integration of political allegory into pastoral drama, his structural innovations in tragédie-sainte and pastoral theater, and his key role in shaping the reading habits of the late Renaissance court firmly establish Nicolas de Montreux as a towering figure in early modern French literary history.

publisher_data: Paris, Chez la veufue de Gabriel Buon, au clos Bruneau á l’image S. Claude, 1598
academic_description: 12mo (143x73 mm). 371, [1] leaves. Collation: A-Hh12. Woodcut printer’s device on the title page, woodcut head-pieces and initials. Restoration-period polished fawn calfskin, signed “Simier, R. du Roi” (Relieur du Roi, 1762-1843) on the spine, panels decorated with a double gilt border, spine with four raised bands, gilt and blind-stamped ornaments, and morocco lettering piece, marbled edges, all edges gilt (Simier was one of the greatest French bookbinders of the 19th century, holding the title of ‘Bookbinder to the King’ under Louis XVIII and Charles X). Joints skillfully repaired. A very good copy. Second edition, which is essentially a reprint of the first edition from 1597. Both editions were published by Jeanne Rondel, the widow of Gabriel Buon, who had died in 1595. The author dedicated the work to Philippe Emmanuel de Lorraine, Duke of Mercoeur and Penthièvre, and Governor of Brittany (1558-1602), with a letter signed from Nantes on 1 January 1597. The privilege granted by the king to Jeanne Rondel is included at the end.This pastoral adventurous novel, written in prose interspersed with verses, forms the second part of a trilogy dedicated to chastity. The first part, published in 1595 simultaneously by the widow of Gabriel Buon and by Saugrain and Des Rues, was entitled Oeuvre de la Chasteté, notable for the Amours de Criniton et Lydie, and was followed by the tragedy Cleopatra. The third part, entitled Les chastes et fidèles Amours de Criniton et Lydie, was published in 1599, again in Paris by Jeanne Rondel.Nicolas de Montreux was born in Sablé-sur-Sarthe, in the province of Maine. He was ordained around 1585. In 1591 he became librarian of the Duke of Mercoeur and fought in the civil wars alongside the Ligue until he was imprisoned. Following his release, he joined the court of Henry IV of France. Montreux signed many of his works with the anagram ‘Ollénix du Mont Sacré’ and left behind a large body of work, including dramas, poems and pastoral novels, as well as a history of the Ottoman Empire from 1565 to 1606 and a lengthy work of spiritual philosophy entitled L’Homme et ses dignités (1599). His most famous work is the pastoral novel/play in five volumes entitled the Bergeries de Julliette (1585-1598). He is considered one of the founders of pastoral drama in France (cf. J. Mathorez, Le Poète Olényx du Mont-Sacré, bibliothécaire du duc de Mercoeur (1561-1610), Paris, 1912, passim).

authors.name: Wallin Georg August
authors.biography: Georg August Wallin (1811–1852), known in the Arab world as Shaykh 'Abd al-Wali, stands as one of the most formidable and groundbreaking figures in the history of nineteenth-century European Orientalism, geographical exploration, and Semitic dialectology. Emerging from the peripheral academic landscape of the Grand Duchy of Finland within the Russian Empire, Wallin transformed the empirical methodology of Middle Eastern scholarship by pioneering an immersive, field-based ethnographic and linguistic approach. Decades before the iconic desert journeys of Sir Richard Francis Burton, William Gifford Palgrave, and Charles Montagu Doughty, Wallin penetrated the formidable interior of the Arabian Peninsula—specifically the Najd, the Northern Hejaz, and the Al-Jawf basin—recording precise geographical, sociopolitical, and dialectological data that fundamentally reshaped Western understanding of the region. His intellectual significance resides not merely in his cartographic and exploratory achievements, but in his revolutionary linguistic precision: Wallin was among the first European scholars to treat spoken Bedouin Arabic dialects not as degraded corruptions of Classical Arabic, but as living, highly structured linguistic systems possessing unique phonetic preservation, sophisticated syntax, and rich oral poetic traditions.Born on October 24, 1811, in the rural parish of Sund on the Åland Islands, Wallin grew up in a Swedish-speaking family during a period of profound geopolitical transition, as Finland was ceded by Sweden to the Russian Empire in 1809. Raised in an environment characterized by Lutheran piety and provincial austerity, he early displayed an extraordinary aptitude for languages. In 1829, he matriculated at the Imperial Alexander University of Helsingfors (now the University of Helsinki), an institution undergoing a vibrant intellectual expansion. Under the tutelage of Professor Gabriel Geitlin, Wallin immersed himself in Classical Arabic, Hebrew, Syriac, and Persian, demonstrating a philological rigor that quickly elevated him above his peers. He earned his Master of Arts degree in 1836 with a dissertation examining Arabic grammatical theory, followed in 1839 by a preliminary treatise on the distinctions between classical and vernacular Arabic idioms (De praecipuis inter Arabicam vulgarem et literale discrimine). In 1842, Wallin defended his doctoral dissertation, an analytical commentary on the mystical elegiac poetry of the medieval Sufi poet Ibn al-Fāriḍ (Carmen elegiacum Ibn al-Fāriḍi). Recognizing Wallin's unprecedented genius for Semitic philology, the Alexander University, supported by imperial research stipends from St. Petersburg, granted him a multi-year traveling fellowship to conduct direct linguistic research in the Orient.Wallin’s journey began in 1843 when he traveled via Constantinople to Cairo, the intellectual capital of the Arab world. Recognizing that superficial European observation yielded only superficial knowledge, Wallin adopted a radical methodology of complete cultural and linguistic assimilation. He donned traditional scholarly dress, perfected his spoken Cairene and scholarly Arabic at the prestigious Al-Azhar Mosque, and adopted the Muslim name and persona of Shaykh 'Abd al-Wali al-Muqaddasi. Between 1845 and 1849, Wallin undertook three monumental expeditions into the Arabian interior and the Levant. His first major desert trek in 1845 took him from Cairo across the Sinai Peninsula to the northern Hejaz, Al-Jawf, and Jubbah, eventually reaching Ha'il, the seat of the powerful Ibn Rashid dynasty. Wallin was the first European scientist to visit Ha'il and provide a detailed account of the political stability, judicial administration, and social structure of the Rashidi Emirate. Continuing south, he visited Medina and Mecca, performing the rites of the Hajj in complete concealment. Subsequent journeys in 1847–1848 and 1848–1849 took him through Palestine, Syria, the Syrian Desert, Najd, and southern Mesopotamia (Baghdad and Basra), culminating in a transit across Persia before returning to Egypt and Europe.The scientific yield of Wallin's travels was immense, particularly in the fields of geography, phonetics, and Arabic dialectology. Unlike many contemporary travelers whose journals were dominated by romanticized impressions, Wallin maintained meticulously detailed daybooks written in Swedish, Arabic, and French. He painstakingly transcribed Bedouin oral poetry, noting subtle variations in pronunciation, stress, interdental consonants, and the retention of archaic grammatical features such as tanwīn (nunation) in Bedouin vernaculars. Upon his return to Europe in 1850, Wallin visited London, where his cartographic observations and notes were presented to the Royal Geographical Society. The Society recognized the monumental value of his geographic and ethnographic corrections to existing maps of Northern Arabia by awarding him its prestigious Founder’s Gold Medal in 1850. Wallin’s reports were published in the Journal of the Royal Geographical Society in 1850 and posthumously in 1854 and 1855, establishing his reputation across the global republic of letters as one of the preeminent Arabic scholars of the nineteenth century.In 1851, Wallin returned to Helsingfors to assume the Chair of Oriental Languages at the Imperial Alexander University. However, his academic tenure was tragically brief. Physical exhaustion from years of arduous desert travel, combined with the psychological difficulty of re-adapting to the rigid academic climate of Northern Europe after years in the Orient, took a heavy toll on his health. On October 23, 1852, on the eve of his forty-first birthday, Wallin died suddenly in Helsingfors, leaving the vast majority of his extensive field notes, journals, and linguistic transcriptions unpublished. His untimely death represented a catastrophic loss to Semitic philology. Posthumously, his Swedish travel journals (Resanteckningar från Orienten åren 1843–1849) were painstakingly edited and published in four volumes between 1864 and 1866 by Sven Gabriel Elmgren and later re-examined by Knut Tallqvist. Historical assessment of Wallin has consistently highlighted his singular ethical approach to field research, his lack of imperialist condescension, and his profound empathy for Bedouin culture. Scholars of Middle Eastern studies today revere Wallin as the true pioneer of modern Arabic sociolinguistics and one of the most remarkable academic explorers of the Victorian era.

publisher_data: Helsinki, Published by (S. Baranovskij for) J. Simelius, 1853
academic_description: 8vo. VII, [1 blank], 126, [2 blank] pp. With a steel-engraved map at the end. It includes printed music for a Bedouin melody and an appendix with Arabic terms and phrases. Contemporary half calf over marbled paper boards (rubbed at extremities, spine worn and with minor losses). On the front flyleaf contemporary ownership entry of John Snellman (1815-1883), Finish senator and relative of renown Johan Vilh. Snellman (1806-1881), statesman and philosopher. A clean copy with occasional toning to pages. First edition, published posthumously in the original Swedish, of the account of Wallin’s journey through Arabia, covering the wastelands of the Nafud Desert, where he reached Ha il, then continued southward to Medina and Mecca after returning to Egypt. More precisely, Wallin “moved eastwards from Wadi al-Araba, first touching upon the upper regions of Wadi Sirhan, then on to the oasis of Djuf (Algawf) and crossed the central regions of Shammar, via Djobbah (Gubbi), the Great Nefud (Nufood), and Hail. Of Shammar and its inhabitants he provided the fullest account, unsurpassed by later travellers in its scholarly precision” (Henze).Wallin, a Finnish orientalist, set out for the Middle-East in 1843 under the name of Abd al-Wali and visited Mecca in 1845, several years before Richard Burton. The account was later translated into English (‘Narrative of a Journey from Cairo to Medina and Mecca’) and published in the “Journal of the Royal Geographical Society” in 1854. The English version, however, does not include the appendix with Arabic terms. The work was probably left incomplete as the indication “fragment” seems to suggest.

authors.name: Graz-Jesuit College
authors.biography: The Graz-Jesuit College (Jesuitenkollegium Graz), which evolved into the Academia Graecensis and subsequently the Karl-Franzens-Universität Graz, stands as one of the most formidable institutional bastions of the Roman Catholic Counter-Reformation in Early Modern Central Europe. Founded in the late sixteenth century within the geopolitical crucible of Inner Austria (Innerösterreich)—a territory encompassing Styria, Carinthia, Carniola, and Gorizia—the college was conceived not merely as a center for humanistic and scholastic instruction, but as an intellectual and ideological fortress designed to roll back the sweeping advance of Lutheran Protestantism across the Habsburg hereditary lands. Under the patronage of the Habsburg dynasty, specifically Archduke Charles II (Erzherzog Karl II. von Innerösterreich) and his devoutly Catholic consort Maria Anna of Bavaria, the college spearheaded an aggressive program of confessionalization, integrating rigorous Ignatius-inspired pedagogy, public disputation, theatrical spectacle, and sophisticated print culture into a unified instrument of ecclesiastical and political restoration.The establishment of the college was forged against the backdrop of acute religious and political polarization in the Holy Roman Empire following the Peace of Augsburg (1555). By the 1560s, the Styrian nobility and burgher estates (Stände) had overwhelmingly embraced the Lutheran confession, securing substantial religious concessions through the Pacification of Bruck (Brucker Pazifikation) in 1578. Alarmed by the perceived erosion of dynastic authority and Catholic orthodoxy, Archduke Charles II sought the intervention of the Society of Jesus (Societas Jesu). Guided by the strategic counsel of Saint Peter Canisius SJ and Father Alfonso Salmerón SJ, negotiations culminated in 1572 with the official invitation of the Jesuits to Graz. The initial contingent of Jesuit fathers arrived in the autumn of 1573, taking residence near the city center adjacent to the parish church (now the Graz Cathedral or Domkirche). The institutional momentum accelerated rapidly: in 1585, Pope Sixtus V issued the papal bull Edictum conferring full university status upon the college, granting it the right to award degrees in Philosophy and Theology. This papal privilege was imperialized the following year, in 1586, when Holy Roman Emperor Rudolf II issued the imperial charter, formally launching the Academia Graecensis as a fully recognized Catholic university operating under the direct control of the Society of Jesus.The intellectual architecture of the Graz-Jesuit College was structured strictly around the humanistic and theological principles codified in the Ratio Studiorum (the standardized Jesuit plan of studies promulgated definitively in 1599).
