Bound in 18th-century stiff vellum, title lettered in gilt on spine, inked date “1549” on spine and inked note on the front panel “Postillati da Latino Latini”, blue edges (slightly soiled and stained). On the front pastedown are the Libreria Loescher Roma bookplate and a pasted leaflet containing notes from a later owner. On the title page ownership entry “Latini Latinij Viterbiens. 1551”, other inked-out note “Coll. Rom. Soc. Iesu ex Leg.o Con. Pallavicini”, and the initials “R.C.”. Annotated throughout by a contemporary hand, with minor additions by one or possibly two other hands. Slightly uniformly browned, two small ink stains with hole on l. y7 of the Columella, all in all a well-preserved, genuine copy. The present volume collecting five editions of the so-called scriptores rei rusticae and their commentators published in Lyon by S. Gryphe, comes from the library of the great philologist Latino Latini and bears extensive annotations (in Latin and occasionally in Greek) in his minuscule yet neat and precise handwriting. Some notes are signed at the end with the letter “L”.Latini devoted much of his life to emending and critically analyzing manuscripts of the Church Fathers, the Sacred Scriptures, and the classics. Though his meticulous work was always carried out with a philological rigor that earned him the unconditional esteem of his contemporaries, it was rarely published in print. In the 17th century, Domenico Magri, the curator of the Capitular Archive of Viterbo where Latini’s library and unpublished manuscripts are housed since his death, recognized the value of the countless critical notes Latini had left in the margins of his library’s books, and published some of these notes in the volume Latini Latinii Viterbiensis Bibliotheca sacra, et profana, sive Observationes, correctiones, coniecturae, et variae lectiones in sacros, et profanos scriptores e marginalibus notis codicum eiusdem (Rome, 1677), in which he recorded the emendations made by Latini to 45 sacred authors and 42 secular writers.During his career Latini also served as a proofreader for the printing house of Paolo Manuzio (1512-1574), who was summoned to Rome in 1561 by Pius IV to establish a printing press for the Curia. Even though the 19th-century note written on the leaflet pasted on the front pastedown states that the inscription “Latini Latinij Viterbiensis 1551” written at the top of the title page is in Manuzio’s handwriting, it is actually Latini’s typical signature on all his books. Considering the connection between the two, however, it is quite plausible that Latini gave Manuzio the volume for a possible publication, which never occurred.Most of the notes are textual amendments, but some are more extensive and contain more detailed comments or personal references. Here are a few examples:-p. 14 Cato: “Lege quae ad calcem operis mea manu adscripsi”;-p. 83 Cato: “Hos catonis de agricoltura libros, cum manuscripto vetusto exemplari meo Romae 1551 contuli…”. He then explains the abbreviations he used to refer to the different manuscripts or “impressos veteres” that he consulted;-p. 106 Varro: “Petrus chaconius locum ita restituendum putat: …”;-p. 464 Columella: “Emendavi Columel: elegantiss. opus, et absolui anno dni 1514. 15 calen. Februarii hora xxiii Geneazani (inquit .i.) hoc ipso loco quare constat ub. non fuisse; […] Marianum e Franciscanorum sodalitiio, Genaciano castro oriundum virum non indoctum fuisse comperi ex iis qui hominis consuetudine usi fuerunt […] Ego vero Romae anno 1551 mense Decembri .L.”;-p. 184 Palladius: “… idest hoc ipso loco scriptum est ita: Absolutus Palladii liber hic et castigatus ann. Dni 1514 die xxviii mensis Januarii […] At postea Franciscani ordinis hominem fuisse accepi, Geneazzano oriundum, neq.; indoctum suo saeculo .L.” (these two notes refer to Mariano da Genazzano (1412-1498), a preacher of the Augustinian Hermits who carried out his ministry primarily in Florence, where he was closely associated with the humanist circles and the Medici family; for this reason, he was a bitter adversary of Savonarola);-l. ee4v Beroaldo: “Defrutare vinum, non est id, quod defrutum facere …”;-p. 5 Vettori: “Codex meus manuscriptus semper posuerunt, et posui, habet, diligenter accurateque ut videtur ex bono descriptus exemplari”.On pp. 56 and 312-315 of Columella there are a few notes possibly in different handwritings. Latino Latini was born in Viterbo in 1513 to Bernardino and Francesca Closia, both from impoverished noble families. From a young age, he suffered from poor health, which influenced some of his future decisions. Around 1533, he moved to Siena with the intention of studying law and remained there for eleven years; his fragile health forced him to abandon the legal studies to devote himself more and more intensely to his beloved Latin classics (especially Cicero) and the Church Fathers. He spent about two years in Viterbo, and between 1544 and 1546 he moved to Rome to seek employment with a member of the clergy. Under Julius III, he was ordained, and around 1552 he was hired as a secretary by Cardinal Jacopo Dal Pozzo. While in his service, Latini began to form friendships with the humanists with whom he corresponded as part of his official duties, and he became associated with the circle of Carlo Borromeo, Cesare Baronio, Guglielmo Sirleto, Fulvio Orsini, Gabriele Faerno, and the future popes Gregory XIII, Pius V, and Sixtus V.On February 14, 1561, Cardinal Dal Pozzo was elected by Pius IV as president of the Council of Trent. While the cardinal and Latini were preparing to travel to Trent, in June 1562 they both fell ill. Dal Pozzo never recovered and died on April 26, 1563. Latini was immediately hired by Cardinal Rodolfo Pio da Carpi, for whom he served as secretary and librarian until the cardinal’s death on May 2, 1564. During that period, Latini devoted himself intensely to publishing sacred authors, undertaking the arduous task of emending the manuscripts, to the point that he fell ill again and returned to Viterbo to recover, primarily through the sulfur-rich waters of the Viterbo thermal baths. Once he had recovered, he returned to Rome in 1565, where he received numerous job offers; he ultimately accepted the offer from Cardinal Ranuccio Farnese, who appointed him as his secretary and took him to Bologna, where Latini established new contacts, particularly with the brothers Gabriele and Camillo Paleotti, with Carlo Sigonio, and with Ulisse Aldrovandi, who submitted his Theatrum naturae to Latini’s judgment, receiving precise corrections in return.Cardinal Farnese also died in 1565, and Latini withdrew from court life for several years, as the repeated deaths that occurred shortly after his appointment had led to him being labeled a jinx. Latini complains about this, for example, in a letter to the Spanish bishop Antonio Agustín. In April 1568, the dying Onofrio Panvinio appointed Latini as his executor (along with the Augustinian friar Giuseppe Panfilo da Verona, Fulvio Orsini, and Girolamo Mercuriale), entrusting him with the task of revising his manuscript works and publishing the complete collection. In the summer of 1568, Latini - along with Vincenzo Pinelli, Mercuriale, and Lorenzo Gambara - was part of the circle of humanists led by Orsini that met in Caprarola, where Orsini was staying in the entourage of Cardinal Farnese. In 1571, Cardinal Marcantonio Colonna took him under his wing and provided him with comfortable lodgings in his own palace, leaving him free to devote himself to literary studies and, above all, to the editions of the Church Fathers. Some time later, perhaps in October 1572, he accompanied the cardinal to Salerno, where he formed a close friendship and began a correspondence with the Jesuit Alfonso Salmerón.After March 1573, Latini returned to Rome and was commissioned by Gregory XIII to revise and restore the text of the Decretum Gratiani, to which so many canons and decretals had been added over time that it had become an extremely tangled web of often contradictory rules. He devoted himself to this work for thirteen years, together with the other members of the commission appointed for that purpose: Cardinals M. Colonna, Alessandro Sforza di S. Fiora, G. Sirleto, Francesco Alciati, G. Paleotti, C. Borromeo, F. Peretti, and others. For this work, Gregory XIII granted him an annual pension of 150 ducats; he also included him in the commission of ten specialists tasked with correcting the Martyrology, among whom was C. Baronio, with whom Latini deepened his friendship. The secretary of the commission was Giovanni Battista Bandini of Florence, who in 1588-89 became one of Latini’s most frequent correspondents.Meanwhile, in 1584, F. Zanetti published in Rome the Loci ex coniectura Latini Latinii Viterbiensis vel restituti, vel aliter lecti in Tertulliano post editionem Iacobi Pamelii Brugen. ann. 1583, based on the edition by Jacques de Joigny de Pamèle. Upon the death of Gregory XIII in April 1585, Latini was commissioned, along with Orsini and Flaminio De’ Nobili, to draft the epitaph for the late pope. In 1587, in a move unusual for him - given his reluctance to publish his works - he published in Rome, in a small pamphlet printed by B. Bonfadini, one of the many opinions and views he was frequently asked to provide: Opinio de ea historiae Socratis Sozomenique parte, qua Nectarii episcopi factum de abrogato paenitentiario presbytero continetur. That same year, he was appointed to the consultors of the Holy Office. Between 1589 and 1590, he sent Michele Mercati some critical remarks on Mercati’s own work De gli obelischi di Roma (1589), to which Mercati replied in 1590 with Consideratio sopra gli avvertimenti del sig. Latino Latini intorno ad alcune cose scritte nel libro de gli obelischi di Roma. Latini continued to work for an entire year on editing the works of Tertullian and St. Cyprian, finding the task increasingly arduous due to his declining physical health, yet enjoying the esteem and respect of his contemporary scholars. His emendations on Tertullian were included in the editions of Tertullian’s Opera, published with extensive scholarly commentary in Paris in 1608 and 1616, and in Cologne in 1617. Latini died in Rome on January 21, 1593. He was buried in the Church of Santa Maria in Via Lata.As mentioned above, most of Latini’s unpublished manuscripts are housed in the Capitular Archive of Viterbo (now part of the Capitular Library). In the mid-17th century, the archivist Domenico Magri was struck by the erudition of the letters - which Latini himself had arranged for publication - and published them between 1659 and 1667, prefacing them with a brief biography of Latini. From the latter’s correspondence - written in Latin and Italian in a very legible hand - emerges a figure who had forged an elite and extensive network of friendships and correspondents, was well-integrated into scholarly society, was listened to with respect - contemporary scholars routinely turned to Latini for advice - and was at times politely challenged. The letters written by Latini during his service to Cardinal Dal Pozzo are addressed primarily to recipients in Poland and Prussia. Of particular interest is the long and uninterrupted correspondence with the Belgian orientalist Andrea Maes, which spanned from 1554 until Maes’s death in 1573. Through Maes, Latini came into contact in 1572 with Benito Arias Montano, an orientalist and librarian at El Escorial. Latini bequeathed his beautiful and extensive library to the Capitular Archives of Viterbo. Some of his books likely came from the library of Cardinal Rodolfo Pio da Carpi. Agustín turned to Latini for assistance in publishing his numismatic works. Together with F. Orsini, O. Pantagato, G. Faerno, A. Chacón, and M.-A. Muret, Latini participated in the lengthy philological work that resulted in a general miscellaneous commentary on Latin historians, which Orsini added to the Fragmenta historicorum published by Agustín in Antwerp in 1595 (cf. M. Ceresa, Latini, Latino, “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 64, Rome, 2005, s.v.).
bibliography: M. Ceresa, Latini, Latino, “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 64, Rome, 2005, s.v.

authors.name: Camerarius Joachim
authors.biography: Joachim Camerarius the Elder (1500–1574) stands as one of the most brilliant, versatile, and influential humanists of the Northern European Renaissance. A scholar of extraordinary linguistic erudition, pivotal university reformer, and tireless textual critic, Camerarius occupied a central position within the intellectual and confessional matrix of sixteenth-century Germany. Alongside his lifelong companion and intellectual collaborator, Philipp Melanchthon, Camerarius served as a primary architect of the Praeceptio Germaniae—the systematic transformation of Northern European education through the integration of classical Greek and Latin philology with evangelical theology. His monumental contributions to classical scholarship, ranging from groundbreaking critical editions of Plautus, Sophocles, and Homer to translations of Galen and Claudius Ptolemy, established standards of textual rigor that bridged the methodology of Italian humanists like Piero Vettori with the emerging philological traditions of early modern Germany. Beyond his textual corpus, Camerarius was an instrumental figure in the institutionalization of the Reformation, drafting foundational documents at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530 and orchestrating the overhaul of major universities, including Nuremberg, Tübingen, and Leipzig.Born on April 12, 1500, in the Franconian imperial city of Bamberg, Camerarius hailed from a patrician family originally named Liebhard. The surname Camerarius was adopted by his ancestors in reference to their hereditary title of Kämmerer (hereditary chamberlain) to the Prince-Bishops of Bamberg. His early educational foundation was established in Bamberg under the guidance of local schoolmasters before he matriculated at the University of Leipzig in 1512 at the exceptionally early age of twelve. At Leipzig, the young scholar came under the profound influence of the English Hellenist Richard Croke and the renowned Latinist Peter Mosellanus (Peter Schade), whose instruction ignited Camerarius’s lifelong devotion to ancient Greek grammar and Neo-Latin eloquence. Seeking an environment more receptive to the new humanist learning, Camerarius transferred in 1518 to the University of Erfurt. There, he entered the celebrated literary circle gathered around Conrad Mutianus Rufus and Helius Eobanus Hessus, immersing himself in the study of classical rhetoric, poetry, and ancient history. In 1521, drawn by the radical intellectual ferment surrounding the early Protestant movement, Camerarius relocated to the University of Wittenberg. This move proved decisive: at Wittenberg, he established an intimate, lifelong friendship with Philipp Melanchthon and entered the immediate circle of Martin Luther. Under Melanchthon’s guidance, Camerarius deepened his command of Greek syntax, began lecturing publicly on Quintilian and Cicero, and engaged directly with the critical translation of Biblical texts.Camerarius’s career as an institutional administrator and educational reformer commenced in 1526, when, upon Melanchthon’s direct recommendation, the Senate of the Imperial City of Nuremberg appointed him rector of the newly established Aegidien-Gymnasium. In Nuremberg, working in close concert with the reformer Lazarus Spengler, Camerarius designed a pioneering humanist curriculum that served as a blueprint for secondary education throughout Protestant Europe. His diplomatic and theological capabilities were put to a severe test in 1530, when he accompanied Melanchthon to the Imperial Diet of Augsburg. Camerarius actively assisted in the redaction, translation, and diplomatic negotiations surrounding the Confessio Augustana (Augsburg Confession), playing a subtle yet critical role in maintaining irenic dialogue with Catholic imperial representatives. Recognizing his institutional genius, Duke Ulrich of Württemberg summoned Camerarius in 1535 to reorganize the University of Tübingen along humanist and evangelical lines, a task he accomplished with remarkable speed by revitalizing the faculties of arts and theology. In 1541, Duke Maurice of Saxony enticed Camerarius to accept the professorship of Greek and Latin literature at the University of Leipzig. For the remaining thirty-three years of his life, Camerarius transformed Leipzig into the premier center of classical philology and humanist erudition in Northern Europe, navigating the immense political and military turmoil of the Smalcaldic War (1546–1547) and the contentious Adiaphoristic controversies with remarkable diplomatic tact and scholarly detachment.The philological legacy of Joachim Camerarius is immense, characterized by unprecedented critical acumen, stemmatological intuition, and deep linguistic sensitivity. His edition of the comedies of Plautus (M. Accii Plauti Comoediae XX), printed at Basel in 1552, represented a watershed moment in Latin textual scholarship. Utilizing the famous Codex Vetus (Vaticanus Lat. 3870), which he examined with meticulous care, Camerarius purged centuries of scribal corruptions, restored ancient metrical structures, and established a text that remained standard for generations. His labor in Greek letters was equally groundbreaking: he produced critical editions and Latin translations of Homer’s Iliad and Odyssey, Sophocles’ tragedies, Hesiod, Theocritus, Demosthenes, Xenophon, and Herodotus. Camerarius did not limit his erudition to literary classics; he was deeply fascinated by ancient science, astronomy, and medicine. In 1535, he published the editio princeps of the Greek text of Claudius Ptolemy’s astrological treatise, the Tetrabiblos (or Quadripartitum), alongside his own Latin translation, accompanied by an edition of the Karbos (Centiloquium). His medical interest led him to translate and annotate works by Galen and Aetius of Amida. In the realm of contemporary history and biography, Camerarius authored two masterworks that remain indispensable primary sources for the Renaissance and Reformation eras: his Narratio de Helios Eobano Hesso (1553) and his monumental De vita Philippi Melanchthonis narratio (1566). The latter represents the first comprehensive biography of Melanchthon, offering an insider’s view of the intellectual dynamics, personal struggles, and theological debates of the Reformation inner circle.The dissemination of Camerarius’s vast literary output was made possible through his intimate, highly strategic relationships with the leading printing houses of Northern Europe. He maintained close working alliances with the great Basel presses, most notably those of Johannes Herwagen, Johann Oporinus, and Hieronymus Froben. These Basel publishers possessed the specialized Greek fonts and scholarly correctors necessary to produce Camerarius’s complex Greek commentaries and critical texts. In Nuremberg, he collaborated extensively with Johannes Petreius, who printed several of his grammatical and astronomical works, while in Leipzig, his texts issued regularly from the presses of Ernst Voegelin, Michael Blum, and Valentin Papa. Camerarius was also a central node in an international republic of letters (*Respublica Literaria*). His voluminous epistolary correspondence—comprising well over one thousand extant Latin and Greek letters—demonstrates active textual exchanges with Italian humanists such as Piero Vettori (Victorius) in Florence and Cardinal Pietro Bembo, as well as Northern scholars like Erasmus of Rotterdam, Johannes Sturm in Strasbourg, and Joachim Vadianus in St. Gallen. Through these networks, Camerarius facilitated the exchange of rare manuscripts, collations, and codicological data across confessional divides, maintaining a steadfast commitment to the universal fellowship of humanist learning despite the religious wars fracturing Europe.Camerarius passed away in Leipzig on April 17, 1574, leaving behind a family that would continue his scholarly legacy, most notably his son, Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534–1598), a celebrated physician, botanist, and emblem author. In the centuries following his death, Camerarius’s reputation as a giant of classical philology remained unshakeable. Polyhistors of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, including Daniel Georg Morhof and Johann Albert Fabricius, praised him as the ultimate exemplar of Northern erudition—a scholar who combined the stylistic elegance of the Italian Renaissance with German textual thoroughness. Modern historiography, led by scholars such as Heinz Scheible, Thomas Fuchs, and Volkhard Wels, has re-evaluated Camerarius not merely as a passive transmitter of classical antiquity, but as an indispensable agent of cultural transformation who shaped the institutional structures of early modern German universities, pioneered modern philological methodologies, and preserved the intellectual coherence of Protestant Humanism during a period of acute ideological crisis.

academic_description: The miscellany contains six works, five from the 16th century (but one is just a fragment) and one from the beginning of the 17th century: BASILIUS CAESARIENSIS Sanctus (330-379) et al. D. Basilij Magni De instituenda studiorum ratione ad nepotes suos oratio paraenetica Graece & Latine, ut cum annotationibus Iustini Gobleri conferri possit. Item Ioannis Pici Mirandulę De homine opusculum omnino diuinum. Eiusdem De Christi regno, & vanitate huius mundi. Loci christianam uitam breuiter complectens. Et Commentaria in Psal. 15. Præterea Rodolphus Agricola De Formando studio, & Erasmi Roterodami ac Philippi Melanchtonis studiorum rationes, atque locorum communium index. Basel, Heinrich Petri, (1537). [16], 229 [of 262] pp. Also lacking the final leaf with the printer’s device. Collation: a8 A-Q8 R4. Over 30 pages (half quire P to R) at the end, containing the Ratio colligendi exempla, the famous method theorized by Erasmus of Rotterdam in his rhetorical-pedagogical treatise De duplici copia verborum ac rerum (1512), have been expunged. Other signs of censorship such as this are also visible on the title page and on l. P3r, where Erasmus’ name has been erased. Additionally, on leaf P4v, the beginning of Erasmus’s aforementioned treatise is covered by a blank leaf and some scribbles. Leaf N8v is also covered by blank paper strips to censor a brief text by Melanchthon and Erasmus. Some old manuscript annotations, partly trimmed by the bookbinder. Woodcut decorative initials. Roman and Greek types. Curiously, and in apparent contradiction with the aformentioned censorships, the owner of the present Sammelband bound between the title page and leaf a2 a dedication that Melanchthon addressed to his friend and fellow scholar Simon Grynaeus taken from Peuerbach’s Theoricae novae planetarum in the Wittenberg 1551 edition printed by Hans Lufft with a preface by Melanchthon (cf. VD16, P-2061).Saint Basil the Great’s famous homily, De instituenda studiorum ratione ad nepotes suos oratio paraenetica, printed here also in its original Greek text, was a cornerstone of Christian humanism, as Saint Basil argues that young Christians should actively study pagan classical texts (like Homer and Plato) for their moral virtues, using them as a preparatory stepping stone before diving into Holy Scripture. This specific edition is accompanied by the annotations of the German jurist and humanist Justin Gobler, providing contemporary readers with philological and practical insights into Basil’s rhetoric.The edition also includes two works by Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, his celebrated Oration on the Dignity of Man and a lesser-known text De Christi regno, & vanitate huius mundi, a sort of commentary on Psalm 15, as well as Rudolph Agricola’s De Formando studio. As said, the final texts by Erasmus and Melanchthon were expurgated by the owner of the volume.VD16, B-650. OLYMPIODORUS (fl. 6th cent.). Olympiodori Doctissima in Ecclesiast. scholia, nova & latinis auribus insueta tralatione inserta, Aquilae videlicet, Theodotionis, & 70. Zenobio Acciaiolo Florentino interprete. Divi Gregorij Neocaesariensis In eundem metaphrasis, uel ut Suidæ placet, […] Ioanne Oecolampadio interprete. Aristeae De 72. legis Hebraicæ interpretatione libellus, […] Matthia Palmerio Vicentino interprete. Basel, Johann Bebel, 1536. 8vo. [8], 248 pp. Collation: α4 a-p8 q4. Printer’s device on l. o8v.These are the commentaries (scholia) attributed to Olympiodorus the Deacon (not to be confused with the Neoplatonic philosopher of the same name), which contain some of the the most ancient lost Greek translations (“unusual to Latin ears”): those of Aquila of Sinope, of Theodotion, and the Septuagint. The translator from Greek to Latin is the Florentine humanist Zenobio Acciaioli (1461-1519), a Dominican friar and prefect of the Vatican Apostolic Library, who rediscovered and translated this commentaries precisely to make fragments of the first Greek biblical translations available to scholars. The second part contains the paraphrase (metaphrasis) of Ecclesiastes written by Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus (or of Neocaesarea), a third-century Church Father. The title cites the Byzantine encyclopedia Suidas for the attribution of the text. The Latin translation here is by Johannes Oecolampadius (1482-1531), a renowned German humanist, Hebraist, and leader of the Protestant Reformation in Basel. The final section is the celebrated Letter of Aristeas to Philocrates, a seminal Hellenistic text that recounts the legendary story of the birth of the Septuagint Bible. The Latin translation is by the humanist Matteo Palmieri (1423-1483).VD16, O-727. ATHENAGORAS ATHENIENSIS (ca. 2nd cent.)-AENEAS GAZAEUS (430-486). Athenagoras De mortuorum resurrectione, Petro Nannio interprete [followed by:] Aeneas Gazaeus De immortalitate animarum, et corporum resurrectione, Ioanne Vuolphio interprete. A fragment from Philo Alexandrinus’ (25-40) Lucubrationes quotquot […] Latinae factae per Sigismundum Gelenium (Basel, Nikolaus Episcopius d.J., 1558). 8vo. 1401-1526, [2 blank] pp. Collation: RR-Aaa8.Athenagoras was one of the most refined Christian philosophers and apologists of the second century. His treatise on the resurrection of the dead is a fusion of Christian theology and Platonic and Aristotelian logic. Rather than relying solely on Scripture, Athenagoras uses pure philosophical argument to demonstrate that the resurrection of the body is logical and morally necessary for the final judgment of humanity. The Latin version is the work of the Flemish humanist Pieter Nanninck (Petrus Nannius, 1500-1557), a highly esteemed professor of Latin at the prestigious Collegium Trilingue in Louvain.Aeneas of Gaza was a Neoplatonic philosopher who converted to Christianity and lived between the fifth and sixth centuries. His work is structured like a Platonic dialogue: in it, Aeneas refutes traditional Neoplatonic doctrines that viewed the body as a prison of the soul to be destroyed, philosophically arguing for the immortality of the soul and the glorification and final resurrection of the material body. The translation from Greek and the philological restoration of the text are due to Johann Wolf (Ioannes Vuolphius, 1521-1571), a theologian and professor in Zurich.VD16, ZV-12449. PLUTARCHUS (45-120)-CAMERARIUS, Joachim, ed. (1500-1574). De natura et effectionibus daemonum libelli duo Plutarchi Cheronensis, cum explicationibus, & proemio Ioachimi Camer. Quibus & eruditae, & rarae & iucundae & non inutiles cognitu rerum mirabilium & singularium expositiones continentur. Leipzig, Ernst Vögelin, [1565]. 8vo. [54], 151 [i.e. 152], [2: errata] pp. Collation: A-N8. Woodcut historiated initials and woodcut geometric figures in the text. Inked marginalia and underlinings in later hand (partly trimmed).Extremely rare first edition (reprinted by Vögelin in 1576). The book combines the text of Plutarch, translated in Latin by Adrien Turnèbe (1512-1565), with the commentary of the German humanist Joachim Camerarius (1500-1574). Plutarch, who was a priest at the Oracle of Delphi, explores in these pages the nature of the “daimones”, understood in Greek culture as intermediary entities between gods and men, responsible for prophetic inspiration. Plutarch’s two works on oracles and prophecy cover a wide range of topics, including spirits, demons, witchcraft, astronomy, and geometry.Camerarius’s lenghty preface, followed at the end by another long text, which features geometrical figures, called Annotatio, is significant because it not only comments on Plutarch’s text on oracles and prophecy (De Defuctu Oraculorum and De Figura ei, consecrata Delphis), but extends the discussion to contemporary concerns about witches.“Joachim Camerarius the Elder is routinely praised for his critical acumen in editing classical texts. In this paper I would like to blame him for his role in fostering the witch craze that swept southern Germany a decade after his death. The fifty years between 1581 and 1631 saw the arrest, trial, and execution of some 2,500 witches in Trier, Bamberg, and Würzburg. Although Camerarius is not associated with those trials, I would like to suggest he be held responsible for helping create the intellectual climate that made them possible.We all go crazy sometimes. Late at night, a sudden noise can set your mind whirring or make you freak out. When that happens, it isn’t always easy to get a grip on yourself and realize that your thoughts are running wild. That happened to Joachim Camerarius one night and it changed his life. He tells us so in the preface to a book he published in Leipzig in or around 1568. The book is a Latin translation of two mystical essays by Plutarch, On the Failure of Oracles and On the E at Delphi, but the surprising thing about it is the title Camerarius gave it: De natura et effectionibus daemonum, ‘On the Nature and Activities of Demons’.The preface takes the form of a letter from Camerarius to a friend, named Adrianus Albinus, who had stopped twice to visit him in Leipzig while on his way to and from Speyer: It is 51 pages long. In it Camerarius says the conversations they had had led him to stay up late one night reading a book, a book that made him rethink everything he thought he knew. In the pages that follow he proceeds to lay out his revised thoughts about the reality of demons, of witches, and of witchcraft. At length he states his new view to Albinus (p. 28):Neque est res ista nova, sed priscis quoque temporibus nota atque usurpata. Nomina tantum et voces mutantur, caetera sunt cadem.That thing you mentioned? It’s nothing new. People knew about it and did it in anti-quity. It’s all the same; only the names have changed.As becomes clear, the meaning of ista res, ‘that thing you mentioned’, is sexual intercourse. Camerarius and Albinus had talked about sex, but not of the typical kind. Rather, the great scholar and his friend had heatedly debated the reality of sexual intercourse between human beings and demons. From the letter it is obvious that Camerarius was already a true believer in ghosts, mediums, and conjuring the dead, but that is nothing unusual for a man of his times. What is unusual, and bizarre, is his newfound conviction that women literally have sex with demons […]An incidental clue allows us to fix the date of the letter. On p. 52 Camerarius remarks that 48 years have passed since he last studied with Richard Croke (1489-1558), a teacher with whom he first read bits of Plutarch. That was in 1517, so Camerarius wrote the letter to Albinus in 1565. As we will see, this is precisely the date to which external indications also point.The letter begins with a convoluted and cryptic sentence (p. 4 = A2r):Cum nuper hac ex Nemetum urbe revertens transires, et me, perpetua consuetudine tua, humanissime salutasses, recordari te puto, Adriane Albine, factae mentionis inter alios sermones nostros, cuiusdam a me, de mirabilibus cogitationibus meis, quibus causam dedissent narrationes tuae superiorum dierum, quando proficiscens ad Rhe-num huc veneras.I bet you remember, Adrianus Albinus, that when you passed through here not long ago on your way back from Speyer and (as kindly as ever) you came to see me, I mentioned, among other things, some strange thoughts I'd been having. They were prompted by what you told me about some recent events (narrationes superiorum dierum) when you stopped here on your way to the Rhine.These ideas certainly could have been stated more clearly. Working backward in time, the sentence says that on a recent trip, Albinus had stopped in Leipzig to see Camerarius, not once but twice. The first time was on his way to Speyer and the second was on his way back. On his first stop, Albinus had told Camerarius about some recent events that set his mind thinking. Camerarius was still brooding on them when Albinus stopped again on his way home, so they discussed them a second time. And after Albinus left again, Camerarius still couldn’t stop thinking about them […] Camerarius goes on (p. 5 = A2v):Extatque liber cuiusdam titulo Mallei maleficarum, et Francisci Pici alter de Strigibus, in quibus huius generis exempla et plurima numero et factis teterrima leguntur. Atque ego me aliquando paulo antequam cubitum irem librum Pici percurrentem, memini noctem illam habuisse valde gravem ac difficilem, obversantibus animo terroribus variis de is quae ibi referuntur.There’s a book out there called Malleus Maleficarum (‘A Mallet for Malefactresses’), and another one by Francisco Pico about witches (strigibus). We see case after case like that - really shocking stuff! - in them. I remember leafing through Pico's book that night just before going to bed and having an awful, simply horrible, night. My mind was haunted by all kinds of frightening thoughts about the stuff in that book.He adds (ibid.):Mihi vero post tuum discessum de istis ita multae et variae cogitationes obstrepere non destiterunt, ut non possem facere quin de tota re anquirere et considerare accu-ratius et diligentius instituerem.After you left, I was obsessed by all kinds of thoughts about what you said, and I couldn’t help it: I just had to investigate the whole thing, had to take a really good, hard look at it.‘The whole thing’ (tota re) turns out to mean not only sex with demons, but demonology as a whole. In the 50 pages that follow Camerarius ransacks classical pagan literature for evidence of the existence and harmful activity of demons, ghosts, nightmares, madness, visions, magic cures, and witches. He conflates fact and fiction; he cites hearsay evidence and stories of evildoing to which no names or dates are attached. Remarkably, he chooses not to invoke his Christian faith for his belief in witches, preferring instead the evidence of classical authors. Fifty pages later, he has concluded that witches are real and that this was a fact known to all ancient authorities. He also concludes that witches celebrate orgies and do have sexual intercourse with demons. Although that was an old rumor in Catholic countries, it was something new in Germany, especially Protestant Germany; I will come back to this point. Camerarius goes on at such length not out of prurience or misogyny but because he is plainly trying to prove to himself that demons (or rather, daimones - meaning both good spirits, like angels, and evil spirits) are corporeal […]When he published it, Camerarius was hailed as the leading light in Europe and the successor of Erasmus. On the last page of the letter, he addresses Albinus once more and makes two important points. First, he reveals why he wrote the letter (p. 51):Tuae, Albine Adriane, narrationes illas cogitationes, quas exposui, commoverunt, casque ut scripto completerer, ne quasi evanescerent, cum alia me impulerunt, tum quod eas ipsas abs te legendo cognosci cuperem.All these thoughts of mine were prompted by what you told me, Adrianus Albinus, and that induced me to write them down, not just to ensure they wouldn’t vanish (so to speak when I became preoccupied with other matters, but also because I wanted you to read and learn from them).He then offers a prediction about the fate of these efforts (p. 53 = p. D2v):Quod autem ad rem ipsam attinet, habes, Adriane Albine, meam sententiam de iis, quae et tractata sunt sermonibus nostris te praesente, et his Plutarchi libellis dis-putantur, habes operam quoque interpretationis. [..] alios, si qui illa forte legerint eruditi et docti, confido studium diligentiae meae non esse improbaturos.And there you have it, Adrianus Albinus - my thoughts on what you and I talked about when you were here, matters that these essays of Plutarch’s also discuss. You’ve also got my best shot at making sense of them. [...] If any other sophisticated readers come across them, I’m positive they won't criticize the careful attention I gave them.It isn’t clear in that last sentence whether Camerarius is referring to his thoughts on demonology or to the annotations he adds to the translations of Plutarch; but at any rate, Camerarius’ Plutarch book was reprinted in Leipzig in 1576, two years after his death. Five years later, in 1581, and closer to Würzburg, the preface was reprinted in Frankfurt am Main. It appeared as a supplement to the Flagellum haereticorum fascinariorum (‘A Scourge for Heretical Witches’), an inquisitor’s treatise that asserted the equivalence of heretics and witches. Two years after that, the flames of a thousand bonfires began to light up the heavens in Trier. The Great Witch Craze had come to southern Germany.Camerarius’ addressee is not a famous man. Who was Adrianus Albinus, and what did he tell his friend to shock him so? Born in Lauban, Silesia (today Lubań, in southwest Poland), Adriarius Albinus (1513-1590) studied law in Poland, Germany, France, and Italy. In 1541, at the age of 28, he briefly taught law in Leipzig. There he probably met Camerarius, who arrived the same year as Professor of Latin and Greek. In 1544 Albinus became Professor of Roman Law at the University of Frankfurt-Oder, in Brandenburg, and the year after that, in 1545, the 32-year old Albinus was named the Chancellor of Neumark (cancellarius Neomarchiae) and legal advisor (consiliarius, Rat) to John, Margrave of Brandenburg-Küstrin" (1513-1571). Thirty-five years later, in 1590, Albinus died and was buried in Küstrin. A contemporary obituary says he had been a devout Christian and lifelong devotee of Plutarch’s Parallel Lives.!? The Plutarch connection could explain why Camerarius dedicated the book to him, but probably not. That brings me to the topic of their conversation, and in particular the narrationes superiorum dierum, as Camerarius called them (pp. 4-5 = A2t-A2v):Commemoravisti enim tunc, quid apud vos compertum prolatumque fuisset, de mulie-rum quarundam veneficarum horribilibus facinoribus, deque superstitionis incredibili efficacitate, et eiusmodi operibus, de quibus non modo sollertiae humanae consideratio quaerens conturbari, sed religiosae quoque pietatis attentio vacillare quoddamodo posset. [..] Atque me ea repetentem animo quae audiveram ex te, percusserunt similia quaedam de aliis cognita. Nam quod tu de consuetudine spirituum quadam occulta ceteris, ipsis illis infelicibus mulieribus manifesta, exposuisti, perquam multa altis temporibus atque locis pariter depraehensa, et atrocibus suppliciis vindicata esse constat.You see, when we spoke you mentioned what an inquiry back home (apud vos) had discovered (compertum) and brought to light about the awful crimes of some poisoner-women (veneficae) and the incredible power of superstition and workings of that sort. As you put it, looking into those things doesn’t just befuddle a clever man’s reason; it can even shake firm religious faith. […] And while I kept brooding on what you told me, I was struck by some legal discoveries about other women (de altis cognita) that resemble the ones you were talking about. You see, what you said - about a certain ‘sexual intercourse with spirits’ that those terrible women themselves can see but nobody else can - well, it’s a fact that lots and lots of cases were detected and punished by dire penalties at other times and places.Camerarius next mentions the awful night he stayed up reading Pico’s book. Since he blames that incident for converting his worldview from skepticism to belief, whatever Albinus told him must have been grave indeed. After some sleuthing, I think I have figured out what it was. The facts are as follows.Mark Brandenburg, where Albinus was from, was one of the earliest regions in central Europe to prosecute and execute witches. Witch trials elsewhere in Germany only began in earnest around 1570, but in Brandenburg the trials peaked before 1580. In its northwest there is a district called Prignitz. Its capital is a small city called Perleberg, whose population before the Thirty Years’ War (1618-1648) was about 3,000. That is where, in 1565, all hell broke loose - literally. In two waves, small groups of women were tried, convicted, and speedily executed for the crime of sorcery. Though he says nothing of the details, Gerhard Schormann considers the second of these trials a watershed: ‘1565 marks the first time’, he observes, ‘that five women were convicted at one trial and with it, the first appearance of witch lore, including Walpurgis Night on the Blocksberg’.It all happened so fast. Four days after Walpurgis Night in 1565 (the night between April 30 and May 1), three women of Perleberg were arrested, interrogated, convicted, and executed for sorcery. A week later five more witches were caught and tried and, like the first, met their fiery fate on the Weinberg hillside in Perleberg. The witches had been accused of poisoning, but […] the Perleberg women [also] admitted to celebrating a witches’ sabbat, just days before their arrest, on the Blocksberg. This was an unprecedented admission in Christian Germany […] The fate of these latter four women is not clear, but in just one week's time, at least eight and perhaps twelve witches were caught, tried and burned in one small city.Those confessions, certified by execution, must have sparked fears that an evil conspiracy was afoot. This was the moral panic Albinus told Camerarius of […] The Perleberg trials took place in Altmark, in West Brandenburg. Although Adrianus Albinus lived in Neumark, in East Brandenburg, he certainly knew about them. As chancellor of Neumark he would not have been a member of the Appeals Panel, but he was well aware of its activities […] [All this brings to the probable conclusion] that it was this spate of witch trials in Perleberg in 1565 that Albinus told Camerarius about during his two stops in Leipzig […] It is clear from the letter that Camerarius had already believed in demons and, presumably, witchcraft or harmful magic (maleficium) - poisoning, uttering oaths, casting spells, and other physical interventions - long before Albinus arrived. His revelation, therefore, was the sudden realization that the witches’ sabbat, replete with lurid demon sex, was real and was being celebrated right there in Germany. The Perleberg confessions, and executions, had just proven it […]By 1580, six years after Camerarius’ death, belief that a witches’ sabbat was celebrated on the Blocksberg had spread throughout Germany. For example, it is the subject of an anonymous treatise printed in Rostock that year titled Concerning the Witches' sabbat in Brocken Mountain, which is also called Blocksberg Camerarius did not mention the sabbat explicitly in his Plutarch book, but he did discuss sex with demons. So did his book - and its reprints - help promote belief in it? […] He took an existing idea and amplified it, and not only as a radio tower amplifies sound. He also amplified it in stature, adding dignity and authority to a rabble-rousing mistake. His authority authenticated and relayed the idea throughout Germany, where it went viral […] What Camerarius did was worse than authenticating a forgery, like spurious fossils or a Vermeer painting. Camerarius - the university reformer, the ‘eye of Germany,’ the heir of Erasmus - authenticated a mistake. Should we condemn him, and Albinus, for their credulity? […]Like many of his contemporaries, Camerarius made the fatal leap of faith from physical harm (poisoning: cf. veneficae) and threats of it (invoking the devil) to supernatural crime - the witches’ sabbat. But that is less a giant leap than a small step on the journey […] Well-entrenched ideologies - such as messianic Christianity had been […] - are, of course, not easily refuted. Once the basic premises of an ideology are accepted, new observations are perceived in its imagery and articulated in its vocabulary. The result is that while no fresh observation can undermine the belief system, new ‘facts generated by the ideology constantly lend further support to it. This was true in the past for the belief in witchcraft and the corresponding prevalence of witches […] Camerarius did this. He relied on his well-entrenched ideology to generate new ‘facts’ about witches and the corresponding prevalence of witches, and lent his support to it […] So I would not be too quick to condemn Albinus and Camerarius for their credulity. His decision to get involved - to speak out publicly - is a different matter. If public intellectuals are responsible for their public statements, we must condemn Camerarius for his. He abused classical literature - taking the fictions of Plautus, Ovid, Apuleius, and others as evidence of reality, and, to judge from the reprints of his letter to Albinus, he persuaded others he was right […]Did Camerarius recant his belief in witchcraft on his deathbed? In Lea [Materials Toward a History of Witchcraft, Philadelphia] 1939, vol. 1, 248 we read:[…] Camerarius was consulted in 1571 by William IV of Hesse Cassel (son of Philip the Magnanimous) [1532-1592] about some women arrested for jugglers’ [i.e. swindlers’] tricks on a boy. Camerarius opposed the use of torture in such cases and also the water ordeal which Wilhelm was disposed to employ, as he was sure that they would sink, and warned him against the cruelty of witch-burning and the prosecutions by which the innocent were obliged to confess.This suggests Camerarius, who died in 1574, repented late in life for the views he expressed in his letter to Albinus a decade earlier. Sadly, it is apocryphal. Lea has mistaken Camerarius the Elder for his son, Joachim Camerarius the Younger (1534-1598), a distinguished physician and naturalist of Nuremberg and a known associate of William’s over many years” (M. Fontaine, Joachim Camerarius on Witches, Witchcraft, and Criminal Responsibility, or, How to Philologize with a Witches’ Hammer, in: “Camerarius Polyhistor”, Th. Baier, ed., Tubingen, 2017, pp. 335-356).While the second 1576 edition occasionally appears on the market, to find another copy of this first edition on the market, one has to go back to the Sotheby’s New York auction sale of 20 April 1931, when a copy was purchased by McLeish.VD16, P-3696. ACRONIUS, Johannes (1520-1564). Miraculorum quorundam et eorundem effectuum descriptio, per Iohannem Acronium Frisium Mathematicum Basiliensem. Basel, Jakob Kündig, 1561. 8vo. [14 of 16], 46, [2] pp. Collation: *8 A-C8. Without the title page, removed probably for security concerns. Woodcut initials and ornaments. Printer’s device on last leaf recto.Rare first edition. Born in Friesland (in Akkrum, hence the name Frisius) around 1520, Johannes Acronius moved to Basel, where he first obtained a chair in mathematics (1547), then in logic (1549), and finally, in the last year of his life (1564), graduated in medicine before tragically dying of the plague. His Miraculorum quorundam et eorundem effectuum descriptio (‘Description of certain miracles and their effects’) was published in 1561, a period of enormous ferment in pre-Galilean astronomy. As a mathematician and expert in astrolabes, Acronius analyzed the phenomena of the upper atmosphere and outer space, attempting to calculate their physical, mathematical, and meteorological effects on Earth. As was almost always the case in the 16th century, the scientific description of comets and meteors was not entirely unrelated to astrology and historical accounts. The text examines the “effects” of these celestial bodies, which the contemporary mindset still considered indicators or physical messengers of major political changes, famines, or climate changes.“Die Schrift […] behandelt Meteore, Kometen und andere Himmelserscheinungen und ihre Einflusse auf das irdische Geschehen. Dabei werden sowohl Ereignisse aus friiheren Epochen als auch Beobachtungen von Acronius und seinen Zeitgenossen erwahnt. Acronius vertritt den Standpunkt, daB die Himmelserscheinungen von Gott geschickt wurden, um seine GroBe zu demonstrieren, dem Menschen Zeichen zu geben und gegebenenfalls kunftiges Unheil anzukundigen. Seine Erklarungen iiber Struktur und Aufbau des Himmels und der uberirdischen Korper steht noch in der Tradition des Aristoteles” (‘The text discusses meteors, comets and other celestial phenomena, as well as their impact on events on Earth. It references events from earlier eras, as well as observations made by Acronius and his contemporaries. Acronius believed that celestial phenomena were sent by God to demonstrate His greatness, provide signs to humanity, and foreshadow future calamities when necessary. His explanations of the structure and composition of the heavens and celestial bodies follow the Aristotelian tradition’) (M. Folkerts, Eine Verwechslung mit Folgen: Die Humanisten Acronius und Atrocianus, in: “Sudhoffs Archiv”, vol. 85.1, 2001, p. 59).VD16, A-135. COGAMANDOLUS, Theonestus. Secreta Secretorum. Calvino-Turcica Secreta, Eorundemque Apocalypsis. XCIV. Considerationibus Exposita, & futuro Principum Conventui exhibenda. In qua praecipue demonstratur, Calvinistas, Catholicis, Lutheranis, Suis Confoederatis Exitium Molitos. Auctore, Theonesto Cogmandolo […] Acta, & revisa in secretissima Cancellaria Anhaltina omnia, cum originalibus collata, & hac tertia editione aucta. Notulas addidit Nicolaus Herris Ab Isecera, Iprensis, Auctoris discipulus. N.pl., n.pr., 1621. 8vo. 94 [i. e. 88] pp. Collation: A-E8 F4.One of three editions printed in the same year. Theonestus Cogmandolus, or Cogamandolus, is a pseudonym that has been erroneously identified with Étienne Moquot (1570-1625). The identity Nicolaus Herris ab Isecera, or Herisbarisecera, is also a pseudonym that cannot be identified.This pamphlet is a Counter-Reformation and anti-Calvinist propaganda pamphlet, most likely published in Germany. The text fits into the tense climate preceding the Thirty Years’ War, aiming to demonize the Calvinist faction in the eyes of European rulers. A text with a similar title and subject matter had already been published in Antwerp in 1597, Calvino-turcismus, id est, calvinisticae perfidae, by the English theologian William Reynolds.The author accuses the Calvinist Church of having entered into a secret political and ideological alliance with the Ottoman Empire (the Turks), then considered the archenemy of Christianity. The work often circulated anonymously or, as in this case, under the pseudonym Theonesto Cogmandolo.VD17, 12:108122C. Six works in one volume (154x95 mm). 18th-century full marbled leather (worn at edges and rubbed), gilt spine with morocco lettering piece (“miscellanea”), red edges. Large restoration to the title page of the first work with loss of text, some leaves of the Basilius detached, worm track to the final four leaves slightly affecting the text, browned at places, some occasional staining.

title: Las Heroidas de Ovidio traducidas por un Mexicano

authors.name: Ovidius Publius Naso
authors.biography: Publius Ovidius Naso (43 BC – AD 17/18), known universally to the Western canon as Ovid, stands alongside Vergil and Horace as one of the three canonical triumvirs of Augustan Latin poetry. Emerging during the momentous transition from the chaotic twilight of the Roman Republic to the consolidated autocratic Pax Augusta under Octavian Caesar, Ovid represented a radically distinct literary sensibility. Unlike Vergil, whose epic national mythos solemnized the divine destiny of Rome, or Horace, who balanced Stoic-Epicurean philosophy with civic virtue, Ovid introduced an unprecedented elegance, psychological complexity, rhetorical brilliancy, and subtle subversion into Roman letters. As the last of the great Augustan love elegists, Ovid transformed the poetic landscape of antiquity by mastering hexameter, pentameter, and elegiac verse, laying the imaginative groundwork for medieval troubadour traditions, Renaissance humanism, Baroque iconography, and modern European literature.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationOvid was born on March 20, 43 BC—a fateful year marked by the deaths of the consuls Hirtius and Pansa at Mutina—in the ancient Paelignian town of Sulmo (modern-day Sulmona), situated in a fertile valley of the Apennines east of Rome. He belonged to an ancient and wealthy equestrian family (equester ordo), a social status that granted him economic independence and access to the highest echelons of Roman education. Alongside his elder brother, who possessed a natural aptitude for jurisprudence but died tragically at the age of twenty, Ovid was sent to Rome to be trained in the art of public speaking and rhetoric. Under the tutelage of the most distinguished rhetoricians of the era—notably Arellius Fuscus, who favored an ornate, highly emotional style, and Porcius Latro, renowned for his rigorous argument and analytical structure—Ovid excelled in declamation, particularly in the genre of suasoriae (persuasive speeches advising historical or mythical figures). The elder Seneca, who observed Ovid in the declamatory schools, recorded that the young poet found forensic argument tedious but delighted in exploring human psychology and ethical dilemmas in verse, displaying an innate inclination toward poetic cadence over legal prose.Following the customary educational grand tour of the Roman elite, Ovid traveled to Athens to study Greek philosophy and literature, visited the historic cities of Asia Minor, and resided for a prolonged period in Sicily alongside his friend, the poet Macer. Upon his return to Rome, Ovid briefly assumed minor judicial posts (tresviri capitales and decemviri stlitibus judicandis) as part of the vigintivirate, the preliminary steps toward a senatorial career (cursus honorum). However, driven by an unyielding poetic vocation and a temperament averse to political ambition, Ovid declined candidacy for the quaestorship, formally abandoning civic administrative life to devote himself entirely to the Muses—a decision that reflected the changing socio-political reality of Rome, where political power was increasingly centralized in the imperial household of Augustus.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksOvid's literary output spans several distinct phases, reflecting a profound evolution from youthful erotic subversion to encyclopedic myth-making and melancholic exilic lamentation. His earliest public success arrived with the Amores ('Loves'), a collection of elegiac poems initially published in five books around 16 BC and later revised into three books. Center-stage in these poems is the elusive figure of Corinna, a literary construct through which Ovid parodied the convention of the tormented elegiac lover popularized by Gallus, Propertius, and Tibullus. Rather than portraying love as a divine affliction or a moral duty, Ovid treated it as a sophisticated, theatrical game governed by wit, irony, and rhetorical bravura. This elegiac phase culminated in the revolutionary Heroides ('Heroines'), a series of fictional epistolary poems written from the perspective of legendary mythic women—such as Penelope, Dido, Ariadne, and Medea—to their absent or treacherous lovers. Through the Heroides, Ovid invented a new literary genre, granting voice and psychological nuance to female perspectives previously marginalized in traditional epic narratives.At the turn of the century, Ovid published his didactic erotic masterpieces: the Ars Amatoria ('The Art of Love'), a three-book manual prescribing technical instruction for men and women on the arts of seduction and flirtation, followed by the Remedia Amoris ('Cures for Love') and Medicamina Faciei Femineae ('Cosmetics for the Female Face'). By applying the solemn, instructional format of Hesiodic and Lucretian didactic poetry to the worldly, illicit realm of urban Roman romance, Ovid achieved a brilliant satire of Roman social norms. However, this playful provocation directly collided with the conservative moral campaign of Emperor Augustus, who had instituted the Lex Julia de adulteriis coercendis to enforce marital fidelity and aristocratic discipline.Between AD 2 and AD 8, Ovid composed his supreme masterpiece, the Metamorphoses ('Transformations'), a colossal narrative poem in fifteen books comprising nearly 12,000 dactylic hexameter lines. Positioned as a continuous song (carmen perpetuum), the Metamorphoses chronicles the history of the cosmos from its primordial creation out of chaos down to the deification of Julius Caesar and the reign of Augustus. Bound together by the central motif of physical transformation, the work weaves over 250 mythological tales into a fluid, highly sophisticated tapestry. Drawing deeply upon Alexandrian poetry (especially Callimachus and Nicander) as well as Hesiodic catalogues, Ovid integrated the Pythagorean philosophy of cosmic flux—the doctrine that all things change, but nothing truly perishes—into a grand narrative that challenged the static eternity claimed by Augustan imperial ideology. Simultaneously, Ovid worked on the Fasti, an ambitious elegiac calendar designed to detail the religious festivals, astronomical occurrences, and historical anniversaries of the Roman year. Although intended to span twelve books corresponding to the months, the project was cut short at six books (January to June) due to the poet's sudden banishment.Ovid's intellectual networks in Rome were vastly influential. He was an active member of the literary circle gathered around the distinguished general and patron Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus, which also nurtured Tibullus and Sulpicia. Ovid maintained close friendships with Horace, Propertius, Ponticus, and Bassus, and enjoyed widespread popularity among the Roman aristocracy. However, his distance from the primary imperial patronage network of Gaius Maecenas positioned him outside the official state-sanctioned propaganda apparatus, leaving his highly provocative works exposed to political scrutiny.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationThe manuscript tradition of Ovid's works survived the collapse of the Western Roman Empire through intensive copying in monastic scriptoria during the Carolingian Renaissance (often termed the Aetas Ovidiana during the 12th and 13th centuries). The textual transmission relied on several key codices, including the 9th-century Codex Parisinus Latinus 8242 (for the Metamorphoses) and the 11th-century Codex Neapolitanus (for the elegiac works). With the invention of movable type in the 15th century, Ovid's works became primary vectors for the spread of Classical Humanism across printed Europe.The editio princeps of Ovid's complete works was produced in Rome in 1471 by the pioneering German printers Conrad Sweynheym and Arnold Pannartz, edited by the humanist scholar Giovanni Andrea Bussi, Bishop of Aleria. Simultaneously, another landmark edition appeared in Venice in 1471 from the press of Balthasar Azoguidus in Bologna. These early incunabula were printed in elegant Roman typefaces designed to mimic humanistic book-hand scripts. The absolute typographical revolution for Ovid, however, occurred in 1502–1503, when the legendary Venetian printer Aldus Manutius issued his milestone three-volume octavo edition of Ovid, edited by the prominent humanist Andrea Navagero. Printed in the newly cut italic typeface designed by punchcutter Francesco Griffo, the Aldine Ovid democratized access to the text. The compact, portable octavo format allowed scholars, poets, and artists across Europe to carry Ovid's works effortlessly, transforming the poet into a ubiquitous cultural force.Throughout the 16th and 17th centuries, Ovid's Metamorphoses became one of the most illustrated books in printing history. Grand illustrated editions, such as those featuring woodcuts by Virgil Solis (Frankfurt, 1563) and copperplate engravings by Hendrik Goltzius (Antwerp, 1589) and Antonio Tempesta (Amsterdam, 1606), served as quintessential visual pattern-books for Renaissance and Baroque painters, sculptors, and craftsmen. In the 17th century, the Dutch philologist Daniel Heinsius and his son Niklaas Heinsius performed monumental textual criticism on Ovid's text, culminating in the authoritative Amsterdam editions printed by the Elzevir Press (1652, 1661), which established the modern critical apparatus for classical Latin scholarship.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyThe defining tragedy of Ovid's life occurred in AD 8, when Emperor Augustus abruptly issued an imperial edict banishing the fifty-one-year-old poet to Tomis (modern Constanța, Romania), a remote frontier garrison on the western shore of the Black Sea (Pontus Euxinus). The banishment took the form of relegatio rather than deportatio, meaning Ovid retained his property and citizenship, but was forcibly confined to a harsh, cold climate surrounded by non-Latin speaking Getae and Sarmatians. Ovid enigmatically identified the causes of his exile as carmen et error ('a poem and a mistake'). The carmen was universally acknowledged to be the Ars Amatoria, which offended Augustus's statutory moral reforms. The nature of the error remains one of the greatest mysteries of classical antiquity. Modern historical scholarship—championed by figures such as Sir Ronald Syme—suggests that Ovid may have been an unwitting witness to or accomplice in a court scandal involving Augustus's rebellious granddaughter, Julia the Younger, who was banished in the same year, or a dynastic conspiracy regarding the succession of Tiberius.In exile, Ovid produced a haunting body of elegiac poetry that transformed his literary persona: the five books of the Tristia ('Sorrows') and the four books of the Epistulae ex Ponto ('Letters from the Black Sea'), along with the invective poem Ibis. Abandoning the playful cynicism of his youth, these late works invented the genre of exilic literature, characterized by profound psychological isolation, elegiac appeals for imperial clemency, poignant descriptions of physical suffering, and meditation on the immortal power of poetry to transcend political tyranny. Despite his relentless petitions to Augustus and subsequently to Tiberius, Ovid was never recalled to Rome. He died at Tomis around AD 17 or 18, leaving behind an indelible mark on Western civilization.Ovid's legacy is immense. In the Middle Ages, despite Christian theological reservations regarding his erotic themes, works like the 14th-century French commentary Ovide moralisé re-interpreted his mythic transformations as allegories of Christian theology. During the Renaissance, Ovid served as the primary literary muse for Giovanni Boccaccio, Francesco Petrarca, Ludovico Ariosto, and William Shakespeare—whose Venus and Adonis, A Midsummer Night's Dream, and The Tempest are steeped in Ovidian lore. In modern classical scholarship, Ovid has been radically re-evaluated not merely as a master of superficial verbal charm, but as a sophisticated thinker who explored fluid identities, narrative instability, structural ambiguity, and resistance to imperial totalitarianism. His voice remains an enduring testament to human creative freedom over autocratic constraint.

academic_description: Two volumes, 8vo (150x96 mm). [4: title page and Advertencia], 229, [1 blank]; [2: title page], 221 [recte 219], [1 blank] pp. Pages 219/220 omitted in pagination. Contemporary or slighlty later calf, gilt spine with lettering piece, marbled endleaves (worn and rubbed). On the front pastedown bookplate of Jesús Guzmán y R.G. (“Ex libris JG RG Cave! ne cadas Mexici Nonis Junii a.D. MDCCCLXIX”) and his stamp on the title page verso (dated 14 June 1920). Some marginal tears, but a very good, clean copy.Extremely rare first and only edition of the Spanish translation by Anastasio María de Ochoa y Acuña of the Heroides (or Letters of Heroines), a collection of epistolary poems written by the Roman poet Ovid in Latin elegiac couplets and presented as though written by various aggrieved heroines from Greek and Roman mythology. Ochoa y Acuña was born in Huichapan, Hidalgo, in 1783. He studied at the College of San Ildefonso and at the Royal and Pontifical University. In 1813, he decided to join the clergy, studying at the Conciliar Seminary of Mexico, where he was ordained a priest in December 1816, at the age of 34. From 1817 to 1827, he served as a parish priest in Querétaro. From 1828 onwards, he devoted himself exclusively to literary work. He was a member of the Arcadia Mexicana and translated classical and modern works from Latin, French, and Italian. Much of his poetic work appeared in “El Diario de México”, but he also published two poetry collections, Poesías satíricas y morales (Mexico, 1812) and Poesias de un Mexicano, printed in 1828 both in Mexico City and New York. He favoured the festive genre and he is considered as the finest chronicler of the social life of his era, much like José Joaquín Fernández de Lizardi. Ochoa is credited with introducing nacionalismo pintoresco (‘picturesque nationalism’) into poetry. He died of cholera in Mexico City in 1833 (cf. A. Muñoz Fernández, Fichero bio-bibliografico de la literatura mexicana del siglo XIX, Mexico, 1995, vol. 2, s.v.).

title: Proef van Letteren, welke gegooten worden in de Nieuwe Haerlemsche Lettergietery van J. Enschedé

authors.name: Enschedé Johannes
authors.biography: Johannes Enschedé (1708–1780) stands as one of the most distinguished figures in the history of eighteenth-century European typography, print culture, and bibliophilia. As the principal architect of the Haarlem-based printing house and type foundry that would come to bear the name Joh. Enschedé en Zonen, he elevated a local civic printing enterprise into an international powerhouse of typographical innovation and historical preservation. Operating during the vibrant twilight of the Dutch Enlightenment, Enschedé bridged the monumental typographical heritage of the seventeenth-century Dutch Golden Age—dominated by master founders such as Christoffel van Dijck and the Elzevir press—with the refined, high-contrast aesthetics of the neoclassical era. His career reflected a rare dual mastery: he possessed an astute commercial acumen that secured financial permanence through newspaper publishing and government contracts, alongside an uncompromising artistic and scholarly devotion to the mechanics of letterforms, punchcutting, and incunabular history.Born in Haarlem on November 10, 1708, Johannes was the son of Izaak Enschedé (1681–1761) and Barentje Gesterkamp. Izaak Enschedé, a printer of Westphalian origin, had established a modest printing workshop in Haarlem in 1703, laying the initial foundations of the family business. Johannes was raised within the rigorous traditions of the Dutch printing guild, receiving an exhaustive education in the technical, manual, and administrative dimensions of the craft. Recognizing the young man's exceptional intelligence and typographical eye, Izaak took Johannes into official partnership in 1734. A decisive juncture in the firm's history occurred in 1737, when father and son acquired the rights to the Oprechte Haerlemse Courant, one of Europe’s most respected and widely circulated newspapers. The steady, highly lucrative revenue generated by the publication of this official journal provided Johannes Enschedé with the financial independence required to pursue ambitious, capital-intensive expansion in typefounding and book collection, turning Haarlem into a rival to the historic printing capitals of Amsterdam, Leiden, and Paris.Enschedé’s defining contribution to graphic arts history was his deliberate strategy to aggregate, preserve, and modernize Western Europe's typographical matrix stock. In 1743, he made a monumental acquisition by purchasing the complete type foundry of the Amsterdam publisher Rudolf Wetstein. This purchase brought into the Enschedé foundry an incredible archive of historic punches and matrices originating from sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Flemish and Dutch masters, including Hendrik van der Keere, François Guyot, Nicholas Briot, and Christoffel van Dijck. Enschedé did not merely archive these historic materials; he actively sought out the finest contemporary artisans to expand his foundry’s repertoire. Most notably, he entered into an extraordinary, decades-long collaboration with the German-born master punchcutter Joan Michael Fleischmann (1701–1768). Fleischmann’s sharp, sparkling, high-contrast transitional roman and italic types—distinguished by their delicate serifs, brilliant modeling, and precise counterpunches—became the signature aesthetic of the Enschedé foundry. Enschedé also commissioned types from the Flemish punchcutter Jacques-François Rosart (1714–1777), further cementing his enterprise as the preeminent source for cutting-edge typography across the Dutch Republic and Scandinavia.The culmination of Johannes Enschedé’s life work as a typefounder was realized in the publication of his celebrated 1768 specimen book, titled Proef van letteren, welke gegooten worden in de nywe lettergieterij van Joh. Enschedé te Haarlem. This monumental volume is widely regarded by modern bibliographers as one of the finest type specimens ever produced. Printed on luxurious paper with meticulous impression control, the specimen systematically showcased the vast range of the foundry's holdings, juxtaposing Fleischmann’s brilliant modern designs with historic Gothic, Civilité, Arabic, Greek, and Music types. Beyond his commercial work, Enschedé was an ardent bibliophile and an obsessive historian of the printed word. Deeply immersed in the contemporary scholarly debates regarding the invention of printing, Enschedé became a fervent champion of the Dutch nationalist claim that Laurens Janszoon Coster of Haarlem—rather than Johann Gutenberg of Mainz—was the true inventor of movable metal type. To substantiate this theory, Enschedé accumulated a vast private library containing rare incunabula, early Dutch blockbooks, and fragment sheets (the so-called Costeriana), turning his residence into a salon for international antiquarians, scholars, and bibliophiles.Johannes Enschedé died in Haarlem on August 21, 1780, leaving behind an unmatched typographical legacy and a flawlessly organized industrial enterprise. The business was seamlessly continued by his sons—Johannes Enschedé II (1750–1826), Jacobus Enschedé (1753–1826), and Abraham Enschedé (1760–1841)—under whose stewardship the firm evolved into Joh. Enschedé en Zonen. Over the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, the company achieved global fame as the official security printer for the Kingdom of the Netherlands, producing banknotes, postage stamps, and high-security state documents, while maintaining its historical foundry and typographical museum. Today, Johannes Enschedé is remembered not only as a visionary industrialist who defined the aesthetic tone of eighteenth-century Dutch printing, but also as an indispensable custodian of European typographical heritage whose preservation of historic matrices enabled modern typographical historians to reconstruct the evolution of Western letterforms.

academic_description: Large 8vo (212x127 mm). Ornamental frontispiece engraved by A. van der Laan after Taco Hajo Helgersma, title page with engraved vignette by A. van der Laan, engraved portrait of Johann Enschedé by C. van Noorde, 2 engravings of the statues of Lourens Janszoon Coster and Adrianus Junius, [32] pp. of introduction, engraved portrait of Johann Michael Fleischmann by C. van Noorde dated 1769, [74] leaves of specimens printed on recto only (includign the often missing ‘Canon Hebreeuwsch’), engraving of another statue of Coster by A. van der Laan after Jelgersma, [4] leaves of supplement with additional specimens printed on recto only (Oude Hollandse letteren zynkde eerstellingen der Boek-Drukkonst), 8 pp. (Lyst der Pryzen), engraved folding view by C. van Noorde of the interior of Enschedé’s typefoundry workshop, dated 1768. The preface is printed in Fleischmann’s cursive script. Title page and each page within a woodcut border. 19th-century half morocco, richly gilt spine, marbled pastedowns. On the front pastedown bookplate Andrzeja Awiuszewskiego, on the front flyleaf verso bookplate W. Kutkiewicz printed in red, and on the frontispiece later ownership entry. A very good copy. First edition of this beautiful type specimen sample book showcasing the designs of the type founder Johann Michael Fleischmann (1701-1768). Fleischmann worked for the Enschedé type foundry from 1743 onwards and created antique typefaces and Gothic letters. The former were of great importance in the development of printed typefaces, particularly the ‘Enschedé typeface’ he designed, which strongly influenced the development of printing types in England.“This is a very interesting and fine specimen-book of all the characters then in the Enschedé foundry. It contains finely-engraved copperplate portraits of the printer J. Enschedé; Junius, the propagator of the Koster legend; another of the celebrated type-cutter, Fleischman; and one of Koster, all being by C. van Noorde. It also gives the view of the two statues of Koster and Junius which Enschedé placed in his own garden, and which still remain there. At the end is a large view of the principal room of the foundry. The titles of the founts are given in Dutch, French, English, and German” (Bigmore & Wyman).The book includes specimens of music types, capital letters, exotic fonts (Greek, Arabian, Hebrew and Armenian), typographical ornaments and black-letter types of the fifteenth and sixteenth centuries. J.M. Fleischmann died just before the publication of the book, and his work and merits are described at length in the foreword by J. Enschedé.“Fleischman, a German, was employed by the Enschedes in the eighteenth century to cut types for their foundry, and his signature is found beneath many fonts shown in their specimen-books. In his hands their output was somewhat changed, though not much bettered. His types are singularly devoid of style, and usually show a drift toward the thinner, weaker typography which was coming in Holland as everywhere else. But Fleischman’s work was much the fashion in the eighteenth century, and it made such excellent fonts as Van Dyck’s appear hopelessly obsolete. In 1810, when Didot type was the mode, Van Dyck’s matrices and types were, without much thought, thrown into the meltingpot -a “gesture” no doubt regretted by later members of the Enschedé family. Various books and broadside specimens of types and ornaments were published by the Enschedés. One of the earliest books was the Epreuve des Caractècres, qui se fondent dans la Nouvelle Fonderie de Lettres d’Isaac et Jean Enschedé à Haarlem. Augmentée & perfectionée jusquà lìAn 1744. The preface alludes to the abilities of Rudolph Wetstein as a printer and type-founder, and mentions that the Enschedés bought his foundry in 1743; Wetstein having died the year before. The Greek types are mentioned with special pride; and the deep cutting of counters, and the solid way in which the types are constructed to escape wear, are emphasized. The roman and italic types shown are all old style. In 1768, the Enschedés published an elaborate specimen called Proef van Letteren, welke gegooten worden in de Nieuwe Haerlemsche Lettergietery van J. Enschedé, prefaced by a portrait of Enschedé and other engravings. An introduction, dated Haarlem, 1768, and signed by J. Enschedé, is printed in a very ugly cursive script letter -a fearful decline from the splendid cursive fonts in use a hundred and fifty years earlier. This is followed by a portrait of J.M. Fleischman, their type-cutter. Then begins a series of types -capital letters in roman and italic of a very Dutch and ugly cut, a series of shaded capital letters, and a great variety of faces of roman and italic types, in some of which the size of the body of lower-case letters is unduly large in proportion to the capitals. Many of the types that we come upon which look more “modern” (some of them being as we should now say “condensed”) were cut by Fleischman -whose name appears beneath them. He uniformly extracted all interest from his fonts, partly through lightening the cut, which gave monotony of colour, and partly by his large, round lower-case letters, made more rolling in effect by shortening the descenders in a very modern way. The smaller types are extremely dull in colour, though here and here we find fonts with a good deal of movement, cut by Van Dyck. Fleischmann’s black-letter is tortured and fanciful, and does not stand comparison with Van Dyck’s simpler and finer black-letter, still less with early Flemish gothic fonts. Fleischmann’s music, both in round notes and square, is also shown. The caractère de finance, an unattractive script, was cut by Rosart. Beyond these fadedlooking characters comes a page of fine old civilité. There is an interesting collection of Greek fonts, and the assortment of ligatured characters which supplement them should be examined. There are Arabic, Hebrew, Armenian, and other exotic types by various hands, and the specimen closes with ornaments which are mostly flat renderings of current English and French designs. Every page in the book is surrounded by type borders, many of them ingeniously contrived […] Two pages of splendid old Dutch black-letter fonts and a folding view of the Enschede foundry at Haarlem close a representative eighteenth century Dutch specimen” (Updike). Bound with: Verzeichnis der werthvollen Bibliothek des Königl. Hof-Kalligraphen u. akad. Künstlers Ernst Schütze. Manuscripte, Schreibebücher, Ornamentwerke, zu verkaufen durch J.A. Stargardt. Berlin, 1861. Pp. [4], 54, [2]. Enchedé’s work is listed here under no. 567.
