authors.name: Speckle Daniel
authors.biography: Daniel Speckle (frequently Latinized as Daniel Specklinus and rendered in French scholarship as Daniel Specklin; 1536 – August 15, 1589) stands as one of the most significant and innovative military architects, cartographers, and urban engineers of the Northern Renaissance. Operating at the crucial historical juncture where Italian Renaissance fortificatory theory intersected with the pragmatic defensive needs of Northern and Central European polities, Speckle transformed the science of permanent fortification. His practical work across the Holy Roman Empire and his monumental treatise, Architectura von Festungen (1589), laid the theoretical and geometric groundwork for the Old German Fortress School (Altdeutsche Befestigungskunst), directly influencing subsequent generations of military engineers, including Wilhelm Dilich, Matthias Dögen, and ultimately the defensive paradigms of Sébastien Le Prestre de Vauban and Menno van Coehoorn.Born in the Free Imperial City of Strasbourg in 1536, Speckle belonged to a family deeply embedded in the vibrant artistic and craft traditions of the Alsatian metropolis. His father, Veit Speckle (died 1555), was an acclaimed woodcutter (Formschneider) celebrated for executing the exquisite woodcuts designed by Albrecht Meyer and Heinrich Füllmaurer for Leonhart Fuchs’s landmark botanical treatise, De Historia Stirpium commentarii insignes (Basel: Michael Isengrin, 1542). Raised in an atmosphere of rigorous draughtsmanship and technical discipline, young Daniel was initially apprenticed as a silk embroiderer (Seidensticker) and punch-cutter. This formative artistic education endowed him with remarkable graphic precision, spatial visualization, and draftsmanship—skills that would later prove indispensable for both his cartographic surveys and his detailed architectural and engineering copperplates.Following the completion of his initial apprenticeship in the mid-1550s, Speckle embarked upon extensive Wanderjahre (journeyman travels) that lasted nearly a decade (c. 1555–1564) and fundamentally reshaped his career trajectory. Travelling through the Low Countries, Denmark, Sweden, Poland, Prussia, Austria, Hungary, and Italy, Speckle transitioned from decorative crafts to practical building engineering and military design. Crucially, during his time along the imperial frontier in Ottoman-threatened Hungary, Speckle observed and participated in field fortification works at Komárno (Komorn). There, he gained direct exposure to the devastating impact of heavy siege artillery and the practical shortcomings of medieval masonry walls. In Italy, Speckle studied the advanced bastioned trace (tracé italien) pioneeringly deployed by Michele Sanmicheli, Baldassarre Peruzzi, and Giovan Giacomo Paleari d'Allio. He absorbed the geometric principles of low-profile angular bastions, integrated casemates, and deep dry ditches, synthesizing Italian theoretical treatises with the practical demands of Northern European terrain and artillery warfare.Upon his return to Alsace in the mid-1560s, Speckle re-established himself in Strasbourg as a master craftsman, surveyor, and engraver. His talent as a cartographer achieved imperial renown with the publication in 1576 of his monumental map of Alsace, titled Alsatiae Superioris et Inferioris Nova Descriptio (commonly known as the Chorographia Elsassia). Printed from three large woodblocks that Speckle himself carved, this masterwork represented the most detailed, scientifically accurate, and visually stunning regional survey of Alsace produced in the sixteenth century. Dedicated to the estates of Upper and Lower Alsace, the map secured Speckle’s status as a preeminent technical authority across the Upper Rhine basin.Speckle’s growing reputation as an expert engineer led to widespread recruitment by princes and imperial cities throughout the Holy Roman Empire. In 1573, he was summoned to Vienna to advise on the modernization of the imperial capital’s fortifications, specifically contributing to the reconstruction of the Schottenbastei and surrounding bastioned fronts. Over the next decade, his consultancies spanned the length and breadth of Southern Germany and the Rhineland. He designed or renovated fortifications, arsenals, and municipal works for Duke Louis of Württemberg at Schorndorf and Stuttgart, Elector Palatine Johann Casimir at Heidelberg and Mannheim, the Margrave of Baden, the Duke of Bavaria at Ingolstadt and Lichtenberg, as well as the Free Imperial Cities of Ulm, Nuremberg, Regensburg, Amberg, and Frankfurt am Main. Speckle’s defensive architecture emphasized wide, straight curtains, spacious bastions with heavy flanks (Orillons), elevated cavaliers for long-range counter-battery fire, and sophisticated subterranean casemates ventilated to disperse gunpowder smoke.In October 1577, the City Council of Strasbourg appointed Speckle to the prestigious post of Stadtbaumeister (City Master Builder and Chief Engineer). In this capacity, Speckle assumed total responsibility for the civil architecture, hydraulic engineering, and military preparedness of one of the empire's most strategically vital Protestant bastions. During his twelve-year tenure as Stadtbaumeister, Speckle thoroughly overhauled Strasbourg’s medieval defenses, constructing modern earthwork ramparts, advanced ravelins, and water-filled ditches. Beyond fortifications, he engineered municipal grain stores, flour mills along the Ill River, public water conduits, and directed major structural renovations on the Frauenhaus (Maison de l'Œuvre Notre-Dame), leaving an indelible imprint on Strasbourg's urban landscape.The culmination of Speckle’s life work occurred in 1589 with the publication of his treatise, Architectura von Festungen (Architecture of Fortifications), printed at Strasbourg by the distinguished press of Bernhard Jobin. A magnificent folio volume lavishly illustrated with 36 double-page copperplate engravings designed and etched under Speckle’s direct supervision, the book was the first comprehensive fortification manual written in the German language. Divided into three exhaustive parts, the work provided systematic instruction on practical geometry, the design of regularity in fortresses, the construction of earthen versus stone ramparts, siege tactics, counter-mine networks, and urban layout within fortified enclosures. Speckle argued passionately for adapting fortresses to specific local topography rather than blindly applying rigid theoretical shapes, advocating for wide bastions capable of accommodating massive defensive artillery.Tragically, Daniel Speckle died in Strasbourg on August 15, 1589, just months after the initial printing of Architectura von Festungen. However, the posthumous influence of his publication was immense. The treatise went through numerous subsequent editions—notably those published in Strasbourg by Lazar Zetzner in 1599, 1608, and 1628, as well as later Dresden reissues in 1658—serving as the fundamental textbook for military officers and engineers across Protestant and Catholic Europe during the Thirty Years' War (1618–1648).In addition to his published architectural work, Speckle was an avid historian and chronicler. He compiled a massive manuscript chronicle of his native city, known as the Collectanea, which recorded Strasbourg’s political, social, architectural, and military history from ancient times up to 1589. Remaining in manuscript for centuries, the Collectanea was edited and published in the late nineteenth century by the historian Rodolphe Reuss, revealing Speckle to be not only an engineering genius but also a astute observer of sixteenth-century urban society and political culture. Today, Daniel Speckle is recognized as a quintessential Northern Renaissance polymath whose synthesis of geometry, art, cartography, and military science profoundly shaped the early modern European built environment.

academic_description: Folio. [8], 112, [i.e. 114: 1-66, (1), 66-112], [1: errata] leaves. Title printed in red and black within an engraved architectural border by Matthias Greuter, woodcut coat of arms of Julius Duke of Brunswig, 21 (20 double-page) engravings (sometimes appearing as two single leaves; one is also signed by Matthias Greuter), and numerous woodcut illustrations in the text. Contemporary limp vellum (a bit smutty), with later added supralibros and spine label, from the library of Walter Hawken Tregellas (1831-1894), an English writer of historical and biographical works and a professional draughtsman (with his presentation label on the pastdown), and from the Royal Engineers Library (gilt stamp on binding, and small ink stamp on title-page and on a few other places). Some very light browning and marginal dampstains, but a very nice genuine copy.Rare first edition of this magnificent work on fortification and town-planning, the first important contribution in the German-speaking world on the subject since Dürer's Etliche Underricht zur Befestigung der Stett (1527). It was to become the standard reference work on the construction of fortresses until there was a decisive change in the manner in which wars where fought. Further editions were published in 1599, 1608, 1705 and 1756.''Speckle writes his treatise from a strongly national motivation as is clear from his preface. He wishes to prove that the Germans are not completely without imagination, and that their invention of printing and of a 'grausam Geschütz' ('fearsome artillery') shows them to be the 'the greatest in the world' in these fields. He attacks, above all, the Italian theorists for their academic disputes, declaring their rules to be outmoded and openly ridiculing their approach ('when someone has no Latin, he cannot understand it, and so has no business to talk about it'). He demonstrates the urgency of fortification, as Dürer has done, by reference to the Turkish threat. Speckle claims to be familiar with fifty or sixty types of fortification, but restricts himself to a few only. He writes in German and avoids foreign words, 'so that every German - such as I too have the honour to call myself - can understand' '' (H.-W. Kruft, A History of Architectural Theory from Vitruvius to the Present, London & New York, 1994, p. 115).In addition to Dürer, whose work Speckle considered very important, he had adopted the work of Francesco de Marchi from Bologna, Della architettura militare, thus proving that he kept abreast of the latest trends. But he was no less a pragmatist, who in his teaching methods took into account whether a fortress was located in flat countryside, in hills or in mountainous terrain. Mathematics and geometry, in conjunction with practical skills and a knowledge of mechanical laws were also the art of building fortresses. Some of his retreats and mountain castles appear on the other hand as fantastic visions of a world that had rid itself of enemies. In a copy of the 1608 edition in the Strasbourg library these castles are labeled by hand and identified as based on reality. In the second part of the treatise Speckle presents plans whose forms are dictated by terrain. He describes inter alia, in great detail, the Turkish siege of Malta (1565) and the rebuilding of La Valetta, and in so doing provides us with one of the most detailed plans we have of Francesco Laparelli's project (cf. J. Zimmer, Daniel Speckle Architectura Von Vestungen, in: ''Architectural Theory from the Renaissance to the Present'', B. Evers & C. Thoenes, eds., Köln, 2003, pp. 511-519).The twenty-eighth chapter of the first part of the treatise contains the essence of Speckle's thinking on town planning. He starts with a description of a regular plan with six bastions, of which he gives a perspective view and which reveals the priority he accords to defensive considerations. He then describes in great detail an ideal type of town plan with eight bastions, in which his political and social ideas are revealed. In the tradition of all military architects of the second half of the sixteenth century, he uses a strict radial pattern. Around the central square are situated the church, royal palace, town hall and staple inn. Religious, secular and economic power are concentrated in this area. The military, on the other hand, are removed to the areas around the bastions. It is interesting that Speckle expressly sets civil law above martial law. Speckle aims overall at a very ordered community: 'mercenaries should be done away with'. Defensive considerations determine the city to the last detail (cf. K. Krüger, Albrecht Dürer, Daniel Speckle und die Anfänge frühmoderner Städteplanung in Deutschland, in: ''Mitteilungen des Vereins für deutsche Geschichte Nürnbergs'', 67, 1980, pp. 79-97; and H. de la Croix, Military Architecture and the Radial City Plan in Sixteenth Century Italy, in: ''The Art Bulletin'', 427/ 4, 1960, pp. 263-290).''Later in the sixteenth century, the instruments and surveying techniques essential to the preparation of ichnographic city plans were made available to an increasingly large circle of northern artists and topographers through a number of publications. One of the most interesting of these books is Daniel Speckle's treatise on fortifications, published in 1589. Speckle's method of surveying, which permitted a ground plan of 'any building, city or castle' to be drawn, is closely related to Hirschvogel's procedure. Unlike Hirschvogel's confusing description of his own invention, however, Speckle's chapter on surveying is a model of clarity and verbal economy. Speckle's straightforward and step-by-step exposition of surveying techniques parallels those of Tartaglia and Bartoli earlier in the century. It permitted any interested artist or architect to learn and apply them easily'' (J.A. Pinto, Origins and Development of the Ichnographic City Plan, in: ''Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians'', 35, 1, 1976, p. 49).In the Architectura are also described several instruments of his invention, especially his set of six reduction compasses (cf. I. Schneider, Der Proporzionalzirkel. Ein universelles Analogrecheninstrument der Vergangenheit, München, 1970, pp. 31-32).Daniel Speckle (Specklin), a native of Strasbourg, was the son of the eminent carver Veit Rudolph Speckle. After completing his apprenticeship as a silk embroiderer, he left Strasbourg in 1552 to go on a study tour, which took him to the fortress of Komorn and Györ in Hungary. By 1555 he was in Vienna, where he first trained as a master mason and later became an architect. The influence of the chief builder in Vienna, Hermes Schallautzer, could well have played a role in influencing Speckle's decision to concentrate in the future on the construction of fortresses. He soon achieved success in this field and was employed as head of constructions for various fortress projects. He visited Antwerp in 1560 and subsequently travelled to Denmark, Sweden, Poland, and Russia. In 1564 he returned to Strasbourg, married and worked again as a silk embroiderer. Having been involved with the construction of fortifications in Düsseldorf and Regensburg in 1567, he was once again in Hungary, this time with his patron, the Imperial general Lazarus von Schwendi, where he was instrumental in the planning of fortifications in VaraÅ¾din, Kashau, and Tokai. During this time he must also have acquired a reputation as a mapmaker, since as a result of Schwendi's connections he was commissioned in 1573 by Archduke Ferdinand to produce a map of Alsace, which he worked on until 1576. He also was engaged in producing an overall plan for fortifying the city of Ulm. To this end he drew up extensive plans and models, as well as a builder's journal, the first of its kind. There followed a journal for Colmar (1579) and a building code for Basle (1589). By now he had also produced elaborate pieces of work for the city of Strasbourg, including a large-scale wooden model of the city. On October 5, 1577 Speckle was appointed City Architect with an annual salary of 250 Guilders, 6 tuns of wine and 1000 bundles of wood. With the authorization of the city council he continued to work for other domains and towns, such as Schlettstadt, Ensisheim, Colmar, Basle, Veldens, Belfort, Cologne, Heidelberg, and Hanau. After being sent on a study trip to Antwerp, he brought back several plans of the fortifications of towns in Brabant and Holland. In September 1587 he submitted his Architectura to the council of Strasbourg. Finally, the city of Heilbronn requested his advice and later sent him the ground plans of a planned fortress for his appraisal, but he was not able to air his opinions on it, as he died on October 18, 1589, aged 53 (cf. K.E. Mayer, Die Lebensgeschichte des Strassburger Stadt- und Festungsbaumeisters Daniel Specklin, Stuttgart, 1928, passim; and A. Fischer, Daniel Specklin aus Strassburg, 1539-1589: Festungsbaumeister, Ingenieur und Kartograph, Sigmaringen, 1996, passim).

authors.name: Aesopus
authors.biography: Aesopus (c. 620–560 BC), known universally in the Western tradition as Aesop, stands as the paramount foundational figure of classical Graeco-Roman fable narrative (ainoi, mythoi) and a seminal icon in the history of European popular ethics. Operating at the cultural threshold where Archaic Greek oral tradition transitioned into written literacy, Aesop represents a crucial counter-weight to the aristocratic, heroic epic tradition of Homer and Hesiod. While the Homeric ethos reflected the aristocratic values (arete) of the warrior elite, the Aesopic corpus articulated the pragmatic wisdom, subversion, and existential caution of the subjugated classes, the disenfranchised, and the unprivileged. Aesop's historical existence, situated firmly within the sixth century BC during the era of the Seven Sages of Greece, has been the subject of profound philological inquiry from antiquity through the modern era. Whether understood as a concrete historical individual or as an idealized, accretive folk-hero persona around whom an expansive corpus of animal apologues coalesced, Aesop embodies the democratization of moral philosophy, transforming the simple animal fable into an enduring instrument of socio-political critique, rhetorical argument, and pedagogical instruction across human history.The biographical traditions regarding Aesop's early life, lineage, and geographic origins are preserved in a complex matrix of classical histories, ancient biographical lexicons (such as the Suda), and the Hellenistic biographical narrative known as the Vita Aesopi (The Aesop Romance). Ancient accounts fluctuate wildly regarding his birthplace, attributing his origins variously to Thrace (specifically Selymbria), Phrygia (Cotyaeum), Lydia (Sardis), the island of Samos, or Ethiopia. The etymological association between the name Aisopos and the Greek word for Ethiopian (Aithiops) prompted ancient commentators and modern scholars—such as Leslie Kurke and Frank Snowden—to explore the textual representation of Aesop as an 'outsider' or ethnic subaltern within the Aegean world. What remains consistent across all biographical streams is his initial status as an enslaved person. Aesop was owned first by a Samian named Demarchus or Xanthus—the latter depicted in the Vita Aesopi as a pomposity-prone itinerant philosopher repeatedly outwitted by his slave—and subsequently by Iadmon of Samos. Through his extraordinary sharpness of wit, keen observational intelligence, and mastery of persuasive allegorical narrative, Aesop secured his enfranchisement from Iadmon. Following his manumission, Aesop's reputation as a counsel and diplomat elevated him to the international stage: he was invited to the court of King Croesus of Lydia in Sardis, where he reportedly interacted with eminent statesmen including Solon of Athens, Thales of Miletus, and Chilon of Sparta, as recorded in Plutarch’s Banquet of the Seven Sages (Septem Sapientium Convivium).The tragic climax of Aesop’s life occurred during a diplomatic or religious mission to Delphi, undertaken on behalf of King Croesus to distribute financial offerings to the shrine of Apollo. According to classical accounts—most notably detailed by Herodotus in his Histories (Book II, 134–135)—a bitter dispute arose between Aesop and the inhabitants of Delphi concerning the allocation of the royal funds. Aesop, disgusted by the Delphians' greed and hypocrisy, refused to distribute the money and sent it back to Sardis. In retaliation, the Delphians framed Aesop by concealing a sacred gold cup from Apollo's temple within his luggage. Accused of sacrilege (hierosylia), Aesop was condemned to death. Despite defending himself through a series of brilliant, cautionary fables warning his executioners against moral blindness, he was cast off the Phaedriades cliffs to his death. Herodotus records that following this unjust execution, Delphi was struck by a severe plague and divine retribution. To expiate their guilt, the Delphians proclaimed a public notice offering compensation to anyone who could claim satisfaction for Aesop's murder; the restitution was eventually claimed by Iadmon’s grandson, also named Iadmon, thereby historically corroborating Aesop's servitude under the Samian family.Literarily and structurally, the Aesopic fable represents a distinct genre characterized by brevity, dramatic economy, anthropomorphic representation, and an explicit or implicit ethical lesson (epimythion). The dramatis personae of the Aesopic corpus consist predominantly of animals—the cunning Fox, the tyrannical Lion, the rapacious Wolf, the innocent Lamb, the plodding Tortoise, and the vain Raven—who act as psychomorphic proxies for human types, power relations, and social hierarchies. Through these allegorical interactions, the fables analyze the ruthless mechanics of power (as in The Lion's Share or The Wolf and the Lamb), the dangers of hubris, the virtue of pragmatic adaptability, and the necessity of self-knowledge. The structural composition typically follows a triadic scheme: an initial narrative premise establishing a conflict or imbalance, a dramatic confrontation or dialogue (agon), and a decisive resolution that lays bare a universal moral reality. During the fifth and fourth centuries BC, Aesopic fables were integrated into Athenian public discourse, drama, and philosophy. Aristophanes frequently cited Aesop in his comedies—such as The Wasps (Vespae), The Birds (Aves), and Peace (Pax)—as a marker of popular, street-smart Athenian culture. Aristotle, in his Rhetoric (Book II.20), classified the Aesopic fable as a potent form of rhetorical proof (paradeigma), citing Aesop’s public defense of a Samian politician through the fable of the fox and the hedgehog. Most famously, Plato records in the Phaedo (60c–61b) that Socrates spent his final days in his prison cell versifying the fables of Aesop, recognizing in Aesop’s popular allegories a parallel to his own philosophical mission of moral awakening.The textual transmission and publishing history of the Aesopic corpus reflect one of the most complex, multi-layered editorial evolutions in Western book history. Aesop himself left no written manuscripts; his fables circulated orally until Demetrius of Phalerum (c. 350–280 BC), the statesman and founder of the Alexandrian intellectual project, compiled the first written collection of Aesopic tales (*Synagoge aesopeia*) at the Library of Alexandria, a work now lost. During the Early Roman Empire, the corpus was transformed into verse by two master poets: Phaedrus (c. 15 BC–c. AD 50), a freedman of Emperor Augustus, who rendered the fables into Latin iambic senarii, infusing them with sharp political critiques of Tiberian authoritarianism; and Babrius (2nd century AD), who composed Greek choliambic verse versions. In Late Antiquity and the Byzantine era, prose recensions multiplied, most notably the Latin collection attributed to Romulus, the metrical distichs of Avianus (5th century AD), and the monumental 13th-century Byzantine compilation prepared by the scholar monk Maximus Planudes (c. 1260–1305), whose *Vita et Fabulae Aesopi* became the primary textual vector for the revival of Greek fable literature in Renaissance Europe.With the invention of movable type printing in the fifteenth century, the Aesopic corpus experienced an unprecedented typographical explosion. The editio princeps of the Greek text of Aesop was published in Milan around 1479–1480 by the Italian humanist editor Bonus Accursius (Buono Accorsi), printed by Antonius Zarotus. However, the most influential early printed book in the entire Aesopic history was the monumental incunabulum produced by the physician and translator Heinrich Steinhöwel, printed in Ulm by Johann Zainer around 1476–1477. Steinhöwel’s Esopus presented a bilingual Latin and German text accompanied by over 190 magnificent, expressively carved woodcut illustrations. This Ulm incunabulum established the visual and textual archetype for Renaissance readers and was rapidly copied, translated, and reprinted across Europe: in England by William Caxton (Westminster, 1484), in France by Julien Macho (Lyons, 1480), and in Nuremberg by Anton Koberger. In 1505, the celebrated Venetian typographical master Aldus Manutius published a seminal Greek edition of Aesop at the Aldine Press (*Vita & Fabellae Aesopi*), incorporating Greek fables alongside works by Gabrias, Aphthonius, and Philostratus, printed in Aldus’s exquisite Greek typefaces. In the seventeenth century, the Aesopic lineage reached its stylistic zenith in early modern literature through the masterwork of Jean de La Fontaine (Fables Choisies, Mises en Vers, Paris, 1668), who transformed the sparse Aesopic prose narratives into sparkling, sophisticated French poetic verse.In modern critical scholarship and philology, Aesop has been the subject of intensive historical-critical scrutiny and structural classification. The landmark Enlightenment study by the English classical scholar Richard Bentley—his Dissertation Upon the Fables of Aesop (1699)—decisively demonstrated that the late prose collections attributed to Aesop and the accompanying Planudean *Life of Aesop* were Hellenistic and Byzantine compilations rather than authentic sixth-century BC writings. In the twentieth century, the field was revolutionized by the monumental work of Ben Edwin Perry, whose monumental Aesopica (University of Illinois Press, 1952) established the authoritative Perry Index, cataloging and cross-referencing 725 Aesopic fable types from Greek and Latin textual traditions. Subsequent structuralist and socio-historical studies by Francisco Rodríguez Adrados (History of the Graeco-Latin Fable, 3 volumes) and Niklas Holzberg (Die antike Fabel) have highlighted the ideological complexity of the Aesopic tradition, framing it as an essential forum for ancient socio-political dialogue. Today, Aesop stands not merely as an ancient chronicler of folklore, but as a central pillar of world literature whose allegorical genius continues to form the bedrock of ethical discourse, literary education, and rhetorical commentary throughout global civilization.

academic_description: 16mo (122x70 mm). 375, [9] pp. Collation: a-z8 A8. Greek portion of title romanized. Greek and Latin text in parallel columns from p. 3 to p. 279, on opposite pages from p. 280 to p. 375. Woodcut printer’s device on title page and prism device to verso of otherwise blank final leaf. With 40 woodcut illustrations in text illustrating the fables of Aesopus, of which 37 are ascribed to Bernard Salomon and 3 (fables 46, 100, 118) are repeated from Tournes edition of La Perrière’s Theatre des bons engines (1545). Woodcut head- and tail-pieces and decorative initials. Early 17th-century blind-stamped panelled calf, spine in compartments, covers with fleur-de-lys centre-pieces, central panel with floral corner-pieces, blue (faded) edges (joints, spine ends, and corners partly skillfully restored). Later ink underlining and occasional marginalia in Greek and Latin (the latter mostly at end, including more extensive notes around prism device). Small restoration to lower margin of title, some occasional spotting and marginal staining, slightly browned, all in all a very good, genuine copy, nicely bound and with a strong impression of the woodcuts. First de Tournes edition in Greek and Latin, edited by Adam Knopff (cf. Typographus Lectori, p. [382]), of Aesop’s fables. A second edition, with sixty-one woodcuts and the addition of the fables of Avianus, was issued by De Tournes in 1570 (cf. R. Brun, Le livre français illustré de la Renaissance, Paris, 1969, pp. 77-81 and 184).The volume also includes the Aesopi fabulatoris vita (pp. 7-118) by Maximus Planudes (c. 1260-1330), the fables (Fabellae) by Babrius or Gabrias (2nd cent.), the Batrachomiomachia by Homerus (8th cent. BC), and the Galeomyomachia by Theodorus Prodromus (12th cent.).

title: Saggio filosofico e critico sulli giuochi di azzardo
academic_description: 8vo (205x 127 mm). VIII, 232, [4] pp. The first leaf, a blank, is included in the pagination. The name of the printer can be found in the printing license at the end of the volume. Typographic ornament on the title page. Decorative head- and tailpieces. Contemporary half calf, gilt spine with lettering piece, marbled boards, sprinkled edges (some minor restoration to spine and corners). On the title page manuscript initials “N.C.”. Contemporary manuscript note at p. 39. Some scattered foxing due to the quality of the paper, all in all a good, genuine copy. Rare first edition, dedicated by the author to John Acton (1736-1811), commander of the navy of the Kingdom of Naples, of this work dealing with gambling from every possible angle: mathematical, statistical, ethical, economical, legal, psychological, and social.In 1790, at the age of twenty-five, Francesco Bernardino Cicala published in Naples the Saggio filosofico e critico sulli giuochi di azzardo, echoing in its title another work on the same subject by P.R. Montmort (Essai d’analyses sure les jeux de hazard, Paris, 1708). The treatise is not a mere examination of mathematical operations, but a series of insights on gambling interpreted in the context of human action and from a historical perspective. The author does not hide his personal involvement, having personally known the gambling tables. His personal experience acquires, however, through introspective analyses a public dimension. Indeed, the self-inquiry broadens to include groups, social classes and the entire nation. Gambling is investigated not only as an individual issue, but also in its collective dimension. The spreading of gambling is seen as a political problem to be dealt with through the critical lenses of the rationalist culture of the Enlightenment.The Saggio consists of two sections, each comprising eight chapters: Human Sensibility, The Passion for the Game, Moral Effects, Consequences, Vicious Habits, Address to the Beautiful Sex, Time, its Use and Abuse, Physical Effects, Origins, Subject of Disputes, Matter of Calculation, Political Aims, Theory of Justice, Legislation, Law of Proscription, Linguet on Examination.In addition to the usual classical and Christian authors, quotations from French, German and English thinkers are particularly numerous in the work: J. De la Bruyère, F. de la Rochefoucauld, H. Grotius, Cl.-A. Helvetius, S. Pufendorf, Ch.-L. Montesquieu, D. Diderot, F.-M. Voltaire, J.J. Rousseau, P.L. Maupertuis, É. Condillac, J. Locke, and W. Balckstone. Significant are also the references to Italian Enlightenment philosophers like A. Genovesi, G. Filangieri and C. Beccaria, remembered for his article on gambling published in the journal “Il Caffè”.In describing the physical effects of gambling, Cicala achieves a remarkable effectiveness by using with confidence his medical knowledge of the functioning of the human organism. Ethical-philosophical reflections, on the other hand, intersect with mathematical theories and the calculus of probability. Cicala is well aware of the latest scientific-mathematical achievements in this field, and quotes Montmort, Bernoulli and Moivre.Cicala also does not forget the role of women in gambling, providing an in-depth analysis of individual male and female behaviors. For Cicala gambling concerns both sexes, but he feels the need to directly addresses the female audience traditionally excluded from the debate of ideas. Concluding his analysis, Cicala also assesses the positive and recreational aspects of gambling if practiced in moderation, considering gambling as permissible when it creates healthy conditions of recreation and sociability that are positive both for the individual and the community (cf. E. Filieri, Francesco Bernardino Cicala 1765-1815, tra passione e ragione: il gioco d’azzardo nella pubblica armonia, in: “Il Canone e la Biblioteca, costruzioni e decostruzioni della tradizione letteraria italiana”, A. Quondam, ed., Rome, 2002, II, pp. 353-360).When he wrote the present work, Cicala was a young man of 25, living in Naples at a time when gambling was a defining moment in society life. He had been for years very sensitive to both social gatherings and the passion for gambling. When he wrote the essay he had long avoided the now hated gambling tables: for him they had become only places to stay away from, because they evoked in him atmospheres and memories of a pathology that were still too vivid in his memory. It is precisely this pathology and the states of mind associated with it that Cicala analyzes in detail, with a particular attention to the interpersonal and social fallout of the gambler’s behaviors. Cicala is at the same time a man of his time and a forerunner of a knowledge that was not yet widespread scientific patrimony at his time. His interpretation of the compulsion for gambling is no more in moralistic terms, but rather in the broader framework of ethics, medicine and psychic introspection. He goes beyond his time by separating the cultural and social dimension of gambling from the individual dimension of the gambler (F.B. Cicala, Il gioco d’azzardo. Saggio filosofico e critico sulli giuochi di azzardo, G. Corrivetti & M.R. Pelizzari, eds., Cava de’ Tirreni, 2006, pp. 11-18).Francesco Bernardino Cicala, born in Lecce in 1765, began writing at a very young age. At 20 he had already composed two tragedies, Marcantonio in Egitto (which remained unpublished) and Gli Arsacidi, which was successfully performed in Naples, replicated in various Italian cities and first published in 1789. His tragedies also include Merope, La dinastia degli Eraclidi, Meride, Erode (remained unpublished), and Ermione, first performed in 1797 and published in 1798. Admitted, at only 22, to the Academy of Arcadia under the name Melindo Alitreo, at 27 he was accepted into the Royal Academy of Sciences and Fine Letters in Naples. He was also a member of the Accademia del Buon Gusto in Palermo and the Accademia dei Pastori Ereini-Imerei. Most of his poems and tragedies were published in the two volumes of the Opere (Lecce, 1814). In 1799 Cicala joined the Republic of Naples. When the Bourbons returned, he was imprisoned for two years, then forced to flee outside the kingdom. Returning home with the arrival of the Napoleonids, he settled in Lecce, where he died in 1815.

authors.name: Antiquari Jacopo
authors.biography: Jacopo was probably the son of the physician Stefano Antiquari. After studying under Giovanni Antonio Campano, who taught at Perugia from 1452 to 1459, he entered the service of the papal governor of that city, Giovanni Battista Savello, and accompanied him to Bologna when he was transferred there in 1468. In the early 1470s he moved to Milan, possibly on the invitation of Bartolomeo Caldo, secretary to duke Galeazzo Maria Sforza. Antiquari served as secretary to the dukes, with supervision over appointments to ecclesiastical benefices. He chose to remain at Milan even after the French removed Lodovico (il Moro) Sforza in 1500. Antiquari was a protector, adviser, and confidant of the greatest literary figures of his day, most notably Angelo Poliziano. He is mentioned in Erasmus’ Ciceronianus as one of the many writers who could not meet the exacting standards of the Ciceronians.

authors.name: Morata Olympia Fulvia
authors.biography: Olympia Fulvia Morata (1526–1555) stands as one of the most formidable intellectual figures of the sixteenth-century European Republic of Letters. A prodigy of Italian humanism, a pioneer of female classical scholarship, and an uncompromising voice of the Protestant Reformation, Morata embodied the dramatic convergence of Renaissance philology and transalpine evangelical theology. Operating at the intersection of the Ferrarese court of the Este dynasty and the radical printing houses of Basel and the Palatinate, her brief life captured both the zenith of Italian Renaissance learning and the tragic violence of early modern religious upheaval. Her surviving writings—comprising Latin and Greek dialogues, Greek psalm paraphrases, humanist declamations, and an expansive epistolary network spanning Europe—attest to an extraordinary intellectual synthesis that bridged classical antiquity, courtly humanism, and radical Reformation soteriology.Born in Ferrara in 1526, Olympia was raised in an environment saturated with humanistic rigor and political significance. She was the daughter of Fulvio Pellegrino Morato (Fulvius Peregrinus Moratus), a distinguished scholar of grammar, rhetoric, and classical literature who served as tutor to the young princes of the Este court, including Alfonso and Ercole d'Este. Pellegrino Morato was deeply embedded in the intellectual networks of Northern Italy, maintaining active correspondence with eminent humanists such as Celio Secondo Curione and Bembo. From her earliest childhood, Olympia demonstrated an extraordinary aptitude for classical philology. Her father personally directed her foundational studies in Latin grammar and syntax, instilling in her a deep devotion to Ciceronian rhetoric and classical poetry. The intellectual milieu of Ferrara during the 1530s was uniquely positioned to foster such precocity; under Duke Ercole II d'Este and his wife, Renée of France (Renata di Francia), the court of Ferrara became a vibrant nexus for intellectual experimentation and international diplomacy.In 1539, at approximately thirteen years of age, Morata's remarkable intellectual gifts earned her an invitation to enter the ducal court of Ferrara. She was appointed as the formal academic companion and tutor to the young Anna d'Este, the eldest daughter of Duke Ercole II and Renée of France (who would later marry François de Guise and subsequently Jacques de Savoie, Duke of Nemours). At court, Morata was afforded unprecedented access to the highest echelons of classical scholarship. Her education was placed under the supervision of the renowned German humanist brothers Johannes Sinapius (Johann Senf) and Kilian Sinapius (Chilianus Sinapius), who had been recruited to Ferrara to lecture on Greek language and medicine. Under their tutelage, alongside continued guidance from Celio Secondo Curione, Morata achieved absolute fluency in ancient Greek and Latin. By her mid-teens, she was delivering formal Latin lectures on Cicero’s Paradoxa Stoicorum, composing original Greek epigrams, and translating portions of Homer’s Iliad into Latin prose. Contemporary observers, including foreign ambassadors and visiting scholars, marveled at her capacity to debate complex philosophical problems in refined classical Latin, earning her recognition as a true virago literata and docta puella.The court of Renée of France was not merely a sanctuary for classical philology, but also the epicenter of evangelical dissent in Counter-Reformation Italy. Duchess Renée, the daughter of King Louis XII of France, maintained strong sympathies for the Reformation and transformed her Ferrarese household into an asylum for exiled French and Italian evangelicals. In 1536, John Calvin visited Ferrara under the pseudonym Charles d'Espeville, leaving an indelible imprint on the duchess's courtly circle, which also included the French poet Clément Marot and the reformer Bernardino Ochino. Morata’s exposure to this environment precipitated a profound internal spiritual metamorphosis. While her early youth had been dominated by the aesthetic and rhetorical ideals of classical pagan antiquity, her engagement with the writings of Martin Luther, Philip Melanchthon, and Calvin redirected her scholarly energies toward biblical exegesis and soteriology. Morata increasingly came to regard classical erudition not as an end in itself, but as a philological instrument to be consecrated to the understanding of Sacred Scripture and the defense of the doctrine of justification by faith alone (sola fide).This period of intellectual and spiritual maturity was soon disrupted by political and personal crises. In 1548, her father Fulvio Pellegrino Morato passed away. Concurrently, political pressure from the Roman Papacy and the Holy Office of the Inquisition intensified upon Duke Ercole II d'Este to purge his court of heresy. As Ercole II moved to suppress evangelical conventicles and curtail his wife’s Protestant network, Morata was compelled to leave the ducal court to care for her ailing mother, Lucrezia, and her younger siblings. Deprived of courtly patronage and facing growing suspicion from local inquisitorial authorities, her situation in Ferrara became increasingly precarious. However, during this period of distress, she met Andreas Grundler (Andreas Grundlerus), a young German physician, classicist, and committed Protestant from Schweinfurt in Franconia, who had come to the University of Ferrara to complete his medical doctorate. The two shared an intense intellectual and religious affinity and were married in late 1549 or early 1550.Fearing active persecution by the Inquisition in Northern Italy, Morata and Grundler resolved to flee across the Alps to the Holy Roman Empire in the summer of 1550, accompanied by Olympia's eight-year-old brother, Emilio Morato. Their journey into exile marked the beginning of a perilous transalpine odyssey. Upon arriving in Southern Germany, the couple sought refuge in Augsburg, where Morata’s reputation as a scholar preceded her. She was warmly received by prominent patricians and patrons of learning, including Johann Jakob Fugger and Antonius Fugger, as well as the humanist Bishop of Augsburg, Urbanus Rhegius's associates. Through these contacts, Grundler was offered a post as municipal physician in his hometown of Schweinfurt, an Imperial Free City in Franconia. Settling in Schweinfurt in late 1550, Morata devoted herself to intense study, translating the Psalms into elegant Greek verse, composing theological dialogues, and maintaining a vast epistolary network with leading figures of the Protestant Reformation, including Matthias Flacius Illyricus, Hieronymus Wolf, Hubert Languet, and her lifelong mentor Celio Secondo Curione, who was by then established in Basel.The violent realities of early modern European warfare shattered this brief period of academic tranquility. In 1553, the Imperial Free City of Schweinfurt became embroiled in the catastrophe of the Second Margrave War (Markgrafenkrieg). The mercenary armies of Albert Alcibiades, Margrave of Brandenburg-Kulmbach, occupied Schweinfurt and converted it into a military stronghold. Subsequently, the city was subjected to a brutal fourteen-month siege by the combined forces of the Bishop of Würzburg, the Duke of Brunswick, and the Elector of Saxony. Schweinfurt was subjected to continuous artillery bombardment, starvation, and a rampant outbreak of pestilence. Morata and her family were forced to live for months in underground cellars to escape the shellfire, during which time Grundler contracted severe epidemic fever. In June 1554, the besieging forces breached the city walls, plundered Schweinfurt, and set fire to the municipality. Morata and her husband escaped the burning city on foot, barefoot and destitute, having lost all their personal possessions, money, and—most devastatingly for Morata—her entire personal library and manuscript collection.Following their traumatic flight across Franconia, during which Grundler was briefly seized and held for ransom by rogue soldiers, the refugees found sanctuary in the territory of Count Erbach, who provided them with clothing, shelter, and medical care. News of their plight rapidly spread through the German scholarly community. Through the intervention of influential patrons and the recommendation of the Protestant Elector Palatine Frederick II (and subsequently Elector Otto Henry, or Ottheinrich), Grundler was appointed Professor of Medicine at the University of Heidelberg in late 1554. Recognizing Morata's phenomenal erudition, the university authorities and imperial administrators took the extraordinary step of offering her a formal academic appointment to deliver public lectures in Greek literature—a proposal almost unprecedented for a woman in sixteenth-century Europe. However, Morata’s physical constitution had been permanently shattered by the horrors of the siege of Schweinfurt and the subsequent flight. Suffering from severe pulmonary consumption (tuberculosis), she was unable to assume full lecturing duties, focusing instead on reconstructing her lost literary corpus from memory and draft letters.Olympia Fulvia Morata died in Heidelberg on October 26, 1555, at the age of twenty-nine. Her husband, Andreas Grundler, and her young brother, Emilio, succumbed to the plague only weeks later, in November 1555, and were buried beside her in the Church of St. Peter (Sankt Peter) in Heidelberg, where her funerary monument remains to this day. Prior to her death, aware of her impending end, Morata entrusted her remaining papers, dictate fragments, and reconstructed letters to her faithful friend and correspondent in Basel, Celio Secondo Curione, entreating him to collect and publish her literary legacy.Curione orchestrated a magnificent editorial crusade to immortalize Morata's life and intellectual achievements. Enlisting the printing press of Pietro Perna in Basel—the premier publishing house for Italian Protestant émigrés—Curione edited and released the first edition of her collected works in 1558 under the title Olympiae Fulviae Moratae Mulieris omnium eruditissimae Latina et Graeca, quae haberi potuerunt, Scripta. This monumental edition included her Latin and Greek dialogues, her Greek translation of the Psalms, her philosophical essays, her funeral orations, and her extensive correspondence with contemporary European intellectuals. The volume was dedicated to Queen Elizabeth I of England, framing Morata as an exemplar of Protestant female piety and supreme humanist learning. Perna’s press issued subsequent expanded and corrected editions in 1562, 1570, and 1580, ensuring the wide distribution of her writings throughout Transalpine Europe, England, and the Low Countries.The historical and critical significance of Olympia Fulvia Morata resides in her unique dual identity as a master of Renaissance classical philology and an articulate theologian of the Transalpine Reformation. In the history of women's writing, she represents a crucial transitional figure between the Quattrocento tradition of Italian female courtly humanists (such as Isotta Nogarola, Laura Cereta, and Cassandra Fedele) and the mid-sixteenth-century confessional polemicists of Protestant Europe. Her correspondence provides invaluable historiographical insight into the transalpine networks of refugee scholars, the internal political dynamics of the Ferrarese court, the reception of classical texts among early modern women, and the devastating human cost of the German wars of religion. Celebrated by her contemporaries as the "fourth Grace" and the "tenth Muse," Morata remains a titan of early modern intellectual history, whose erudition and tragic destiny continue to illuminate the complex intersections of gender, humanism, and religious reform in sixteenth-century Europe.

academic_description: 8vo. [16], 278 pp., [1: errata] leaf. *8, A-R8, S4. With Morata's epitaph by Johannes Herold within a full-page woodcut border. 18th century calf with gilt fillets and floreal ornaments on the panels, gilt back and edges, marbled endpapers. With the book-plates of the French linguist and book-collector Pierre-Alexandre Gratet-Duplessis (1792-1853) and of the architect Jules-Édouard Potier de la Morandière (1813-1905).Second, greatly enlarged edition, published by the Italian emigrant scholar Celio Secondo Curione (1503-1569) with a new dedication to Queen Elizabeth of England, dated Basel, September 1, 1562.The first edition was published in 1558 and contained thirty letters by and to Morata as well as some letters by others. In the present edition the number of letters was raised to 74, of which 50 were by Morata, 14 to her and 10 by others. In the third edition (1570), which was reprinted in 1580, two Italian letters by Morata were added.The volume contains furthermore a declamation on Cicero's Stoic Paradoxes and another In Praise of Mutius Scaevola (the latter in both Greek and Latin), a Latin translation of the first two stories of Boccaccio's Decameron,two dialogues in Latin, eleven poems (eight in Greek and three in Latin), and the translation into Greek of seven Psalms, as well as several poems in Greek and Latin in her praise and some epitaphs (cf. O.F. Morata, Briefe, R. Kössling, ed., Leipzig, 1990, pp. 215-216).At the end of the volume is printed the famous letter in form of an elegy variously attributed to Ippolita Torelli (1499-1520), wife of Baldassarre Castiglione, who was one of the most influential representatives of courtly culture in Italy and author of the Courtier (1528). This poem was first included in his Latin poetry as by himself. It was written in 1518, when Baldassarre was ambassador to the Gonzaga at Rome. In it she laments his absence from home and calls his attention to the dangers of the court of Leo X. She mentions as a great comfort the portrait Raphael had painted of him. Added is also her epitaph by Pietro Bembo, which is found on her tomb in the Santuario delle Grazie near Mantua (cf. J.D. Falvo, The Economy of Human Relations: Castiglione's ‘Libro del Cortegiano', New York, 1992, pp. 159-166).“Es ist eine bunte Vielfalt von Begegnungen und Verbindungen zwischen italienischen sowie deutschen und in einem Falle auch schweizerischen Gelehrten, die sich in Olympia Moratas Korrespondenz widerspiegelt. Diese gründete im wesentlichen auf der Gemeinsamkeit Renaissance-humanistischer Bildung und - mehr oder weniger ausgeprägt - auf reformatorischer Glaubenshaltung. Möglicherweise hatte der deutsche Dichter Goethe auch diese Kontakte im Blick, als er unter dem 30. Januar 1828 in seinem Tagebuch notierte: ‘Las in den Briefen der Olympia Fulvia Morata, und es ging mir über den eigentlichen, damaligen, protestantischen Zustand ein ganz neues Licht auf. Meine Bemerkungen denke niederzuschreiben' ” (R. Kössling, Die Korrespondenz der Olympia Fulvia Morata (1526-1555) als Dokument italo-deutscher Begegnungen, in: “Acta Conventus Neo-Latini Bariensis”, Tempe, AZ, 1998, p. 377).Celio Secondo Curione was born the youngest of twenty three children in Moncalieri in the province of Turin. He first studied law and humanities at Turin and continued his studies in Milan, where he also started to teach in 1528. He became more and more interested in the writings of the German reformers. He taught at Pavia and Venice, where he met Bernardino Ochino. He lived for a short time at the court of Ferrara and in Lucca. After several narrow escapes from the Inquisition he fled to Switzerland via the Grisons where he met with Camillo Renato, an Antitrinitarian, and became rector of the newly founded University of Lausanne in 1542. In 1546 he went to Basel, where he taught ancient classics at the University until his death. He gained a wide reputation and attracted many students coming from foreign countries. He declined invitations by the Pope to Rome, by the Duke of Savoy to Turin, from the Emperor to the University of Vienna, and from the prince of Transylvania to the new college established at Alba Julia. He was not a confessed theologian, nevertheless he wrote a treatise Christianae religionis institutio (1549), from which he omitted any mention of the Trinity or the deity of Christ as a doctrine necessary for salvation. In 1550 he attended the Anabaptist Council at Venice and in 1554 wrote a work dedicated to the Polish king, De amplitudine beati regni Dei, in which he opposed Calvin's doctrine of predestination. He was accused by Vergerio in 1559 of heresy, but was exonerated by the University of Basel. Curione was very careful not to commit himself to any compromising doctrinal position, nevertheless his writings and his association with Castellio, Ochino, and Lelio Sozzini make him one of the precursors of the Unitarian-Socinian movement (cf. M. Kutter, Celio Secondo Curione. Sein Leiben und sein Werk, Basel & Stuttgart, 1955, passim). (Liber I:)Sinapius, Kilian (p. 73)from Morato, Fulvio Pellegrino. Speyer, May 15, 1562 (p. 224) Olympia (or Olimpia) Morata was born in Ferrara, the eldest child of Fulvio Morato, a humanist scholar who was tutor to the younger sons of Alfonso d'Este, duke of Ferrara. She learned her subjects so well that at the age of twelve or thirteen she was invited to the court of Ferrara as a companion of study to Anna d'Este, the daughter of Duke Ercole II and Duchess Renée of France. There she continued her classical studies with Anna under the guidance of her father and two German brothers, Johannes and Kilian Sinapius.She was considered a “fanciulla prodigio”, and won the praise of many intellectuals for her fluency in Latin and Greek. It is highly probable that her sympathies for the Reformation began at the court of Ferrara since the Duchess herself supported the efforts of the reformers. Also Olympia's father shared these views, and in 1532 was forced to leave Ferrara. For six years the family lived in other northern cities, where Morato lectured on the teachings of Luther and Calvin. In 1547, her father became ill, and Olympia left court to help her mother care for him until his death the following year.Morata then returned to court, but things had changed there: Anna had left for France to be married to François de Guise, and Ercole had finally succumbed to pressure from Rome to purge the court of religious reformers. In Ferrara, Morata met a young German follower of Luther, Andreas Grundler, who was finishing a medical degree. In late 1549 or early 1550, they married. By the end of 1550, the couple moved to Germany to evade the Roman Inquisition, accompanied by Morata's 8-year-old brother Emilio and settled at Grundler's home in Schweinfurt, in central Germany (Morata's mother and sisters remained in Italy), never to return to Italy.Grundler accepted a position as medical doctor for the Imperial Spanish troops who were stationed in Schweinfurt. From 1553-54, they were caught in the middle of war. Schweinfurt was occupied by the soldiers of Albert Alciabides, and Morata, Grundler, and Emilio lived in dangerous and difficult conditions, at one point taking refuge in a wine cellar. Ultimately, the city was sacked and burned by Albert's enemies. The Grundler household left the city as refugees, having lost everything, including most of Morata's written work. They went eventually to Heidelberg, where Grundler accepted a position as professor of medicine at the university and Morata tutored students in Greek and Latin.However, the fever that Morata caught in Schweinfurt never subsided, and a few months later she died. She was not quite 29 years old. Less than two months later, Grundler and Emilio also died, most likely of the plague that had taken hold of the residents of Heidelberg. Although most of Morata's writing had been lost, her friends gathered up all they could find and in 1558 one of them, Celio Curio, published the first edition of her works, along with letters to her from others and laudatory poems; other items were found and added in later editions.From these, we can hear the voice of a woman trying to balance her humanist ideals with her religious beliefs, and trying both to live in an uncertain world and to help her friends to do the same. For her, learning was not a mere ornament, but her true identity. She also was one of the very first women whose writings were put on the Index. In fact her name is found on the list of prohibited authors of ‘second class' in the Clementine Index of 1596 (cf. A. Rabil, Jr., Olympia Morata, in: “Italian Women Writers: A Bio-bibliographical Sourcebook”, Westport, CT, 1994, pp. 267-279; J. Stevenson, Women Latin Poets: Language, Gender and Authority from Antiquity to the Eighteenth Century, Oxford, 2005, pp. 285-288; and C. Franceschini, ‘Literarum studia nobis communia': Olimpia Morata e la corte di Renata di Francia, in: “Schifanoia”, 28/29, 2005, pp. 207-232).

title: Mückenkrieg, Darin zu befinden, Welcher Gestalt die Mücken, neben ihren Mitverwanthen und Bundsgenossen, sich wider die Ameissen, und derselben Beistand, in mercklicher anzal un[d] übergrossem Heer zu Feld gelagert: [...] und ein überauß greuliche und blutige Schlacht einander geliefert haben. Alles mit sondern Fleiß verfasset in unterschiedliche Drey Bücher [...]
academic_description: 8vo (152x98 mm). 116, [2 blank] pp. Collation: A-C8 D8-1 E-G8 H4. Leaf H4 is a blank. Title page printed in red and black with a woodcut vignette in the center. Later cardboards, inked title on spine (slightly rubbed), sprinkled red edges. Slightly browned. A very good copy.Earliest obtainable edition. According to earlier bibliographers at least three editions preceded the present one, of which, however, no copies are known: one printed at Schmalkalden in 1580, one printed in Amberg without printer nor date, and one with the title Mückenkrieg, Tractatus de bello muscarum, dated 1600 (cf. F.W. Genthe, ed., H. C. Fuchs's heroisch-komisches Gedicht der Mückenkrieg : Nach der Ausg. von a. 1600, mit den Varianten der Schnurr'schen Bearbeitung von 1612, und einer Einleitung, Eisleben, 1833, pp. 9-12).It is considered “possibly the least known, but probably also the most underestimated text of its kind” (G. Riedl, “...deren beyspiel man sol volge tun”. Das satirische Tierepos als lehrhaftes Geschichtsexempel, in: “Tierepik und Tierallegorese: Studien zur Poetologie und historischen Anthropologie vormoderner Literatur”, B. Jahn, ed., Frankfurt/Main, 2004, p. 279).The work is a rather free adaptation of Teofilo Folengo’s juvenile mock epic Moscheide, written in macaronic verses and first published in his Maccheronee (Toscolano, 1521). In his preface Fuchs explicitly mentions Folengo and his peculiar style, which, however, he did not want to imitate.“Die Grobstruktur des Mückenkriegs ergibt sich aus der bei Teofilo Folengo vorlie- genden Einteilung des Textes in drei Bücher, die die Entstehung und Verlauf einer kriegeri- schen Auseinandersetzung zwischen Mücken und Ameisen schildern. Ausgehend von einer vernichtenden militärischen Niederlage be- schliesst Mückenkönig Sanguileo die Einberu- fung und Rüstung des alliierten Mückenheeres und somit die Kriegserklärung an das Ameisen- reich. Nach einer detaillierten Beschreibung der einzelnen Truppenkontingente endet das erste Buch mit der Einschiffung des Heeres. Das zweite Buch handelt von der Ankunft und Rüs- tung der Ameisen und ihrer Verbündeter, der gefährlichen Seefahrt der Mücken sowie ersten militärischen Erfolge. Das dritte und letzte Buch berichtet die Feldschlacht, die dem Schei- tern einen angebotenen Stellvertreterkampfs zwischen Myrnuca und Siccaboron folgt. Die Schlachtschilderung wird dabei in Einzel- kampfsequenzen zerteilt; die Schlacht endet mit der Flucht des Mückenheeres und der Tötung des tollkühnen Siccaboron... Stand bei Folengo das gebildete Sprachspiel, der formale Spra- chwitz, im Vordergrund, so ist bei Fuchs eine Umgewichtung der Aussageintention zu konstatieren, bei der die instruktive, didaktische Funktion der Fürstenspiegelliteratur bzw. der literarisierten Kriegslehre ins Zentrum rückt... Wenn Fuchs auf der einen Seite die komische Aufzählung von Mückenstädten tilgt und auf der anderen Seite sein Tierepos durch Rekurs auf reale Städte (z.B. Antwerpen oder Venedig) konsequenter an die ausserliterarische Realität anbindet, kann dies Ausdruck einer bewussten Authentifizierung der Handlung sein” (H.C. Fuchs, Der Mückenkrieg. Ein frühneuzeitliches Tierepos herausgegeben und mit einem Kommentar von Sabine Schu, St. Ingbert, 2012, pp. 405, 447; see also C. Struwe-Rohr, Von Mücken und Ameisen und einem toten Ochsen. Überlegungen zur Problematik der Geltung und Durchsetzung von Herrschaft sowie Freiheit der Massen im ‘Mückenkrieg’, in: “Reflexionen des Politischen in der europäischen Tierepik, J. Glück et al., eds., Ol- denburg, 2016, pp. 182-208).Little is known about Hans Christoph Fuchs life. He was hereditary lord of Wallenburg in Franconia (cf. O. Gerland, Hans Christoph Fuchs der Altere zu Wallenburg und Arnschwang, ein humanistischer Ritter des 16. Jahrhunderts, in:“Zeitschrift des Vereins für hessische Geschichte und Landeskunde”, Neue Folge 23, 1898, pp. 204-246).

authors.name: Taubmann Friedrich
authors.biography: Friedrich Taubmann (1565–1613) stands as one of the most brilliant, versatile, and complex figures of late German Humanism (Späthumanismus), occupying a pivotal historical position at the intersection of classical philology, Neo-Latin poetry, academic oratory, and Protestant educational reform. Operating from the prestigious Chair of Poetry and Eloquence at the University of Wittenberg (the Leucorea), Taubmann mediated between the rigorous textual traditions of Northern Renaissance philology and the emerging demands of early modern university pedagogy. While 18th-century popular culture often reduced his memory to a quasi-legendary court jester and author of witty anecdotes (the ubiquitous Taubmanniana), contemporary historical and literary scholarship recognizes him as an erudite editor of Roman comedy, a master of Latin metrics, and a key architect of the late 16th- and early 17th-century Republic of Letters in the Holy Roman Empire. His life's work reflects the vibrant, albeit politically precarious, intellectual climate of Saxon academia on the eve of the Thirty Years' War, demonstrating how classical erudition was deployed to cultivate civic virtue, linguistic precision, and Lutheran confessional identity.Born on May 16, 1565, in the small Franconian village of Wonsees, near Kulmbach, Friedrich Taubmann was the son of a modest tailor and smallholder who died during Friedrich's early childhood. Raised in severe financial hardship by his widowed mother, Taubmann's exceptional intellectual acuity was recognized by local patrons, enabling him to attend the Latin school in Kulmbach. His academic trajectory was decisively shaped when he secured admission to the renowned princely school (Fürstenschule) at the former Cistercian monastery of Heilsbronn (Heilsbronn Abbey) in 1582. Under the rigorous curriculum established by the Margraves of Brandenburg-Ansbach, Taubmann received an intensive grounding in Greek and Latin philology, dialectic, and classical rhetoric. In 1592, sponsored by noble patronage, he matriculated at the University of Wittenberg, an institution still reverberating with the intellectual legacy of Philipp Melanchthon. At Wittenberg, Taubmann distinguished himself almost immediately through his extraordinary facility in Neo-Latin verse, earning his Master of Arts degree in 1593 and receiving the coveted imperial poetical coronation (Poeta Laureatus) from Friedrich Wilhelm, Duke of Saxe-Weimar. By October 1595, at the remarkably young age of thirty, Taubmann was appointed Professor of Poetry and Eloquence at Wittenberg, a position he retained with immense distinction until his untimely death on March 24, 1613.Taubmann's scholarly and literary output represents a monumental synthesis of creative Neo-Latin composition and critical textual editing. His creative poetical reputation was inaugurated with the publication of Columbae (1594), a sophisticated collection of Neo-Latin lyrics that showcased his mastery of Catullian hendecasyllables, Martial-esque epigrams, and Horatian odes, followed by the expanded Schediasmata poetica (1610) and Otia Friderici Taubmanni. However, his lasting philological monument is his seminal edition of Titus Maccius Plautus, published as T. Macci Plauti Comoediae XX (Wittenberg, 1605; revised and expanded in 1612). Before Taubmann, early Roman comedy was frequently misunderstood metrico-linguistically, treated with skepticism by scholars accustomed to Augustan Latinity. Taubmann applied an unprecedented level of paleographical scrutiny, metrical reconstruction, and lexicographical analysis to Plautus, restoring archaic Latin usages and establishing a baseline for early Latin linguistics that influenced scholars across Europe for generations. Following his triumph with Plautus, Taubmann turned his attention to Publius Vergilius Maro, preparing a colossal commentary on the Aeneid, Georgics, and Eclogues (posthumously completed and published by his student and successor, Caspar von Barth, in 1618). As an orator, Taubmann's published speeches—such as his Oratio de lingua Latina—defended the living vitality of Latin as the universal medium of international scholarship, arguing passionately against the linguistic decay and pedantry of contemporary academic pedants.The dissemination of Taubmann's works provides a vivid window into the early modern print culture of Saxony and the commercial mechanisms of the Frankfurt and Leipzig book fairs. His principal texts were issued through the eminent presses of Wittenberg printers, most notably Zacharias Schürer, Paul Helwig, Clemens Schleich, and the printing house of Christian Tham. These production houses utilized sophisticated typography, employing crisp Roman types for main texts flanked by dense, smaller-font Italic and Greek commentary in the margins—a typographical layout that visually encoded the humanist method of active reading and scholarly annotation. The commercial success of Taubmann's Plautus edition of 1605 was such that it was quickly pirated and reprinted in Frankfurt, Leiden, and Geneva, testifying to the pan-European reach of the Wittenberg book market. Furthermore, Taubmann maintained an extensive epistolary network with leading European humanists, including Joachim Camerarius the Younger, Jan Gruter, Joseph Justus Scaliger, and Isaac Casaubon, exchanging rare manuscripts, emendations, and typographical proofs that crossed political and religious boundaries across the Holy Roman Empire and the Low Countries.The critical reception of Friedrich Taubmann underwent a dramatic dual evolution in the centuries following his death. Within academic circles, he was revered by 17th-century polymaths like Daniel Georg Morhof and Johann Albert Fabricius as a prince of philology who rescued Roman comedy from medieval corruption. However, parallel to his academic fame, a popular folk tradition emerged around his persona. Due to his legendary quick wit, biting humor, and habit of using satire to critique courtly hypocrisy and academic pomposity, stories of his life were collected into popular chapbooks. The most famous of these, the Taubmanniana (first published systematically by Christian Hübner in 1703 and continuously reprinted throughout the 18th century), recast the serious Wittenberg professor as an unruly, jesting folk hero operating in the tradition of Till Eulenspiegel. This popular image led Enlightenment critics, including Johann Christoph Gottsched and G. E. Lessing, to launch efforts to rescue Taubmann's serious scholarly legacy from anecdotal trivialization. In the 19th and 20th centuries, modern philologists such as Friedrich August Wolf, Otto Ribbeck, and later 20th-century scholars of Späthumanismus like Wilhelm Kühlmann and Heinz Entner reaffirmed Taubmann's foundational role in early modern Latin studies, establishing him as a crucial intellectual bridge between the Renaissance humanism of Melanchthon and the modern scientific altertumswissenschaft of the German University tradition.

authors.name: Meibom Heinrich
authors.biography: Heinrich Meibom the Elder (1555–1625) stands as one of the most prominent intellectual figures of late German Humanism (Späthumanismus), serving as a quintessential bridge between sixteenth-century philological erudition and seventeenth-century institutional historiography. As a distinguished Professor of Poetry and History at the famous Academia Julia in Helmstedt, an official historian to the Ducal House of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and a imperial Poeta Laureatus crowned by Emperor Rudolf II, Meibom shaped the scholarly identity of Protestant Northern Germany. His literary production, characterized by masterful Neo-Latin verse and rigorous archival compilation, exerted a profound influence on early modern conceptions of German imperial history, territorial statecraft, and academic humanism. Operating within a dense network of European polymaths, Meibom transformed the study of medieval chronicles from mere moralistic compilation into an empirical instrument of historical and legal evidence, directly laying the foundations upon which later scholars such as Hermann Conring and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz would erect modern German historiography.Born on December 4, 1555, in the Westphalian town of Lemgo within the Principality of Lippe, Meibom belonged to an established burgher family deeply integrated into municipal administration. He received his foundational education at the renowned Lateinschule in Lemgo under the guidance of committed Lutheran humanists, who instilled in him a rigorous command of Classical Latin, Greek grammar, and ancient rhetoric. Seeking advanced instruction, Meibom progressed to the Gymnasium in Dortmund before matriculating in May 1577 at the newly founded University of Helmstedt (the Academia Julia), which had been established in 1576 by Duke Julius of Brunswick-Lüneburg as the primary intellectual powerhouse of Lutheran Northern Germany. At Helmstedt, Meibom came under the transformative influence of eminent scholars, most notably the famed humanist Johannes Caselius, whose ecumenical classical vision and irenic rhetoric profoundly shaped Meibom's intellectual ethos. Under Caselius and the theologian Polycarp Leyser the Elder, Meibom immersed himself in classical philology, ancient philosophy, poetry, and imperial legal traditions, quickly establishing a reputation as one of the academy's most gifted Latin stylists.In 1583, at the remarkably young age of twenty-eight, Meibom was appointed to the prestigious Chair of Poetry and History at the University of Helmstedt, a position he would hold with distinction for over four decades until his death. His academic lectures at the Academia Julia became legendary for synthesizing classicizing poetic eloquence with deep critical engagement with medieval historical texts. Meibom argued that poetry and history were twin pillars of humanistic education: poetry cultivated civic rhetoric and ethical virtue, while history provided the empirical exempla necessary for governance and legal jurisprudence. His scholarly talents quickly attracted the patronage of Duke Heinrich Julius of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, a ruler famed for his intense commitment to the arts, drama, and university expansion. Meibom became the duke’s trusted court historiographer, tasked with assembling archival proof of the antiquity, prestige, and imperial privileges of the House of Welf. In recognition of his elevated literary genius and his heroic panegyrics on the Holy Roman Empire, Emperor Rudolf II formally invested Meibom with the title of imperial Poeta Laureatus at Prague in November 1590, elevating him into the elite realm of recognized imperial poets.Meibom's scholarly output was divided between brilliantly crafted Neo-Latin poetry and seminal editorial monuments of German medieval history. Among his poetic works, his panegyrics, epicedia, and historical verse—such as Irrenreitender Martinus (a sharp satirical poem targeting contemporary theological polemicists) and his elegiac celebrations of Welf princes—demonstrated complete mastery of Ovidian and Vergilian prosody. However, his most enduring contribution to European scholarship lay in his monumental historiographical compilations. Meibom was among the first German humanists to systematically hunt for unpublished medieval codices in monastic archives across Lower Saxony and Westphalia. His critical compilations, including the Opuscula historica ad res Germanicas spectantia (1688 posthumous expansion) and his specialized regional studies such as the Chronicon Waldeccense and De Saxonum inferiorum historia, transformed medieval manuscript fragments into clean, annotated printed texts. He famously defended the imperial legitimacy of Emperor Otto IV in his Apologia pro Ottone IV imperatore, utilizing charter evidence to rehabilitate the Welf emperor's historic reputation.The printing history of Meibom’s works offers a fascinating window into the early modern publication market of the Holy Roman Empire and the institutional typography of the Academia Julia. The vast majority of Meibom's initial dissertations, panegyrics, and historical treatises were issued by the official university press at Helmstedt, managed by the distinguished printer Jakob Lucius the Elder and subsequently his son, Jakob Lucius the Younger. These Helmstedt editions were celebrated for their crisp Roman and Italic types, elaborate woodcut coats-of-arms, and the prominent display of the university's official crest. Larger historical treatises were published through major regional print centers such as Magdeburg, Goslar, and Frankfurt am Main, allowing his research to circulate across the Republic of Letters. The ultimate monument to Meibom’s scholarship was realized posthumously by his grandson, Heinrich Meibom the Younger (1638–1700), himself a world-renowned physician and historian. In 1688, the younger Meibom thoroughly edited, expanded, and published his grandfather's accumulated collection of medieval sources under the title Rerum Germanicarum Scriptores in three massive folio volumes at Helmstedt and Leipzig, printed by Gottlieb Henricus Gropius. This monumental set became an indispensable foundational text for European historical scholarship throughout the Enlightenment.Throughout his academic career, Meibom maintained an expansive correspondence network that connected Helmstedt with the highest echelons of European scholarship. He exchanged letters, philological notes, and rare manuscript readings with international humanists including Joseph Justus Scaliger, Justus Lipsius, Janus Gruterus, and Isaac Casaubon. His academic presence at Helmstedt helped elevate the Academia Julia into an international intellectual destination, drawing students from Scandinavia, the Baltic regions, and across the Holy Roman Empire. Within university politics, Meibom consistently advocated for humanistic moderation against the encroaching tide of rigid Lutheran scholastic orthodoxy, upholding Johannes Caselius's ideal of open, irenic academic inquiry.Heinrich Meibom the Elder died in Helmstedt on September 20, 1625, amidst the darkening turmoil of the Thirty Years' War, which would soon disrupt the flourishment of the university he had served for forty-two years. His historical legacy remained immensely powerful. In the late seventeenth century, Hermann Conring praised Meibom as the indispensable pioneer who rescued Northern German history from medieval fable. Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, when undertaking his grand task of writing the history of the House of Brunswick (Annales Imperii Occidentis Brunsvicenses), drew continuously upon the documentary foundation laid by Meibom. Modern scholars of late Renaissance Humanism recognize Meibom as a pivotal figure who successfully combined the stylistic elegances of Renaissance poetry with the rigorous empirical demands of critical historiography, securing his place as a master bibliographer and chronicler of the Holy Roman Empire.
