authors.name: Lauro Pietro
authors.biography: Pietro Lauro (also known as Pietro Lauro Modenese, ca. 1510 – 1568) stands as one of the most versatile, industrious, and influential poligrafi—professional translators, press correctors, and vernacular editors—active in Venice during the golden age of Renaissance print culture. Operating at the dynamic intersection of humanist erudition and the commercial book market, Lauro played a paramount role in democratizing classical, scientific, philosophical, and foreign literature for the rapidly expanding Italian vernacular readership of the mid-sixteenth century. While often overshadowed in romanticized literary histories by more flamboyant contemporaries such as Pietro Aretino, Ludovico Dolce, or Niccolò Franco, Lauro’s monumental corpus of translations provided the intellectual foundation for early modern European cross-cultural transfer. His linguistic agility allowed him to bridge Latin, Greek, Spanish, and vernacular Italian, turning the printing shops of the Venetian lagoon into international hubs of knowledge dissemination.Born in Modena around the first decade of the sixteenth century, Lauro received a rigorous humanist education grounded in classical philology, rhetoric, and moral philosophy. Though precise details regarding his early domestic lineage remain sparse, his early writings reveal a deep familiarity with scholastic Latin traditions, ancient Greek syntax, and the emerging prestige of the Tuscan vernacular as canonized by Pietro Bembo. Drawn to the economic vitality and intellectual liberty of the Republic of Venice, Lauro migrated to the lagoon around the late 1530s or early 1540s. Venice was then experiencing an unprecedented expansion in its typographical industry. The city's printers were shifting from expensive, Latin-dominated folios toward accessible, vernacular octavos and duodecimos aimed at merchant elites, educated women, civic administrators, and provincial scholars. Recognizing that his classical training could be converted into economic subsistence within the print shop, Lauro integrated himself into the flourishing networks of Venetian publishing houses.Lauro’s bibliography of translations is extraordinary in its thematic breadth, spanning botany, medicine, agronomy, history, Christian humanism, and romance literature. One of his most celebrated contributions to early modern science was his translation of Leonhard Fuchs’ landmark botanical treatise, De historia stirpium octo commentarii. Published in Venice by Vincenzo Valgrisi in 1544 under the title Historia de le piante, Lauro’s translation brought Northern European botanical classification and medical herbalism directly to Italian apothecaries, physicians, and natural philosophers. In doing so, Lauro had to navigate not only complex Latinized botanical nomenclature but also the subtle theological risks associated with translating Protestant authors like Fuchs into post-Tridentine Italy. His work in the natural sciences extended to classical agriculture; his Italian vernacularization of Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella’s De re rustica (published by Michele Tramezzino in 1544) provided Renaissance landowners with a practical, vernacular handbook on estate management, soil cultivation, and animal husbandry.Beyond scientific literature, Lauro was a central agent in translating the Northern European Renaissance and Iberian humanism for Italian readers. He undertook vernacular renderings of Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, including popular editions of the Enchiridion militis christiani and selections from the Apophthegmata, framing Erasmian moral piety for Italian devotional contexts before such works faced strict censorship under the Roman Index of Prohibited Books. Equally significant was his introduction of Spanish moral and chivalric literature to the Venetian press. Lauro translated Juan Luis Vives’ treatises on female education and domestic duty (such as De institutione feminae christianae, rendered as De l'ufficio del marito and related moral guides) and Antonio de Guevara’s celebrated mirror-for-princes, the Reloj de príncipes (as Horologio de' principi). Furthermore, Lauro was instrumental in catalyzing the immense Italian craze for Iberian chivalric romances. Working in close collaboration with the publisher Michele Tramezzino, Lauro translated significant portions of the Amadís de Gaula cycle, Palmerín de Oliva, and Primaleón, adapting the courtly ethics and fantastic geography of Spanish romance into fluid, elegant Italian prose that captivated Italian aristocratic readers.The operational locus of Lauro’s career was inextricably linked to the typography and business strategies of Venice’s premier publishing dynasties, notably those of Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari, Vincenzo Valgrisi, and Michele Tramezzino. Working as an editor and translator for Giolito, Lauro contributed directly to the publisher's famous series of vernacular classics and educational treatises. The physical format of Lauro’s translations reflected cutting-edge Venetian book design: clean italic fonts, woodcut initials, elegant architectural title pages, and detailed thematic indexes compiled by Lauro himself to maximize usability for non-scholarly readers. His prefatory epistles, addressed to prominent Venetian patricians, noblewomen, and intellectual patrons, offer invaluable insight into the economic realities of sixteenth-century authorship, where translators navigated tight printing deadlines, rival unauthorized editions, and the patronal patronage system.Pietro Lauro died in Venice around 1568, leaving behind a legacy that fundamentally shaped the Italian Renaissance vernacular revival. Modern bibliographical scholarship has reassessed Lauro not merely as a passive translator for hire, but as an active cultural mediator who helped construct the vernacular encyclopedia of the sixteenth century. By translating complex Latin science, classical historiography, Erasmian philosophy, and foreign fiction into clear, accessible Italian, Lauro expanded the boundaries of vernacular literacy and literary culture. His work paved the way for the institutionalization of Italian as a global language of print, solidifying Venice’s reputation as the vibrant capital of the early modern European book trade.

academic_description: 8vo. [16], 240 pp. Collation: a8, A-P8. Printer's device on title-page. Italic types. Later full vellum.First edition, second issue (the first bears the date 1552), dedicated by the author to Francesco Chimenti.“Pietro Lauro presentava la sua raccolta di lettere al dedicatario Francesco Chimenti, 'nobile fiorentino', come una raccolta di ‘concetti', frutto di conversazioni: ‘Vengo dunque con le mie lettere, ne le quali vostra Signoria leggerà molti bei discorsi e piacevoli ragionamenti e vi sovvenirà di molti similari parlari, che voi et meco ne la casa vostra, e in più altri luochi con diverse persone virtuose havete trattato. Et io tenendone memoria, me ne sono in molte mie lettere servito' ” (L. Braida, Libri di lettere. Le raccolte epistolari del Cinquecento tra inquietudini religiose e ‘buon volgare', Bari, 2009, p. 243).“Le recueil contient 125 lettres [including the dedicatory] non datées, écrites, de l'aveu de l'auteur, à partir d'études et de conversations. D'après la Tavola delle materie, il y aurait 6 l. ‘consolatorie', 3 d' 'esortatione', 1 ‘giocosa', 1 ‘famigliare', etc. Plus que les destinataires (des noms apparemment fictifs se mêlent à d'autres de personnes connues: Ortensio Lando, Fausto da Longiano, Lucrezia Gonzaga da Gazuolo,…) comptent les sujets, un par lettre: aux plus nombreux traités dans la ligne de la morale traditionelle (le mariage, l'éducation des enfants, la consolation,…), s'opposent quelques attitudes inhabituelles ou paradoxales: Lauro se déclare contre la pauvreté puisque la société n'estime pas les qualités du pauvre; il invite l'écrivain à justifier son oeuvre et à la louer lui-même, il engage à douter de la rhétorique en se fondant sur une des règles de la rhétorique,…). Non sans raison, ce recueil est parfois attribué à O. Lando” (J. Basso, Le genre épistolaire en langue italienne, 1538-1662, Roma, 1999, I, pp. 170-171).“Il Sanesi [Tre epistolari del Cinquecento, in: “Giornale storico della Letteratura italiana”, 23, 1894, pp. 26-32] accosta l'epistolario di Lucrezia Gonzaga a quello di Pietro Lauro: mentre il primo potrebbe essere opera del Lando (e il Sanesi ne è convinto) per via dello stile, ricco di ‘citazioni della storia e della mitologia' e caratterizzato da ‘una certa maniera di filosofare tutta propria del Lando', è proprio questo stile, paradossale e basato sull'accostamento di contrari, che il Lauro vuole apertamente imitare in quelle che, secondo l'opinione di Sanesi, sono lettere fittizie scritte à la Lando. Certo è che la dedicatoria a Francesco Chimenti, nobile fiorentino del primo libro di Lettere del Lauro si può considerare esattamente speculare a quella appena vista al Manfrone [Pietro Paolo Manfrone, dedicatee of Lucrezia Gonzaga's letters, see p. XXX]: laddove nella prima il dedicatario veniva liquidato con la titolazione della soprascritta, qui l'autore si diffonde in numerose variazioni sul tema della generosità del Chimenti nei confronti dei virtuosi, ma soprattutto nei confronti del dedicante, tanto che il Lauro lo vedeva ‘tanto disposto ai suoi comodi, che lui à saper desiarli'. Altro aspetto sottolineato in più riprese è il piacere provato dal Chimenti nell'intrattenersi in dotte conversazioni, conversazioni che il Chimenti ritroverà in parte divenute materiale per queste lettere (‘Et io tenendone memoria, me ne sono in molte mie lettere servito')” (C. Schiavon, Una via d'accesso agli epistolari. Le dediche dei libri di lettere d'autore nel Cinquecento. Prima parte, in: “Margini. Giornale della dedica e altro”, 3, 2009, p. 28).Lauro published a second volume of letters seven years later, Delle lettere di messer Pietro Lauro. Libro secondo (Venice, 1560), dedicated to Johann Jakob Fugger.All the letters in the collection are without place and date. A certain number of recipients can certainly be considered as fictitious. For that we have decided to render their names exactly as they are given in the printed text. In brackets is found the modern spelling of the names of the identified recipients. Born in Modena around 1510, he probably made medical studies in Bologna or Padua, considering the many translations of medical works he did during his career.Around 1542 he moved to Venice, where he started collaborating with some local typographers (mainly Giolito, Tramezzino, and Valgrisi) as a translator from Greek and Latin. He continued this activity until 1568, together with those of schoolmaster and scribe.Among the many works he translated into Italian stand out the De inventoribus rerum by Polidoro Virgili (1543) and Erasmus' Colloquia (1545), which were both subsequently put on the Index. He also translated De officio mariti by Juan Luis Vives (1546) and Leon Battista Alberti's De re aedificatoria (1546).The relationships Lauro had with several Italian figures close to the Evangelical movement, like Ortensio Lando, Lucrezia Gonzaga, and Renée of France (to whom he dedicated his Colloqui famigliari di Erasmo), and the many letters he addressed to German correspondents, (all found in his letter collections), testify to his sympathy for the Lutheran doctrines (cf. S. Seidel Menchi, Erasmus als Ketzer: Reformation und Inquisition im Italien des 16. Jahrhunderts, Leiden & New York, 1992, pp. 435, 467). Besides that, the friar Ambrogio da Milano referred to him as a Lutheran in a deposition made before the Inquisition in 1557. So did a certain Ettore Donati during another trial. Lauro died in Modena after 1568 (cf. G. Dini, Lauro, Pietro, in: “Dizionario biografico degli Italiani”, Roma, 2005, LXIV, pp. 119-122).

title: Il primo libro delle lettere

authors.name: Martelli Nicolò
authors.biography: Nicolò (or Niccolò) Martelli was the scion of a wealthy family of merchants from Florence. At the age of fourteen he was sent to Rome to make practice in the trade. Here he met his idol, Pietro Aretino, who encouraged him to compose poems. Back in Florence he took over the family business.In 1531, exiled for a few months in Prato, he met the “letterati” Baldinaccio Martellini, Pandolfo Martelli, and Agnolo Firenzuola, and had a love affair with Maria Minerbetti, wife of Tommaso Minerbetti, Duke Cosimo de' Medici's local representative. In 1536 he married Lucrezia di Francesco Ciampelli. In 1540 he founded, together with Giovanni Mazzuoli, Antonio Grazzini and many others, the Accademia degli Umidi (cf. M. Maylender, Storia delle Accademia d'Italia, Bologna, 1930, V, pp. 363-367), which a year later was transformed into the more institutional Accademia Fiorentina (cf. Plaisance, Une première affirmation de la politique culturelle de Côme Ier: la trasformation de l'Academie des ‘Humidi' en Académie Florentine (1540-1542), in: “L'Accademia e il suo principe”, Roma, 2004, p. 140, 185-186).Martelli remained member of the academy with the name of “Gelato” and in 1544-45 was appointed consul. In 1543 he travelled to France in search of business venture, following the footsteps of his friend Luigi Alamanni, but already after a month he returned to Florence to assume the new position as mayor of Impruneta. He died in Florence in 1555.Martelli was the author of many occasional pieces dedicated to members of the Medici family. He also wrote love verses addressed to Maria Minerbetti and several comical compositions. His entire poetic production remained unpublished, except the Stanze sopra le nozze del duca Cosimo Medici secondo (Firenze, 1539).

publisher_data: Florence, (at the author's expenses) [Anton Francesco Doni], 1546
academic_description: 4to. [4], 5-91, [1] leaves. Collation: A-Z4 (lacking Z4, a blank). With the woodcut portrait of the author on the title-page. Seventeenth century vellum over boards, marbled edges. First edition, published at the author's expenses, of this collection of 209 letters arranged in chronological order. The second book, which was almost ready when the first appeared, was never published. It is preserved in a manuscript of the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale of Florence (cf. C. Marconcini, ed., Dal primo e dal secondo libro delle lettere di Niccolò Martelli, Lanciano, 1916, pp. 5-12).The present edition, variously attributed to the Guinta press, has more recently been assigned to Anton Francesco Doni. “Il nome del Doni non si legge nella data, ma apparisce chiarissimo che ne fosse lo stampatore, non solo per la forma de' caratteri, ma per esservi detto in una lettera del Martelli, a pag. 84, e per altri certi riscontri: onde si vede quanto sbagliassero il Bandini ed il Renouard, nei loro cataloghi Giuntini, quando attribuirono questa edizione ai Giunti. Il Doni, quale ne fosse la causa, dopo avere dato mano alla stampa di questo libro, lo criticò nella Prima Libreria” (S. Bongi, Catalogo delle opere di A.F. Doni, in: A.F. Doni, “I marmi”, P. Fanfani, ed., Firenze, 1863, II, p. 303).Bongi does not seem, however, to have noticed the letter addressed to a certain Gian Francesco da Pavia (“car. e bidello della sacra Accademia Fiorentina”, l. 63v), in which the author invites the unidentified recipient (called “virtuoso giovane”) to undertake the printing of his letters, to choose a nice paper and elegant types, and to accept a remuneration for the edition.“Anche Nicolò Martelli, che stampò il suo libro di lettere presso la stamperia di Doni a Firenze, dedica la sua raccolta a una donna: si tratta di Maddalena Bonaiuti, moglie di Luigi Alamanni. Nell'incipit lo scrittore ricorda subito il noto marito, dicendo di aver pensato in un primo momento di dedicare a lui il libro, ma aggiunge: ‘facendolo errava, & tale errore meritava riprensione: ma haveria risposto, che non meno si conveniva alle sue nobili qualitati & magnanime Eccellenze d'esser sacrati purissimi inchiostri, che egli stesso s'habbia fatto si divinamente quelle d'altri'; così Martelli si rivolge a Maddalena: ‘ma ecco che voi per essere il cuore dell'anima sua; come egli l'animo de l'anima vostra: indirizzandole alla candidezza di quello splendore: che vi adorna il pellegrino spirito di si pregiate lodi: ci haverà parte in ogni modo'. Con la donna, in ogni caso, Martelli ha debiti personali diretti: di lei infatti viene lodato ‘l'offitio di cortesia' e la sua capacità di intercedere efficacemente ‘dalle gran Madame & dalle persone deputate, à ciò per le vie ch'ella sa più brevi & migliori', sostenendo che, vista l'influenza che già esercita alla giovane età di ventidue anni, è facile pensare che ‘tutte le faccende importanti di cotesto Christianissimo Regno, si guideranno un giorno nel dignissimo cospetto vostro per conferirle nella Maestà della Sereniss. Madama Caterina unica vostra Signora & mia sempiterna Patrona, acciò ch'ella ne risolva poi col grande Arigo Marito suo, quello che Dio gli spirerà'. In effetti la Bonaiuti era dama di compagnia della potente Caterina de' Medici, futura regina di Francia. Il Martelli, ricorda poi un episodio preciso: ‘quando non havendo di me à gran pena conoscenza vi degnaste introdurme a villa Cutrea la vigilia del Batista hora ha due anni, davanti al sacro cospetto della Giovane Reale: per presentarle il libro delle Donne Illustri, che presto verrà a luce'. Le lettere che le vengono donate, inoltre, sostiene Martelli, parlano in più punti delle dame di compagnia della regina, che Maddalena stessa gli ha permesso di conoscere. La dedica si conclude unendo negli auspici la dedicataria ‘insieme con l'Eccellenza del suo gran Consorte in quella Realissima di Madama la Dalfina, unica sua Regina'. Grazie alla mediazione della Bonaiuti, Martelli aveva ottenuto dalla Delfina di Francia, prima della pubblicazione del libro di lettere, una donazione di cento scudi d'oro e delle raccomandazioni per il granduca Cosimo I. Non sembra invece che questa dedica sia stata particolarmente gradita alla dama di compagnia di Caterina de' Medici, visto che in una lettera al marito di lei, Alamanni, Martelli si lamenta: ‘Meritava un certo che, se non d'altro, di gratitudine di parole, dove io non ho mai havuto risposta alcuna, né da V. S., né da Lei, né dal Sr abate vostro figlio'; lo stralcio, riportato da Hauvette [Luigi Alamanni (1495-1556). Sa vie et son oeuvre, Paris, 1903, p. 133] è tratto da una lettera dell'epistolario inedito, destinato probabilmente a diventare il secondo libro di lettere, poi mai stampato e conservato nella Biblioteca Nazionale di Firenze (cl. VIII, cod. 1447); se non ci sono errori nella data indicata da Hauvette (10 gennaio 1545) si tratterebbe di un pentimento piuttosto precoce, visto che il Primo libro verrà stampato nel 1546” (C. Schiavon, Una via d'accesso agli epistolari. Le dediche dei libri di lettere d'autore nel Cinquecento. Prima parte, in: “Margini. Giornale della dedica e altro”, 3, 2009, pp. 36-37).“Le lettere di Niccolò Martelli […] costituiscono il più coerente esempio di ortodossia al modello aretini ano […] Sin dallo strato più esterno – l'apparato paratestuale – è evidente la volontà, esplicitamente dichiarata, di ricalcare il modello. Sono infatti presenti gli elementi caratterizzanti dei volumi aretiniani: l'inclusione, già nel titolo della prima raccolta, del numero ordinale (Il primo libro delle lettere) e un ritratto dell'autore, di buona fattura, in posa di tre quarti. Aretino aveva usato il libro di lettere per imporsi definitivamente come il più influente ‘uomo di penna' del proprio tempo; analogamente, anche se in tono minore, Martelli, che proviene da una famiglia di mercanti, affida alla stampa delle proprie epistole la speranza di essere accolto nel novero dei letterati ‘illustri'. Un desiderio che stenta a realizzarsi, come egli stesso ammette con amarezza in diverse occasioni […] L'immagine che Martelli vuol dare di sé […] è quella del letterato che insegue con un certo grado di successo una vocazione difficile. È in questo senso significativa la scelta di proporre un primo blocco di epistole che sono per la maggior parte accompagnatorie o dedicatorie di scritti occasionali […] Si tratta di un insieme che, pur tradendo l'imperativo aretiniano della varietas che allontana il ‘tedio', risulta funzionale per lanciare in limine uno sguardo retrospettivo sulla propria biografia intellettuale […] Per saldare la frammentarietà di questa sezione suggerendo una lettura di essa in chiave autobiografica, Martelli inserisce tra le prime una lettera indirizzata all'Aretino, anch'essa fondamentalmente concepita per accompagnare alcuni versi, che riassume in poche righe la storia della propria vocazione” (G. Genovese, La lettera oltre il genere. Il libro di lettere, dall'Aretino al Doni, e le origini dell'autobiografia moderna, Roma & Padova, 2009, pp. 153-159). Marguerite de Navarre. Firenze, June 10, 1546 (l. 91r) Nicolò (or Niccolò) Martelli was the scion of a wealthy family of merchants from Florence. At the age of fourteen he was sent to Rome to make practice in the trade. Here he met his idol, Pietro Aretino, who encouraged him to compose poems. Back in Florence he took over the family business.In 1531, exiled for a few months in Prato, he met the “letterati” Baldinaccio Martellini, Pandolfo Martelli, and Agnolo Firenzuola, and had a love affair with Maria Minerbetti, wife of Tommaso Minerbetti, Duke Cosimo de' Medici's local representative. In 1536 he married Lucrezia di Francesco Ciampelli. In 1540 he founded, together with Giovanni Mazzuoli, Antonio Grazzini and many others, the Accademia degli Umidi (cf. M. Maylender, Storia delle Accademia d'Italia, Bologna, 1930, V, pp. 363-367), which a year later was transformed into the more institutional Accademia Fiorentina (cf. Plaisance, Une première affirmation de la politique culturelle de Côme Ier: la trasformation de l'Academie des ‘Humidi' en Académie Florentine (1540-1542), in: “L'Accademia e il suo principe”, Roma, 2004, p. 140, 185-186).Martelli remained member of the academy with the name of “Gelato” and in 1544-45 was appointed consul. In 1543 he travelled to France in search of business venture, following the footsteps of his friend Luigi Alamanni, but already after a month he returned to Florence to assume the new position as mayor of Impruneta. He died in Florence in 1555.Martelli was the author of many occasional pieces dedicated to members of the Medici family. He also wrote love verses addressed to Maria Minerbetti and several comical compositions. His entire poetic production remained unpublished, except the Stanze sopra le nozze del duca Cosimo Medici secondo (Firenze, 1539) (cf. E. Stumpo, Nicolò Martelli, in: “Dizionario biografico degli Italiani”, Roma, 2008, LXXI, pp. 61-64).

authors.name: Aventinus (Thurmair) Johannes
authors.biography: Johannes Aventinus (born Johannes Thurmair or Turmair; July 4, 1477 – January 9, 1534) stands as one of the most formidable figures of Northern European humanism, universally acclaimed as the pioneer of modern scientific historiography within the Holy Roman Empire and revered as the 'Bavarian Herodotus.' Operating at the volatile intersection of Renaissance philology, Germanic archaism, and the early confessional ruptures of the Protestant Reformation, Aventinus transformed the writing of history from medieval annalistic compilation into a critical, source-driven, and epigraphically verified discipline. His monumental dual historiographical achievements—the Latin Annales Boiorum and its vernacular counterpart, the Bayerische Chronik—redefined the cultural and political self-consciousness of the Duchy of Bavaria and the wider German-speaking lands. By subjecting monastic charters, ancient inscriptions, numismatic evidence, and medieval chronicles to rigorous philological scrutiny, Aventinus established a new methodology for territorial history while simultaneously articulating a fiercely anti-curial, proto-nationalist political philosophy that deeply impacted the intellectual landscape of early modern Europe.Born in the Lower Bavarian town of Abensberg—from whose Latinized name, Aventinum, he adopted his humanist pseudonym—Aventinus was the son of Peter Thurmair, a prosperous and respected innkeeper of the establishment 'Zum Rothaase.' From his early youth, Thurmair exhibited an extraordinary intellectual capacity, receiving his initial schooling at the Latin school of Abensberg before matriculating at the University of Ingolstadt in 1495. The academic environment at Ingolstadt, though still dominated by scholastic traditions, was beginning to absorb the fresh currents of Italian humanism. Seeking a broader engagement with classical studies, Aventinus relocated in 1498 to the University of Vienna, which had recently become the undisputed epicenter of German humanism following the arrival of Conrad Celtis (1459–1508). Under Celtis’s charismatic tutelage, Aventinus was initiated into the Sodalitas Litteraria Danubiana, absorbing Celtis’s vision of a revitalized Germanic culture capable of rivalling Italian intellectual supremacy through the rediscovery of native antiquities and classical poetry.Aventinus’s educational pilgrimage continued across the major university centers of Central and Western Europe. In 1503, he spent time at the University of Kraków, then a renowned center for mathematical and astronomical studies, where he deepened his knowledge of geography and classical science under humanists such as Laurentius Corvinus. In 1504, he traveled to the University of Paris, enrolling at the Collège de Lemoine. In Paris, Aventinus came under the profound influence of Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples (Jacobus Fabricius Stapulensis, c. 1455–1536), whose Christian humanism, Aristotelian commentaries, and irenic pedagogical reform left an indelible mark on the young Bavarian scholar. Obtaining his Master of Arts degree from Paris in 1507, Aventinus returned to Bavaria equipped with an unrivaled mastery of Latin philology, Greek literature, pedagogical theory, and historical method, positioning himself as one of the premier intellectuals of the Wittelsbach realm.Upon his return to Munich in 1507, Aventinus was quickly integrated into the courtly and academic circles of the House of Wittelsbach. In 1509, Duke William IV and his brother Duke Louis X of Bavaria entrusted Aventinus with the prestigious responsibility of serving as private tutor to their younger brother, Duke Ernest of Bavaria (1500–1560), who would later become the Prince-Bishop of Passau and Archbishop of Salzburg. Establishing his residence at the ducal court in Burghausen, Aventinus devised an innovative pedagogical curriculum based on classical philology, music theory, mathematics, and geography, rejecting the dry scholastic manuals of the medieval schoolmen. To facilitate this elite education, Aventinus authored a series of groundbreaking educational manuals, including the Rudimenta grammaticæ (1512), the Musica monographia (1516), and the Grammatica nova (1517), which synthesized Latin grammar with humanistic elegance.Aventinus’s pedagogical success in Burghausen solidified his reputation among the German intelligentsia. In 1516, he orchestrated the establishment of the Sodalitas Litteraria Angilostadensis at the University of Ingolstadt, an academic society designed to foster humanist scholarship, publish classical texts, and coordinate historical research across Bavaria. Through this network, Aventinus maintained an extensive correspondence with the leading luminaries of European humanism, including Willibald Pirckheimer (1470–1530), Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547), Hieronymus Gebwiler (1473–1545), and Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam (1466–1536). Recognized by the Wittelsbach dukes as a scholar of exceptional promise, Aventinus was officially appointed in February 1517 as the official Bayerischer Geschichtsschreiber (Historiographer of the Duchy of Bavaria)—a groundbreaking institutional appointment that liberated him from pedagogical duties and provided him with the financial patronage necessary to execute a comprehensive history of the Bavarian state.As official historiographer, Aventinus initiated an unprecedented research project that anticipated the modern archival revolution. Armed with ducal letters of authorization, he spent years traveling across the Holy Roman Empire, conducting extensive field research in imperial archives, municipal registries, and monastic libraries. He systematically examined and transcribed manuscript collections at major Benedictine and Augustinian abbeys, including St. Emmeram in Regensburg, Tegernsee, Niederaltaich, Weltenburg, Mondsee, Passau, Freising, and Salzburg. Unlike medieval chroniclers who uncritically copied mythic genealogies, Aventinus interrogated his primary sources with rigorous philological skepticism. He pioneered the use of auxiliary historical sciences in Germany, meticulously collecting Roman stone inscriptions (epigraphy), ancient coins (numismatics), medieval charters (diplomatics), and geographical landmarks. In 1523, he produced the Bavariae Descriptio, the very first printed geographical and topometrical map of Bavaria, printed via woodblock in Landshut.The culmination of this exhaustive archival labor was his Latin magnum opus, the Annales Boiorum (Annals of the Bavarians), composed between 1517 and 1521. Spanning seven massive volumes, the Annales provided a panoramic history of Bavaria from its legendary antique origins under the mythical king Tuisco and Celtic-Germanic tribes down to the imperial Diet of Worms in 1521 and the death of Emperor Maximilian I. Aventinus framed Bavarian history within the broader narrative of the Holy Roman Empire and European geopolitics, displaying an astonishing mastery of classical prose modeled on Livy, Tacitus, and Sallust. Recognizing that his Latin masterpiece remained inaccessible to the broader German public, Aventinus spent the years between 1526 and 1533 translating, recasting, and expanding the text into the vernacular, producing the Bayerische Chronik. Written in a powerful, evocative Early New High German (Frühneuhochdeutsch), the Bayerische Chronik transcended mere translation to become a vibrant piece of vernacular literature, rich in cultural detail, social commentary, and political polemic.Aventinus’s historiography was defined by a fiercely critical political and ecclesiastical ideology. Imbued with the irenic humanism of Erasmus and affected by the early developments of the Lutheran Reformation, Aventinus utilized his historical narratives to deliver a scathing critique of medieval papal overreach, monastic corruption, and ecclesiastical encroachment upon secular authority. He argued that the political decline of the German Empire was directly linked to the interference of the Roman Curia, detailing historical instances of papal interdicts, simony, and financial exploitation of the German populace. While Aventinus never formally severed his ties with the Catholic Church nor officially embraced the Lutheran church structure, his trenchant anti-clericalism and published critiques of ecclesiastical privileges aroused the intense hostility of conservative Catholic theologians in Munich and Ingolstadt, notably Johannes Eck (1486–1543).The intensifying confessional polarization of the Holy Roman Empire eventually engulfed Aventinus in severe persecution. In October 1528, while residing in Abensberg, he was abruptly arrested by the local inquisitorial authorities on charges of suspected Lutheran heresy, anti-clerical agitation, and violating fast laws. He was imprisoned in the castle of Abensberg, facing potential execution or life imprisonment. However, his high-ranking academic prestige and the immediate intervention of his former pupil, Prince Ernest of Bavaria, alongside Duke William IV, secured his prompt release after eleven days of confinement. Shaken by his imprisonment and realizing that his intellectual freedom was untenable in Catholic Munich or Ingolstadt, Aventinus sought sanctuary in the Free Imperial City of Regensburg, a municipal republic that was increasingly receptive to humanist reform and intellectual independence.In Regensburg, Aventinus spent the final years of his life in scholarly retreat, continuing his historical, linguistic, and musical investigations. In November 1529, at the age of fifty-two, he married Barbara Kraseis, the daughter of a Regensburg burger, with whom he had two children. Despite ongoing financial hardships and the persistent threat of confiscation of his manuscript collection, Aventinus refined his historical manuscripts until his sudden death on January 9, 1534, at the age of fifty-six. He was solemnly interred in the church of St. Rupert adjacent to the famous Benedictine Monastery of St. Emmeram in Regensburg, where his grave monument remains a testament to his enduring legacy.Because of their radical anti-curial content and the sensitive political environment of the Counter-Reformation in Bavaria, neither the Annales Boiorum nor the Bayerische Chronik could be published unexpurgated during Aventinus’s lifetime. The manuscript of the Annales Boiorum underwent a highly contentious publishing history. The editio princeps was printed posthumously at Ingolstadt in 1554 by the press of Alexander and Samuel Weissenhorn; however, this edition was heavily censored and expurgated by the Catholic humanist Hieronymus Ziegler, who excised hundreds of passages attacking the papacy and medieval clergy. It was not until 1580 that the complete, uncensored Latin text was published in the Protestant printing hub of Basel by Pietro Perna, meticulously edited by the Lutheran theologian and historian David Chytraeus (1530–1600). Similarly, the vernacular Bayerische Chronik was first published in Frankfurt am Main in 1566 by Georg Rab and Han Weigand, quickly becoming a central text for Protestant humanists and early modern political theorists across Central Europe.In the nineteenth century, the intellectual legacy of Aventinus underwent a massive revival, led by the emergence of modern professional historical science in Germany. The Royal Bavarian Academy of Sciences (Königliche Bayerische Akademie der Wissenschaften) recognized Aventinus as the founding father of Bavarian national history and undertook the monumental publication of his complete works. Between 1881 and 1908, the Academy published the definitive critical edition, Johannes Aventinus' Sämmtliche Werke, in six monumental volumes under the editorial direction of Sigmund von Riezler, Matthias von Lexer, and Gotthold Oldenbourg. Today, Aventinus is celebrated not only as a master of Renaissance Latinity and German prose, but as an indispensable architect of historical empiricism whose archival rigor, epigraphical precision, and courageous intellectual independence permanently transformed the writing of history in the Western tradition.

academic_description: 4to. 32 unnumbered leaves (the last is a blank). Collation: a6, b-c4, d6, e-g4. Title within an ornamental woodcut border. Wrappers, a fine copy.First edition. Although Aventinus had contacts with many fellow humanists and noblemen, his extant correspondence with them is surprisingly small. Among a little more than twenty extant letters written by and addressed to him we find among others the names of Konrad Celtis, Urbanus Rhegius, Beatus Rhenanus, Joachim Vadian, Philipp Melanchthon, Conrad Peutinger, and Willibald Pirckheimer.Aventinus' letters in this volume mostly concern the publication of the life of emperor Henry VI from a codex in the library of the monastery of Saint Emmeram. The first three letters, to the prior of Saint Emmeram, Ambrosius Münzer, to the librarian of the monastery Dionysius Menger and to the priest Ulrich Preu of Pföring, are letters of thanks for their help in the publishing venture. The letter to Leonard von Eck (1480-1550), a powerful figure in the political life of the time and an important councillor to duke William VI of Bavaria, and the two letters by Frederick III the Wise of Saxony to Aventinus are about a project of a chronicle of Saxony and Thuringia the Elector had entrusted to the humanist Georg Spalatin (1484-1545) (cf. Johannes Aventinus, Briefwechsel, in: “Sämmtliche Werke”, S.v. Riezler, ed., München, 1881, I/2, pp. 632-654).This work also testifies of the short lived Sodalitas literaria Angilostadiensis, an association of men of letters and learning from the environment of the University of Ingolstadt. The society benefited of the patronage of Duke Ernst of Bavaria and was presided by Leonard von Eck. It was licensed by the University (its statutes having been approved by the philosophical faculty), and it drew some local talent into the circle of companionship and scholarly activities. Most members, however, returned to other pursuits when the first flush of enthusiasm had subsided. The organisation languished for a while, then dissolved without formalities. But it was an interesting group while it lasted, and it provided stimulating companions for Aventinus. His first close acquaintance with Leonard von Eck came at this time. Another member, the Greek and Hebrew scholar Matthias Kretz, was destined to play an important part as opponent of Luther. Melchior Seuter was the author of several books on the Turkish wars, which Aventinus read with profit. Urbanus Rhegius lectured on poetry and rhetoric at the University before he was drawn to the side of the reformers and became a preacher in North Germany. A distinguished member was Georg Spies, or Cuspinus, a well-known jurist. There must have been good talk and lively debates, but in Aventinus' eyes the group's essential function was not discussion but publication. However, only the present edition of a medieval life of Emperor Henry IV was published under the auspices of the Sodalitas (cf. G. Strauss, Historian in an Age of Crisis. The Life and Work of Johannes Aventinus, Cambridge, MA, 1963, pp. 67-68).The present volume opens with the already mentioned biography (attributed to Erlung von Würzburg) of emperor Henry IV (1050-1106), who was chosen German King at Tribur in 1053, crowned at Aix-la-Chapelle in 1054, and appointed duke of Bavaria in 1055, and inherited after his father's death the kingdoms of Germany, Italy and Burgundy. Because of his early age these territories were governed in his name by his mother Agnes. In 1069 Henry took the reins of government into his own hands. No historical incident had more impressed the imagination of the western world than his abasement at Canossa, which represented the king as standing in the courtyard of the castle for three days in the snow, clad as a penitent, and entreating to be admitted to the presence of pope Gregory VII. It was, however, a move of policy to weaken the pope's position at the cost of a personal humiliation to himself. Henry was seen as a friend of the lower orders, was capable of generosity and gratitude, and showed considerable military skill. Unfortunate in the time in which he lived, and in the troubles with which he had to contend, he holds an honourable position in history as a monarch who resisted the excessive pretensions both of the papacy and of the ambitious feudal lords of Germany. Henry's biography is followed by nine of his letters. The volume closes with some Latin poems by the members of the Ingolstadt Sodalitas, i.e. Georg Spies, Johannes Kneissel, Urbanus Rhegius, Otto von Pack, Hieronymus Anfang, Melchior Soiter, Matthias Kretz, Magnus Haldenberger, David Rotmund, Georg Bossus, Georg Schack, and Augustinus Merbolt. Torgau, October 4, 1514 (l. e3v)Eck, Leonhard von (l. f1v) Johannes Aventinus was the son of an innkeeper in Abensberg, Lower Bavaria. He attended the local school of the Carmelite monastery and matriculated at the University of Ingolstadt in 1495. In 1496 he received the lower orders and pursued his humanistic studies in Vienna, Cracow and Paris. In 1517 he was appointed tutor to the dukes Louis and Ernest of Bavaria and was named historiographer to the dukes of Bavaria. His Annales Boiorum were severely anticlerical and thus unsuited for publication under the auspices of the Catholic dukes, and the Church set them on the Index. Not until 1554 was an expurgated version of the Annales published at Ingolstadt. Later in his life Aventinus continued to work on a chronicle of all Germany, of which, however, only the first book and an index were completed. He spent the rest of his life in the free imperial city of Regensburg, which remained aloof when the dukes of Bavaria began to repress all Lutheran tendencies. All of Aventinus' works were put on the Venetian Index in 1554 (cf. C. März, op. cit., cols. 72-77).

authors.name: Borghesi Diomede
authors.biography: Diomede Borghesi was born in Siena around 1540. He was a pupil of Ludovico Meneghini, professor at the local “Studio”. At an early age he was banned from the city for unknown reasons and confined for two years to Portoferraio on the island of Elba. He managed to escape to Mantua, where he gained the protection of Cardinal Federico Gonzaga.After the latter's death in 1564, he moved to Padua, and completed there his literary apprenticeship under Sperone Speroni, Francesco Piccolomini and Scipione Gonzaga. Although Borghesi had established his home in Padua, he nevertheless did not cease to roam through Italy. Between 1564 and 1587 he visited Venice, Bergamo, Verona, Rome, Viterbo, Perugia, Siena, Florence, Bologna, Ferrara, Reggio Emilia, Correggio, and Turin, where he became particularly known as a poet, composing various occasional poems for Carlo Emanuele of Savoy. Between 1566 and 1571 he published five volumes of Rime.In 1588 Borghesi entered the service of Ferdinando de' Medici, Grand Duke of Tuscany, who established a chair of ‘lingua Toscana‘, the very first in any Italian university. This chair was especially created for Borghesi to teach Tuscan to the many German and North Italian students present in Siena at that time (cf. A. Cappagli, Diomede Borghesi e Celso Cittadini lettori di toscana favella, in: “Tra Rinascimento e strutture attuali. Atti del primo convegno della Società Internazionale di Linguistica e Filologia Italiana, Siena, 28-31 marzo 1989”, Torino, 1991, I, pp. 23-35; and P. Rossi, La prima cattedra di lingua toscana dai ruoli allo studio senese, 1588-1743, Torino, 1910, passim).“His lecture notes, which are now in the Siena library and his tenure of the chair have been described by Rossi in his paper on the Tuscan language chair [see supra]. There are also two inaugural lectures by him delivered in connection with his academic duties [published respectively in 1589 and 1590], to which may be added an Oratione intorno agli onori della poesia e della eloquenza, printed in Siena in 1596. Most of Borghesi's extant philological works were written by him in epistolary form, and appear to have enjoyed some degree of popularity [...] Borghesi published some Lettere famigliari, the first [and only] volume bears the Padua imprint and the date 1578. In 1868 an edition of Borghesi's [unpublished] correspondence, edited by G. Campori, saw the light in Bologna from the press of G. Romagnoli” (R. Weiss, The Sienese Philologists of the Cinquecento. A Bibliographical Introduction, in: “Italian Studies” 3, 1946, pp. 44-45). From then on until his death on January 28, 1598, he lived in Siena, completely devoting himself to the study of grammar and language.

academic_description: 4to. [12], 136 pp. Collation: a4 b2 A-R4. With the printer's device on the title-page, ornamental woodcut initials. 18th century vellum over boards, red label with gilt title on spine, marbled endpapers, contemporary marginal annotations, entry of ownership by count Leonardo Trissino (1780-1841) dated 1837 (cf. D. Bortolan, Leonardo Trissino, celebre avventuriero, in: “Nuovo Archivio Veneto”, 1892, pp. 5-46). First edition, edited by Francesco Salce and dedicated by the author to Bianca Cappello (Padua, August 11, 1578), first lover and then from 1579 wife of Ferdinando de' Medici, of Diomede Borghesi's Lettere famigliari, so called to distinguish them from the Lettere discorsive, which he published in three parts (La prima [-II, -III] parte delle lettere, Padua, Lorenzo Pasquati, 1584; Venice, Francesco de' Franceschi, 1584; Siena, Luca Bonetti, 1603) and in which he exposed his grammatical theories on the Italian language.The collection contains 158 letters, arranged more or less in chronological order. “Un certain nombre est daté, de 1564 à 1578; leur classement est chronologique à l'exception de la première lettre du livre, du 1er juillet 1578, la plus récente, et des dernières qui marquent un retour en arrière. La plupart des lettres sont de compliment et assez brèves. Parmi les exceptions, on relèvera la première lettre du livre addressée à Scipion Gonzague prince d'Empire pour souligner l'estime attachée ‘oggidì' à ‘il parlar nobilmente et lo scriver con vaghezza et regolatamente' en général, et en particulier à la forme épistolaire, puis une lettre qui traite de la supériorité de la nature sur l'art c'est-à-dire de la poèsie sur les sciences (pp. 26-39) et une longue lettre de consolation (pp. 51-58). Le commerce littérarire tient aussi une certaine place dans ce recueil. Les destinataires principaux, parmi lesquels Bianca Capello, reçoivent entre 5 et 6 lettres” (J. Basso, Le genre épistolaire en langue italienne (1538-1662). Répertoire chronologique et analytique, Rome-Nancy, 1990, I, p. 279).“La reputazione del Borghesi assai più che alle Rime e alle Orazioni si raccomanda alle Lettere familiari e discorsive. Infatti mentre queste vanno lodate dei buoni precetti che porgono su vocaboli e frasi e su la più retta intelligenza della lingua nostra, quelle si pregiano di eleganza non artificiosa né studiata. Esse possono offrirsi ad esempio ai giovani e a chi voglia perfezionarsi in tal sorta di componimenti così necessaria ad ogni condizione di persone, perché non si discostano dall'uso moderno se non in quanto la purezza della lingua che negli scrittori moderni così raramente s'incontra scompagnata dall'artifizio e dalla fatica, appare nel Borghesi affatto naturale e spontanea” (Diomede Borghesi, Lettere, G. title: Lettere amorose di madonna Celia gentildonna romana, scritte al suo amante

authors.name: Celia Romana
authors.biography: Celia Romana (fl. second half of the sixteenth century) represents one of the most compelling and enigmatic figures within the landscape of Italian High Renaissance lyric poetry, situated at the vibrant intersection of mid-sixteenth-century Petrarchism, aristocratic female authorship, and the material history of early modern print culture. Writing during the pivotal decades of the Counter-Reformation and the consolidation of Bemban poetic orthodoxy, the author published under the intriguing designation of "M. Celia, gentildonna romana" (Madonna or Madama Celia, Roman noblewoman). Her sole surviving literary monument—a slender yet intensely expressive collection entitled Amorose rime di M. Celia, gentildonna romana, issued from the Emilian presses of Piacenza in 1562—occupies a singular place in the canon of petrarchismo al femminile. Alongside illustrious female contemporaries such as Vittoria Colonna (1492–1547), Veronica Gambara (1485–1550), Gaspara Stampa (1523–1554), Laura Terracina (1506–c. 1575), Tullia d'Aragona (c. 1510–1556), Chiara Matraini (1515–1604), and Laura Battiferri (1523–1589), Celia Romana contributed significantly to the democratization and diversification of early modern vernacular lyricism. However, unlike the spiritualized Neoplatonism of Colonna or the courtly panegyrics of Battiferri, Celia's verse is characterized by an unvarnished, visceral intensity, charting the psychological disintegration and emotional agony of an unrequited, agonizing passion with unmatched dramatic urgency.The biographical identity of Celia Romana has constituted one of the most enduring historical and philological puzzles in Renaissance literary scholarship. Operating in mid-sixteenth-century Rome—a city undergoing profound sociopolitical and religious transformations under the pontificates of Julius III (Giulio III Ciocchi del Monte, r. 1550–1555), Paul IV (Gian Pietro Carafa, r. 1555–1559), and Pius IV (Giovanni Angelo Medici, r. 1559–1565)—the poet moved within an environment where aristocratic female intellectual expression was tightly policed by patrician family structures and the tightening moral strictures of the Tridentine Church. Philologists and bibliophiles have long debated whether "Celia" was a baptismal name, a family surname (such as the Roman Debbia or Celli lineages), or an elaborate poetic pseudonym. Nineteenth-century archival hypotheses occasionally suggested that Celia might have been a high-ranking cortigiana onesta (an educated courtesan) operating within the elevated humanistic salons and papal diplomatic circles of Rome, drawing structural comparisons to Tullia d'Aragona or Veronica Franco. Conversely, competing theories hold that she was an authentic Roman patrician living in enforced social seclusion or religious retreat, whose highly personal manuscript notebook (scartafaccio) was surreptitiously obtained and transmitted to the printing press without her explicit public sanction. While early twentieth-century skepticism occasionally pondered whether the collection was an exercise in male prosopopoeia—a heteronym created by a male humanist constructing a female voice—modern scholarship, led by Italianists such as Carlo Dionisotti, Francine Daenens, Tatiana Crivelli, and Virginia Cox, overwhelmingly affirms the authenticity of her distinct female agency and subjective perspective.Literarily and stylistically, the Amorose rime consists of forty-five sonnets and several madrigals that together form an exceptionally tight, narrative-driven lyric sequence. Philological analysis demonstrates that Celia Romana operated with complete technical mastery over the Italian vernacular as codified by Pietro Bembo in his seminal Prose della vulgar lingua (1525). She adopted the traditional hendecasyllabic meter and Petrarchan rhyme schemes (primarily ABBA ABBA CDE CDE or CDC DCD), yet radically subverted the conventional emotional dynamics of the Petrarchan tradition. Where Petrarca and his male emulators constructed an idealized, distant female object of desire (the inaccessible Laura) viewed through a reflective, Neoplatonic lens, Celia inverted the gaze: she positioned herself as the agonized female subject, addressing a distant, cruel, or unfaithful male lover. Her poetry eschews the transcendent, sublime resolution typical of mainstream Renaissance Neoplatonism, refusing to convert earthly heartbreak into divine contemplation. Instead, her verses delve into the raw psychological realities of jealousy, betrayal, temporal decay, and existential despair. Intertextually, her work displays deep thematic affinities with the elegiac tradition of Catullus and Ovid, as well as the impassioned, immediate lyric voice of Gaspara Stampa, whose Rime had been posthumously printed in Venice in 1554. Celia's sonnets frequently utilize dramatic apostrophe, urgent interrogatives, and stark antitheses to articulate the claustrophobic confinement of a woman bound by societal decorum while consumed by an unquenchable internal fire.The material and printing history of Celia's work provides crucial insights into the editorial transmission of sixteenth-century vernacular poetry outside major publishing capitals. The princeps edition was issued in 1562 in Piacenza with the title Amorose rime di M. Celia, gentildonna romana. The choice of Piacenza—a key urban center within the Duchy of Parma and Piacenza under the rule of Ottavio Farnese—as the place of publication highlights the decentralized nature of Emilian print culture during the 1560s. Printing operations in Piacenza, represented by typographers such as Seth Viotti, Francesco Conti, and Giovanni Bazachi, frequently catered to elite manuscript circulation and regional humanistic academies, offering a discreet alternative to the massive commercial printhouses of Venice (such as those of Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari or Vincenzo Valgrisi). The publication of Celia's work reflects a broader mid-century publisher strategy: capitalizing on the immense public appetite for female-authored lyric collections, which were viewed as modern marvels of vernacular eloquence. However, unlike the widely reprinted anthologies of Vittoria Colonna or Laura Terracina, the print run of Celia's Amorose rime was exceptionally modest. The work was never granted a contemporary second edition, rendering original copies extraordinarily rare in European research libraries. Today, surviving exemplars are preserved in elite institutions, including the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana, the Biblioteca Nazionale Centrale di Firenze, and the British Library.The critical reception and historiographical legacy of Celia Romana underwent a dramatic evolution across four centuries. Following its initial appearance in 1562, the collection fell into relative obscurity during the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, overshadowed by the dominant counter-reformation religious poetry and the baroque extravagances of the Seicento. The literary re-emergence of Celia Romana began in the late nineteenth century, driven by the rise of scientific bibliography and historical philology in unified Italy. In 1888, the Venetian scholar Giuseppe Giuriati published a pioneering critical study and re-edition of her poetry, bringing her back to the attention of Renaissance specialists. This was followed in 1895 by Emilio Teza's rigorous textual analysis presented to the Reale Accademia dei Lincei. The decisive turning point in her critical fortunes arrived in 1945, when the eminent philosopher and literary critic Benedetto Croce dedicated an influential essay to her in his Poeti e scrittori del Pieno e Tardo Rinascimento. Croce praised Celia's verse for its psychological authenticity, emotional directness, and freedom from artificial rhetorical ornamentation, establishing her as one of the most original poetic voices of the Italian Cinquecento. In contemporary scholarship, Celia Romana is recognized as a vital component of the early modern female canon. Feminist literary historians and bibliographers, including Louise George Clubb, Laura Benedetti, Brian Richardson, and Abigail Brundin, continue to examine her work as a primary exemplar of female self-fashioning, subversion of patriarchal literary codes, and the complex mechanics of manuscript-to-print transmission in Renaissance Italy.

academic_description: 8vo. 76 leaves. A-I8, K4. With the printer's device on the title-page. Printed in italic. Eighteenth-century vellum over boards, lettering piece on spine, marbled edges. Ownership entries on the title page including "Mario de Candia", possibly the great Sardinian tenor with the same name (1810-1883).Fifth edition of this collection of sixty-eight fictitious love letters signed by Madonna Celia under her name or the pseudonym of Zima. First published in Venice by Antonio degli Antonii for Francesco Rampazzetto in 1562, it was reprinted 10 times until 1628.Towards the end of the century the book was put in the Index as all the works related to profane love, and therefore could be printed only donec expurgetur. “Lo stesso [Fabrizio] Zanetti ripubblicò nel 1600 le Lettere amorose di Madonna Celia Romana, con numerose variazioni rispetto alla prima edizione del 1562: veniva soppressa la dedica dell' ‘Amante alla Signora Lisa', sostituita con una lettera dedicatoria firmata dallo stesso Zanetti a Ottavio Sfoglio, ‘gentiluomo trevigiano'. In un avviso ai lettori, lo stampatore giustificava la sua operazione con il fatto che la raccolta da molti anni non aveva avuto riedizioni, eccetto alcune ‘mal corrette'. Anche in questo caso numerosi erano gli interventi sul testo: in modo particolare l'espurgatore eliminava tutti i termini religiosi usati per esprimere la passione amorosa […]” (L. Braida, Libri di lettere. Le raccolte epistolari del Cinquecento tra inquietudini religiose e “buon volgare”, Bari, 2009, pp. 284-285).The letters are all addressed by Celia to her anonymous lover, who is also the editor of the collection. In the dedication to Signora Lisa, he says that from the thousand letters he had received in the fifteen-year-long love affair with Celia, he had decided to select some of them in order to warn all men and all women against the dangers of love, and to demonstrate the intellectual and human qualities of Celia which, despite she had not received a proper education, leaked clearly even from her hasty letters. Most of the letters are dated. The earliest date is February 2, 1549; the latest December 30, 1560.“As the sixteenth century progressed, early modern writers continue to capitalize on the converging trends of epistolary literature and widespread interest in describing the female experience, turning increasingly to manuals and repertories for guidance. On the one hand, popular epistolary narratives such as the Lettere amorose of Madonna Celia and those of Girolamo Parabosco began to codify representations of the woman writer as an epistolary character motivated by passion and lovesickness. Models for such fictionalized and generalized female narrators, who fell from grace as they abandoned the feminine ideals of chastity and silence to follow their hearts, abounded” (M.K. Ray, Writing Gender in Women's Letter Collections of the Italian Renaissance, Toronto, 2009, p. 123).“The genre, and the pseudonymous publication, would lead us to suspect that the author was a fictional creation, though the fact that a sonnet by a Celia Romana appears in a verse collection of the period (Tempio, 1568, l. 31v) leaves open the possibility that she may have existed” (V. Cox, Women's Writing in Italy 1400-1650, Baltimore, MD, 2008, p. 317, no. 5).

authors.name: Melanchthon Philipp
authors.biography: Philipp Melanchthon (born Philipp Schwarzerdt; February 16, 1497 – April 19, 1560) stands alongside Martin Luther as one of the twin pillars of the Wittenberg Reformation and arguably the most decisive intellectual architect of Protestant educational, philosophical, and theological codification in early modern Europe. Known reverently to posterity as the Praeceptor Germaniae ("Teacher of Germany"), Melanchthon accomplished a monumental synthesis between the Greek and Latin philological rigor of Renaissance Humanism and the radical evangelical doctrines of salvation by faith alone. Where Martin Luther provided the charismatic, prophetic impulse and raw rhetorical power of the Reformation, Melanchthon supplied the systematic order, dialectical precision, pedagogical frameworks, and diplomatic formulations that enabled Protestantism to crystallize from an explosive religious protest into enduring ecclesiastical, academic, and political institutions.Born in the Palatinate town of Bretten to Georg Schwarzerdt, an armorer and keeper of the electoral artillery, and Barbara Reuter, the daughter of a prosperous merchant, young Philipp was raised in an environment that valued craftsmanship, piety, and civic responsibility. Following the premature death of his father and grandfather in 1508, the child’s intellectual trajectory was guided by his maternal grand-uncle, the renowned Christian humanist and Hebrew scholar Johannes Reuchlin. Recognizing the boy’s extraordinary aptitude for classical languages, Reuchlin served as his mentor, enrolling him in the Latin school at Pforzheim directed by Georg Simler. It was Reuchlin who, adhering to the prevailing humanist custom, hellenized the family name Schwarzerdt (meaning "black earth") into the Greek equivalent Melanchthon (Μελ΄αγχθων). In 1509, at the astounding age of twelve, Melanchthon matriculated at the University of Heidelberg, completing his Bachelor of Arts in 1511. When denied the Master’s degree due to his youthful age, he moved to the University of Tübingen in 1512, where he immersed himself in Aristotelian philosophy, scholastic dialectic, mathematics, astronomy, and Greek literature, receiving his Master of Arts in 1514 at the age of seventeen.Melanchthon’s early career in Tübingen established him as a rising prodigy within the international Republic of Letters. He edited texts for the print shop of Thomas Anshelm, composed Latin verse, and published his celebrated Greek grammar, the Grammaticae Graecae libri duo (1518), which would remain a standard textbook across Europe for generations. In 1518, upon the recommendation of Johannes Reuchlin, Elector Frederick the Wise of Saxony appointed the twenty-one-year-old scholar to the newly established Chair of Greek at the University of Wittenberg. On August 29, 1518, Melanchthon delivered his epochal inaugural lecture, De corrigendis adolescentiae studiis ("On Reforming the Studies of Youth"), in which he issued a scathing critique of medieval scholasticism and articulated a bold humanist vision for academic reform. He advocated for a direct return to classical original sources (ad fontes), prioritizing Greek philology, classical rhetoric, and authentic Aristotelian textuality as essential instruments for purifying both secular learning and Christian theology.The arrival of Melanchthon at Wittenberg initiated one of the most famous intellectual partnerships in Western history. Martin Luther, who occupied the Chair of Theology, immediately recognized the young classicist's genius. Under Luther's influence, Melanchthon applied his formidable philological skills to biblical exegesis, formalizing evangelical theology in his groundbreaking work, the Loci Communes Rerum Theologicarum ("Common Topics of Theology"), published in 1521 by the Wittenberg printer Johann Rhau-Grunenberg. The Loci Communes represented the very first systematic treatment of Protestant theology, organizing biblical doctrines not through the abstract metaphysical categories of scholasticism, but through the thematic, rhetorical loci of law, sin, grace, faith, and sacraments. The work achieved instant international fame, going through dozens of printings and revisions during Melanchthon’s lifetime.Melanchthon’s diplomatic acumen and systematic clarity reached their zenith at the Diet of Augsburg in 1530. With Luther under imperial ban and unable to attend, Melanchthon served as the primary author and chief negotiator of the Confessio Augustana (the Augsburg Confession), the foundational confession of faith of the Lutheran Church presented to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. In drafting the document, Melanchthon sought to demonstrate that the evangelical reforms were not radical heresies, but rather a faithful restoration of the historic, catholic Christian faith rooted in Scripture and the early Church Fathers. When Roman Catholic theologians drafted the Confutatio Pontificia in response, Melanchthon composed the Apologia Confessionis Augustanae (1531), a masterpiece of theological defense and rhetorical strategy that further solidified Protestant confessional identity.Beyond his theological endeavors, Melanchthon transformed the European intellectual landscape through his sweeping educational reforms and philosophical manuals. He fundamentally reshaped the curricula of German universities—including Wittenberg, Marburg, Leipzig, and Heidelberg—and spearheaded the creation of the Protestant Gymnasium system. Believing that natural philosophy, mathematics, and human reason were gifts of God essential for maintaining moral order and understanding divine creation, Melanchthon composed standard university textbooks across the entire spectrum of the arts curriculum. His works on logic (Dialectica), rhetoric (Elementa Rhetorices), moral philosophy (Ethicae doctrinae elementa), psychology (De Anima), and natural science (Initia Doctrinae Physicae) reinstated a purified, humanist Aristotelianism that served as the philosophical foundation for Protestant scholasticism and early modern scientific inquiry.The printing and circulation of Melanchthon’s works constitute a major chapter in early modern typographical history. Wittenberg became the undisputed center of Protestant publishing, where prominent printers such as Melchior Lotter the Younger, Hans Lufft, Joseph Klug, and Georg Rhau worked in close proximity to Melanchthon and Luther. Melanchthon personally oversaw the editorial quality and layout of his texts, collaborating with Lucas Cranach the Elder and his workshop for illustrative woodcuts and portrait frontispieces. Beyond Saxony, his writings were aggressively reprinted across major European printing hubs, including Basle (by Johann Bebel, Andreas Cratander, and Heinrich Petri), Strasbourg (by Wendelin Rihel and Johann Herwagen), Leipzig, and Frankfurt. Italian printers in Venice and Lyons frequently issued pirated or pseudonymous editions of his pedagogical texts, masking his name under latinized variants like Philip de Schwarzerdt to bypass the censors of the Roman Inquisition, thereby testifying to the universal demand for his scholastic textbooks even within Catholic territories.The final decade of Melanchthon’s life was marred by fierce theological controversies following the death of Martin Luther in 1546 and the military defeat of the Schmalkaldic League in 1547. Forced to navigate the political impositions of the Augsburg and Leipzig Interims, Melanchthon advocated a policy of concession on non-essential ecclesiastical rites (adiaphora) to preserve the core of evangelical preaching. This compromise ignited the intense Adiaphoristic Controversy, during which strict, ultra-orthodox Lutherans—known as the Gnesio-Lutherans, led by Matthias Flacius Illyricus—accused Melanchthon of treason against the Reformation. Concurrently, debates erupted over the human will in salvation (the Synergistic Controversy) and the nature of Christ’s presence in the Eucharist, with critics accusing Melanchthon of leaning toward Calvinist or Crypto-Calvinist positions in later revisions of his works (such as the Variata edition of the Augsburg Confession).Philipp Melanchthon died in Wittenberg on April 19, 1560, and was buried alongside Martin Luther in the Schlosskirche (Castle Church). Despite the bitter late-sixteenth-century confessional polemics that sought to overshadow his legacy, modern historical scholarship has reaffirmed Melanchthon’s monumental status. He was neither a mere shadow of Luther nor a compromised vacillator, but an intellectual titan who provided Protestantism with its pedagogical apparatus, its philosophical vocabulary, its legal and political framework, and its ecumenical vision. His integration of classical humanism with biblical faith permanently altered the trajectory of Western education, leaving an indelible imprint on the cultural and intellectual history of early modern Europe.

academic_description: 8vo. [16], 550 [i.e. 590, with errors in the pagination], [2] pp. Collation: α8, a-z8, A-O8. With the printer's device on the title-page. Contemporary blind-stamped pigskin. With the autograph entry of ownership of Johannes Sagittarius (Schütz), Protestant theologian (1531-1584), and the engraved book plate of the jurist Christian Carl Ludwig von Savigny (1684-1740). First edition of Melanchthon's first published letter collection. His correspondence, larger than that of Luther and Erasmus combined (nearly ten thousand letters), spanned the European continent. He had contacts in every major court and university in Europe (cf. C. Mundhenk, Melanchthons Briefwechsel, in: “Die Forschungsvorhaben der Heidelberger Akademie der Wissenschaften 1909-2009”, V. Sellin, E. Wolgast & S. Zwies, eds., Heidelberg, 2009, pp. 156-157).Published five years after Melanchthon's death, this collection was compiled by Johannes Manlius (d. after 1571). A native of Ansbach, he came as a young student to Wittenberg in 1548, obtained a master degree in 1558 and started to teach in the philosophical faculty in 1559. Later he was active as a pastor in various small German towns. In 1562 he publish in Basel his Locorum communium collectanea, a collection of sayings and anecdotes, which Melanchthon had used in his lectures. The work was a great success, in fact until 1600 appeared 14 editions and 2 German translations. Manlius had access to many of Melanchthon's letters mainly during his position as the latter's secretary (probably from 1556 to 1557) (cf. M. Simon, Johann Manlius, der erste Herausgeber von Melanchthonbriefen, in: “Zeitschrift für bayerische Kirchengeschichte”, 24, 1955, pp. 141-149).Manlius' edition was sharply criticized by Melanchthon's son-in-law and editor of his Opera Omnia, Caspar Peucer, who quickly countered with his own letter collection (Epistolae selectiores, Wittenberg, 1565, see item no. XXX). Soon thereafter in 1569 Joachim Camerarius provided a rich resource with a volume of some six hundred letters, which he had personally received from Melanchthon himself. In 1570 Peucer published a second collection of Melanchthon's letters, a libellus tertius was issued by Christoph Pezel in 1590 and a liber quartus was edited by Johannes Saubert in 1640, followed by the liber quintus et ultimus in 1646 and by a sixth book edited by Ludwig Camerarius (Leiden, 1647).The volume contains 422 pieces (70 of which are not by Melanchthon) and opens with a prefatory letter by Manlius to Christoph Jonas, Thomas Matthias, and Christoph Meienburger, all councilors to George Frederick of Brandenburg-Ansbach, to which follows a letter from Heinrich Claviger to Manlius dated [August 2], 1564.“Melanchthon hatte ein ganz anderes Verhältnis zu seiner Korrespondenz als die Mehrzahl der Humanisten. Seine Privatbriefe sind echte Augenblickserzeugnisse. Formale oder inhaltliche Rücksichten auf eine Veröffentlichung kennt er nicht. Er schreibt ohne Umschweife, was er zu sagen hat. Und er hat immer etwas Wichtiges zu sagen. Blumige Redewendungen einzuflechten, die Briefe ‘unter die Feile zu nehmen', verbot ihm der Drang der Geschäfte. Er merkte selbst, dass er sich von der ‘eleganten' Schreibweise der Humanisten, derer auch in seiner Jugend gezollt hatte, immer weiter entfernte. ‘Trocken' nennt er seinen Stil. Uns heutzutage spricht diese Sachlichkeit mehr an als die allzuoft nichtssagende Verschraubtheit mancher Humanisten, und auch Zeitgenossen stellten den Inhalt über die Form und rühmten die Klarheit der Sprache Melanchthons” (H. Scheible, Überlieferung und Editionen der Briefe Melanchthons, in: “Melanchthon und die Reformation”, G. May & R. Decot, eds., Mainz, 1996, p. 136). (Pars prima:)George [III] of Anhalt[-Dessau]. [Wittenberg,] (p. 550, i.e. 559, Dedi nuper ad te literas) Philipp Melanchthon (Schwarzterdt) was born in Bretten (Palatinate) on February 16, 1497. His mother was the niece of Johann Reuchlin, who later bestowed on him the Greek name of Melanchthon. Privately taught as a child by Johann Unger, in 1508 he attended the Latin school in Pforzheim, where the director Georg Simler introduced him to the study of Greek.In 1509 he matriculated at the University of Heidelberg, where he met Jacob Wimpfeling, and two years later at the University of Tübingen, where he obtained his MA in 1514. Between 1514 and 1516 he taught some courses at the university and collaborated as a corrector at the press of Thomas Anshelm.In 1518 he was appointed to the new chair of Greek at the University of Wittenberg. Already since his inaugural speech (De corrigenda adulescentiae studiis), he proposed a through reform program of education. Early on he also began to support Luther's theological reform and defend him in his publications. In 1523 Melanchthon was elected rector of the Wittenberg University, despite its statutes requested a celibate for that position, and in 1536, under the university's new constitution, he, like Luther, received the privilege to organize his courses independently of faculty regulations. His lectures formed the basis for those numerous commentaries and textbooks that, revised and rewritten many times, have earned him the title of ‘Praeceptor Germaniae'.Besides his scholarly work, he was deeply involved in ecclesiastical politics: he prepared memoranda, undertook many journeys (in particular he attended the diet of Augsburg in 1530, the political meetings in Schmalkalden, and the colloquy of Worms in 1541), and composed milestone works as Loci communes rerum theologicarum and the Confessio Augustana. During the war of Schmalkalden (1546-1547), which led to the siege and occupation of Wittenberg, he fled to Nordhausen. In 1557 he attended in Worms his last religious colloquy and helped reorganize the University of Heidelberg. On a trip to Leipzig to an examination of candidates at the university he caught a cold from which he died in Wittenberg on April 19, 1560. He was laid to rest next to Luther in the castle church.Melanchthon's importance for the Reformation lay essentially in the fact that he systematized Luther's ideas, defended them in public, and made them the basis of a religious education. These two, by complementing each other, could be said to have harmoniously achieved the results of the Reformation.As a reformer, Melanchthon was characterized by moderation, conscientiousness, caution, and love of peace; but these qualities were sometimes said to only be lack of decision, consistence, and courage. Often, however, his actions are shown stemming not from anxiety for his own safety, but from regard for the welfare of the community and for the quiet development of the Church.As a scholar Melanchthon embodied the entire spiritual culture of his age. At the same time he found the simplest, clearest, and most suitable form for his knowledge; therefore his manuals, even if they were not always original, were quickly introduced into schools and kept their place for more than a century. In ethics Melanchthon preserved and renewed the tradition of ancient morality and represented the Evangelical conception of life. His books bearing directly on morals were chiefly drawn from the classics, and were influenced not so much by Aristotle as by Cicero. Melanchthon's formulation of the authority of Scripture became the norm for the following time. The principle of his hermeneutics is expressed in his words: “Every theologian and faithful interpreter of the heavenly doctrine must necessarily be first a grammarian, then a dialectician, and finally a witness”.In the sphere of historical theology the influence of Melanchthon may be traced until the seventeenth century, especially in the method of treating church history in connection with political history. His was the first Protestant attempt at a history of dogma.As a philologist and pedagogue Melanchthon was the spiritual heir of the South German Humanists, of men like Reuchlin, Wimpheling, and Rudolph Agricola, who represented an ethical conception of the humanities. The liberal arts and a classical education were for him only a means to an ethical and religious end. The ancient classics were for him in the first place the sources of a purer knowledge, but they were also the best means of educating the youth both by their beauty of form and by their ethical content. By his organizing activity in the sphere of educational institutions and by his compilations of Latin and Greek grammars and commentaries, Melanchthon became the founder of the learned schools of Evangelical Germany, a combination of humanistic and Christian ideals. In philosophy also Melanchthon was the teacher of the whole German Protestant world (cf. H. Scheible, Melanchthon. Eine Biographie, München, 1997, passim).
