authors.name: Guevara Antonio de
authors.biography: Fray Antonio de Guevara (c. 1481 – 3 April 1545) stands as one of the most widely read, translated, and culturally influential prose authors of the European Renaissance. A Franciscan friar, royal chaplain, official court chronicler (cronista real), and imperial preacher to Emperor Charles V, who subsequently elevated him to the bishoprics of Guadix (1528–1537) and Mondoñedo (1537–1545), Guevara constructed a distinctive literary oeuvre that bridged late medieval moral didacticism, Christian humanism, Stoic philosophy, and courtly satire. His works—characterized by a highly stylized, balanced, and antithetical prose style—exerted an overwhelming impact on early modern European vernacular literature, shaping the development of Renaissance epistolary art, the political genre of the mirror for princes (speculum principis), the court-versus-country topoi, and early English prose aesthetics, most notably Tudor Euphuism.Early Life, Noble Lineage, and Formative EducationBorn in Treceño (in the Cantabrian region of Asturias de Santillana) around 1581, Antonio de Guevara belonged to a prestigious, albeit cadet branch of the aristocratic House of Guevara. His father, Juan Beltrán de Guevara, and his mother, Elvira de Noroña y Calderón, maintained ties to the high nobility of Castile. Details regarding his earliest years remain wrapped in the self-fashioning narratives of his own writings, but it is firmly established that his youth was spent in the environment of the royal court of the Catholic Monarchs, Queen Isabella I of Castile and King Ferdinand II of Aragon. There, Guevara received an elite courtly education alongside the royal pageboys, absorbing the chivalric, political, and early humanist ideals circulating in late fifteenth-century Spain.Following the death of Prince Juan in 1497 and Queen Isabella in 1504, the young courtier underwent a profound spiritual crisis and decided to renounce his secular career. Around 1504, Guevara entered the Order of Friars Minor (OFM), joining the Observant Franciscan branch. He undertook rigorous theological, scholastic, and classical studies within Franciscan monasteries in Castile, quickly gaining recognition for his exceptional oratorical talents, legal acumen, and mastery of rhetoric. Within the order, he rose through the administrative hierarchy, serving as guardian of several friaries, provincial definitor, and custodian of the Franciscan province of Concepción. Imperial Service: Court Preacher, Chronicler, and Diplomat under Charles VGuevara's definitive entry into imperial politics occurred in 1521 when he was appointed court preacher (predicador real) to the young King Charles I of Spain (soon to become Holy Roman Emperor Charles V). During the turbulent period of the Revolt of the Comuneros (1520–1521), Guevara positioned himself as a steadfast defender of royal authority. He participated actively in diplomatic missions on behalf of the Crown, negotiating with the rebellious cities and drafting moralizing letters—such as his famous Epístola a los comuneros—admonishing the rebels to lay down their arms and submit to the emperor. His loyalty during the crisis solidified his standing at the imperial center.In 1526, Charles V appointed Guevara to the prestigious position of Imperial Chronicler (Cronista Real) and royal chaplain. In this capacity, Guevara accompanied the imperial court on its restless itineraries across Spain, Italy, and North Africa. He was present at the historic Cortes of Toledo, Madrid, and Valladolid, and attended Charles V during his triumphant campaign against the Ottoman-backed corsair Hayreddin Barbarossa in the Conquest of Tunis in 1535. Guevara's proximity to the monarch allowed him to observe firsthand the inner workings of imperial diplomacy, courtly sycophancy, and military strategy, providing the empirical raw material for his political treatises and courtly satires. His royal favor culminated in his promotion to the episcopate: first as Bishop of Guadix in the Kingdom of Granada (1528), where he worked to enforce religious conformity among the newly converted Moriscos, and later as Bishop of Mondoñedo in Galicia (1537), where he governed until his death in 1545.Major Literary Works, Ideology, and Pseudo-Historical MethodGuevara’s literary production ranks among the most published and republished in sixteenth-century Europe. His debut work, the Libro áureo de Marco Aurelio con el Relox de príncipes, was born out of a long composition process. Initially compiled in the mid-1520s as an invented biography and fake letter collection attributed to the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius, an unauthorized draft was pirated and published in Seville by the German typographer Jacobo Cromberger in 1528. Deeply incensed by this pirated release, Guevara thoroughly expanded and restructured the text, officially publishing the definitive version as the Relox de príncipes (Clock of Princes) through the royal printer Nicolás Tierri in Valladolid in 1529.The Relox de príncipes is a monumental example of the Renaissance speculum principis. Presented as a newly recovered classical biography of Marcus Aurelius, the work fuses Stoic philosophy, Christian morality, advice on governance, war, justice, and marital duties. Crucially, Guevara employed a technique of deliberate pseudo-epigraphy and historical invention: he manufactured classical citations, forged ancient laws, and invented historical episodes to serve his moral and political arguments. For Guevara, historical truth was subordinate to moral pedagogical utility. Through Marcus Aurelius, Guevara offered Charles V and early modern rulers an ideal model of the philosopher-king who balances absolute imperial prerogative with self-restraint, justice, and Christian piety.In 1539, while residing in Valladolid, Guevara oversaw the printing of a masterly cluster of four distinct works: Epístolas familiares (First Part, with the Second Part published in 1541), Menosprecio de corte y alabanza de aldea, Aviso de privados y doctrina de cortesanos, and De las vidas de los diez Césares. The Epístolas familiares (Family Letters) represented a crucial milestone in European epistolary literature. Blurring the boundary between real correspondence and fictional essayism, these letters addressed contemporary historical figures, aristocrats, and intellectuals on subjects ranging from medical advice and anti-courtly satire to classical philosophy, antiquarian curiosities, and moral theology.In Menosprecio de corte y alabanza de aldea (Scorn for the Court and Praise of the Countryside), Guevara articulated the classic Renaissance antithesis between the corrupting, deceptive atmosphere of the imperial court and the peaceful, virtuous life of rural retreat. Drawing upon Horatian (beatus ille) and Stoic topoi, the book offered a penetrating psychological critique of ambition, power, and courtly anxiety, resonating deeply with readers across a bureaucratizing Europe. Simultaneously, his Aviso de privados y doctrina de cortesanos provided a pragmatic, cynical, yet morally framed manual for royal favorites, exploring the perilous dynamics of proximity to sovereign power. Towards the end of his life, Guevara returned to explicit theological composition, producing the Monte Calvario (Part I, 1545; Part II, posth. 1550), a monumental Franciscan treatise on the Passion of Christ that combined affective meditation with patristic erudition.Printing History, Typographical Context, and International CirculationThe material production and print circulation of Guevara's works represent a phenomenal success story in early modern publishing history. His texts were magnificent commercial successes for printers across the Iberian Peninsula, Flanders, France, Italy, and England. The premier Iberian print workshops—including those of Nicolás Tierri and Juan de Villaquirán in Valladolid, Juan Cromberger in Seville, and Miguel de Eguía in Alcalá de Henares—issued numerous folio and quarto editions of his complete works throughout the 1530s and 1540s.Driven by an insatiable European demand for Spanish imperial culture, major typographical centers across Europe quickly began producing vernacular translations and Latin adaptations. In Antwerp, the presses of Martin Nuncio (Martin Nutius) and Johannes Steelsius regularly printed Spanish and translated editions to supply the Flemish and Northern European markets. In France, the renowned Lyonnese publishers Jean de Tournes and Guillaume Rouillé, along with Paris printers, produced elegant octavo and duodecimo editions translated by Antoine de Alaida, René Binet, and later Antoine de Belleforest. In Italy, Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari and Vincenzo Valgrisi in Venice published influential Italian translations rendered primarily by the Spanish expatriate scholar Alfonso de Ulloa.The English printing landscape was similarly transformed by Guevara. Lord Berners (John Bourchier) translated the Golden Book of Marcus Aurelius (published posthumously in 1535 by Thomas Berthelet), which became an immediate best-seller at the Tudor court. This was followed by Sir Thomas North’s monumental translation, The Diall of Princes (1557), printed by John Wayland. North’s translation served as a primary stylistic model for Elizabethan writers. The intricate, highly structured prose style of Guevara—replete with rhetorical parallelisms, balanced clauses, antitheses, and elaborate metaphors—was directly adopted and amplified by John Lyly in his 1578 novel Euphues: The Anatomy of Wit, thereby giving birth to the literary style known as Euphuism.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyWhile Guevara achieved unprecedented popularity during his lifetime, his penchant for historical fabrication provoked fierce contemporary polemics. The most famous attack came from the Valencian humanist Pedro de Rhua, a professor of rhetoric at Soria. In a series of famous critical letters (Cartas a Fray Antonio de Guevara, 1540–1548), Rhua rigorously exposed Guevara’s historical inaccuracies, fabricated classical citations, and forged ancient inscriptions. Rhua demanded that as an imperial chronicler, Guevara adhere strictly to historical truth rather than publishing moral fictions passed off as ancient history. Guevara treated these attacks with courtly disdain, maintaining that his primary objective was moral instruction rather than pedantic antiquarian accuracy.In modern historiography and literary scholarship, Guevara’s reputation has undergone significant re-evaluation. Marcelino Menéndez y Pelayo recognized him as a master of Spanish prose, albeit flawed by excessive rhetorical ornamentation. Américo Castro analyzed Guevara as a quintessential figure of Spanish Renaissance contradiction, caught between the imperial court and Franciscan asceticism. Later scholarship by Augustin Redondo, José Antonio Maravall, and Asunción Rallo Gruss re-established Guevara as a brilliant political ideologist and rhetorical innovator who understood the power of print media to shape public opinion and elite consciousness in Renaissance Europe. Today, Antonio de Guevara is celebrated as a pivotal architect of early modern European prose, whose writings provide an indispensable lens into the imperial ethos, literary taste, and philosophical anxieties of the sixteenth-century world.

Valladolid, June 25, 1539 (l. 33v)Allons, Alvaro (l. 59v)Manrique, Iñigo de (l. 66r) Antonio de Guevara was the major prose writer of sixteenth century Spain. The enormous success of his works, made him the first Spanish writer to achieve a status comparable to that of the great authors of antiquity. He was born around 1481 in the city of Treceño and moved in 1492 to the royal court, where he stayed until the mid 1510s. Around 1506 he joined the Franciscan Order. In 1521 Charles V summoned him to serve as preacher in the royal chapel, a post that he occupied, however, only two years later. In 1525 and 1526 he was sent to Valencia and Granada as a commissioner of the Inquisition to evangelize the Islamic population. As a reward, the emperor appointed him royal chronicler.In 1528 Guevara wrote the Libro aureo de Marco Aurelio, followed a year later by the Libro llamado Relox de principes, a reworking of the previous book, both of which became two of the most frequently published works in Europe. In 1529 he was elected bishop of Guadix, and in 1537 bishop of Mondoñedo. Three years later, probably because he felt uncomfortable, he asked for a different position in Valladolid, which, however, was denied to him. His disappointment is clearly manifest in his last works, including the second book of letters, which became more spiritual and ascetic. He died in 1545, while he was finishing La segunda parte del libro llamado Monte Calvario. By that time he had gained international renown and his writing where widely read and imitated all over Europe (cf. E. Grey, Guevara, A forgotten Renaissance Author, The Hague, 1973 passim; see also J.R. Jones, Antonio de Guevara, Boston, 1975, passim; and A. Redondo, Antonio de Guevara (1480?-1545) et l'Espagne de son temps. De la carrière officielle aux oeuvres politico-morales, Genève, 1976, passim).

authors.name: Ginanni Giuseppe
authors.biography: Count Giuseppe Ginanni (1692–1753) stands as one of the most distinguished figures in eighteenth-century Italian natural history, serving as a vital intellectual bridge between the microscopic revolution initiated by Marcello Malpighi and Francesco Redi and the systematic, empirical naturalism of the late Enlightenment. Born in Ravenna on November 23, 1692, into an ancient and patrician family of the Romagnol nobility, Ginanni devoted his life to the meticulous observation of the natural world, transforming his ancestral estates and the unique ecological habitats of the Venetian and Adriatic littoral into a living laboratory. At a time when European natural philosophy was gradually shedding the remaining speculative remnants of scholasticism, Ginanni introduced rigorous empirical protocols, quantitative field observations, and pioneering microscopic inspections to the study of avian reproduction, marine botany, zoophytology, and agricultural phytopathology. His work not only elevated the intellectual stature of Ravenna within the Republic of Letters but also profoundly influenced scientific academies across Bologna, Venice, Padua, and Paris.The Ginanni lineage was deeply entrenched in the administrative, legal, and intellectual fabric of the Legation of Ravenna within the Papal States. Giuseppe was the son of Count Giovanni Battista Ginanni and Maria Maddalena Vaini, and grew up in a household that venerated civic duty and humanistic learning. His older brother, Marco Antonio Ginanni (1690–1770), would achieve international acclaim as a scholar of heraldry and sigillography, authoring the seminal treatise L'arte del blasone. Giuseppe’s early education followed a classical course, encompassing Latin rhetoric, scholastic philosophy, and mathematics. However, his formative intellectual awakening occurred through his self-directed engagement with modern experimental philosophy. Inspired by the groundbreaking treatises of Giovanni Alfonso Borelli, Lorenzo Bellini, Antonio Vallisneri, and Count Luigi Ferdinando Marsili, the young Ginanni turned his back on pure speculative philosophy to immerse himself in the physical study of nature. He established a personal museum of natural history—a cabinet of specimens collected from the pine forests of Ravenna (the famed Pineta di Classe and Pineta di San Vitale), the surrounding marshlands, and the littoral waters of the northern Adriatic.Ginanni’s first monumental contribution to European science arrived with the publication of his masterpiece on avian oology and ethology, entitled Delle uova e dei nidi degli uccelli libro primo..., published in Venice in 1737. Prior to this landmark treatise, European ornithology had treated birds' eggs and nesting behaviors as mere peripheral curiosities or culinary footnotes. Ginanni approached the topic with revolutionary scientific rigor, conducting systematic field observations across the seasonal cycles of native and migratory birds. He analyzed the architectural mechanics of nest construction, the physical properties and pigmentation of eggshells, the internal embryonic structures observable through early-stage incubation, and the physiological mechanics of laying. The treatise was conceived on a grand scale, featuring exquisite full-page copperplate engravings that depicted eggs at full size alongside intricate structural details of nests. Ginanni’s methodical classification predated modern oological taxonomies and earned immediate acclaim from European naturalists, including René Antoine Ferchault de Réaumur and Buffon, who recognized the work as an unprecedented monograph in field biology.Parallel to his ornithological research, Ginanni turned his attention to marine biology and zoophytology, an area of fierce debate among eighteenth-century scientists regarding the boundary between the plant and animal kingdoms. Spending months along the coastlines of Ravenna, Cervia, and Venice, Ginanni collected, dried, and micro-dissected hundreds of marine specimens. He conducted exhaustive investigations into seaweeds, corals, calcifying algae, polyps, and sponges. Opposing the antiquated theories of spontaneous generation, Ginanni demonstrated through careful dissection and microscopic observation that many structures previously categorized as sub-aquatic plants were in fact animal colonies or organo-mineral structures generated by living polyps. His research directly built upon and refined Luigi Ferdinando Marsili’s Histoire physique de la mer (1725). Furthermore, Ginanni made foundational contributions to agricultural science through his field studies on cereal diseases, particularly grain smut and wheat rust (la nebbia del grano). By examining infected stalks under compound microscopes, Ginanni identified structural anomalies in plant tissues caused by parasitic fungi and climatic fluctuations, laying essential groundwork for modern plant pathology decades before the formalization of modern phytopathology by European agronomists.The publishing history and typographical execution of Ginanni’s works reflect the vibrant print culture of mid-eighteenth-century Venice. His 1737 treatise Delle uova e dei nidi degli uccelli was produced in a magnificent quarto format by the Venetian printer Antonio Tiauto under the typographical supervision of Ercole Lami. The work was praised for its crisp Latin and Italian typography, wide margins, and exceptional plate quality. Following Giuseppe’s death on October 23, 1753, his natural history collections and extensive unpublished manuscripts were preserved and edited by his nephew, Count Francesco Ginanni (1716–1766)—himself a distinguished scholar and author of Delle malattie del grano in erba (1759). Between 1755 and 1757, Francesco overseen the posthumous publication of Giuseppe’s complete marine and botanical research, issued in two lavish folio volumes in Venice by the printer Guglielmo Zerletti under the title Opere postume del conte Giuseppe Ginanni ravennate. The first volume contained descriptions and copperplates of 114 marine plants, while the second volume contained 152 plates dedicated to corals, zoophytes, and shell structures, preceded by a celebrated biographical memoir written by Francesco.Throughout his mature life, Giuseppe Ginanni maintained an active role in European intellectual networks. He was a corresponding member of the prestigious Accademia delle Scienze dell'Istituto di Bologna and maintained regular scientific correspondence with leading naturalists of the Italian Peninsula, including Giovanni Battista Morgagni, Scipione Maffei, and Antonio Vallisneri. The historiographical reception of Ginanni’s legacy has consistently highlighted his pioneering role in empirical observation. Nineteenth-century historians of science, such as Georges Cuvier and Julius von Sachs, cited Ginanni’s contributions to marine zoology and plant physiology as fundamental milestones in the development of modern natural history. In the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, scholarship by scientific historians has re-evaluated Ginanni’s extensive archival legacy preserved at the Biblioteca Classense in Ravenna, solidifying his status as a master of Enlightenment natural philosophy whose meticulous field methodologies helped transform descriptive natural history into a modern, empirical science.

academic_description: WITH 22 COPPERPLATE ENGRAVINGS OF BIRD EGGS AND 8 PLATES OF GRASSHOPPERSFolio (mm. 290x208). Pp. [10, including the engraved frontispiece and title page], 130, [2], 55, [3] and [1: Classe prima delle uova degli uccelli terrestri non rapaci], XIII, [1: Classe seconda delle uova degli uccelli terrestri rapaci], XIV-XVI, [1: Classe terza delle uova degli uccelli aquatici], XVII-XXII, [1 blank], VIII leaves of plates. Collation: [A]4 B-Bb4. Leaf Bb4 is blank. Woodcut initials, headpieces, and tailpieces. The Dissertazione delle cavallette commences with its own title page on leaf Z1r. Contemporary cardboard binding with raised bands and manuscript title on the spine. On the front free endpaper, the ex-libris of the gastronomic collection of Jacques and Hélène Bon. The volume is slightly loose, yet a splendid copy, as new, uncut, and largely unopened.This is the first edition of the first printed book entirely devoted to the eggs and nests of birds. These are categorized into three groups: terrestrial raptors, other terrestrial birds, and aquatic birds. Each plate depicts between one and nine eggs, encompassing a total of 111 species.Giuseppe Ginanni (or Zinanni) was born in Ravenna in 1692. After completing his studies at the college of nobles in Ravenna, directed by the Jesuits, he traveled to Padua in 1715, where he met Antonio Vallisneri, who guided him towards naturalistic studies. In the garden of his own home, Ginanni established a veritable botanical garden, which he continuously expanded and enriched with exotic plants, obtained from Giulio Pontedera, the prefect of the botanical garden of Padua. In 1732, he established contact with the Florentine botanist Pier Antonio Micheli, to whom he supplied numerous plants from the Ravenna region. Besides Vallisneri and Micheli, Giovanni Bianchi (Janus Plancus), considered an authority in marine biology, also exerted significant influence on Ginanni. Between 1732 and 1737, he devoted himself to observations on grasshoppers and the collection of bird eggs and nests. He subsequently traveled to Venice to personally oversee the publication of the work in which he presented these studies. This work garnered him considerable fame as a naturalist and in 1737 led to his affiliation with the Academy of the Institute of Sciences of Bologna. Ginanni later focused on the study of mollusks, brachiopods, and other marine animals, as well as insects, fossils, and algae. These researches, left unpublished, were posthumously published in two volumes by his nephew Francesco Ginanni (Venice, 1757) (cf. G. Ongaro, Ginanni, Giuseppe, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 55, Rome, 2001, s.v.).

authors.name: Hulak Mykola Ivanovich
authors.biography: Mykola Ivanovych Hulak (also rendered in imperial Russian historiography as Nikolai Ivanovich Gulak; May 25 [June 6], 1821 – May 26 [June 7], 1899) stands as one of the most intellectually formidable, morally resolute, and polymathic figures of the nineteenth-century Ukrainian national awakening (Vidrodzhennya). A jurist, historian, mathematician, philologist, and public activist, Hulak was a co-founder and the principal organizational mind behind the Brotherhood of Saints Cyril and Methodius (Kirillo-Mefodiyevskoye bratstvo), a secret political society established in Kyiv in late 1845. Operating at the confluence of Romantic nationalism, Pan-Slavic federalism, and Christian democratic radicalism, Hulak articulated a vision of total social emancipation—demanding the abolition of serfdom, the eradication of autocratic Tsarist rule, and the establishment of a decentralized, democratic federation of equal Slavic republics. His unwavering defiance during the Imperial Russian political trials of 1847, followed by three years of solitary confinement in the notorious Shlisselburg Fortress and lifelong exile from his homeland, transformed him into a archetype of intellectual martyrdom. Later in life, while exiled in the Caucasus, Hulak transformed into a pioneering scholar of Georgian, Persian, and Azerbaijani literatures, as well as a philosopher of science and non-Euclidean geometry, embodying the highest ideals of nineteenth-century European universal humanism.Early Life, Nobility, and Formative Education at DorpatMykola Hulak was born into an educated family of the Ukrainian Cossack-gentry nobility (starshyna) in Warsaw, where his father, Ivan Hulak, served as an official in the imperial administration before retiring to the family estate in the Poltava Governorate. The Hulak lineage traced its ancestry back to prominent Cossack military commanders of the Hetmanate, a background that deeply ingrained in young Mykola a profound historical memory of Ukrainian autonomy and constitutional traditions. Raised in an environment that prioritized intellectual rigor, Hulak demonstrated an extraordinary aptitude for classical and modern languages from early childhood, mastering Latin, Ancient Greek, German, French, and Polish alongside his native Ukrainian and Russian.In 1838, Hulak matriculated at the Imperial University of Dorpat (modern Tartu, Estonia), one of the preeminent centers of legal and scientific learning in the Russian Empire. Dorpat occupied a unique cultural space: heavily influenced by Baltic German academic traditions, the university served as a conduit for Kantian and Hegelian philosophy, German historical jurisprudence (specifically the ideas of Friedrich Carl von Savigny), and European constitutional theory. Hulak immersed himself in Roman law, comparative jurisprudence, historical linguistics, and higher mathematics. He graduated in 1843 with the degree of Candidate of Law, presenting a thesis that showcased an advanced mastery of legal history and institutional philosophy. The intellectual atmosphere of Dorpat fostered in Hulak a profound commitment to constitutionalism, civil liberties, and rationalist enquiry, distinguishing his legal philosophy from the purely emotional or romantic Slavophilism that prevailed in Moscow and St. Petersburg.The Kyiv Period and the Cyril and Methodius BrotherhoodFollowing his graduation, Hulak spent a brief period working in the administrative bureaucracy in St. Petersburg before securing a post in Kyiv in 1845 as an official in the chancellery of the Governor-General of Kyiv, Podolia, and Volhynia. Kyiv at the mid-nineteenth century was undergoing a turbulent cultural revival, centered around the Imperial University of Saint Vladimir. It was in this vibrant academic milieu that Hulak forged deep intellectual bonds with the historian Mykola Kostomarov and the educator Vasyl Bilozersky. Together, in December 1845 or January 1846, they founded the secret political organization known as the Brotherhood of Saints Cyril and Methodius.The Brotherhood soon attracted the premier minds of the Ukrainian intelligentsia, most notably the national poet Taras Shevchenko, the writer and translator Panteleimon Kulish, and the ethnographer Opanas Markovych. Within this intellectual cadre, Hulak represented the ideological vanguard and the legal-organizational backbone. While Kostomarov authored the society's mystical-historical manifesto, The Book of the Genesis of the Ukrainian People (Knyhy Bytiya Ukrayins'koho Narodu), Hulak was instrumental in drafting the organization's charter (Statut) and its foundational proclamations to the Slavic nations. Hulak’s vision was sharply political and uncompromisingly republican: he advocated for the absolute destruction of Russian imperial autocracy, the total emancipation of the peasantry from serfdom without compensation to landowners, universal literacy, and the creation of a pan-Slavic democratic federation anchored by an equal alliance of Ukrainians, Poles, Russians, Czechs, Slovaks, Serbs, Croats, and Bulgarians, with Kyiv serving as the federal capital and parliamentary seat.Positioned on the radical wing of the Brotherhood alongside Shevchenko, Hulak rejected passive educational gradualism, arguing that fundamental political transformation required structured organizational networks, covert agitation, and uncompromising ideological clarity. He maintained extensive correspondence with radical thinkers across the empire and amassed a massive personal library of prohibited political, philosophical, and legal literature, including works on Western European constitutional law and utopian socialism.Betrayal, Interrogation by the Third Section, and ImprisonmentThe existence of the secret society was betrayed in March 1847 by Alexey Petrov, a university student and police informant who overheard discussions among the brothers and gained access to their written draft documents. The Imperial Third Section (the secret political police), acting under the personal orders of Tsar Nicholas I and under the direction of Count Alexey Orlov, launched a swift and ruthless crackdown across Ukraine and Russia. Hulak was arrested on March 18, 1847, at his residence in St. Petersburg, where police seized a hoard of political manuscripts, ciphered documents, and personal journals.During the harrowing interrogations in St. Petersburg, Hulak displayed a legendary stoicism and intellectual composure that confounded the investigators of the Third Section. Refusing to succumb to psychological coercion, physical exhaustion, or promises of imperial clemency, Hulak steadfastly took sole responsibility for the political writings found in his possession. He shielded his comrades—particularly Shevchenko, Kostomarov, and Kulish—by asserting that the Brotherhood was merely a philosophical circle and that all radical political programs were his own personal, theoretical exercises. Recognizing his extraordinary legal acumen and immovable willpower, Imperial officials classified Hulak as the most dangerous and unrepentant conspirator of the entire circle.While Kostomarov and Kulish received lighter sentences or periods of exile, and Shevchenko was condemned to penal military service in the Transcaspian desert, Hulak was handed the harshest sentence among the non-military members: three years of solitary confinement in the terrifying Alexis Ravelin of the Shlisselburg Fortress, followed by indefinite administrative exile under strict police surveillance. His incarceration in the damp, subterranean casemates of Shlisselburg severely damaged his physical health, yet he utilized his years of solitary confinement to deepen his mastery of foreign languages, higher mathematics, and theoretical physics.Exile in Perm, Riazan, and the Caucasian RenaissanceUpon his release from Shlisselburg in 1850, Hulak was exiled to Perm, and later transferred to Riazan in 1855, remaining under constant surveillance by the Secret Police. Deprived of his noble status and barred from entering his native Ukraine or the imperial capitals of St. Petersburg and Moscow, Hulak turned to pedagogy and private scholarship to earn a livelihood. Following the death of Nicholas I and the general political thaw under Alexander II, Hulak was granted permission in 1859 to enter civil employment as a teacher in the peripheral regions of the empire.In 1859, Hulak relocated to the Caucasus, a region that would become his intellectual home for the remaining four decades of his life. He served as a professor of history, geography, mathematics, and classical languages in various gymnasiums, notably in Kutaisi, Tiflis (Tbilisi), Kerch, Stavropol, and Elizavetpol (Ganja). Free from the immediate pressure of Ukrainian political life but permanently alienated from his homeland, Hulak redirected his monumental intellectual energy toward the study of Caucasian and Oriental cultures.Hulak quickly acquired fluency in Georgian, Armenian, Azerbaijani Turkish, Persian, and Arabic. He became one of the foundational figures of scientific Kartvelology (Georgian studies) and Oriental philology in the Russian Empire. Between 1870 and 1890, Hulak accomplished monumental literary translations and critical studies. He translated the epic Georgian poem The Knight in the Panther's Skin (Vepkhistqaosani) by Shota Rustaveli into Russian verse, appending detailed philological, historical, and philosophical commentaries that placed Rustaveli alongside Dante and Shakespeare in the canon of world literature. Furthermore, he translated major portions of Ferdowsi's Persian epic, the Shahnameh, as well as works by the Azerbaijani poet Nizami Ganjavi. In addition to his literary achievements, Hulak published groundbreaking scientific essays on non-Euclidean geometry (advancing interpretations of Nikolai Lobachevsky), higher algebra, pedagogical theory, and regional ethnography in regional journals such as Kavkaz and Sbornik materialov dlya opisaniya mestnostey i plemen Kavkaza.Historiographical Legacy and Critical SignificanceMykola Hulak died on May 26 (June 7), 1899, in Elizavetpol (modern Ganja, Azerbaijan), where he was buried far from his native Ukrainian soil. For decades, the Tsarist censorship suppressed his political legacy, attempting to reduce his memory to that of an obscure provincial schoolteacher and translator. However, nineteenth- and twentieth-century historiography gradually restored Hulak to his rightfully exalted position in the pantheon of Eastern European intellectual history.Scholars of the Ukrainian national awakening—ranging from Vasily Semevsky and Pyotr Zaionchkovsky to modern historians like George Luckyj and Johannes Remy—recognize Hulak as the primary systemic theorist of democratic federalism within the nineteenth-century Slavic world. Unlike many contemporary Romantic intellectuals whose nationalism was rooted purely in poetic or ethnographic sentimentality, Hulak grounded Ukrainian national aspirations in rigorous legal philosophy, institutional constitutionalism, and universal human rights. His heroic stoicism during the 1847 trials preserved the survival of Ukraine's intellectual elite at a critical juncture, ensuring that the ideological seeds sown by the Cyril and Methodius Brotherhood would blossom into the broader political movements of the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

academic_description: 8vo (250x165 mm). [6], 150, [4] pp. and one large folding plate with geometrical figures. Editor's printed wrappers (worn, marginal paper loss, spine broken and roughly repaired). Some quires loose. A genuine copy preserved in a cloth box.Incredibly rare first and only edition of this pioneristic work on four-dimensional geometry. Mykola Ivanovich Hulak (or Nikolai Ivanovich Gulak or Goulak) was born in Warsaw in 1821 into a noble, but poor family from the Zolotonish district of the Poltava province. He spent his childhood and youth in the village of Mykolaivka, in the Kherson region. After graduating from the local gymnasium, he studied law at the University of Tartu in Estonia, graduating in 1844. From 1845 he served the Kiev governor-general as a translator and archaeographer.Hulak played an active part in the founding of the Cyril and Methodius Brotherhood (cf. P.S. Goncharuk, The harbinger of friendship and cooperation of peoples: to the 180th anniversary of the birth of Cyril and Methodius M.I. Hulak, Kyiv, 2002). He belonged to the radical wing of the organization, which defended national-democratic ideals and the idea of a peasant revolution. He advocated the elimination of autocracy and serfdom, the abolition of estates, universal education, and the unification of Slavic people. In January 1847 he moved to St. Petersburg, where he was arrested in March for his political activism. During interrogation, he refused to testify or name any of the brotherhood's members. He spent three years in the Shlisselburg Fortress, after which he was exiled to Perm. It was only 12 years later that he returned to Ukraine and began teaching. He taught geography and mathematics at the Russian-language lyceum in Odessa (1859-1861), history at the Kushnikov Women's Institute in Kerch (1861-1862), mathematics at the Stavropol gymnasium (1862-1863), physics and cosmography at the Kutaisi Gymnasium (1863-1867), and mathematics, physics, Latin and Greek at the Tiflis Gymnasium (1867-1886). After retiring, he moved to the Azerbaijani city of Yelizavetpol (later Kirovabad, today Ganja), where he died. A street in that city is named after him.Hulak had been interested in mathematics even before the Brotherhood was founded. While in prison, he studied the subject and later carried out research primarily related to non-Euclidean geometries and four-dimensional space. In 1859, he published “Studies on Transcendental Equations” in Odessa, and in 1877, he published the present work in Tbilisi (cf. M. Briefly & O. Antonyuk, Mikola Gulak as a mathematician: Monograph, Lutsk, 2004).In particolar, Hulak's second book aroused great interest. He published it with a dedication “To the memory of Lobachevsky”. He considered Lobachevsky's discoveries in non-Euclidean geometry to be of revolutionary importance. The introduction to the book is titled “A Conversation about Space”. Written in the form of a dialogue between the author and his friend “V”, it contains an exchange of thoughts about the theories of Nicolaus Copernicus and Nikolai Lobachevsky. The book, one of the first ever published in this field, deals with synthetic geometry and explores the properties of figures in a four-dimensional space. Hulak invented neologisms for the new concepts he was explaining (such as ‘sphero-sphere', ‘plano-planes', ‘prismo-prisms', ‘pyro-pyramides', so forth), and was one of the first to systematically treat four-dimensional geometry in a synthetic way, anticipating by decades some of the best-known developments in the West (even though his works remained little known outside certain circles). Hulak also wrote a continuation to the “Attempt at Four-Dimensional Geometry” entitled “Analytical Geometry with Four Dimensions and with Spherical Tetrahedronometry”, but this work remained unpublished. The original manuscript ended up in the collection of Professor I.K. Andronov (cf. I.K. Omelchenko, Gulak, Mykola Ivanovich, in: “Great Ukrainian Encyclopedia”, online; G. Bevz, Mykola Hulak, in: “Mathematics at School”, 2011, no. 9, pp. 46-47).Hulak (pp. 25-26) claims that he had reached his conclusions in 1876, completely independently of Carl Friedrich Zöllner's Prinzipien einer elektrodynamischer Theorie der Materie (‘Principles of an Electrodynamic Theory of Matter', 1876): ‘Such a coincidence of my thoughts with those of a renowned scientist can only bring me joy because it confirms that we are both addressing a genuinely advanced issue that aligns with modern science'.During the Soviet era, Hulak was completely forgotten. It is only in recent years that he and his work have been rediscovered. He himself was quite an impressive figure. He was the first Ukrainian orientalist. He spoke Ukrainian, Russian, German, French, Latin, Greek and several Oriental languages (cf. Z.K. Aliyeva, Intelligentsia in linguistic studies and Georgian-Azerbaijani-Ukrainian relations, in: “Scientific notes of the Nizhyn State University named after Mykola Gogol. Series: Philological Sciences”, 2013, 4, pp. 302-308). Roman Ivanychuk's 1984 historical novel, “The Fourth Dimension”, is dedicated to Hulak and his passion for mathematics. In the afterword to the novel, Ivanychuk writes: “Mykola Ivanovich Hulak was the most active organiser of the Cyril and Methodius Brotherhood. He was an outstanding mathematician, lawyer, literary scholar, orientalist, translator and philosopher with encyclopaedic knowledge. He was also a political scientist who knew twenty languages perfectly”.“Interestingly, [the renowned Russian polymath and religious philosopher Pavel] Florensky understood it [the concept of the fourth dimension] not only as time, but also as ‘depth' -a peculiar quasi-metaphysical depth of reality that should not be confused with depth in a usual, three-dimensional sense, and especially not with perspectival depth. This rather uncommon notion came from a book called An Essay on the Geometry of Four Dimensions. Synthetic Geometry (“Opyt geometrii o chetyrekh izmereniyah. Geometriya sinteticheskaya”, 1877) by a Ukrainian scholar and educator named Nikolai Goulak (alternatively spelled as Mykola Hulak), whose biography Florensky considered writing during his university years. In the introduction, echoing Johann Carl Friedrich Zöllner's reflections on the non-Euclidian character of cosmic space, Goulak suggested that space in the universe may be most accurately described through Bernhard Riemann's elliptic geometry and conceived of as a closed ‘sphero-sphere' (sharo-shar) with constant positive curvature. ‘And having once assumed that our space has constant positive curvature, in all its points, we thus allow the existence of the fourth dimension-depth', which is ‘imperceptible by our sensory organs, but nevertheless as real as length, width, and height' (Goulak 1877, 13-14). The following exchange between the author (‘I') and his fictional interlocutor (‘V') is particularly instructive: ‘V. All this is wonderful, but I can't understand what exactly this fourth dimension-depthis, and why isn't it perceptible by our sensory organs? After all, you said yourself that the direction of depth is as real as the directions of length, width, and height […] I. Indeed, and I even claim that the depth axis is mutually perpendicular to the other axes and makes 90-degree angles with them. V. Well, here's the point O in space: I will pass through it, in fact or in imagination, three mutually perpendicular axes: length, width, and height, and you pass through this point, mentally, the fourth axis of depth. I. With pleasure. First of all, notice that the depth axis has, like the other three axes, two opposite directions: a positive direction and a negative direction. Consequently, this axis will pass through the point O, and at this point -but only at this one point- will cross our space […] Departing from the point O in the positive direction of the depth axis, we will leave our space and deepen into the sphero-sphere, for which Riemannian space serves as the outer edge. Take a good look at the ex-pression: deepen. So, the direction of the fourth axis lies not to the right or left, not above or below, not at the front or behind the point O, but straight inside it. Following the positive direction of the depth axis, we will finally reach the center of the universe […] (Goulak 1877, 20-21). Further on, to account for the inability of the human senses to perceive this mysterious ‘axis of depth', Goulak employed a popular explanatory device -the analogy with imaginary sentient inhabitants of two-dimensional space who would have no idea of a higher dimension. ‘Similarly, in our material world of three dimensions, we see and perceive not the very essence of external objects, but only their three-dimensional projection, just as in a picture we see their projection in two dimensions' (Goulak 1877, 21). In support of this argument, he cited several acclaimed sources, such as Plato's Republic, Goethe's Faust, and Louis Claude de Saint-Martin's Of Errors and Truth (Des erreurs et de la vérité, 1775). But the most important text (referenced even on the cover of the book), where the word ‘depth' seems to have originated, was a verse from Apostle Paul's epistle to the Ephesians (3:18). In his article on ‘The Meaning of Idealism' (Smysl idealisma, 1915), Florensky acknowledged Goulak as the first person to notice this verse (in the geometrical context) and cited it along with several previous ones: ‘I bow my knees before the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ... May He grant you, -writes St. Apostle to the Ephesians,-... to be strengthened with His Spirit in the inner man, and may Christ dwell in your hearts through faith, so that you, being rooted and grounded in love, could comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth and length and depth and height'. Florensky could recall this passage (which directly connects the concept of the ‘inner man' to four dimensions), and the obscure book on ‘synthetic geometry' along with it, thanks to the work of Pyotr Ouspensky, the main Russian theorist of the fourth dimension and promoter of Charles Howard Hinton's ideas. In the conclusion to his Tertium Organum (1911), discussing the words of St. Paul, ‘startling by reason of their mathematical exactness', Ouspensky remarked that they not merely connect sanctity to knowledge, but imply ‘that sanctity gives a new understanding of space'. Florensky borrowed this idea and, in a way, turned it against Ouspensky: criticizing ‘the methods of distillation of new capabilities', devised by Hinton and popularized by his Russian counterpart, as ‘unnatural' and ‘violent' to the ‘spiritual organism', he described the fourth dimension as ‘the depth of the world, which can be perceived only by a righteous soul'. This four-dimensional depth, therefore, served as a kind of alternative to the habitual three-dimensional one, which Hermann von Helmholtz had shown to be a psychological phenomenon produced by the so-called ‘unconscious inference'. For Florensky, the latter seems to have represented a by-product of the fallen human mind that lost the capacity to see the world in its original and supertemporal unity. Identifying Goulak's axis of depth with the axis of time, he explained that, being seen properly, ‘any reality is stretched in the direction of time no less than it is stretched in each of the three directions of space', which means that it has a certain ‘time depth' and ‘constitutes some kind of formation of the four-dimensional geometry, i.e. not a body, but a super-body, or, in N.[I.] Goulak's terminology, body-body [telo-tela]': ‘Now, any reality extends in four dimensions and is isolated in an image of four dimensions. And time, the fourth coordinate of this image, is organized in it as its own [internal] time […] This time is not an external time, which is the time of lifeless things devoid of strong individuality. And that is why the time of a given image cannot be measured by the time of other images […]: it is necessary either to enter into the proper time of a given image and consider it as a self-contained unity or to ascend by contemplation to an image [of a higher order] that concretely encompasses this image and others […] Then this new image, in relation to those particular images, will act as their common space, with its own special time, i.e. the four-dimensional space, and they, these particular images, in relation to the common image, will be the objects within it, connected between themselves by power and energy interaction' ” (P. Yushin, The Cover of the Journal Makovets and Pavel Florensky's World Picture, in: “In anderen Zeiten/In Other Times. Zeitdiskurse im Wandel/Changing Discourses of Time across Human History”, B. Hohenwald, N. Illner & J. Renn, eds., Berlin, 2022, pp. 170-174).We were not able to trace a copy of this book in any public library worldwide.

title: Historie fiorentine di Niccolo Machiavelli cittadino, et segretario fiorentino

authors.name: Machiavelli Niccolò
authors.biography: Niccolò di Bernardo dei Machiavelli (3 May 1469 – 21 June 1527) stands as one of the most transcendent and pivotal figures in the history of Western political thought, diplomatic theory, and Renaissance humanism. Operating at the tumultuous juncture of the Italian High Renaissance and the devastating Italian Wars, Machiavelli redefined the parameters of political philosophy by divorcing the analysis of statecraft, power dynamics, and governance from scholastic theology, Christian morality, and teleological idealism. Serving as Secretary to the Second Chancery of the Republic of Florence from 1498 to 1512, he was not merely a theoretical observer of political phenomena but an active diplomatic practitioner whose firsthand experience with monarchs, popes, condottieri, and regional despots forged a empirical methodology anchored in what he famously termed the verità effettuale della cosa—the effectual truth of the matter—rather than the imaginary republics conceived by classical philosophers. Through his seminal political treatises—most notably De Principatibus (The Prince) and the Discorsi sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio (Discourses on Livy)—as well as his historical writings, military manuals, and dramatic literature, Machiavelli inaugurated modern political science, establishing a secular theoretical framework focused on the dialectic of virtù (human agency, energy, and political skill) and fortuna (contingency and cosmic instability), the mechanics of state preservation, the nature of republican liberty, and the institutional dynamics of civic corruption.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationMachiavelli was born in Florence into an ancient and noble, though economically diminished, patrician family whose roots traced back to the rural nobility of the Val di Pesa. His father, Bernardo di Niccolò Machiavelli, was a doctor of laws and a jurist of modest financial means who nevertheless maintained an ardent commitment to humanist learning and classical literature. Bernardo’s meticulous personal diary, the Ricordi, provides priceless historiographical insights into young Niccolò’s upbringing and education in the heart of Lorenzo de' Medici’s Florence. From an early age, Niccolò was immersed in the studia humanitatis, receiving instruction in Latin grammar, rhetoric, and classical literature from esteemed tutors such as Maestro Matteo and later the noted humanist Paolo da Ronciglione. While Machiavelli did not master ancient Greek—a limitation that set him slightly apart from elite Florentine humanists like Angelo Poliziano or Marsilio Ficino—his command of Latin prose was rigorous and expansive. He studied the works of Cicero, Terence, Caesar, Sallust, Xenophon (in Latin translation), and above all, Titus Livius (Livy), whose monumental history of early Rome would form the intellectual backbone of his mature political thought. A surviving manuscript copy of Lucretius’s epicurean poem De rerum natura, meticulously transcribed in Machiavelli’s own hand during his youth, further attests to his early exposure to classical atomism, naturalism, and a non-providential view of cosmos and history.Machiavelli’s formative years unfolded against the backdrop of dramatic political transformations in Florence. He witnessed the decline of the Medicean hegemony following the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent in 1492, the French invasion led by King Charles VIII in 1494 which expelled Piero de' Medici, and the subsequent rise and fall of the Dominican friar Girolamo Savonarola. Savonarola’s radical religious republic, marked by moral puritanism and apocalyptic rhetoric, deeply affected the young Machiavelli. Attending Savonarola’s sermons at the Duomo and San Marco, Machiavelli analyzed the friar’s political maneuvers with acute realism, famously characterizing Savonarola in his later correspondence as an "unarmed prophet" (profeta disarmato) whose lack of military force and institutional stability rendered his political project doomed to eventual destruction once public sentiment shifted.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksThe execution of Savonarola in May 1498 opened political opportunities within the restructured Florentine Republic. In June 1498, at the age of twenty-nine, Machiavelli was appointed Head of the Second Chancery of the Republic of Florence, and shortly thereafter was designated Secretary to the Dieci di Balìa (Ten of War), the chief magistrate committee governing Florence’s foreign policy and military operations. For fourteen years, under the leadership of Gonfaloniere a vita Piero Soderini, Machiavelli operated at the nerve center of Florentine diplomatic and administrative life. He undertook numerous diplomatic missions across Europe and the Italian peninsula, encountering the major political figures of his age: King Louis XII of France, Emperor Maximilian I of Habsburg, Pope Julius II, and most decisively, Cesare Borgia (Duke Valentino), the illegitimate son of Pope Alexander VI. Borgia’s ruthless consolidation of power in the Romagna, his calculated elimination of rebellious captains at Senigallia in 1502, and his strategic use of force, fraud, and administrative severity left an indelible imprint on Machiavelli’s political philosophy, serving as a primary case study for executive decisiveness in Il Principe. Furthermore, Machiavelli’s practical experience with the disastrous reliance on mercenary troops (condottieri) during the protracted siege of Pisa led him to champion a radical military reform: the establishment of a native Florentine citizen militia (the ordinanza), authorized by the government in 1506, which successfully recaptured Pisa in 1509.The geopolitical catastrophe of 1512 permanently shattered Machiavelli’s diplomatic career. Following the defeat of French forces by the Holy League at Ravenna, Spanish troops sacked Prato and forced the collapse of Soderini’s republican regime. The Medici family returned to rule Florence, dissolved the Republic, and abolished Machiavelli’s Chancery post. Accused in early 1513 of complicity in an anti-Medicean conspiracy organized by Pier Paolo Boscoli and Agostino Capponi, Machiavelli was arrested, imprisoned in the Bargello, and subjected to the tratti di fune (strappado torture). Maintaining his innocence under interrogation, he was released under a general amnesty declared upon the election of Giovanni de' Medici as Pope Leo X. Stripped of office and banned from the Palazzo della Signoria, Machiavelli retreated to his modest family estate, Sant'Andrea in Percussina (the Albergaccio), near San Casciano in the Val di Pesa.It was during this period of forced political isolation that Machiavelli produced his greatest masterworks. In a celebrated letter to his friend Francesco Vettori dated 10 December 1513, Machiavelli described his daily routine of rural labor, followed by evening studies where he donned his courtly garments to enter the ancient courts of classical authors: "Ho composto uno opuscolo De Principatibus..." This treatise, Il Principe (written in late 1513, though revised later), was conceived as a concise manual on executive power, statecraft, and the acquisition, maintenance, and defense of political dominions. Dedicating the work eventually to Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino (grandson of Lorenzo the Magnificent), Machiavelli broke radically with the medieval and Renaissance "mirror-for-princes" genre. Rather than advising the ruler to cultivate traditional Christian virtues such as justice, mercy, and piety, Machiavelli argued that a prince must learn how not to be good when political survival demands it. He articulated a revolutionary doctrine of political ethics: a prince must possess the agility of both the fox (to recognize traps) and the lion (to frighten wolves), navigating the relentless friction between human virtù and unpredictable fortuna. Crucially, Machiavelli asserted that the preservation of lo stato and the security of the political community supersede conventional moral norms, establishing what later theorists would designate as the autonomy of politics.Concurrently and in the years following, Machiavelli engaged deeply with the intellectual circle of young Florentine humanists and patricians who gathered in the gardens of the Rucellai family, the Orti Oricellari. Exposed to the theoretical discourses of Cosimo Rucellai, Zanobi Buondelmonti, and Luigi Alamanni, Machiavelli composed his longest and most profound theoretical work: the Discorsi sopra la prima deca di Tito Livio (Discourses on Livy, c. 1513–1519). If Il Principe analyzed the mechanics of autocratic order during times of emergency, the Discorsi presented a comprehensive defense of classical republicanism, civic liberty, and popular sovereignty based on the model of the Roman Republic. Machiavelli argued that dynamic political conflict between the elite (i grandi) and the common people (il popolo) had not caused Rome’s downfall, but had instead generated civic freedom and military strength through constitutional checks and robust laws. He explored the causes of political corruption (corruzione), the necessity of mixed constitution government, the crucial role of civic religion, and the dangers of autocratic tyranny, asserting that a republic composed of a virtuous citizenry is inherently more stable and enduring than a state governed by a single prince.In 1520, through the patronage of Cardinal Giulio de' Medici (later Pope Clement VII) and the academic sponsorship of the Studio Fiorentino, Machiavelli was re-admitted into official favor and commissioned to write the history of his native city. The resulting Istorie fiorentine (8 books, completed in 1525) utilized a sophisticated humanist historical framework to examine the internal factions, economic conflicts, and foreign policy blunders that had plagued Florence from the fall of the Western Roman Empire down to the death of Lorenzo the Magnificent in 1492. In addition to his political works, Machiavelli achieved major literary acclaim as a playwright. His masterpiece comedy, La Mandragola (written c. 1518 and printed shortly thereafter), provided a hilarious yet devastating satirical allegory of Florentine moral decay, social deception, and political manipulation through the figures of Callimaco, Ligurio, and Fra Timoteo. His other notable works included the dialogue Dell'arte della guerra (The Art of War, published in 1521)—his only major political/historical prose work published during his lifetime—the novella Belfagor arcidiavolo, and the comedy Clizia.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationThe publishing history of Machiavelli’s works represents a dramatic chapter in Renaissance typography and the spread of early modern political literature. During his lifetime, Machiavelli saw only a fraction of his major writings enter print. His military treatise, Dell'arte della guerra, was issued in Florence by the celebrated printer Bernardo Giunta in 1521 in a fine quarto format, set in elegant Roman and italic types characteristic of the Giunti press’s scholarly production. His comedy La Mandragola saw small, clandestine printings in Rome and Venice during the late 1510s and 1520s. However, Machiavelli’s two central theoretical works—Il Principe and the Discorsi—as well as the Istorie fiorentine, circulated exclusively in manuscript copies among networks of humanists, diplomats, and aristocratic friends prior to his death in 1527.The posthumous dissemination of Machiavelli’s major works began in the early 1530s through rival publishing enterprises in Rome and Florence, operating with papal privileges granted by Pope Clement VII (Giulio de' Medici). In late 1531 and early 1532, the printer Antonio Blado in Rome issued the editio princeps of the Discorsi (1531) followed by Il Principe and the Istorie fiorentine (1532). Simultaneously, the press of Bernardo Giunta in Florence produced competing editions of Il Principe, the Discorsi, and the Istorie in 1532. These early octavo and quarto editions featured distinct typographical designs: Blado’s Roman editions utilized clear, legible chancery italic types based on the designs of Ludovico Vicentino degli Arrighi, appealing to Roman curial scholars and humanists, while the Giunta editions established the canonical Florentine readings of Machiavelli's vernacular text. Throughout the 1530s and 1540s, Venetian presses—most notably those of Gabriele Giolito de' Ferrari and Vincenzo Valgrisi—reprinted these texts in massive quantities, introducing pocket-sized duodecimo formats that facilitated widespread readership across the Italian peninsula and beyond.This period of open publishing ended abruptly with the Counter-Reformation. In 1559, Pope Paul IV placed the entirety of Machiavelli’s works (*opera omnia*) on the first Roman Index Librorum Prohibitorum in the strict category of absolute prohibition (first class), a prohibition reconfirmed by the Tridentine Index of 1564 under Pope Pius IV. The Papal condemnation banned the printing, ownership, reading, or distribution of Machiavelli’s texts across Catholic Christendom under pain of excommunication. This suppression catalyzed a fascinating underground printing tradition. Protestant printers in Basel, Geneva, and London began issuing clandestine editions of Machiavelli. In the 1580s, the Italian Protestant exile printer Pietro Perna in Basel, along with the English printer John Wolfe in London (issuing books with false Italian imprints such as "Piacenza" or "Palermo"), produced subterranean editions of Il Principe and the Discorsi. Most famously, from 1550 through the late sixteenth century, a series of mysterious pirated editions known as the Edizioni Testina (named for the small woodcut portrait head of Machiavelli on their title pages, bearing the false imprint "In Yverdon, 1550") circulated thousands of copies throughout Europe, ensuring that Machiavelli’s political theory bypassed ecclesiastical censorship.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyThe reception of Machiavelli’s political thought is one of the most intense, controversial, and influential trajectories in intellectual history. Almost immediately following his death and the posthumous printing of Il Principe, his name became synonymous with political amoralism, tyrannical deception, and ruthless statecraft. The term "Machiavellian" was coined to denote sinister, unscrupulous political intrigue. The Counter-Reformation launched a ferocious ideological assault against him, led by Cardinal Reginald Pole, the Jesuit Pedro de Ribadeneyra, and the French Huguenot Innocent Gentillet, whose Discours contre Machiavel (1576) popularized the black legend of Machiavelli across Europe. In Elizabethan and Jacobean drama, the "Machiavel" emerged as a stock theatrical villain—a demonic figure of atheism and cunning featured in the plays of Christopher Marlowe (The Jew of Malta) and William Shakespeare (Richard III, Othello). Catholic theorists of the Counter-Reformation, such as Giovanni Botero in his Della ragion di Stato (1589), sought to absorb Machiavelli’s empirical insights into state preservation while ostentatiously re-subordinating statecraft to Catholic orthodoxy.Despite this moral condemnation, the world’s greatest political thinkers recognized Machiavelli’s profound brilliance and analytical honesty. Francis Bacon praised Machiavelli for writing about what men do, not what they ought to do. During the seventeenth century, Baruch Spinoza in his Tractatus Politicus reinterpreted Machiavelli not as a advisor to tyrants, but as a wise and courageous defender of republican liberty who exposed the methods of princes to warn free citizenries. This republican reinterpretation was amplified by the English Commonwealthmen, including James Harrington (in The Commonwealth of Oceana, 1556), John Milton, and Algernon Sidney, who found in Machiavelli’s Discorsi the foundational blueprint for a balanced, anti-monarchical republic. During the Enlightenment, Jean-Jacques Rousseau famously proclaimed in Du contrat social (1762) that "in pretending to give lessons to kings, Machiavelli gave great lessons to the people: The Prince is the book of republicans."In the nineteenth century, during the Italian Risorgimento, Machiavelli was re-evaluated as a patriotic visionary whose passionate final chapter of Il Principe—an ardent exhortation to liberate Italy from foreign barbarians (barbari)—foreshadowed the nineteenth-century movement for Italian national unification. Historians such as Pasquale Villari and literary critics like Francesco De Sanctis celebrated Machiavelli as the founder of modern secular national consciousness. In the twentieth century, scholarly debate over Machiavelli reached unprecedented depth and complexity. Friedrich Meinecke traced the evolution of statecraft back to Machiavelli in Die Idee der Staatsräson (1924), while Marxist philosopher Antonio Gramsci re-conceptualized Il Principe in his Prison Notebooks, proposing that the modern political party serves as the collective "Modern Prince" capable of mobilizing popular political will. Leo Strauss offered an influential conservative reading in Thoughts on Machiavelli (1958), characterizing Machiavelli as a "teacher of evil" who consciously broke with classical natural law to inaugurate modern philosophical nihilism. Conversely, the "Cambridge School" of intellectual history, spearheaded by Hans Baron, Felix Gilbert, Quentin Skinner, and J.G.A. Pocock (whose landmark 1975 study The Machiavellian Moment placed Machiavelli at the core of the Atlantic republican tradition), re-established Machiavelli as a central pillar of civic humanism and constitutional liberty. Modern Italian historiography, led by scholars such as Roberto Ridolfi, Federico Chabod, Gennaro Sasso, Giorgio Inglese, and Jean-Jacques Marchand, has established rigorous critical editions of his works, solidifying Niccolò Machiavelli’s stature as an indispensable architect of global political thought.

academic_description: 4to (205x133 mm). [4], 9-224 leaves. Signatures: [A]4 B-Z8 AA-EE8. As is often the case, lacking the final 4 leaves (quire FF4) containing the errata (ll. FF1-2), a blank FF3, and the printer's device (FF4v). Moreover, due to a mistake in the composition of quire S, leaves 139v, 140r, 141v, and 142r have been omitted, while leaves 139r, 140v, 141r, and 142v are incorrectly repeated. Printer's device on the title page. Contemporary flexible vellum (recased, new endleaves). Preserved in a cloth case. Slightly browned, light marginal damp stains, all in all a good, genuine copy.Rare first Florence Edition, possibly the first edition overall, of this landmark of historiographical literature. After Machiavelli's death in 1527 there was a rush to publish his remaining works, and a fierce competition began between the Roman printer Blado and the Florentine printer Guinta to be the first to press. Although Giunta had been given the approval of Machiavelli's heirs and rushed to honor his fellow Florentine with elegant editions of his works, both Blado's and Giunta's editions of “The Florentine History” appeared almost simultaneously. It is generally presumed that Blado's Roman edition, dated 25 March 1532, preceded Giunta's by two days. Some copies of the Giunta edition, (as in the present copy), are dated 27 March 1532 in the colophon, while others are dated 16 March 1532. It is possible that Giunta printed an incorrect 16 March date to convince the public that his edition was indeed the first and to match the date of Giunta's dedication to the duke Alessandro de' Medici, printed on the title-page verso, which is followed by Machiavelli's dedication addressed to Pope Clemens VII. In 1520, Machiavelli was commissioned by Giulio de' Medici to write an account of the history of Florence. The book he produced “is the first example in Italian literature of a national biography, the first attempt in any literature to trace the vicissitudes of a people's life in their logical sequence, deducing each successive phase from passions or necessities inherent in preceding circumstance, reasoning upon them from general principles, and inferring corollaries for the conduct of the future” (Britannica).
