authors.name: Philandrier Guillaume
authors.biography: Guillaume Philandrier (latinized as Guilielmus Philander; 1505–1565) stands as one of the most formidable intellectual bridges between the Italian High Renaissance and the French Renaissance scholar-architectural tradition. A profound philologist, diplomatic secretary, theologian, and pioneering architectural theorist, Philandrier's crowning achievement—his commentary on Marcus Vitruvius Pollio's De Architectura—fundamentally transformed early modern European architectural theory. Working at the intersection of humanist textual criticism and practical antiquarianism, Philandrier systematically codified the classical canon of the Five Orders of Architecture, providing the northern European continent with its first rigorous, philologically grounded, and iconographically illustrated guide to the classical antiquity of Rome. His career exemplifies the mid-sixteenth-century Renaissance ideal, wherein humanistic scholarship was directly applied to the material arts, bridging the divide between textual erudition and architectural practice.Born in Châtillon-sur-Seine in Burgundy in 1505, Philandrier received an extraordinarily rigorous education in classical literature, Greek philology, and jurisprudence. Early in his formative years, he entered the intellectual orbit of the great French humanist Guillaume Budé, whose methodology of rigorous textual collation and philological archaeology profoundly shaped Philandrier's analytical mind. Philandrier's intellectual trajectory shifted decisively in the early 1530s when he entered the service of Georges d'Armagnac, the erudite Bishop of Rodez (later Cardinal and diplomat). As principal secretary and confidential advisor to Armagnac, Philandrier gained access to the highest echelons of diplomatic, ecclesiastical, and intellectual nobility across Europe. When Armagnac was appointed French Ambassador to the Republic of Venice by King Francis I in 1536, Philandrier accompanied his patron across the Alps, initiating an extended period of residency in the Italian peninsula that would define his life's work.During his stay in Venice between 1536 and 1539, Philandrier immersed himself in the vibrant Venetian humanist network. He studied Greek under the guidance of the renowned scholar Marcantonio Flaminio and established close connections with the intellectual sphere surrounding the printer Paolo Manuzio, as well as the satirist Pietro Aretino and the architectural theorist Sebastiano Serlio. It was during this Venetian period that Philandrier began his intensive study of ancient architectural treatises and surviving classical monuments. Serlio's preliminary publications on the architectural orders (such as Book IV of his Tutte l'opere d'architettura, published in Venice in 1537) exercised an immediate influence on Philandrier, prompting him to combine textual scholarship on Vitruvius with visual and geometrical analysis.In 1540, Cardinal Georges d'Armagnac was reassigned to Rome as the representative of the French Crown at the Papal Court of Paul III Farnese. Philandrier accompanied Armagnac to the Eternal City, an environment that provided an unprecedented opportunity for direct antiquarian research. In Rome, Philandrier became an active member of the celebrated Accademia della Virtù (also known as the Accademia Vitruviana), founded under the leadership of the Sienese humanist Claudio Tolomei and patronized by Cardinal Marcello Cervini (later Pope Marcellus II). The Accademia brought together the most brilliant minds of the era—including scholars, humanists, and artists such as Jacopo Barozzi da Vignola and Guillaume Du Choul—with the ambitious goal of producing a comprehensive, encyclopedic edition of Vitruvius accompanied by exhaustive archaeological commentaries, maps, and drawings of Roman ruins.Philandrier took upon himself the primary responsibility for the textual critique of Vitruvius. He meticulously collated ancient manuscripts preserved in the Vatican Library and private Roman collections, comparing scribal errors, corrupt Latin terms, and obscure Greek borrowings. The fruits of this monumental labor appeared in Rome in 1544, published by the printer Andrea Dost, under the title In decem libros M. Vitruvii Pollionis de Architectura annotationes. Dedicated to King Francis I, this work was not merely a set of glosses, but a exhaustive, line-by-line critical commentary that elucidated Vitruvian terminology—ranging from technical details of masonry construction (*eustylos*, *pycnostylos*, *entasis*) to complex theories of acoustic vessels in ancient theaters and classical proportions. The 1544 Roman edition was illustrated with exquisite woodcuts that translated Vitruvius's notoriously obscure verbal descriptions into clear geometric and architectural diagrams.Following the resounding success of the first edition, Philandrier returned to France and settled in the diocese of Rodez, where his patron Cardinal d'Armagnac bestowed upon him major ecclesiastical appointments, including Canon of Rodez Cathedral and Archdeacon of Saint-Antonin. However, Philandrier continued to refine his scholarly work. In 1552, he published a drastically expanded and revised edition of his commentary in Lyons, produced by the premier humanist printer Jean de Tournes. The 1552 Lyons edition of the Annotationes represents a masterpiece of Renaissance typography and book design, featuring detailed woodcut illustrations attributed to the circle of Bernard Salomon. In this edition, Philandrier incorporated a formal treatise on the Five Orders of Architecture (Tuscan, Doric, Ionic, Corinthian, and Composite), establishing precise mathematical ratios and modular systems for column shafts, capitals, bases, and entablatures. He was among the very first theorists to formally codify the Composite order alongside the traditional four described by Vitruvius, synthesizing Serlio's visual models with rigorous Latin scholarship.Philandrier's contribution extended beyond theoretical literature into practical architectural patronage. In his role as Archdeacon and Canon at Rodez, he was commissioned to design the monumental upper storey and gable end of the West Facade of Rodez Cathedral. Completed around 1562, this extraordinary structure—often referred to as the clocher or Renaissance crest of the cathedral—seamlessly integrated classical Corinthian and Composite pilasters, entablatures, and a high Renaissance pediment atop a severe medieval Gothic edifice. This architectural intervention remains one of the most sophisticated examples of mid-sixteenth-century French Renaissance architectural design, directly reflecting the classical principles Philandrier had articulated in his writings.The impact of Philandrier's work on European architecture was profound and immediate. His Latin commentary was widely utilized by contemporary translators and architects across Western Europe. When Jean Martin produced the first French translation of Vitruvius in 1547 (Architecture ou Art de bien bastir), he relied heavily on Philandrier's Latin notes and anatomical diagrams, effectively using Philandrier as the interpretive key to unlock Vitruvius for French stonemasons, master builders, and patrons. Philibert de L'Orme, Jacques Androuet du Cerceau, and later theorists such as Roland Fréart de Chambray and Claude Perrault all acknowledged Philandrier as the supreme philological authority on ancient architecture. Guillaume Philandrier passed away in Rodez on February 8, 1565, leaving behind a legacy that permanently embedded classical humanism and Vitruvian theory into the architectural fabric of Early Modern Europe.

authors.name: Vitruvius Pollio
authors.biography: Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, more commonly known as Vitruvius, stands as a monumental figure in the annals of architectural history. His comprehensive treatise, 'De Architectura', composed in the late 1st century BC, is the oldest surviving work on architecture and has profoundly influenced architectural theory and practice through the ages, particularly during the Renaissance. Vitruvius's work is not merely a technical manual but a profound synthesis of architectural knowledge, reflecting the cultural and intellectual milieu of Augustan Rome. His treatise covers a wide array of topics, from the principles of building design to the theoretical underpinnings of architecture, and serves as a bridge connecting ancient Greek architectural traditions with Roman innovations.Vitruvius's early life remains shrouded in mystery, with scant biographical details available. His full name, Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, suggests a connection to the Roman gens Vitruvia, though the precise details of his lineage are uncertain. The nomenclature 'Pollio' may indicate his association with the Pollia tribe, particularly in the region of Fanum Fortunae, modern-day Fano. His education likely encompassed a broad spectrum of disciplines, typical of Roman intellectuals of his time, including studies in mathematics, engineering, and the liberal arts. Vitruvius himself mentions his role as a scriba armamentarius, overseeing the construction of war machines, which underscores his technical expertise and the practical experience that informed his writings.'De Architectura', dedicated to Emperor Augustus, is Vitruvius's magnum opus, comprising ten books that systematically address the principles of architecture. The treatise begins with a dedication to Augustus, highlighting Vitruvius's gratitude for the patronage and pension he received. The work covers a wide range of topics, including the selection of building sites, materials, and the design of various structures, from temples to private homes. Vitruvius's emphasis on symmetry, proportion, and the triadic principles of firmitas (strength), utilitas (utility), and venustas (beauty) reflects his philosophical grounding in Pythagorean and Stoic thought. His work also engages with the broader intellectual currents of his time, drawing on the writings of Greek architects and philosophers, thereby positioning him within a network of Roman and Hellenistic scholarship.The transmission of Vitruvius's text through the centuries is a testament to its enduring significance. The first printed edition appeared in Rome in 1486, edited by Giovanni Sulpicio da Veroli and Pomponio Leto. This incunable marks the beginning of Vitruvius's Renaissance revival, as architects and humanists sought to reconnect with the classical past. Subsequent editions, such as the 1511 Venetian edition by Fra Giocondo, expanded the treatise's reach, incorporating illustrations to compensate for the lost original diagrams. The Italian translation by Cesare Cesariano in 1521 further facilitated its dissemination, making Vitruvian principles accessible to a broader audience. The typographical landscape of the 15th and 16th centuries, characterized by the burgeoning of print culture, played a crucial role in cementing Vitruvius's legacy in architectural theory and practice.Vitruvius's treatise, while not immediately influential in antiquity, gained prominence during the Renaissance, becoming a cornerstone of architectural education and practice. Figures like Leon Battista Alberti, Andrea Palladio, and Leonardo da Vinci drew extensively from Vitruvian principles, integrating them into their own works and treatises. The 'Vitruvian Man' by Leonardo, for instance, exemplifies the application of Vitruvian concepts of human proportion to artistic and architectural design. Despite debates regarding the precise dating and authorship of the treatise, its impact is undeniable. The 'De Architectura' continues to be a foundational text in the study of architecture, reflecting the rich interplay of technical, aesthetic, and philosophical ideas that have shaped the built environment from antiquity to the modern era.

academic_description: 8vo (155x99 mm). [16], 369, [39] pp. Collation: a8 A-Z8 &8 AA8 BB4. Large printer's device on the title page and 65 woodcut illustrations in text. Colophon on last leaf verso. Woodcut initials. Italic, Greek, and Roman type. Contemporary flexible vellum with overlapping edges and inked title on spine (traces of ties). Small hole on l. H1 with some loss of text, quire T slightly browned, otherwise a very good, extremely genuine copy in its first binding.Provenance. Ownership entry on the title page “Joan. Bap.ta Gabii”. Giovan Battista Gabia, born in Verona in the early 16th century, was a professor of Greek at the University of Rome from around 1553 until 1582. Alongside teaching, he was also active as a translator and editor of Greek and Hebrew texts. In 1583, he published in Rome a translation of the Gregorian calendar into Greek. He probably died around 1590 (cf. E. Del Gallo, Gabia, Giovan Battista, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 51, 1998, s.v.).Scarce first edition, dedicated to the King of France Francis I, of Philandrier commentary on Vitruvius, that was reprinted in Paris in 1545 and later issued accompanying Vitruvius's actual text in Strasbourg in 1550 in 16mo and in De Tournes' enlarged 4to format in Lyons in 1552.The edition opens with a note to the scholars (“studiosis”), a six-page long list of quoted authors, and a short life of Vitruvius based on the autobiographical references that can be found in his own work.As secretary to Cardinal Georges D'Armagnac, Philandrier lived in Rome for a few years, becoming a member of the famous Accademia della Virtù, which, founded by Claudio Tolomei in 1538 under the protection of Cardinal Ippolito de' Medici, had been established for the main purpose of studying and commenting on the work of Vitruvius (see M. Maylender, Storia delle accademie d'Italia, Bologna, 1926-‘30, V, pp. 478-480). The academy, whose members included Marcello Cervini (the future Pope Marcellus II), Jacopo Barozzi called Il Vignola, Alessandro Manzuoli, Luca Contile, Annibal Caro, Marco Antonio Flaminio, and Francesco Maria Molza, to name but a few, met twice a week at the residence of Archbishop Francesco Colonna; during the meetings Vitrivius' De Architectura was read and discussed in order to publish a comprehensive annotated edition of the work. The activity and goals of the Accademia della Virtù are outlined by Tolomei in a very interesting letter to Count Agostino Landi, dated 14 November 1542 (cf. D. Wiebenson, ed., Architectural Theory and Practice from Alberti to Ledoux, Chicago, IL, 1982, pp. 1-13).It was precisely during his stay in Rome that Philander (known in Italian as Filandro and in Latin as Philander) produced his Annotationes, which remained the only published outcome of the ambitious project of the Accademia della Virtù (cf. F. Lemerle, Philandrier et le texte de Vitruve, in: “Mélanges de l'École française de Rome, Italie et Méditerranée”, 106, no. 2, 1994, pp. 517-529).“Philander's commentary is composed of sections of the text followed by practical explanations and definitions, each passage heavily reinforced with scholarly and classical examples […] Philander's work is at once a learned study and a practical manual of architecture, incorporating the methods of both the humanists and architects […] It is the first synthesis of academic and practical interpretations of Vitruvius' treatise to appear in published form. The contribution of Philander and of the Accademia delle Virtù to mid-sixteenth-century architectural theory is of the greatest importance […] Philander's notes would be cited almost without exception by every Vitruvius commentator and translator, from the date of its first appearance until the nineteenth century” (D. Wiebenson, ed., The Mark J. Millard Architectural Collection, I: French books, New York, 1993, no. 165 for the 1552 edition).Guillaume Philandrier, a native of Châtillon-sur-Seine, was a pupil of Jean Perelle. As secretary to Georges d'Armagnac, French ambassador first to Venice, then to Rome, he visited Italy and got to know influential artists of the time, most notably Sebastiano Serlio, who taught him architecture. At an unspecified date between 1544 and 1549 he returned to France, to Rodez, where, having taken the ecclesiastical habit, he was appointed canon of the cathedral and archdeacon. He died in Toulouse in February 1563, while visiting Georges d'Armagnac, who had meanwhile become bishop of that city. His annotations to Vitruvius had a considerable influence on later commentaries such as that of Barbaro and became a reference text especially on the four orders, to which Philandrier added a fifth, the Varronian order (cf. M. Carpo, L'architettura dell'età della stampa. Oralità, scrittura, libro stampato e riproduzione meccanica dell'immagine nella storia delle teorie architettoniche, Milan, 1998, pp. 64-71).

authors.name: Marx Karl
authors.biography: Karl Heinrich Marx (1818–1883) stands as one of the most influential intellectuals, political theorists, economists, and historians in modern world history. Operating at the intersection of nineteenth-century German idealist philosophy, French socialist theory, and British classical political economy, Marx forged a comprehensive method of critical analysis—subsequently codified as historical materialism—that reconfigured the parameters of humanistic and social inquiry. His intellectual trajectory reflects a relentless attempt to synthesize theoretical rigor with revolutionary practice, articulating a critique of capitalist modernity that problematized the categories of political emancipation, economic value, alienation, and social class. Through his partnership with Friedrich Engels and his pivotal role in international labor organizations such as the International Workingmen’s Association (the First International), Marx provided the conceptual foundation for modern communism, socialism, and critical social theory, shaping the geopolitical and ideological landscape of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries.Born on May 5, 1818, in the ancient Rhineland city of Trier—then a recently annexed province of the Kingdom of Prussia—Marx was raised in a milieu defined by modernizing social shifts and lingering religious tensions. His father, Heinrich Marx (formerly Herschel Levi), was a prosperous lawyer of Jewish descent who converted to Evangelical Protestantism to maintain his legal practice under Prussian anti-Semitic decrees. His mother, Henriette Pressburg, belonged to a well-connected Dutch Jewish family. Marx received his formative secondary education at the Gymnasium zu Trier under the headmastership of Hugo Wyttenbach, a proponent of the Enlightenment and liberal humanism. In 1835, Marx matriculated at the University of Bonn to study law, but his interest soon gravitated toward literature and philosophy. Transferring to the University of Berlin in 1836, Marx entered an intellectual environment dominated by the posthumous legacy of Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel. There, he immersed himself in Hegelian dialectics and joined the Doktorklub, an informal circle of radical young intellectuals known as the Young Hegelians (Junghegelianer), which included Bruno Bauer, Arnold Ruge, and Ludwig Feuerbach. Influenced by Feuerbach’s materialist critique of theology and Hegel’s idealist philosophy of history, Marx completed his doctoral dissertation, The Difference Between the Democritean and Epicurean Philosophy of Nature (Differenz der demokritischen und epikureischen Naturphilosophie), receiving his doctorate in absentia from the University of Jena in April 1841.Barred from an academic career due to the Prussian government’s suppression of radical Hegelianism, Marx turned to journalism, serving as editor-in-chief of the liberal opposition newspaper Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne in 1842. His radical economic commentaries—particularly on the legal debates surrounding the customary right of peasants to gather windfall wood—marked his initial transition from abstract philosophical critique to concrete socioeconomic analysis. Following the suppression of the paper by Prussian censors in March 1843, Marx married his childhood sweetheart, Jenny von Westphalen, the daughter of a progressive Prussian aristocrat, Ludwig von Westphalen, who had nurtured Marx’s early interest in Romantic poetry and Saint-Simonian socialism. The couple migrated to Paris in late 1843, where Marx co-edited the short-lived Deutsch-Französische Jahrbücher alongside Arnold Ruge. In Paris, Marx experienced an intense period of intellectual maturation. He studied French socialist theory (Pierre-Joseph Proudhon, Henri de Saint-Simon, Charles Fourier) and classical political economy (Adam Smith, David Ricardo). It was during this Paris period that Marx began his lifelong intellectual collaboration and personal friendship with Friedrich Engels. In his unpublished manuscripts of 1844 (the Economic and Philosophic Manuscripts), Marx introduced his groundbreaking analysis of alienated labor (entfremdete Arbeit) under private property, arguing that capitalism estranges workers from the products of their labor, the act of production, their species-essence (Gattungswesen), and their fellow human beings.Expelled from Paris at the instigation of the Prussian government in early 1845, Marx relocated to Brussels, where he formally renounced his Prussian citizenship. In Brussels, Marx and Engels sharpened their theoretical distance from both bourgeois liberalism and rival socialist factions. In The German Ideology (Die deutsche Ideologie, written 1845–1846, though published posthumously), they formulated the premises of historical materialism, asserting that human history is fundamentally determined by the material conditions of production and the socio-economic relations arising from them, rather than by autonomous idealist concepts. Marx subsequently published The Poverty of Philosophy (Misère de la philosophie, 1847), a devastating critique of Proudhon’s idealist economics. In late 1847, Marx and Engels joined the League of the Just (renamed the Communist League) and were commissioned to draft its manifest program. The resulting document, the Manifesto of the Communist Party (Manifest der Kommunistischen Partei), published in London in February 1848 on the eve of European-wide revolutionary outbreaks, famously declared that 'the history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.' Returning to Germany during the revolutions of 1848–1849, Marx edited the radical daily Neue Rheinische Zeitung in Cologne, championing democratic rights and radical social transformations. Following the collapse of the revolutionary movements and his subsequent expulsion from Germany and France, Marx sought permanent asylum in London in August 1849.Marx’s exile in London was marked by severe financial hardship, personal tragedy—including the early deaths of several of his children—and relentless scholarly labor. Supported financially by Engels, who worked in his family’s textile firm in Manchester, Marx spent decades conducting exhaustive empirical and theoretical research in the Reading Room of the British Museum. His economic research yielded massive manuscript drafts, most notably the Grundrisse der Kritik der politischen Ökonomie (written 1857–1858) and Theories of Surplus Value (Theorien über den Mehrwert). In 1859, Marx published A Contribution to the Critique of Political Economy (Zur Kritik der Politischen Ökonomie), which contained his classic preface summarizing the dynamic relationship between the economic structure (base) and the legal, political, and ideological superstructure. Marx’s magnum opus, Capital: A Critique of Political Economy (Das Kapital: Kritik der politischen Ökonomie), saw its first volume published in Hamburg by Otto Meissner in September 1867. In Das Kapital, Marx unveiled his analysis of the commodity form, the dual character of labor, the creation and extraction of surplus value (Mehrwert), and the systemic contradictions inherent to capital accumulation. Alongside his theoretical writing, Marx remained intensely active in working-class politics. He served as the dominant theoretical authority of the International Workingmen’s Association from its founding in 1864 until its dissolution in the 1870s, producing its Inaugural Address and its celebrated defense of the Paris Commune of 1871, The Civil War in France. Marx passed away in his London home on March 14, 1883, and was buried in Highgate Cemetery.The publishing history of Marx’s works is exceptionally complex, marked by severe censorship, exile printings, posthumous editoral reconstructions, and ideological debates over text-critical fidelity. The printings of his early journalism in the Rheinische Zeitung and Neue Rheinische Zeitung relied on localized German presses operating under constant threat of confiscation by Prussian authorities. The first edition of the Communist Manifesto was printed anonymously in London by the Workers' Educational Association (Bildungs-Gesellschaft für Arbeiter) as a modest 23-page pamphlet in German, before being translated into English, French, and Russian. The publication of Das Kapital encountered significant commercial resistance; publisher Otto Meissner printed an initial run of 1,000 copies of Volume 1 in 1867, which sold slowly across German-speaking territories. Marx spent his final years revising the French translation (published in installments between 1872 and 1875 by Maurice Lachâtre in Paris) and preparing material for subsequent volumes. Following Marx’s death, Friedrich Engels performed a monumental task of transcription and editorial organization, publishing Volume 2 of Das Kapital in 1885 and Volume 3 in 1894. Later in the twentieth century, the Marx-Engels Institute in Moscow, under the direction of David Riazanov, initiated the first scholarly edition of their complete works (Marx-Engels-Gesamtausgabe or MEGA1), which unveiled crucial early manuscripts such as the 1844 Manuscripts and The German Ideology. This effort was succeeded by the MEGA2 edition, established in the late twentieth century as an international, non-ideological text-critical edition restoring all extant manuscripts, notebooks, and correspondence to their unedited historical forms.The critical reception of Karl Marx’s thought represents one of the most contentious chapters in modern intellectual history. In the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, his theories were adopted as official dogma by social democratic parties and later by Marxist-Leninist regimes across the Soviet Union, Eastern Europe, Asia, and Latin America. However, scholarly reception within Western Marxism—spearheaded by theorists such as György Lukács, Karl Korsch, Theodor W. Adorno, Max Horkheimer, Walter Benjamin, Antonio Gramsci, and Louis Althusser—severed Marx’s philosophical critique from dogmatic state ideologies, re-emphasizing his theories of alienation, reification, dialectical method, and structural critique of political economy. Contemporary academic scholarship in economic history, sociology, literary theory, and philosophy continues to engagement with Marx’s analysis of globalized commodity production, economic crises, financialization, and social inequality. Recognized today not as a dogmatic prophet but as an indispensable historian and critic of modern capitalism, Marx’s legacy remains a central pillar of global social and political thought.

academic_description: Folio (mm. 276x192). Pp. 351, [1] comprising: the half-title page adorned with an allegorical vignette and the indication “1re Livraison, Prix de la Livraison: dix centimes”; the title page featuring a vignette depicting the Pantheon on the recto and the mark of Typographie Lahurf on the verso; a full-page portrait of Marx with his signature beneath; a facsimile of a letter sent by Marx to the publisher Maurice Lachâtre (with a reply on the verso: “Au citoyen Karl Marx”); the Préface de la première édition dated 25 July 1875 (p. [9]); the Avis au lecteur dated London, 28 April 1875 (p. 348); the Extraits de la postface de la seconde édition allemande (pp. 348-351); the errata (p. 351); and finally the index of subjects on the last page. The work is embellished with engraved headpieces and tailpieces. The text is printed in two columns starting from p. [13]. Modern half morocco binding with the title in gilt on the spine, while the boards are crafted from transparent plexiglass panels, allowing the original publisher's wrappers to remain visible. There is some minor foxing, yet it remains an excellent copy.This is the first edition, first issue, of the inaugural French translation of the first volume of Das Kapital. The translation by M.J. Roy is based on the manuscript of the second German edition. Marx had revised the original text and dispatched a copy of the revised manuscript to the Parisian socialist publisher Maurice Lachâtre, a friend of Proudhon, even prior to the publication of the Hamburg edition in June 1872. Marx regarded this French translation as an original work, “which possesses an independent scientific value from the original and should be consulted even by readers familiar with the German language” (see the Avis au lecteur, p. 348).As with the Russian edition, Marx was directly involved in the printing operations and commended the publisher's decision to distribute the book initially in parts. The edition was indeed released in fascicles between August 1872 and May 1875. The work was subsequently reprinted between 1878 and 1880 by Librairie du Progrès with the preliminary pages recomposed.From Marx's correspondence, it is evident that the French government was apprehensive about the book's publication and sought to prevent it. Despite this, the publication proceeded, though its sale was temporarily prohibited, and Lachâtre initially hesitated to offer the copies for sale. In the second issue, which appeared under the name of Librairie du Progrès, the preliminary pages, including Lachâtre's dedication to Marx, were altered or omitted.

authors.name: Volta Alessandro
authors.biography: Alessandro Giuseppe Antonio Anastasio Volta (1745–1827) stands as one of the quintessential figures of the European Enlightenment and a foundational titan in the history of experimental physics. Operating at the intersection of late eighteenth-century natural philosophy and the emerging empirical disciplines of chemistry and electrodynamics, Volta transformed the scientific understanding of electricity from an unpredictable, transient electrostatic phenomenon into a manageable, continuous source of electromotive force. Born in Como within the Duchy of Milan—then under the Enlightened reformist rule of the Austrian Habsburg Monarchy—Volta’s life coincided with a profound restructuring of northern Italian academic institutions, scientific societies, and global communication networks. His invention of the electric battery (the voltaic pile) in 1800 not only resolved the intense international debate regarding 'animal electricity' but also provided the indispensable technological impetus for nineteenth-century electrochemistry, electromagnetism, and industrial technology.Genealogy, Early Life, and Formative EducationAlessandro Volta was born on February 18, 1745, into an aristocratic yet financially modest family of Lombardy. His father, Filippo Volta, belonged to an ancient noble lineage of Como, while his mother, Donna Maddalena dei Conti Inzaghi, reconnected the young Volta to prominent regional clerical and administrative elites. Remarkably slow in his early linguistic development—he did not speak articulate sentences until the age of four—Volta soon displayed an exceptional intellect and an insatiable curiosity regarding natural phenomena. Following the death of his father in 1752, his education was directed by his paternal uncles, particularly Canonico Ascanio Volta, who steered the young noble toward a traditional humanist curriculum administered by the local Jesuit college in Como.While the Jesuits sought to recruit the precocious youth into their order, Volta resisted clerical vows, drawn instead to the burgeoning fields of natural philosophy and experimental physics. During the 1760s, he taught himself the fundamentals of Newtonian mechanics, optics, and pneumatic chemistry, maintaining a lively correspondence with leading scholars across the Italian peninsula. Most notable among his early mentors was Giambatista Beccaria, professor of experimental physics at the University of Turin and the premier Italian authority on Benjamin Franklin’s single-fluid theory of electricity. In 1769, at the age of twenty-four, Volta published his first theoretical treatise, De vi attractiva ignis electrici, ac phaenomenis inde pendentibus ('On the Attractive Force of Electric Fire, and the Phenomena Dependent Thereon'), addressed to Beccaria. In this early work, Volta laid the groundwork for his lifelong methodology: an insistence on quantitative instrument-driven measurement, a mechanical interpretation of imponderable fluids, and a profound skepticism toward unobservable occult qualities in physical nature.Early Inventions, Pneumatics, and the Pavia ProfessorshipVolta’s career as an inventor gained rapid international momentum during the 1770s. In 1775, while serving as rector and professor of physics at the Royal Grammar School (*Regio Ginnasio*) of Como, he perfected and popularized the elettroforo perpetuo (electrophorus). Building upon earlier experiments by Johan Carl Wilcke, Volta created a device consisting of a resinous disc excited by friction and a metallic plate with an insulating handle. This instrument allowed for the repeated transfer and accumulation of static charge without requiring continuous rubbing, serving as an early prototype for modern electrostatic generators. The widespread acclaim of the electrophorus established Volta's reputation throughout Europe's leading scientific academies.Between 1776 and 1778, Volta turned his intellectual energies toward pneumatic chemistry, spurred by the discovery of various gases by Joseph Priestley and Antoine Lavoisier. While exploring the marshlands of Lake Maggiore near Angera, Volta observed bubbles of inflammable gas escaping from the muddy sediment. Through rigorous experimentation, he isolated this substance—which he named aria infiammabile delle paludi ('inflammable air of the marshes')—now recognized as methane ($CH_4$). Volta analyzed its combustion properties, constructed the eudiometer to measure the oxygen content of atmospheric air via controlled electrical explosions, and developed the 'electric pistol' (*pistola di Volta*), a precursor to the internal combustion engine mechanism wherein an electric spark ignited a gaseous mixture to propel a lead projectile.Recognizing his scientific brilliance, Empress Maria Theresa of Austria appointed Volta to the Chair of Experimental Physics at the University of Pavia in 1778. Pavia was then undergoing a radical Habsburg-sponsored institutional renaissance designed to make it a premier center of European Enlightenment science. Over his three decades at Pavia, Volta transformed the physics cabinet into one of the most sophisticated laboratories in Europe, procuring state-of-the-art instruments from London and Paris. He proved to be a dedicated educator, drawing hundreds of students from across Europe and engaging in extensive scientific voyages through Switzerland, France, Germany, and England, where he established personal ties with Antoine Lavoisier, Pierre-Simon Laplace, Benjamin Franklin, and Sir Joseph Banks, President of the Royal Society.The Galvanic Controversy and the Invention of the Voltaic PileThe defining chapter of Volta’s career began in 1791 following the publication of De viribus electricitatis in motu musculari commentarius by Luigi Galvani, professor of anatomy at the University of Bologna. Galvani reported that dissected frog legs twitched violently when their exposed nerves and muscles were touched simultaneously by a bimetallic arc (such as copper and iron). Galvani interpreted this phenomenon as evidence of an intrinsic, physiological 'animal electricity' generated by the brain, carried by the nerves, and stored in the muscles.Initially receptive to Galvani's findings, Volta undertook a meticulous series of replication experiments in his Pavia laboratory throughout 1792 and 1793. Armed with exceedingly sensitive electrometers of his own design—incorporating delicate straw indicators and condensing plates—Volta arrived at a radically different conclusion. He asserted that the frog’s muscular contractions were not caused by an inherent biological electricity, but rather by an external electrical current generated by the simple contact of two dissimilar metals mediated by the moisture of the organic tissue. This formulation, known as the theory of 'contact electricity' or 'heterogeneity,' ignited one of the most fierce and productive debates in the history of modern science.To prove conclusively that metals acted as active generators of electricity rather than mere passive conductors, Volta systematically removed all animal tissue from his experimental apparatus. He arranged pairs of heterogeneous metallic discs—most effectively zinc and silver or zinc and copper—separated by non-metallic cardboard or leather pads soaked in salt water or acid solution. By stacking these alternating elements in a vertical column, Volta multiplied the electromotive force, creating the world's first primary electrochemical cell: the voltaic pile (pila voltaica), alongside its variant, the 'crown of cups' (*couronne de tasses*).On March 20, 1800, Volta announced his revolutionary invention in a historic French-language letter addressed to Sir Joseph Banks, entitled On the Electricity excited by the mere Contact of Conducting Substances of different Species. Published in the Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society, Volta described an apparatus capable of delivering an unending, continuous stream of electricity, contrasting sharply with the instantaneous spark and discharge of the Leyden jar. Volta’s pile effectively unified the fields of electricity and chemistry, instantly enabling William Nicholson and Anthony Carlisle to accomplish the electrolysis of water in May 1800, and providing Sir Humphry Davy with the tool to isolate alkali metals such as sodium and potassium shortly thereafter.Napoleonic Patronage, Political Honors, and Twilight YearsThe geopolitical upheavals of the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars profoundly impacted Volta’s later life. Following Napoleon Bonaparte's conquest of northern Italy and the establishment of the Cisalpine Republic, Volta retained his prestigious academic standing. In November 1801, Napoleon invited Volta to Paris to present his discovery before the *Institut de France*. Over three session presentations attended by Bonaparte himself, Volta demonstrated the properties of the pile. Enraptured by Volta’s physical demonstrations, Napoleon bestowed upon him a massive gold medal, a generous pension, the title of Count of the Kingdom of Italy, and a seat in the Italian Senate.Despite these immense political honors and administrative appointments, Volta remained deeply committed to a quiet, private life. He married Donna Teresa Peregrini in 1794, with whom he had three sons: Zanino, Flaminio, and Luigi. The premature death of Flaminio in 1814 cast a shadow over his final years. Volta gradually withdrew from public academic duties at Pavia, retiring to his country estate in Camnago, near Como, where he spent his twilight years in agricultural management, religious devotion, and quiet reflection.Alessandro Volta passed away at Camnago on March 5, 1827, at the age of eighty-two. In recognition of his foundational contributions, the International Electrical Congress of 1881 officially named the SI unit of electric potential and electromotive force the Volt in his honor. His home town of Como erected the Tempio Voltiano in 1928, a neoclassical museum housing his original manuscripts, instruments, and physical apparatus, enduring as a physical testament to the father of modern electrical technology.

academic_description: In 8vo (mm. 201x126); pp. 147, (1), c. (1) aggiunta successivamente. Segnatura: a-h8 i10 [χ]1. Vignetta calcografica al frontespizio accompagnata dal motto: “Alpino modo quae certare rigori. Audebatis aque non cediti ignibus ipsis”. Armi del dedicatario, il marchese Francesco Castelli, alla carta a2r. Con inoltre 12 finissime incisioni su rame nel testo, alcune delle quali raffiguranti degli esperimenti. Capilettera xilografici. Al recto dell'ultima carta, aggiunta probabilmente in un momento successivo alla pubblicazione, è stampato: “Didicistis, nihil forte im Physicis intellectu difficilius, quam quidnam proprie sit illud corporei, quod unice combustils sit in materia combustili. Boerh. de Alim. dic. Ign. Exp. XIII.”. Alone all'angolo inferiore destro dei fascicoli a-f, che progressivamente tende ad attenuarsi, ed alone all'angolo superiore sinistro dei fascicoli a-c. Cartoncino coevo colorato un po' sbiadito, lievi abrasioni. Nota manoscritta al dorso. Buona copia genuina. Dedica manoscritta autografa dell'autore al risguardo anteriore (“Dono dell' chiarissimo Autore a Pietro Cernezzi oggi 17. Marzo 1777.”). I Cernezzi, famiglia decurionale già presente a Como nel 1447, ottennero il 28 gennaio 1817, con una sovrana risoluzione, la conferma della propria nobiltà. Pietro, membro del Consiglio Comunale di Como nel 1813 (Bollettino delle Leggi del Regno d'Italia. Parte II. N° 17 al N° 22), ebbe una lunga relazione epistolare con il Volta.EDIZIONE ORIGINALE di questo importante trattato, composto di sette lettere, nel quale l'autore espone a Carlo Giuseppe Campi le ricerche da lui compiute sul gas che risale dalle paludi (metano), che in precedenza non era stato distinto dall'idrogeno. L'opera stimolò i ricercatori a nuovi esperimenti che portarono successivamente alla scoperta della composizione dell'acqua.“Per la storia della chimica è della massima importanza la scoperta degli idrocarburi. Il primo e più importante idrocarburo, dal quale tutti gli altri e tutti i composti organici derivano, è contenuto nel gas delle paludi, che fu poi detto metano. Fu nel 1776 che il Volta scoprì il gas delle paludi in seguito ad un'osservazione accidentale del P. Campi. Egli descrive questo nuovo gas e le località in cui l'ha trovato in sette lettere al suo amico P. Campi...” (Guareschi, La chimica in Italia dal 1750 al 1800, in Suppl. ann. Enc. Chim., 1912, pp. 395- 403).“The discovery of marsh gas... is described by Volta in some letters to Campi, dated from Como (November 1776 to January 1777)... He distinguished it from the inflammable air from metals (hydrogen) by its azure-blue flame and slower combustion, and by its requiring 10-12 vols. Of air for detonation. A much larger electric spark was necessary to ignite marsh gas than to ignite hydrogen. Volta, who invented the electric pistol, thought detonating gas could be used as a propellant...” (Partington, History of Chemistry, III, p. 814).

authors.name: Benzi Ugo
authors.biography: Ugo Benzi, also known in Latin as Hugo Bentius, Hugo de Senis, and Hugo Senensis, was born at Siena on 24 February 1376 and died at Ferrara on 30 November 1439. Earlier scholarship commonly placed his birth between about 1360 and 1370, but the precise date was established from the Vita Ugonis composed shortly after his death by his son Socino and preserved in a miscellany of the Biblioteca Comunale Ariostea at Ferrara. Although older accounts described the Benzi as a noble family, Socino states that they belonged neither to the nobility nor to the poor, but to the Sienese urban bourgeoisie and politically to the faction of the Dodici. Ugo's father, Andrea, was a magistrate whose fortunes deteriorated after the defeat of his faction and during the conflict between Siena and Florence; his paternal uncle Marco was an established physician and university teacher. These circumstances help to explain both the financial difficulty of Benzi's early education and the pronounced mobility of his subsequent academic career.Benzi received grammatical instruction at Siena, but warfare interrupted his studies. About 1393 he went to Florence, reportedly financing the journey through the sale of a valuable garment, and there began the study of philosophy. He continued at Bologna under Pietro Mantovano, although the relationship soon ended in disagreement. At Pavia he received a doctorate on 17 October 1396, probably in logic and philosophy rather than medicine, as was formerly supposed. He then taught logic at the Pavian Studium from 1396–97 until 1402, except during the academic year 1399–1400, when the university was transferred to Piacenza because of plague. His lost De logicae artis ratione belongs to this period. The renewed disruption caused by epidemic disease in 1402 marked a decisive change in his intellectual direction: after an interval devoted to Latin literature, he undertook the systematic study of medicine.Called to Bologna, Benzi taught philosophy there from approximately 1402 to 1405 and promoted the study of Averroes and Albert the Great. His surviving philosophical production, though fragmentary, included a paraphrastic treatment of Aristotle's Parva naturalia and a series of questions on natural philosophy. At Bologna he also studied medicine under Marsilio di Santa Sofia and soon began to teach the discipline. On 5 February 1405 he was appointed to the medical chair at Siena with an annual salary of two hundred gold florins. During this Sienese residence he married a woman named Laia, from Percena, and established a large family; his sons included Socino, later his biographer, and Francesco, both of whom pursued medical careers. Benzi visited Perugia and disputed with members of its Studium, but the evidence does not support the once frequent assertion that he occupied a chair there.Benzi left Siena in 1409 after falling under political suspicion. He was present at Pisa during the council of that year as an observer for the Sienese government and subsequently entered the service of Cardinal Baldassarre Cossa, the future antipope John XXIII, as personal physician. He followed Cossa to Bologna and taught medicine there until 1412. His reputation as a disputant was reinforced by an encounter with French scholars associated with the Council of Pisa; this episode, magnified in Socino's laudatory biography, appears to have contributed to the later but unsubstantiated tradition that Benzi taught at Paris or served the French king. In 1412 Niccolò III d'Este summoned him to Parma, where the university had recently been reconstituted. During four productive years there Benzi lectured on medicine and prepared substantial commentaries on Galen's Tegni, the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, and sections of Avicenna's Canon, as well as questions concerning natural and medical philosophy.He returned to Siena for the academic year 1416–17 and remained until 1421, notwithstanding invitations from other cities. A protracted competition between Siena and Florence then ended with his appointment to the Florentine Studium, where he taught from 1421 until 1423 and published his Quaestio de malitia complexionis diversae in January 1422. After leaving Florence, probably amid another epidemic, he again taught at Bologna until 1425. In January 1424 Cardinal Gabriele Condulmer, later Pope Eugenius IV, granted Bolognese citizenship to Benzi and members of his family. Benzi's standing in philosophical as well as medical debate is illustrated by his service in 1425 as judge in a controversy between Paolo Veneto and Niccolò Fava concerning the powers of the soul and the unity of the intellect.On 19 November 1425 Filippo Maria Visconti appointed him ordinary professor of morning medicine at Pavia, initially at a salary of five hundred ducats. Benzi remained there through the academic year 1428–29, lecturing on Hippocrates and Avicenna and issuing a revised form of his Quaestio de putrefactione. He subsequently went to Padua, where he is associated with a human dissection undertaken about February 1430. Soon afterwards Niccolò III d'Este called him to Ferrara as court physician. Benzi does not appear to have held a regular university chair there, but he taught privately and exercised considerable influence; Angelo Decembrio, who named him as his teacher in a work on plague, was among those associated with his instruction. His learned standing also brought him into contact with humanists. Leonardo Bruni answered an inquiry from him concerning the Latin expression summum bonum in Bruni's translation of Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, while Enea Silvio Piccolomini later celebrated his dialectical command of conflicting Platonic and Aristotelian positions.Benzi's Ferrara years combined court practice, teaching, consultation, and authorship. His surviving consilia include opinions prepared for members of the Este and Malatesta circles and demonstrate the geographical and social reach of his medical practice. In 1438, during the presence at Ferrara of Greek and Latin dignitaries connected with the council, he participated in an extended philosophical discussion on causation, celestial motion, the eternity of the world, the immortality of the soul, separate intelligences, and God. The accounts of this occasion are encomiastic, but they attest the esteem accorded to his extemporaneous command of scholastic philosophy. His service to Niccolò III was generously rewarded with salary, money, and landed property in the territory of Rovigo. Between February and May 1439 he made a final visit to Siena, where he was ceremonially received. He died at Ferrara on 30 November and was buried in the Dominican church there.Benzi's principal importance lies in the conjunction of scholastic natural philosophy, university medical commentary, and the practice of consultation. His commentaries did not present a fundamentally new medical system; rather, they exemplify the mature Italian academic method of expounding authoritative texts through exposition, objections, distinctions, and formally organized quaestiones. Avicenna supplied the principal systematic framework, while Galen and Hippocrates remained indispensable authorities for physiology, diagnosis, prognosis, and therapeutics. Benzi's writings consequently preserve the intellectual substance of university lectures and the interaction between a master's exposition and questions generated in the classroom. The incompleteness of some commentaries reflects their origin in successive courses and, in the case of his treatment of Avicenna, the interruption of work by death.The Consilia ad diversas aegritudines constitute his most consequential contribution to practical medical literature. Arranged around individual cases, they ordinarily proceed from the patient's condition and symptoms to prognosis, regimen, and pharmaceutical treatment. They are not clinical histories in the modern sense, yet they document the application of learned Galenic and Arabic medicine to particular bodies and circumstances. The collection was first printed at Bologna on 3 October 1482 by Johann von Nördlingen and Heinrich von Haarlem, in an edition prepared by Lorenzo Gozzadini; enlarged and rearranged versions followed during the sixteenth century. Benzi's commentaries on Galen, Hippocrates, and Avicenna likewise circulated in manuscript before entering print, notably in Venetian folio editions produced in 1498 by Boneto Locatello for the publisher Ottaviano Scoto. Their posthumous publication confirms their continuing utility within the medical curriculum of the early print period.Special caution is required concerning the Tractato utilissimo circa la conservatione della sanitade, printed at Milan in 1481 under Benzi's name and long regarded as one of the earliest medical regimens printed in Italian. No manuscript of the work is attributed to him, it is absent from Socino's Vita, and it is not mentioned in contemporary documentation of Benzi's writings. Juliana Hill Cotton demonstrated that its text derives from an Italian translation of the Libellus de conservatione sanitatis by Benedetto Reguardati of Norcia; the attribution to Benzi in the Milanese edition is therefore spurious. The Tractato remains important in the history of vernacular medicine and early printing, but it can no longer be treated as evidence for Benzi's authorship or medical thought. His securely attributable legacy rests instead upon his academic commentaries, philosophical questions, and extensive body of medical consultations, which together place him among the best-documented itinerant professors and court physicians of early fifteenth-century Italy.

publisher_data: Turin, Heirs of Giovanni Domenico Tarino, 1618
academic_description: 16mo (mm. 122x87). Pp. [32], 850 [i.e. 800]. Signatures: †-†8 A-Ddd8. Printer's device on the title page. Woodcut initials. Contemporary limp vellum binding with four raised bands, yapp edges, and manuscript title on the spine (spine slightly darkened). Ex-libris of Jacques and Hélène Bon. Ownership inscriptions on the front free endpaper, one of which is dated 1763. Light scattered foxing, slight stain on the outer margin of the last leaves, but an excellent and genuine copy.This is the first edition of the treatise on dietetics and hygiene by the Sienese physician Ugo Benzi, accompanied by annotations from the Turin-based physician Giovanni Lodovico Bertaldi, who also contributed an appendix, printed here for the first time, addressing the misuse of alcohol and tobacco. The edition was reprinted in Turin two years later.The Tractato utilissimo circa la conservazione della sanitade by Ugo Benzi, first printed in Milan in 1481, was among the earliest works on hygiene and dietetics to be published in Italian. It is likely that this work, for which no manuscript copies exist, was initially composed in Latin and subsequently translated into Italian by Benzi himself or another author. The reappearance of Benzi's work in Turin in 1618 is a testament to its enduring relevance and simultaneously indicates that ordinary medical practice lagged at least a century behind the advancement of scientific theory. A sort of compendium of Galenic diet, the work discusses air, physical exercise, sleep, and nutrition, with the majority devoted to a detailed description of the properties, qualities, and medicinal uses of various foods and beverages, arranged alphabetically up to the entries for “sugar,” “grape,” and “wine.”Bertaldi's appendix addresses exotic foods, the “passions of the soul” (including love, anger, fear, jealousy, hope, hatred, ambition, avarice, envy, and sadness), and proceeds to consider the abuse of tobacco and alcohol, adding several remedies for inebriation not mentioned by Benzi, some rather harsh, such as the practice in Geneva of spinning drunkards on a giant wheel until they vomited.Ugo Benzi was born in Siena in 1376. His uncle Marco was a renowned physician in Siena. The economic conditions of his father Andrea, a magistrate by profession, were favourable until his faction was defeated and war broke out between Siena and Florence, leading to his ruin and imprisonment for debt, from which his son would free him in 1405. After attending the grammar school of a certain Bennazio in Siena, he likely moved to Florence in 1393, where he began studying philosophy, continuing later in Bologna under Pietro Mantovano, with whom he had a falling out in 1394 for unclear reasons. Following this dispute, Benzi retired to his home, dedicating himself to the study of logic, philosophy, medicine, astronomy, arithmetic, geometry, music, grammar, and rhetoric. He then moved to Pavia, where in 1396 he graduated in logic and philosophy and shortly thereafter began teaching logic until 1402. Subsequently called to the University of Bologna, Benzi reorganised the teaching of philosophy, promoting the study of the works of Averroes and Albertus Magnus. In Bologna, he also studied medicine under Marsilio of S. Sofia. In February 1405, Benzi was engaged by the University of Siena to teach medicine. In 1409, having fallen under suspicion by the rulers, Benzi left Siena and entered the service of Cardinal Baldassarre Cossa as a physician, following him first to Pisa, then to Bologna. Later, called to Parma by Niccolò d'Este, shortly after the reopening of the university, which was due to him, in November 1412, Benzi taught medicine in that city for four consecutive years, years particularly fervent with work; during this time, he wrote three of his principal commentaries, on Galen, the aphorisms of Hippocrates, and Avicenna, as well as some Quaestiones rerum naturalium. Recalled to Siena, where he was absolved of all previous accusations, Benzi taught there from 1416 until 1421, when he moved first to Florence, then again to Bologna, where he remained until 1425. In November 1425, Benzi was engaged by Filippo Maria Visconti as an ordinary professor of medicine in the morning at the University of Pavia, a position he held until the year 1428-29. Benzi left Pavia after completing the reading of the aphorisms of Hippocrates, leaving the commentary on Avicenna incomplete, to go to the University of Padua, during which period a dissection of a cadaver is noted (1430). Shortly thereafter, he moved to Ferrara, called by Niccolò d'Este as a court physician, without however holding a university chair. The teaching must have been conducted only privately and occasionally; among his disciples was Angelo Decembrio, whose treatise on the plague bears the title De cognitione et curatione pestis egregia Ugone praeceptore. From 9 February to 6 May 1439, under the protection of Niccolò d'Este, Benzi made his last visit to Siena, received with great honours. A few months later, on 30 November 1439, he died in Ferrara.Benzi's fame is primarily linked to his qualities as a practical physician and as a master and scholar of theoretical medicine; although he is not distinguished for novel discoveries, nor for absolute novelty of thought, he nevertheless demonstrates a vast knowledge of medical doctrine and uncommon technical-therapeutic experience. His Consilia saluberrima ad omnes aegritudines, a broad series of clinical cases chosen to interest a wide sector of medicine, constitute one of the earliest examples we have of systematic collections of various diseases. He was also the author of commentaries on some fundamental medical texts studied in universities: on Galen, the Aphorisms of Hippocrates, the Canon of Avicenna (cf. Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani, vol. 8, Rome, 1966, s.v.).

title: Orlando furioso [...], ornato di varie figure, con cinque canti d'un nuovo libro, & altre stanze del medesimo, nuovamente aggiunti: con belle allegorie: & nel fine, vna breve espositione de gli oscuri vocaboli: con la tavola di tutto quello che nell'opera si contiene

authors.name: Ariosto Ludovico
authors.biography: Ludovico Ariosto (1474–1533) stands as the supreme poet of the High Italian Renaissance, a monumental figure whose literary masterpiece, the epic romance Orlando Furioso, re-articulated the boundaries of European narrative poetry, humanistic philosophy, and vernacular aesthetics. Operating at the vibrant intersection of classical revival and vernacular innovation within the courtly environment of the House of Este in Ferrara, Ariosto synthesized the chivalric tradition of the Carolingian and Arthurian cycles with the structural discipline, epic gravity, and mythic resonance of Vergil, Ovid, and Catullus. Beyond his poetic endeavors, Ariosto was a pioneer of Renaissance vernacular theatre, a diplomatic servant of state, an astute political commentator through his Satire, and a central protagonist in the linguistic standardisation of Italian literature during the early sixteenth century.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationLudovico Ariosto was born on September 8, 1474, in the fortress town of Reggio Emilia, where his father, Count Niccolò Ariosto, served as the military commander and governor of the citadel on behalf of the Dukes of Ferrara. His mother, Daria Malaguzzi Valeri, belonged to a distinguished noble family of Reggio. As the eldest of ten siblings, young Ludovico spent his earliest years exposed to the administrative and military apparatus of the Este state. In 1484, following his father's reassignment, the family relocated permanently to Ferrara, the intellectual and artistic epicentre of northern Italy under Duke Ercole I d'Este.Between 1489 and 1494, at the insistence of his paternal patriarch, Ariosto reluctantly pursued legal studies at the University of Ferrara. This legal training, though deeply unsuited to his artistic inclinations, imbued him with an acute understanding of jurisprudence, statecraft, and administrative mechanics that would later inform both his satirical works and his diplomatic service. Upon securing his father's permission in 1494, Ariosto abandoned the law to immerse himself entirely in Humanistic letters. Under the tutelage of the Augustinian humanist Gregorio da Spoleto, Ariosto acquired a deep mastery of Latin classical literature, analyzing Catullus, Horace, Ovid, and Propertius, and composing his initial Latin lyrics (such as De diversis amoribus and Carmina). His burgeoning intellectual network expanded rapidly, connecting him with prominent humanists including Ercole Strozzi, Pietro Bembo—who resided in Ferrara between 1502 and 1503—and the court humanists surrounding Isabella d'Este and Alfonso d'Este.The sudden death of Count Niccolò in 1500 abruptly terminated Ariosto's period of unencumbered scholarly retreat. As the head of a large household burdened with modest financial resources, Ludovico was compelled to assume public office to sustain his family. He accepted the captaincy of the fortress of Canossa in 1502 and subsequently entered the formal service of Cardinal Ippolito d'Este, son of Duke Ercole I, in 1503. This appointment initiated a long, arduous, and frequently fraught career as a courtier, diplomatic envoy, and administrative officer, binding his creative life directly to the political vicissitudes of the House of Este.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksAriosto's literary output is remarkable for its generic breadth and structural sophistication. While his early Latin verse demonstrated a refined command of neo-Latin lyricism, his transition to the vernacular marked a revolutionary turn in European letters. In the realm of drama, Ariosto established the foundations of Renaissance commedia erudita—vernacular theatre modeled on the classical structures of Plautus and Terence. His plays, including La Cassaria (1508), I Suppositi (1509), Il Negromante (1520), and La Lena (1528), combined classical comic devices (mistaken identities, cunning servants, romantic entanglements) with razor-sharp observations of contemporary Ferrarese and Italian urban society.Between 1517 and 1525, Ariosto composed his seven Satire, a collection of autobiographical, epistolary poems written in terza rima and addressed to relatives and close friends, including his brother Galasso and the humanist Bembo. Modeled after the Satires and Epistles of Horace, these poems present a poignant, witty, and fiercely independent critique of courtly servitude, ecclesiastical corruption, political ambition, and the precarious existence of the Renaissance intellectual. In these verses, Ariosto articulates a moral philosophy rooted in stoic self-reliance, intellectual freedom, and the quiet pursuit of poetic domesticity.Ariosto's supreme achievement remains Orlando Furioso, conceived as a continuation of Matteo Maria Boiardo's unfinished Orlando Innamorato (1495). Written in flawless ottava rima (ABABABCC), the poem weaves three primary narrative strands: the war between the Christian forces of Charlemagne and the Saracen invaders led by King Agramante; the tragic descent into madness of the paladin Orlando following his discovery of the romance between Angelica and Medoro; and the dynastic romance of the Saracen warrior Ruggiero and the female Christian knight Bradamante, designed as the mythical foundation of the House of Este. Through a sophisticated narrative architecture known as entrelacement (interlacing multiple plot lines), Ariosto creates a vast, cosmic tapestry wherein human desires, illusions, and frailties are examined with sublime ironical detachment. The famous episode of Astolfo's journey to the Moon on the hippogriff to retrieve Orlando's lost sanity serves as an enduring philosophical allegory on the vanity of human ambition, the instability of reason, and the pervasive nature of earthly folly.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationThe printing history of Orlando Furioso represents one of the most critical case studies in early modern textual transmission and authorial revision. Ariosto was meticulously attentive to the print medium, actively participating in the production, typographical design, and distribution of his masterpiece across three distinct major redactions:1. The First Redaction (1516): Printed in Ferrara by Giovanni Mazocco da Bondeno, this editio princeps contained 40 cantos. Written in a vernacular heavily influenced by the regional Ferrarese and northern Italian literary dialects, the edition was produced under Ariosto's immediate oversight in a run of approximately 1,250 copies.2. The Second Redaction (1521): Published in Ferrara by Giovan Battista della Pigna and Giovan Battista da Panico, this edition retained the 40-canto structure but underwent meticulous stylistic polishing, textual correction, and minor structural modifications aimed at smoothing dialectal irregularities.3. The Third Redaction (1532): Printed in Ferrara by Francesco Rosso da Valenza, this definitive edition expanded the poem to 46 cantos (incorporating new episodes such as the story of Olimpia and the tragic tale of Marganorre). Most importantly, Ariosto executed a massive linguistic overhaul of the entire text, systematically aligning its phonology, morphology, and syntax with the archaic Tuscan literary model championed by Pietro Bembo in his seminal grammatical treatise, Prose della vulgar lingua (1525). By purging northern regionalisms and adopting Petrarchan lexical norms, Ariosto rendered the Furioso a pan-Italian masterpiece capable of nationwide circulation.Following Ariosto's death in 1533, the publication of Orlando Furioso expanded exponentially, particularly through the commercial print houses of Venice. Publishers such as Gabriele Giolito de' Ferrari (who issued his iconic illustrated edition in 1542) and Vincenzo Valgrisi (1556) transformed the text into an international best-seller, introducing visual woodcuts, marginal glosses, allegorical commentaries (such as those by Girolamo Ruscelli), and detailed indexes that codified how early modern readers engaged with epic poetry.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyThe impact of Ariosto's work upon European literature was immediate, profound, and contentious. During the mid-to-late sixteenth century, the Furioso became the focal point of intense critical debates among Italian literary theorists, contrasting Ariosto's romantic, polycentric narrative freedom with Torquato Tasso's Aristotelian, unified epic model in Gerusalemme Liberata. Theorists such as Giovan Battista Pigna (I Romanzi, 1554) and Giovan Battista Giraldi Cinzio defended Ariosto's romance structure as a valid, modern evolution of classicism, whereas orthodox Neo-Aristotelians criticized its episodic digressions and lighthearted irony.Abroad, Ariosto's influence profoundly shaped the Northern Renaissance. Edmund Spenser drew directly upon the Furioso for the structure, allegorical method, and characterization of The Faerie Queene (1590), while William Shakespeare adapted the plot of Hero and Claudio in Much Ado About Nothing from Ariosto's tale of Ariodante and Ginevra (Canto IV–VI). Sir John Harington's celebrated English translation of 1591 introduced Ariostean verse to the Elizabethan court.In the Enlightenment and Romantic eras, Ariosto received widespread acclaim from figures such as Voltaire—who praised the poet's boundless imagination and stylistic clarity—and Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, who portrayed the poet's life in his drama Torquato Tasso. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, critics transformed the understanding of Ariosto's genius. Francesco De Sanctis identified Ariosto as the poet of pure form and harmonic artifice, while Benedetto Croce famously characterized his output as the supreme expression of 'cosmic harmony' (l'armonia cosmica). Modern scholarship, led by figures such as Santorre Debenedetti, Cesare Segre, Carlo Dionisotti, Lanfranco Caretti, and Albert Russell Ascoli, has emphasized the complex historical, political, and psychological anxieties underlying Ariosto's deceptive ironical elegance. Today, Ludovico Ariosto remains universally recognized as one of the towering titans of world literature, whose monumental vision of human frailty, romantic illusion, and poetic grace continues to resonate across global culture.

publisher_data: Lyon, Jacques Faure for Sebastien Honorat, 1556
academic_description: 4to (249x156 mm). 508, [44] pp. Collation: A-Z8 Aa-Ll8 Mm4. Printer's device on title page and ll. Ff1r, Kk1r, and Mm4r. Leaf Ii8 is a blank. Colophon on l. Ii7v. Text printed in two columns, italic and roman type. With a woodcut architectural title page, numerous decorated initials, and 52 woodcut vignettes printed at the beginning of every book of the poem and the final stanza. On l. Ff1r Gli Cinque canti opens with a separate title page; on l. Kk1r Le sposizione di tutti i vocaboli […] raccolte da M. Lodovico Dolce begins, likewise with a separate title page. Contemporary Lyonnaise binding in richly gilt-tooled light brown morocco, flat spine, panels with large gilt-stamped centre- and corner-pieces, gilt and gauffered edges (skillfully restored, lower joint slightly cracked). On l. A2r the ownership inscription “Juris Consulti D. Joseph Lishri [?]”; on the last back flyleaf the manuscript note “Respize”. Upper margin of l. Ff1 repaired, some staining, slightly and uniformly browned, small round wormhole to the lower margin in the first half of the volume, not affecting the text. A good copy ruled in red throughout. Preserved in a cloth box.The very rare first Italian-language edition printed in France of Ariosto's poem. In the same year Faure-Honorat also issued an 8vo edition and Rouillé an edition in 16mo. The Furioso had previously been printed in Paris and Lyons only in its French and Spanish translations.The significant production of Italian books that came out of French presses in the 1540s and 1550s were intended not only for Italians residing in France, but also the many French speakers who had learned Italian over the course of war, study, or business, including many impressive noblewomen (cf. J. Balsamo, L'italianisme lyonnais et l'illustration de la langue française, in: “Lyon et l'illustration de la langue française à la Renaissance”, Lyon, 2003, pp. 211-229).
