authors.name: Champier Symphorien
authors.biography: Symphorien Champier (ca. 1474–1539) stands as one of the most prolific, enigmatic, and quintessential figures of the early French Renaissance. Operating at the dynamic intersection of late medieval scholastic encyclopedism and the emergent humanist movement, Champier was a practicing physician, a civic magistrate, a royal historiographer, and an insatiable polymath. Based primarily in Lyon—the supreme commercial and typographical crossroads of Western Europe during the early sixteenth century—he acted as a primary conduit through which Italian Renaissance Neoplatonism, medical humanism, and Hermetic philosophy were translated, adapted, and disseminated into the French intellectual vernacular. Far from being a mere passive compiler, Champier utilized his vast literary output to construct an ambitious, syncretic worldview that sought to reconcile ancient Greek medicine with Christian theology, Aristotelian physics with Platonic metaphysics, and chivalric French historiography with classical erudition.Born around 1474 in Saint-Symphorien-le-Château, in the Lyonnais region, Champier belonged to a family of modest local prominence. His early intellectual formation took place at the University of Paris, where he was exposed to the vibrant circle of Christian humanists centered around Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples. This Parisian experience proved seminal: Lefèvre’s pious Aristotelianism and his enthusiasm for the newly translated corpus of Marsilio Ficino and Hermes Trismegistus profoundly shaped Champier’s lifelong intellectual trajectory. Seeking a professional vocation, Champier subsequently migrated south to the renowned Faculty of Medicine at the University of Montpellier, the historical citadel of Western medical pedagogy. There, he absorbed both the traditional Arabo-Galenic medical curriculum and the emerging critical philology of the early medical humanists, culminating in the attainment of his doctorate in medicine around 1503.Upon completing his medical studies, Champier established himself in Lyon, where he rapidly integrated into the city’s ruling patriciate and intellectual elite. His professional prestige earned him appointment as personal physician to Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, whom Champier accompanied on military campaigns during the Italian Wars, most notably participating in the expedition that culminated in the Battle of Marignano in 1515. For his valiant service on the battlefield, Champier was knighted by the Duke. Returning to Lyon with elevated social status, he served multiple terms as a city consul (échevin) and was instrumental in founding the Collège des Médecins of Lyon in 1536, an institution designed to regulate medical practice, combat empiricism and charlatanry, and elevate the scholarly standing of the medical profession against the encroachment of uneducated apothecaries and barbers.Champier’s published oeuvre is astonishing in its thematic range and volume, reflecting an unyielding commitment to intellectual synthesis. Among his most influential philosophical works is the Symphonia Platonis cum Aristotele et Galeni cum Hippocrate, published in Lyon in 1516 by Jean Marion. In this monumental treatise, Champier applied the concordist methodology pioneered by Pico della Mirandola and Marsilio Ficino, seeking to demonstrate the fundamental harmony underlying Platonic philosophy, Aristotelian logic, Hippocratic etiology, and Galenic physiology. For Champier, natural science and medicine were not autonomous empirical disciplines but integral components of a universal Christian theology. His medical treatises, such as the Rosa gallica (1514) and the Cribratio medicamentorum (1515), participated vigorously in the fierce contemporary debates over the authority of medieval Islamic authorities like Avicenna and Rhazes. Championing a form of French medical nationalism, Champier advocated a return to the pristine Greek and Roman sources, attempting to purge pharmacology of Arabist accretions while defending traditional Galenic humoral theory against radical innovation.Simultaneously, Champier was a pioneering pioneer in the realm of medical historiography and bio-bibliography. His De medicinae Claris Scriptoribus (1506) represents one of the earliest systematic histories of medical literature ever printed, offering critical notices and bio-bibliographical sketches of ancient, medieval, and contemporary medical authors. Beyond medicine and philosophy, Champier authored numerous vernacular treatises aimed at aristocratic patronage and moral edification, including La Grant Nef des folz du monde (1503), an adaptation of Sebastian Brant’s famous satire, and La Nef des dames vertueuses (1503), a major contribution to the querelle des femmes in which he defended the moral and intellectual dignity of women using Neoplatonic arguments concerning spiritual beauty. His historical works, such as Les Grandes Chroniques des gestes et vertueux faictz des tresexcellens ducz et princes des royaumes de Hierusalem, de Cypre, de Sicile et de Calabre (1516), served to legitimize the territorial and dynastic ambitions of his patron, the Duke of Lorraine.The physical production of Champier’s works offers a vivid window into the gold age of Lyonnese and Parisian printing. Champier maintained intricate, highly strategic relationships with the foremost printer-publishers of his day, including Josse Bade (Jodocus Badius Ascensius) in Paris, as well as Jacques Sacon, Guillaume Balsarin, and Jean Marion in Lyon. Champier was extraordinarily attentive to the visual and typographic presentation of his books, frequently supervising the inclusion of intricate woodcut illustrations, elaborate architectural title borders, and complex marginal annotations. His texts were designed not merely for academic consumption but as luxurious physical artifacts meant to appeal to noble patrons, wealthy merchants, and international scholars. The print runs of his works circulated extensively across France, the Italian peninsula, the Holy Roman Empire, and the Low Countries, cementing Lyon’s reputation as an international hub of humanist book trade.Despite his immense popularity and social prominence, Champier was a controversial figure during his lifetime and in subsequent historiography. His complex position—standing firmly with one foot in medieval scholastic syncretism and the other in Renaissance humanism—made him a target for younger, more radical humanist reformers. Most famously, François Rabelais, a contemporary physician at the Hôtel-Dieu of Lyon, parodied Champier’s dense, eclectic, and often verbose style in Pantagruel, mocking his pedantic citations and conservative medical positions. Furthermore, Champier’s aggressive stance against radical astrology and magic, set forth in his Dialogus in magicarum artium destructionem (ca. 1500), drew criticism from traditional astrologers, even as his own reliance on Hermetic and Neoplatonic occult sympathies left him open to charges of inconsistency.Symphorien Champier died in Lyon around 1539, leaving behind a monumental bibliographical legacy that bridges two cultural epochs. Modern historiography, led by scholars such as Paul Allut and Brian P. Copenhaver, has re-evaluated Champier no longer as a mere pedantic compiler, but as a crucial historical agent who facilitated the naturalization of Italian Renaissance philosophy within Northern Europe. His life and works remain indispensable for understanding the transmission of Neoplatonism, the evolution of early modern medical humanism, and the vital role of the printing press in shaping the intellectual contours of sixteenth-century Europe.

publisher_data: [Lyon], Jean Phiroben & Jean Divineur for Jacques François Giunta, 1519
academic_description: 8vo (157x105 mm). [96] leaves. Collation: a-m8. Title printed in red and black and a full-page woodcut at the end showing the author with his patron and his wife kneeling in prayer. 20th-century gilt calf, marbled endleaves. Skilfully repaired worm track to the outer margin of several leaves not affecting the text, small repaired hole to l. e8 with loss of some text (the missing text has been supplied by hand), uniformly browned, still a good copy.Rare first edition of Champier's most interesting work, a significant document for the development of cultural nationalism among Renaissance intellectuals. Champier was in Italy three times: in 1506, in 1509 and in 1515. During his last travel he spent some time at Pavia, where he was admitted to the ‘collegium artistarum et medicorum'. The speech by Pietro Antonio Rustico, lecturer on logic and medicine, held on that occasion and printed toward the end of the volume, shows how proud Champier was about this honor. Rustico also alludes to Champier's family ties in Italy, which he sees in the Campeggi families of Bologna and Pavia. At the end of the speech Rustico enumerates and praises the hitherto books published by Champier, important as an early bibliography. The main part of the volume though consists of a ‘epistolary duel' with Girolamo da Pavia, an Augustinian monk from Asti, with whom Champier had for five years an intensive correspondence through the Lyonese publisher Balthazar de Gabiano (cf. P. Jodogne, La correspondence de Symphorien Champier avec Jérôme de Pavie dans le ‘Duellum epistolare', in: “The Late Middle Ages and the Dawn of Humanism Outside of Italy”, G. Verneke & J. Ijsewijn, eds., Den Haag, 1972, pp. 44-56).In the Duellum Champier defends the French culture against the pretended superiority of the Italian claimed by some scholars, namely Sabellico, Foresti and Battista Mantovano. He also sees in many Italian writers detractors moved only by jealousy and malice and mentions Valla, Merula, Poggio, Pico and Girolamo Balbo. Fierce of his Lyonnais origins he praises the antique origins of his native city on the authority of Berosus, which however was rightly questioned by Girolamo da Pavia and Raphael Maffei of Volterra. Even though Champier was not familiar with Annius of Viterbo's Antiquities (1498), in which the Berosus tradition made its first appearance, Champier contributed to the Gallican, anti-Italian Italia mendax narrative based on Berosus' assertions about the origin of the names “Gallia” and “Lugdunum” (cf. R. Cooper, Symphorien Champier et l'Italie, in: “L'Aube de la Renaissance”, Genève, 1991, pp. 233-246; see also W. Stephens, Giants in Those Days, Lincoln, 1989, pp. 171-174).The volume contains furthermore various letters by Champier to others, e.g. a letter to Erasmus (Ep. 680a), in which Champier intervenes in his favor in the latter's dispute with Lefèvre d'Etaples over Psalm 8; a letter to Lefèvre d'Etaples followed by Champier's commentary on the Definitiones Asclepii (first published with Lazzarelli's translation in 1507), expressing his attitude to the Hermetic writings. But the book also contains letters addressed to Champier, mainly from other scholars and physicians, among them Alessandro Benedetti and Robert Cockburn, bishop of Ross (cf. A. Broadie, James Liddell on Concepts and Signs, in: “The Renaissance in Scotland: studies in literature, religion, history and culture”, A.A. MacDonald, et al. eds., Leiden, 1994, p. 82; see also J. Durkan, Robert Cockburn, bishop of Ross and French humanism, in: “Innes Review”, IV, 1953, pp. 121-2.).The volume closes with Catalogus preceptorum, patronorum, familarium et auditorum, in which Champier lists his teachers, patrons, friends and students.Though some scholars believe the work to be printed either at Basel or at Venice, it was in fact printed at Lyon, where the two printers Johann Froben and Jean Divineur were active for several Lyonese publishers such as Luxembourg de Gabiano, Jacques Giunta and François Fradin.Symphorien Champier, was born into a bourgeois family at Saint-Symphorien-sur-Croise, near Lyon and studied at the University of Paris before 1495, when he matriculated at the medical school of Montpellier, which granted him his doctorate in 1504. He taught liberal arts in Grenoble and took a doctorate in theology in 1502. In 1509 he was appointed physician to Antoine Duke of Lorraine, who brought him to Nancy. Champier followed the duke several time to Italy, where he was involved in the battles of Agnadello (1509) and Marignano (1515). During his stays in Italy he won recognition as an academic teacher from the University of Pavia. In 1519 he became an alderman in Lyon, and for the last twenty years of his life he was at the center of the cultural Renaissance of that city, while simultaneously promoting the study of medicine by helping to found the College of the Holy Trinity and sponsoring translations of, and writing commentaries on, the works of Hippocrates and Galen. In the 1530s he was involved in a controversy on the merits of Greek and Arab medicine with the German physician Lorenz Fries and also with the botanist Leonhard Fuchs. Michael Servetus, who was his student, wrote a defense of Champier against Fuchs, In Leonardum Fuchsium Apologia. Defensio pro Symphoriano Campeggio (1536). Champier became more and more hostile to Arabic medicine and in Clysteriorum campi contra Arabum (this work was ironically put by Rabelais in his library of Saint-Victor), he even goes so far to advise his readers to refrain from reading the Arabs. With over fifty titles to his credit, Champier was a very prolific author, editor and compiler. His most important writings were in medicine, pharmacy, philosophy, and occultism, but he also worked in theology, history, biography, genealogy, poetry, patristics, and many other fields. The famous scholar printer Etienne Dolet remarked in his Commentariorum linguae latinae (Lyon, 1536): ‘From the schools of the physicians these rushed to the battle: Symphorien Champier, Jacques Dubois, Jean Ruelle, Jean Cop, François Rabelais, Charles Paludan. From all sides this serried band of doctors made such inroads into the camp of the barbarian that, wherever they stood, no place was left to the enemy' (cf. B.P. Copenhaver, Symphorien Champier and the Reception of the Occultist Tradition in Renaissance France, The Hague, 1978, pp. 45-86; see also R. Cooper, Les derniers année de Symphorien Champier, in: “Réforme, Humanisme, Renaissance”, 47, 1998, pp. 25-50).

title: Descrittione del nobil palazzo, posto nel contà di Bologna. Detto Tusculano, del molto Illustre, et Reverendiss. Monsignore, il Sig. Gio. Battista Campeggi, Vescovo di Maiorica. Composta da M. Giulio Cesare Croce

authors.name: Croce Giulio Cesare
authors.biography: Giulio Cesare Croce (1550–1609) stands as one of the most ubiquitous, prolific, and culturally significant figures of early modern Italian literature, serving as an irreplaceable bridge between the vibrant oral traditions of the public square and the rapidly expanding market for cheap printed vernacular books. Born in March 1550 in the rural township of San Giovanni in Persiceto, within the agricultural hinterland of Bologna, Croce embodied the paradoxical identity of the artisan-author: a working blacksmith who transformed himself into an iconic street performer (cantastorie), polymathic rhymester, and court entertainer. Writing in an era defined by the rigid religious orthodoxy of the Counter-Reformation and the formalistic constraints of late Renaissance classicism, Croce carved out an expansive artistic domain dedicated to the material, linguistic, and humorous realities of the lower social strata. Over a career spanning four decades, he authored over four hundred distinct works—ranging from broadside ballads, moral fables, carnival songs, and rustic comedies to prognostications, riddles, and his undisputed masterpiece, the rustic narrative cycle of Bertoldo and Bertoldino. Through his unique mastery of both regional dialects and vernacular Italian, Croce articulated the anxieties, bodily pleasures, economic hardships, and folk wisdom of early modern Europe's subaltern classes, securing a permanent place in the annals of Western popular culture.The formative years of Giulio Cesare Croce were shaped by humble social origins and severe personal adversity. He was the son of Ercole Croce, a smith of modest means, and Laura Varotti. Following the premature death of his father during Giulio's early childhood, the family was cast into financial precarity, prompting his mother to entrust the young boy's upbringing and training to his paternal uncle, a blacksmith operating in the neighboring rural community of Medicina. It was within the sparks, soot, and rhythmic iron-striking of the smithy that Croce spent his formative youth, absorbing the trade that would forever anchor his public identity. Despite receiving no formal humanistic or university education, Croce exhibited an astonishing aptitude for self-directed learning. He taught himself to read and write, developed a proficient mastery of the lute and violin, and began improvising verses inspired by classical mythology, chivalric romances, and local folklore. In the mid-1570s, Croce permanently relocated to Bologna, the second city of the Papal States and a bustling metropolis characterized by a prestigious university, flourishing printing houses, and an intense civic life.In Bologna, Croce devised an extraordinary dual existence that defined his career: by day, he labored at the forge to earn a meager living, while during evenings, festival days, and carnival seasons, he took to the public arenas—most notably the vast expanse of Piazza Maggiore—as a professional storyteller and musician. Dressed in modest artisanal attire and carrying his instrument, he gathered dense crowds of urban laborers, peasants, merchants, students, and foreign visitors, performing original verse narratives that combined topical satire, slapstick humor, and profound moral observations. Crucially, Croce's talent was not confined to the street pavement; his sharp intellect and innate poetic agility earned him entry into the aristocratic salons of the Bolognese nobility and the refined meetings of elite literary academies, such as the famous Accademia dei Gelati. Despite this cross-class mobility, Croce remained economically vulnerable throughout his entire life. Burdened by the financial demands of supporting two successive wives—first Chiara della Seta, with whom he had fourteen children, and after her death, Giulia Pazzaglia, who bore him another child—he lived in continuous risk of poverty, reliant on the volatile proceeds from his printed broadsides and small patronage gifts from wealthy patrons.The literary production of Giulio Cesare Croce is staggering in its volume, thematic diversity, and stylistic heterogeneity. Operating at the intersection of oral performance and typographical reproduction, Croce composed across a bewildering array of genres. His early publications consisted of ephemeral broadsheets (fogli volanti) and inexpensive octavo pamphlets (libretti da doi quattrini) that featured street songs, lamentations on natural disasters, praises of humble trades, and festive dialogues. His linguistic repertoire was exceptionally rich: he moved fluidly between standard Tuscanized Italian, the authentic Bolognese dialect of his native region, macaronic Latin, and the specialized jargon of wandering beggars, peddlers, and thieves. Croce's artistic vision reached its absolute zenith in his prose narratives dedicated to the figure of Bertoldo. Published in Bologna in 1606 under the title Le sottilissime astutie di Bertoldo ('The Subtle Cunning of Bertoldo'), the work adapted medieval folk motifs—specifically the tradition of the dialogue between King Solomon and Marcolf—transposing them into the early medieval court of the Lombard King Alboin (Alboino) in Verona.In Bertoldo, Croce created an indelible archetype of the unpolished, ugly, yet supremely intelligent peasant whose natural cunning, practical common sense, and earthy wisdom consistently outwit the pompous courtiers, arrogant philosophers, and legalistic scholars surrounding the royal throne. Bertoldo represents the physical and mental resilience of the agrarian poor; his grotesque bodily features—a massive head, small eyes, broad mouth, and rough hands—mirror his rejection of refined courtly aesthetics. The narrative achieves profound tragicomic power in its conclusion: brought to live at court as a reward for his cleverness, Bertoldo falls ill and dies because he is deprived of his natural diet of turnips, beans, and coarse onions, symbolizing the insurmountable, lethal conflict between rustic authenticity and elite courtly decadence. Sensing the immense commercial success of the work, Croce published a sequel in 1608, Le piacevoli et ridiculose simplicità di Bertoldino, which introduced Bertoldo's dim-witted son, whose absurd innocence and literal-minded blunders create a brilliant comic contrast to his father's sharp intellect. Combined decades later with Adriano Banchieri's Cacasenno, Croce's narrative cycle became one of the most widely printed, translated, and read books in European publishing history.Beyond the Bertoldo cycle, Croce's bibliography includes pivotal works of social observation and comic anthropology. In L'eccellenza et trionfo del porco (1594), he composed a mock-heroic treatise celebrating the pig, transforming a humble livestock animal into a symbol of economic survival and culinary joy for the popular classes. In works such as La fiera di Saletto, Sincerità d'Amore, and his autobiographical verse essay Descrittione della vita del Croce, he rendered meticulous descriptions of contemporary fairs, market dynamics, trades, domestic arguments, and the material anxieties of everyday life in early modern Italy. Furthermore, Croce was an innovator in the genre of comic theater, authoring numerous farsette and ridicolose (short rustic plays) that prefigured elements of the Commedia dell'Arte, featuring stock characters such as the boastful soldier, the pedantic doctor, and the sly servant, all speaking in distinct regional dialects.The printing and publication history of Giulio Cesare Croce represents a landmark chapter in the sociology of early modern typography. Bologna during the late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries was a vibrant center of print production, boasting prominent workshop presses such as those of Bartolomeo Cochi, Giovanni Rossi, the Heredi di Giovanni Rossi, Tebaldini, and Viola. Croce established close working relationships with these printer-publishers, often selling his manuscripts outright for small immediate cash payments to buy raw materials or feed his large family. Because modern copyright protections did not exist, printers across Northern Italy—including major centers such as Venice, Ferrara, Milan, Padua, and Florence—pasted together unauthorized reprints of Croce's works, distributing hundreds of thousands of copies throughout the peninsula. These cheap editions were printed on low-quality paper using worn movable type and adorned with simple woodcut illustrations (xilografie) that were frequently reused across different titles. They were sold by itinerant peddlers (strazzaruoli, ciarlatani), broadside sellers, and market stallholders, penetrating every level of society, from illiterate peasants who heard them read aloud in taverns to noblewomen and scholars who collected them for light entertainment.Giulio Cesare Croce passed away in Bologna in January 1609 at the age of fifty-eight, leaving his family in dire financial distress but bequeathing a monumental textual legacy that would profoundly shape European literature for centuries. While seventeenth- and eighteenth-century academic literary historians often marginalized Croce as a mere rustic entertainer or vulgar street scribbler, the Enlightenment and Romantic eras began to recognize his profound importance as a custodian of authentic popular culture. Giambattista Vico and later nineteenth-century folklorists such as Giuseppe Pitrè recognized in Croce's verse a precious repository of folk psychology and oral linguistic memory. In the twentieth century, a dramatic historiographical shift occurred, led by the eminent scholar Piero Camporesi. Through groundbreaking critical studies such as La maschera di Bertoldo (1976), Camporesi restored Croce to the center of early modern intellectual history, demonstrating that Croce's writings offered an unparalleled map of the lower-class mentalities, bodily anxieties, food culture, and carnivalesque inversions of Counter-Reformation Europe. Today, Giulio Cesare Croce is celebrated not merely as a master of popular comedy, but as a towering figure of European vernacular culture whose works continue to illuminate the complex, dynamic interplay between the street, the press, and the literary canon.

academic_description: 4to (202x136 mm). 80 pp. Collation: †4 A-I4. Campeggi's woodcut arms on the title page. Woodcut historiated and decorative initials. Roman and italic types. 19th-century quarter calf with lettering piece on spine (slightly worn). Some minor foxing and staining, marginl hole repaired to the last two leaves not affecting the text, a good copy.Extremely rare first and only edition of this poem, divided into three parts and consisting of two hundred and fourteen octaves, which provides a detailed description of the interior and exterior of the beautiful palace purchased by Giovanni Battista Campeggi, Bishop of Majorca, in 1567. Known as Tusculano, the palace was located four miles north of Bologna on the Saliceto (today Corticella) plain and became a gathering place for eminent learned and noble figures. The detailed account of the rooms (including the kitchen, the pantry and the cellar), frescoes, paintings, furnishings, silverware, drapery, leathers and crockery vividly depict the palace, which no longer exists today, while arousing curiosity and awe. As such, the poem is an excellent example of Croce's poetics, which frequently finds inspiration in the enumeration of objects.The book opens with a dedicatory epistle to Giacomo Campeggi, primicerius of the Cathedral of Bologna, dated 21 December 1582, and a sonnet addressed to readers, in which the author admits that he is not very familiar with the Tuscan language.The edition bears the Campeggi coat of arms on the title page and is adorned with woodcut ornaments and initials at the beginning of each section. Also the choice of the 4to format (larger than Croce's usual 8vo pamphlets) denotes the work's illustrious destination.Croce felt most at ease in the piazzas, streets and taverns, rather than the palaces of the lords, although he always sought to be welcomed there. And when, quite occasionally, he happened to enter the luxurious villa of G.B. Campeggi, it seemed to him that he was entering an incredible, prodigious place that was completely foreign to his experience. He was so stunned and amazed that he felt compelled to describe every minute detail, from the frescoes and crockery to the furniture, books, draperies and linens. He could not tear himself away from it, lingering in his description for over two hundred octaves, a considerable lenght even for someone as generous as he was when it came to inventories of all kinds.Giulio Cesare Croce was a self-taught poet and storyteller who, due to his ability to bridge the gap between the cultured and popular worlds and between oral and written culture, occupies a unique position in the Italian literary scene. Born in San Giovanni in Persiceto near Bologna in 1550 to a family of blacksmiths, he received an irregular education and was supported by the Fantuzzi family of Medicina. He divided his time between blacksmithing and storytelling in Bologna until, in 1575, he devoted himself entirely to storytelling. He travelled from market to market, staying in the homes of the wealthy, but despite his popularity, he remained poor. He also spent some time in Venice, where he performed for local dignitaries. Appreciated by the renowned Modenese musician Orazio Vecchi for his talent as a versifier, Croce collaborated with him on the celebrated Amfiparnaso (1597), widely considered to be the first Italian “melodramma giocoso”. He died in Bologna in 1609.More than four hundred works are attributed to Croce, most of which were published in modest, poorly printed booklets. Written in Italian or Bolognese dialect, in prose or verse, his pamphlets contain lively descriptions of the lives of the poor, as well as jokes, humorous stories, proverbs and accounts of popular festivals and calamities.

title: Nova auris internae delineatio

authors.name: Folli Cecilio (1614-1682)
authors.biography: Cecilio Folli (1614–1682), also Latinized in early modern academic literature as Caecilius Follius or Cecilius Folia, stands as one of the most brilliant and idiosyncratic figures in seventeenth-century European anatomy and Venetian state medicine. Operating at the vibrant intersection of the Paduan empirical anatomical school and the civic medical administration of the Republic of Venice, Folli achieved enduring international renown through his precise anatomical dissections, his pioneering contributions to neuro-otology, and his early, nuanced intervention into the fierce pan-European debates surrounding William Harvey’s revolutionary theory of cardiovascular circulation. Best remembered in the annals of anatomical nomenclature for his discovery of the long anterior process of the malleus—traditionally designated by medical historians as the processus Folianus or processus gracilis Folii—Folli embodied the quintessential Baroque physician-scholar. He combined rigorous micro-anatomical observation with sophisticated copperplate illustration, public anatomical demonstrations, and high administrative responsibilities as Protomedico of Venice and Knight of Saint Mark (Cavaliere di San Marco).Born in Modena in 1614 into a family of respected social standing, Folli spent his formative years relocating to Venice, the cosmopolitan capital whose imperial maritime networks and vibrant publishing apparatus offered an unmatched stage for ambitious men of science. Drawn to the study of natural philosophy and medicine, the young Folli enrolled at the University of Padua, which had served since the era of Andreas Vesalius, Realdo Colombo, and Hieronymus Fabricius ab Aquapendente as the undisputed capital of Western anatomical inquiry. At Padua, Folli studied under the tutelage of illustrious professors of anatomy and surgery, absorbing the rigorous empirical methodology of the Paduan dissecting theater. He was particularly influenced by the anatomical demonstrations of Johann Wesling (Giovanni Veslingio) and the anatomical tradition maintained by the Marchetti lineage. Demonstrating extraordinary technical dexterity in micro-dissection and an acute critical intellect, Folli completed his studies with high honors, receiving his doctorate in medicine and philosophy in 1636. Shortly after his graduation, his exceptional talent attracted the attention of the Venetian Magistracy of Health (Provveditori alla Sanità), leading to his appointment in 1636–1637 as public lecturer of anatomy (Anatomico del Pubblico Studio di Venezia), a prestigious civic position charged with conducting official public dissections for the training of surgeons and physicians within the dominant guild structures of the lagoon city.Folli’s scholarly output blossomed rapidly following his appointment. In 1639, at the astonishingly young age of twenty-five, he published his first major treatise, titled Sanguinis a dextro in sinistrum cordis ventriculum defluentis facilis inthaepatica chyli praeparatio..., printed in Venice by the renowned typographic house of Francesco Baba. This work arrived at a crucial historical juncture, just eleven years after William Harvey had published his epoch-making Exercitatio Anatomica de Motu Cordis et Sanguinis in Animalibus (Frankfurt, 1628). Folli was among the very first Italian anatomists to publicly engage with, validate, and critically examine Harvey’s model of systemic blood circulation. In his treatise, Folli subjected the cardiovascular system, fetal circulation, and the mechanics of the cardiac septum to intense empirical scrutiny. He conducted detailed dissections of human fetuses and animals, carefully illustrating the functional mechanics of the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus. While acknowledging the mechanical reality of the circulatory movement of blood through the arteries and veins, Folli sought to synthesize Harveian hemodynamics with classical Galenic and Aristotelian notions regarding the hepatic role in chyle processing and sanguification. His text sparked lively intellectual exchanges throughout the Republic of Letters, drawing the attention of continental anatomists such as Jean Riolan the Younger, Thomas Bartholin, and Gassendi, and placing Venice at the center of mid-seventeenth-century cardiovascular discourse.Despite the significance of his cardiovascular studies, Folli achieved his most lasting scientific breakthrough in the field of sensory organ anatomy. In 1645, again from the press of Francesco Baba, Folli issued his masterpiece of micro-anatomy: Nova auris internae delineatio. Issued as an elegant folio treatise adorned with exquisitely detailed copperplate engravings, this work presented an unprecedentedly precise anatomical mapping of the human middle and inner ear structures. Through painstaking dissection of the temporal bone using delicate instruments of his own design, Folli isolated and described for the first time a previously unrecorded bone projection extending from the neck of the malleus toward the petrotympanic fissure. This slender anatomical structure—the anterior process of the malleus—was immediately recognized by contemporary anatomists as a major discovery and became known universally across European medical faculties as the processus Folianus (Folian process). Folli’s Nova auris internae delineatio extended beyond the malleus to provide exceptionally clear descriptions and visual plates of the incus, stapes, tympanic membrane, and auditory ossicular chain, laying fundamental empirical groundwork for the later neuro-otological research of Antonio Maria Valsalva, Raymond Vieussens, and Giovanni Battista Morgagni.Folli’s intellectual life was deeply intertwined with the civic institutions and publishing infrastructure of Venice. During the mid-seventeenth century, the Venetian book trade was undergoing a period of profound transformation, transitioning from the broad humanist production of the sixteenth century toward specialized scientific, medical, and technical publishing. The workshop of Francesco Baba, printer to the Venetian Academy and specialist in high-end scientific texts, served as Folli’s primary publisher. Baba’s presses utilized advanced intaglio printing techniques, deploying finely etched copperplates that allowed Folli to convey the minute, complex structures of the inner ear and fetal vasculature with a fidelity that woodcuts could no longer achieve. Folli personally supervised the draftsmanship and engraving of these plates, establishing a model of visual accuracy that rendered his treatises prized collector’s items among contemporary European scholars and bibliophiles. Copies of Folli’s works were rapidly exported across the Alps, circulating through major academic hubs in Leiden, Oxford, Paris, Basel, and Nuremberg.Beyond his scholarly publications, Folli emerged as one of the most powerful medical administrators in the Venetian Republic. His profound clinical acumen, combined with his energetic leadership during recurrent outbreaks of infectious disease and seasonal epidemics in the Venetian lagoon, earned him the total confidence of the Venetian Senate and the Magistracy of Health. He was eventually elevated to the supreme medical office of the state, serving as Protomedico of Venice. In this capacity, Folli oversaw the regulation of the city’s apothecaries, supervised the licensing of medical practitioners, enforced quarantine regulations, and governed the municipal public health apparatus. In recognition of his extraordinary services to both science and the State, the Venetian Senate bestowed upon him the prestigious honorific title of Cavaliere di San Marco (Knight of Saint Mark), a distinction rarely conferred upon practicing physicians. Folli maintained an extensive network of academic correspondence, maintaining intellectual ties with leading members of the Accademia degli Incogniti in Venice and corresponding with scholars across Italy and northern Europe. He continued his medical practice and administrative oversight until his death in Venice in 1682, leaving behind a legacy of profound anatomical discovery and institutional service.The historiographical assessment of Cecilio Folli reflects his pivotal position in the transition from Renaissance Galenism to Baroque experimental science. In the eighteenth century, the great Swiss anatomist and bibliographer Albrecht von Haller offered high praise for Folli in his monumentally comprehensive Bibliotheca Anatomica (1774), celebrating Folli’s structural precision and his priority in the discovery of the anterior process of the malleus. Similarly, Antoine Portal, in his monumental Histoire de l'Anatomie et de la Chirurgie (1770), highlighted Folli’s crucial role in validating Harveian circulation within Italy during an era when conservative faculties in Paris and Madrid still fiercely resisted the doctrine. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, medical historians such as Joseph Hyrtl, Pietro Capparoni, Arturo Castiglioni, and Giuseppe Ongaro re-evaluated Folli’s place in anatomical history, confirming his technical mastery in otology and his critical contribution to the institutionalization of public anatomical teaching in post-Renaissance Venice. Today, Folli stands recognized not merely as the eponym behind the processus Folianus, but as a towering exemplar of the seventeenth-century Venetian scientific renaissance who bridged the gap between empirical anatomical dissection, visual print culture, and public health governance.

academic_description: 4to. [4] leaves. Collation: A4. Printer's device on title page (an eagle with spread wings above a vase containing three lilies supported by a hand coming out of the clouds, in a figurative frame). Woodcut initial and headpiece. On l. A3r full-page engraving by Giacomo Pecini (c. 1617-1669) containing six numbered figures. Some light foxing, traces of folding as the pamphlet was presumably sent as a letter, a very good, wide-margined copy.EXCEEDINGLY RARE ORIGINAL EDITION (first issue) of the most accurate description of the ear up to its time.The work, sent as a letter - the dedication is dated Venice, May 10, 1645 - to the a Danish physician, mathematician, and theologian Thomas Bartholin (1616-1680), became immediately sought-after and rare. Its fame and importance are due to the engraved plate containing six figures that offer an extremely accurate and analytical description of the middle and inner ear. Folli describes some structures of the hearing organ never previously observed and, among the many remarkable morphological details showed in the plate and described in the pamphlet, of particular importance is the depiction in figure 2 (Figura Secunda) of the long process of the malleus, also called “Folli or Follian process”, that is a slender spur running anteriorly from the neck of the malleus toward the membrane of the tympanum. Folli also identifies the lenticular process of the anvil which he calls “os globulus”, whose discovery is attributed to S. de Le Boë. However, Folli mistakenly considers it as an independent bone. Figure 3 (Figura Tertia) gives “the first illustration of the so-called fourth ossicle (stapedis, osseus globulus); it appears to be an extension of the head of the stapes to which it is attached” (C.D. O'Malley & Edwin Clarke, The discovery of the auditory ossicles, in: “Bulletin of the history of medicine”, September-October 1961, vol. 35, no. 5, p. 441 and fig. 5).The fact that the work is addressed to Bartholin is a clear indication of the esteem and friendship that existed between the two; Folli went often to Padua, where Bartholin resided, both to discuss with him the development of his research and to make practical demonstrations of anatomy. In Bartholin's correspondence (Epistolarium medicinalium a doctis vel ad doctos scriptarum centuriae, Hagae Comitum, 1740, cent. I, epist. LXXII, p. 251), besides the Nova auris there is another letter written by Folli, dated 4 November 1644 and titled Observationes quaedam anatomicae, which contains several anatomical observations on the skin, peritoneum, cardiac ventricular ulcerations, and intestinal worms. Bartholin also contributed to the circulation of the Nova auris internae delineatio as is shown in the copy now preserved at the Augsburg State Library which bears his dedication to the German physician Lucas Schrockius (Lucas von Schröck, 1620-1689).“Caecilius Folius […] is known to have written three works, but the single one of these which brought him such renown as he ever enjoyed was his ‘New Delineation of the Internal Ear,' an opuscule of six fairly well executed plates with a brief explanatory text for each, and said to have been the most nearly accurate description of the inner ear up to its time. More than a hundred years later Antoine Portal said of it, ‘This is the manner in which judicious and perspicuous spirits know how to describe in a few words the most complicated objects and how to explain the most interesting discoveries. If everyone had followed the method of Folius there would be fewer books but just as much positive knowledge. It has been said that Vesling used Folius' drawings and description in his own Syntagma Anatomicum, published from Padua in 1641, a date at which Folius would be twenty-six years of age. But Vesling nowhere acknowledged any debt, and the name of Folius is conspicuously absent from the rather long list of anatomists mentioned in Vesling's Syntagma” (G. Kasten Tallmadge, Caecilius Folius on the circulation, in: “Bulletin of the history of medicine”, January-February 1954, vol. 28, no. 1, pp. 15-16). The book was reprinted a century later, in 1745, to commemorate its first publication by the Venetian primary physician Giambattista Paitoni, and then again in Göttingen in 1749 (Disputationum anatomicarum selectarum, Abram Vandenhoeck, 1749, vol. 4, pp. 365-368).Paitoni was a bibliophile and book-collector. In 1745, on the occasion of the centenary of the publication of the Nova auris internae delineatio, he entrusted a Venetian typographer to issue a facsimile reprint of the pamphlet, with a note, printed on title-page verso, which says: “Hoc rarissimum opusculum recusum est Venetiis in usum Jo: Baptistae Paitoni juxta autoris editionem, Dominico Burgo typographo MDCCXLV”. A couple of years after Paitoni's death, his exceptional medical library was auctioned in London by the bookseller James Robson, who gave a detailed description of it in a printed catalog, calling it “one of the finest [libraries] ever offered to public sale” (Bibliotheca Paitoniana: a catalogue of the truly-valuable and justly celebrated library of the late eminent Sig. Jo. Bapt. Paitoni, M.D. [...], London, 1790).The Italian Union Catalogue lists 7 copies of the Nova auris internae delineatio, but likely only 6 of them are truly belonging to one of the two variant issues of the original edition and not to the 1745 reprint. ICCU confusingly mentions three different issues of the first edition, mistakenly confusing the two issues of the original edition with the Paitoni's reprint, which was entirely reset (including the plate which was recast as some minimal variants show) and has a different printer's device on the title page, depicting a woman symbolizing the Concordia.This is certainly the case of the vellum copy recorded in the Italian Union Catalogue among the copies of the 1645 edition and preserved in Venice at the Marciana Library (MEMBR. 0052), which, even though it doesn't have the aforementioned note on title-page verso, does not belong typographically to either issues of the original edition, and is rather to be considered as part of Paitoni's celebratory initiative.The two variants of the 1645 edition have a different fingerprint and a different version of the printer's device with the eagle and the vase with the lilies described above. Our copy certainly corresponds to issue A with the larger version of the eagle/vase device on the title page.OCLC records only one copy in the US at the National Library of Medicine in Bethesda. It would be interesting and useful to check how many copies of this extremely rare pamphlet listed in public libraries worldwide are actually belonging to the 1645 original edition and are not the 1745 or a later reprint. Cecilio Folli (also known as Folius, Follius, Fuoli) was born into a wealthy family in Fanano near Modena on August 1, 1614. His father, the son of the doctor Bartolomeo, was captain of the Venetian Republic and died shortly after Cecilio's birth in the war of Gradisca (1616-1617). Cecilio was entrusted to the care of his paternal uncle Giambattista, an illustrious Venetian doctor and primary physician of the Venetian Republic, who raised him and provided for his scientific education.The spread of the plague that struck Venice in the summer of 1630 contributed to push the young Cecilio to embrace the medical studies. In opposition to most doctors, Cecilio's uncle Giambattista, together with G. degli Aromatari, fought to affirm the contagious nature of the disease and the necessity of implementing severe measures in order to circumscribe the epidemic, attracting upon himself the hostility of the College of Doctors. Cecilio, although still very young, took an active part in the story, assisting his uncle and later, under his guidance, addressing to the Magistrate of Health an accurate report on the spread and severity of the contagion: Vero racconto di tutto quello è occorso l'anno 1630 nel contagio pestilente che disertò l'inclita città di Venezia (‘True account of all what happened in 1630 during the plague that decimated the illustrious city of Venice', Venice, Biblioteca Civica Museo Correr, cod. Cicogna 1509).Cecilio later moved to Padua, where he had the opportunity to attend J. Vesling's lessons and where he graduated in philosophy and medicine, showing a major interest in anatomical and physiological investigations. Back to Venice, he immediately gained notoriety and on August 27, 1636 he was elected public anatomist. In 1639, at the age of 25, he published in Venice his first work, a treatise on blood circulation (Sanguinis a dextro in sinistrum cordis ventriculum defluentisfacilis reperta via, cui non vulgaris in lacteas nuper patefactas venas animadversio praeponitur) dedicated to the Doge Francesco Erizzo. In this book, as in his subsequent publication Discorso anatomico, nel quale si contiene una nuova opinione circa la generatione, et uso della pinguedine, con altri principij Hippocratici (Venice, 1644), Folli states that he was the first to demonstrate in a public anatomy session the presence of lacteal vessels in human corpses, which Gaspare Aselli had described by exclusively dissecting animals.After the publication of these works, as well as of the Nova auris internae delineatio, Folli's fame spread further and on April 11, 1650 he took the place of his uncle Giambattista as primary physician in Venice. A member of the priory of the College of Doctors since 1638, in the years 1652 and 1671 he was appointed its prior.Using his personal prestige, Folli promoted the construction in Venice of an anatomical theater on the model of that of Padua. He conceived its architecture and worked closely with T. Zuccati and F. Bernardi so that the work could be completed in the shortest possible time and in the best possible way. The theater was inaugurated on February 2, 1671, but on January 8, 1800 it was devastated by a fire and with it also the library and the archives were destroyed. Besides his public assignments, Folli also treated many private clients and, most probably, it was this intense practical activity that did not allow him to complete many of his scientific studies.In addition to the admiration of Bartholin who, in the preface to the Anatomical institutions of his father Caspar, quotes him among the most famous anatomists in Europe, Folli enjoyed the esteem and friendship of many contemporary scholars and with many of them he exchanged letters on specific topics related to medical research.In the fire of the anatomical theater was also destroyed a memorial bust which dated Folli's death to 1682. This date appears to be confirmed by other documents, even though it is not clear whether he died in Venice or elsewhere. His health condition had started to deteriorate the year before and he had been forced to reduce his activities and entrust his pupil I. Grandi with many of them (cf. A. Pagano, Folli Cecilio, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, XLVIII, 1997, s.v.). (bound with:)CIMA, Francesco (1633-?)-MOLINETTI, Antonio ed. (1620-1675). Exercitationis medicae de recta acceptione arthritidis, & podagrae ab excellentissimo Antonio Molinetto Patavini Lycaei anatomico, & theorico editae. Examen Francisci Cimae medici Veneti. Venice, ex typographia Leniana, 1662.4to. 28 pp. Collation: A-B4 C6. Woodcut ornament on title page. Small hole to the lower inner margin of the first quire not affecting the text, a fine copy.Extremely rare first and only edition (no copy recorded in US libraries) of this account of a medical case concerning a 36-year-old noble German lady (matrona) affected by arthritis and podagra. The young physician Francesco Cima attended the controversy arisen by the case between his mentor Raimondo Giovanni Fortis (1603-1678) on one side and count Girolamo Frigimelica and Antonio Molinetti on the other side. The text, edited by Molinetti, contains the two medical consultations and Cima's considerations on the case.Nothing is known about the life and work of Francesco Cima. Antonio Molinetti was born in Venice in 1620. After graduating from the University of Padua, he returned to Venice, where he distinguished himself in medical practice and anatomical dissections. This talent enabled him to obtain in 1649 the chair of anatomy and surgery at the University of Padua, succeeding Johann Vesling, and from 1661 also the chair of theoretical medicine, which was vacant after the death, in 1657, of Fortunio Liceti. Molinetti's fame grew rapidly, both in Italy and abroad. The Duke of Bavaria and the Duke of Parma asked for his services. Molinetti's only publication is the Dissertationes anatomicae, et pathologicae de sensibus, & eorum organis (Padua, 1669). (and:)PATIN, Charles (1633-1693). De febribus oratio, habita in Archi-Lycaeo Patavino, die 4. Nov. 1677. A Carolo Patino Doctore Medico Parisiensi Medicinam Praticam Interpretante. Padua, Pietro Maria Frambotto, 1677.4to. [4] leaves. Collation A4. Engraved coat-of-arms on title page. A fine copy on thick paper.Rare first and only edition of this oration on fever dedicated to Leonardo Pesaro and read by the author, on November 4, 1677, in front of the medical faculty of the University of Padua. (and:)CIMA, Francesco (1633-?). Vindicata veritas a Francisco Cima medico veneto in epistolam admonitoriam nomine cuiusdam Baijer typis mandatam. Venice, ex typographia Leniana, 1663.4to. [8], 41, [3] pp. Collation: [π]4 A-D4 E6. Satirical engraved vignette on title page. Woodcut initials and headpieces. A fine copy.Extremely rare first and only edition (no copy in US libraries) of this polemic work written in response to the Epistola admonitoria ad Franciscum Cimam medicum venetum (Padua, 1662) by the physician Johann Michael Bayer, who attacked Cima's Exercitationis medicae de recta acceptione arthritidis, & podagrae (see above).In the pamphlet Cima defines himself ironically as a trigenarius puer (30-yeard-old boy) as his accuser tried to discredit him for his young age and inexperience. He also states that he was pushed to reply to Epistola admonitoria by Fortis and Molinetti themselves.Four works in one volume (216x164 mm). Contemporary boards, label with manuscript title on spine, the letter “C” on the front panel and an inked-out note on the back panel, original flyleaves preserved (back panel stained and with a worm track). On the back pastedown manuscript note “numo. 5. fogli no. 12÷”. Folli is bound as number 2 in the miscellany.A VERY WELL PRESERVED SAMMELBAND OF FOUR EXTREMELY RARE MEDICAL TEXTS ALL LINKED TO THE UNIVERISTY OF PADUA.

Bosatra, La “Nova auris intemae delineatio” di Cecilio Folli, in: “Acta medicae historiae Patavina”, I, 1954-55, pp. 1-16 (includes a facsimile of the 1645 edition); M. Portal, Histoire de l'anatomie et de la chirurgie, Paris, 1770, II, pp. 548-552; Italian Union Catalog, IT\ICCU\MILE\022684; Garrison-Morton, 1542; C. Folli, Caecilii Folii equitis nova auris internae delineatio, Padua, Clinica Otologica dell'Università di Padova, 1970 (photographic reprint of the first edition); S. Minuzzi, Sul filo dei segreti. title: Dei delitti e delle pene

authors.name: Beccaria Cesare
authors.biography: Cesare Bonesana, Marquis of Beccaria (15 March 1738 – 28 November 1794), stands as a monumental pillar of the European Enlightenment (Illuminismo) and the foundational architect of modern criminal jurisprudence, penology, and reformist political economy. Operating at the vibrant intersection of Lombard intellectual radicalism and transatlantic legal humanism, Beccaria reconfigured the conceptual architecture of justice, state sovereignty, and human rights. His masterpiece, Dei delitti e delle pene ('On Crimes and Punishments'), published anonymously in Livorno in 1764, shattered centuries of inquisitorial tradition, canon law supremacy, and arbitrary judicial tyranny. By subjecting the archaic apparatus of Roman-canonical criminal procedure to the rigorous calculus of Sensationalist psychology, Utilitarian ethics, and Social Contract theory, Beccaria formulated an unprecedented critique of state violence. His systematic condemnation of judicial torture, secret accusations, disproportionate punishment, and capital execution transformed criminal law from a mechanism of sovereign vengeance into a secular instrument for preserving social utility and civic liberty.Born in Milan into the landed aristocracy of the Duchy of Milan—then under the dominion of the Austrian Habsburg Monarchy—Beccaria was the eldest son of Giovanni Saverio Bonesana, Marquis of Beccaria, and Donna Maria Visconti di Saliceto, an aristocratic lineage linking him to the historic ruling elites of Lombardy. His early education was entrusted to the aristocratic Collegio dei Nobili in Parma, a rigorous Jesuit institution where he spent eight years (1747–1755) submerged in classical rhetoric, scholastic logic, and dogmatic theology. Beccaria later recalled this period with profound aversion, characterizing his Jesuit schooling as a stifling environment that suppressed intellectual curiosity and emotional development.However, it was during his subsequent university studies at the venerable University of Pavia that his intellectual awakening occurred. Graduating with a doctorate in law (laurea in utroque iure) in September 1758, Beccaria was initially unimpressed by the fossilized Roman law glosses and statutory complexity of the ius commune. His true philosophical baptism came shortly after graduation through his encounter with Montesquieu’s Lettres persanes (1721), a text that ignited his passion for socio-political critique, followed by intensive readings of Claude-Adrien Helvétius, Étienne Bonnot de Condillac, John Locke, David Hume, and Jean-Jacques Rousseau.Beccaria's entry into the radical intellectual vanguard of Milan was precipitated by a dramatic domestic rupture. In 1761, defying the stern opposition of his aristocratic father—who briefly placed his son under house arrest to prevent a misalliance—Beccaria married Teresa Blasco, a sixteen-year-old woman of noble descent but lacking financial dowry. Disinherited and cast out from his ancestral palace, Beccaria found sanctuary and financial sustenance in the home of Count Pietro Verri. This crisis cemented an extraordinary intellectual fraternity. Pietro Verri and his brother Alessandro Verri had gathered a coterie of brilliant young Milanese patricians, including Luigi Lambertenghi, Alfonso Longo, and Sebastiano Franci, into an informal academy dubbed the Accademia dei Pugni ('Academy of Fists'). Meeting regularly in Pietro Verri’s private library, this dynamic intellectual circle rejected the traditional erudition of Italian academies in favor of urgent economic, legal, and political reform. Between June 1764 and May 1766, the group published Il Caffè, a highly influential periodic journal modelled on Addison and Steele's Spectator. Beccaria’s initial contribution to economic literature emerged from these academy discussions: Del disordine e de' rimedi delle monete nello Stato di Milano nel 1762 (printed in Lucca, 1762), a incisive treatise analyzing currency devaluation, monetary standard instability, and minting reform within the Milanese duchy.The genesis of Dei delitti e delle pene between October 1763 and January 1764 represents one of the most intense collaborative episodes in early modern European intellectual history. Prompted by Pietro Verri—who suggested the topic of criminal justice and provided critical data regarding prison conditions and administrative mechanics—and fueled by Alessandro Verri’s firsthand observations as the official protector of prisoners (protettore dei carcerati) in Milan, Beccaria drafted the text on loose scraps of paper. Pietro Verri subsequently organized, copied, and edited the manuscript, polishing its stylistic cadence while preserving Beccaria's devastating philosophical precision. The treatise synthesized three distinct intellectual currents: the contractualist framework of Locke and Rousseau (asserting that individuals surrender only the minimum necessary portion of liberty to the sovereign to maintain public peace), the Utilitarian imperative of Hutcheson and Helvétius ('the greatest happiness shared among the greatest number'), and the Sensationalist epistemology of Condillac (arguing that human behavior is driven by the avoidance of pain and pursuit of pleasure).From these premises, Beccaria derived revolutionary conclusions: laws must be clear, written, and interpreted strictly according to their literal text by magistrates; punishments must be proportional to the harm inflicted upon society (misura dei delitti è il danno alla società); and the ultimate goal of penology must be prevention rather than retribution.Crucially, Beccaria’s treatise executed a radical secularization of criminal law by establishing a rigid distinction between peccato (sin against God) and delitto (crime against society), arguing that the temporal state possesses no theological authority to punish moral depravity, but only civic actions that infringe upon the social contract. His critique of judicial torture (la tortura) exposed its intrinsic absurdity, demonstrating that physical torment functions not as a test of truth, but as a test of muscular resistance, inevitably convicting frail innocent men while exonerating robust criminals. Furthermore, Beccaria articulated the earliest comprehensive philosophical argument against the death penalty (pena di morte). Asserting that no individual ever included the right to be killed in the original social covenant, he argued that state execution constitutes a war of the sovereign against a citizen, lacking both legal legitimacy and deterrent efficacy. Instead, he advocated perpetual servitude (hard labor), arguing that the long-term, visible spectacle of a prisoner deprived of liberty acts as a far more potent and humane deterrent than the momentary horror of a public execution.The publication and circulation of Dei delitti e delle pene constituted an international typographical and political phenomenon. To bypass the vigilant Habsburg and Papal censorship apparatus in Milan, the manuscript was secretly dispatched to Tuscany, where the printer Marco Coltellini published the first edition in Livorno (Leghorn) in July 1764, bearing a false imprint to shield its authors. The book created an immediate sensation throughout Europe. A second expanded edition appeared in 1764, followed by a definitive third edition in 1765 featuring Beccaria's celebrated response to theological critics. In Paris, the treatise was embraced passionately by the Philosophes. André Morellet produced a reordered French translation in 1766, to which Voltaire appended his famous Commentaire sur le livre des délis et des peines. Voltaire’s endorsement catapulted Beccaria to global fame, though the radical nature of the work drew violent condemnation from conservative scholastic theologians, most notably the Venetian friar Ferdinando Facchinei, who published a fierce attack in 1765 accusing Beccaria of 'socialism,' impiety, and subversion of monarchy. In response to Facchinei’s assault, the Congregation of the Index of the Roman Catholic Church formally placed Dei delitti e delle pene on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum on 3 February 1766, a prohibition that remained active for nearly two centuries.Despite ecclesiastical condemnation, the book's European triumph was unstoppable. In the autumn of 1766, Beccaria and Alessandro Verri undertook a triumphant journey to Paris upon the invitation of the Baron d'Holbach and Claude-Adrien Helvétius. Received with adulation in the salons of Madame Geoffrin and Mademoiselle de Lespinasse, Beccaria nevertheless suffered from intense social anxiety, hypochondria, and acute homesickness for his wife Teresa. His sudden, hasty departure from Paris back to Milan alienated the French intellectuals and created an enduring rift between him and Pietro Verri, who viewed Beccaria's withdrawal as a betrayal of their collective intellectual mission. Upon his return to Milan, Beccaria turned his analytical focus toward political economy and civil administration. In November 1768, Empress Maria Theresa appointed him to the newly created Chair of Public Economy and Commerce (Cattedra di Economia Pubblica e Commercio) at the Scuole Palatine in Milan. His inaugural lecture, along with his groundbreaking course lectures—posthumously published as Elementi di economia pubblica (1804)—predated Adam Smith's Wealth of Nations in systematically applying mathematical analysis, demographic modeling, and division-of-labor principles to state governance and resource allocation.In 1771, Beccaria was appointed to the Supreme Council of Economy (Regio Supremo Consiglio dell'Economia), stepping fully into the ranks of the Habsburg civil administration.Over the remaining twenty-three years of his life, he transitioned from a radical philosophical agitator into a meticulous, pragmatic senior magistrate and bureaucratic reformer under Maria Theresa and Emperor Joseph II. He authored exhaustive administrative reports on monetary stabilization, public health, grain trade regulation, judicial reform, and the standardization of weights and measures across Lombardy. Following the death of his first wife Teresa in 1774, he married Anna de' Barnabati. His daughter from his first marriage, Giulia Beccaria, would later give birth to Alessandro Manzoni, the titan of Italian Romantic literature, ensuring an extraordinary generational continuity of intellectual brilliance. Cesare Beccaria died suddenly of an apoplectic stroke in Milan on 28 November 1794 at the age of fifty-six. In accordance with his modest personal wishes, he was buried without ostentation at the Foppone di San Giovannino outside the Porta Tosa.The enduring historical legacy of Cesare Beccaria is vast and foundational to modern constitutional democracy. His theoretical doctrines directly inspired the legal reforms of the most prominent enlightened monarchs of the late eighteenth century: Catherine the Great of Russia incorporated large sections of Dei delitti e delle pene into her famous Nakaz (Grand Instruction) of 1767; Grand Duke Leopold of Tuscany enacted the historic Codice Leopoldino of 1786, making Tuscany the first sovereign state in the Western world to permanently abolish the death penalty and torture; and Joseph II incorporated Beccarian proportionality into the Austrian Penal Code of 1787. Across the Atlantic, Beccaria's writings profoundly influenced the American Founding Fathers, particularly Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, and James Rush; Jefferson laboriously copied extensive passages of Beccaria’s text into his personal legal commonplace book, utilizing them to shape the Eighth Amendment's prohibition against 'cruel and unusual punishments.' Today, Beccaria's masterpiece remains the bedrock text of international human rights law, modern criminological theory, and the ongoing global campaign for the universal abolition of capital punishment.

topics: Printing and the Mind of Man
academic_description: 4to (mm. 203x145). Pages 104, [2]. Signatures: A-N4 χ1. Bound in a 19th-century French half red morocco binding, with marbled paper boards, spine with four raised bands adorned with gilt decorations and title, marbled endpapers and edges. Within the endpapers, there is a loose sheet penned by a 19th-century hand containing an excerpt against torture from Voltaire's Ode à la verité. The title page bears the ownership signature of one “C. Minoret”. The title page is slightly stained, with uniform light browning and scattered foxing, yet it remains an excellent copy with wide margins.First edition (one of the rare copies containing the final errata leaf with twenty-one corrections) of the most significant and renowned work of the Italian Enlightenment, which upon its appearance was met with enthusiastic acclaim throughout Europe. For prudential reasons, the author's name does not appear in the text, which, indeed, was placed on the Index of Prohibited Books by a decree issued on 3 February 1766. Following the first Livorno edition, the work was reprinted numerous times, often with false places of publication (Munich, Lausanne, Haarlem, etc.), in editions of varying accuracy and legitimacy—some of which are counterfeits of counterfeits—testifying to its immense impact and the challenges it faced in dissemination. Through translations into all the principal languages of the time, Dei delitti e delle pene came to influence, directly or indirectly, Catherine of Russia, Joseph II, Leopold II, and the legislators of both the American and French revolutions.In this treatise, Beccaria vehemently criticizes the prevailing legislation and the treatment of prisoners, particularly the abhorrent yet widespread practice of torture, rejecting wholesale much of the preceding legal tradition and centering his discourse on the respect for individual rights, particularly the so-called natural rights, such as the right to liberty and property. In accordance with the rationalistic and utilitarian ideas of the Enlightenment, which he originally combines with a profound love for humanity, Beccaria argues that the fundamental tool to eradicate privileges and abuses committed in favor of the few is the rationalization of law through legislation: a general and unequivocal law that governs clearly and impartially. The first and most important step in this direction is to separate law and religion, thereby promoting the secular nature of law and fostering religious tolerance. In this sense, Beccaria distinctly delineates the difference between crime and sin, criticizing capital punishment as an ineffective deterrent and theorizing the educational and rehabilitative value of punishment.Cesare Beccaria was born in Milan to a noble family of Pavia origin. After completing his studies at the Jesuit College Farnesiano in Parma and at the University of Pavia, where he graduated in 1758, he had a violent disagreement with his father due to his infatuation with the daughter of a lieutenant colonel. Struck by the reading of Montesquieu's Lettres persanes (he himself spoke of a “conversion”), he decided to devote himself to philosophy. Together with the brothers Pietro and Alessandro Verri (the latter had just become an advocate “protector of prisoners”), he was among the founders of the Accademia dei Pugni in 1762 and a contributor to the journal Il Caffè. The role that the Verri brothers played in the genesis and drafting of Dei delitti e delle pene cannot be underestimated. After the condemnation of the book, in 1766 Beccaria undertook a brief journey to Paris, where he was received with great enthusiasm by the intellectual community. Upon returning to Milan, in 1768 he was appointed professor of cameral sciences at the Palatine Schools. After two years of teaching, in 1771 he requested and obtained the position of counsellor of the Supreme Council of Economy. In the following years, as a high-ranking official of the Habsburg administration, he actively sought to introduce new Enlightenment-inspired reforms. He died in Milan on 28 November 1794.
