authors.name: Giraldi Cinzio Giovanni Battista
authors.biography: Giovanni Battista Giraldi Cinzio (born late November 1504 in Ferrara; died December 30, 1573 in Ferrara), also frequently styled in Latinized and European vernacular variants as Cinthio, Cyntio, or Cinthius, stands as one of the most prominent humanists, dramatists, literary theorists, and prose writers of the Italian High and Late Renaissance (Cinquecento). Operating at the intellectual crossroads of the Este court in Ferrara, the Studio Ferrarese, and the flourishing print networks of Venice and Piedmont, Giraldi Cinzio decisively reshaped early modern European literature. His polymathic career bridged medical philosophy and courtly diplomacy, while his creative output laid the theoretical and formal foundations for Senecan vernacular tragedy, the pastoral satyr play, and the Counter-Reformation novella. Beyond the Italian peninsula, his narrative creations served as primary source material for Elizabethan and Jacobean playwrights, most notably William Shakespeare, who adapted Giraldi’s prose tales into the dramatic masterworks Othello and Measure for Measure.Born into a respected citizen family of Ferrara during the reign of Duke Alfonso I d'Este, Giraldi received a rigorous humanist and scientific education at the University of Ferrara (the Studio Ferrarese). His formative years were marked by close contact with leading intellectual figures of the northern Italian Renaissance, most notably the distinguished humanist polymath Celio Calcagnini and the eminent philologist Lilio Gregorio Giraldi, a relative whose scholarly circles exposed young Giovanni Battista to classical philology, rhetoric, and Greek literature. Concurrently, Giraldi pursued higher studies in natural philosophy and Galenic medicine under the guidance of Ludovico Bonaccioli, earning his doctorate in philosophy and medicine in 1531. Immediately following his graduation, Giraldi was appointed to the faculty of philosophy at the University of Ferrara, where for over a decade he delivered lectures on Aristotle’s Physics and Nicomachean Ethics. This deep grounding in Aristotelian philosophy and natural medicine profoundly shaped his later literary theory, imparting a systematic, empirical, and psychological rigor to his analysis of human passions, moral agency, and dramatic catharsis.Giraldi’s formal entry into the political and cultural life of the Ferrarese court occurred under Duke Ercole II d'Este. Following the death of Celio Calcagnini in 1541, Giraldi succeeded his master as the principal professor of rhetoric at the university and was increasingly entrusted with diplomatic and administrative responsibilities by the ducal house. In 1547, Ercole II appointed Giraldi as official Ducal Secretary (segretario ducale), a prestigious post he held until the Duke’s death in 1559. During these decades, Giraldi was at the center of court spectacle, theatrical production, and ideological debates. It was within this vibrant courtly setting that Giraldi executed his historic dramaturgical breakthrough with the tragedy Orbecche, written in 1541 and performed with sensational success in Giraldi’s private residence in Ferrara before Duke Ercole II, Cardinals, and foreign dignitaries. Featuring original stage music composed by Alfonso della Viola and stage designs by Girolamo da Carpi, Orbecche was the first regular vernacular tragedy constructed on the Senecan model to be brought to the physical stage in early modern Europe. Rejecting the restraint of classical Greek tragedy in favor of Seneca’s chilling atmosphere of horror, ghost apparitions, psychological cruelty, and graphic violence, Giraldi inaugurated a genre of dramatic moral shock that would echo across European theatre for over a century.Giraldi’s dramatic experiments expanded throughout the 1540s and 1550s to encompass a broad tragic corpus—including Didone, Altile, Cleopatra, Gli Antivalomeni, Epitia, Euphimia, Arrenopia, and Selene. Crucially, Giraldi formulated the dramatic genre of the tragedia a lieto fine (tragedy with a happy ending), a structural hybrid that avoided ultimate catastrophe for virtuous characters while preserving tragic tension, thereby anticipating the development of modern tragicomedy. In 1545, Giraldi further demonstrated his genre-defining ambitions with Egle, designated as a favola satirica (satyric fable). Drawing upon fragments of Euripides' Cyclops and ancient descriptions of satyr plays, Egle represented an explicit attempt to revive the third canonical dramatic genre of antiquity, positioning itself as a direct predecessor to Torquato Tasso’s Aminta and Battista Guarini’s Il pastor fido in the evolution of the pastoral drama.Giraldi’s theoretical treatise, the Discorsi intorno al comporre de i romanzi, delle comedie, e delle tragedie (published in Venice by Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari in 1554), established him as one of the most original literary critics of the Cinquecento. Writing in response to strict Neo-Aristotelian commentators who condemned Ludovico Ariosto’s Orlando Furioso for failing to adhere to classical unities and epic structures, Giraldi forcefully defended the legitimacy of modern genres. He argued that modern vernacular authors were not rigidly bound by Aristotle's Poetics—which had been written without knowledge of modern romance—and that genre conventions naturally evolve across history according to language, custom, and audience pleasure. This historicist defense of the romanzo ignited a fierce priority controversy with his former student and rival courtier Giovan Battista Pigna, who claimed ownership of the theoretical principles published in Giraldi’s treatise. The bitter quarrel with Pigna alienated Giraldi from Duke Alfonso II d'Este (who had succeeded Ercole II in 1559 and favored Pigna), ultimately forcing Giraldi to leave Ferrara in 1562.The subsequent decade of Giraldi’s life was defined by intellectual exile and mobility across northern Italy. He moved first to Mondovì in Piedmont under the patronage of Duke Emanuele Filiberto of Savoy, where he taught humanities at the newly established ducal academy. It was during his residence in Piedmont that Giraldi published his monumental prose collection, Gli Hecatommithi (or Ecatommithi, meaning "The Hundred Tales"), printed in two monumental octavo volumes in Monte Regale (Mondovì) by Lorenzo Torrentino in 1565. Framed around a group of Ferrarese noblemen and women fleeing the horrific sack of Rome in 1527 by sea toward Marseilles, the Hecatommithi comprises ten decades of moralizing novellas exploring themes of martial fidelity, tyrannical abuse of power, treacherous friendship, illicit passion, and ultimate divine retribution. Written under the shadow of the Council of Trent, the work explicitly rejected the perceived licentiousness of Boccaccio’s Decameron, adopting a grave Counter-Reformation moral purpose while supplying vivid narrative plots that achieved immense transnational success.Giraldi’s typographical history reflects his prominent status within the early modern Italian book trade. His long-standing collaboration with the eminent Venetian printer-publisher Gabriel Giolito de' Ferrari ensured that works such as Orbecche (1543), Egle (1545), and the Discorsi (1554) were distributed throughout Europe in elegant, highly readable italic fonts decorated with Giolito's iconic phoenix woodcut emblem. When Giraldi migrated to Piedmont, he established a strategic partnership with the heirs of the ducal printer Lorenzo Torrentino in Mondovì for the princeps of Gli Hecatommithi (1565), before subsequent Venetian publishers (including Domenico Farri, Girolamo Scotto, and Cesare Arrivabene) reissued multiple editions across the late sixteenth century. In 1568, following an invitation from the Venetian Senate, Giraldi accepted the prestigious Chair of Rhetoric at the University of Pavia, where he taught with great acclaim until failing health compelled him to return to his native Ferrara shortly before his death in December 1573.The critical reception and legacy of Giraldi Cinzio are vast and multifaceted. Although nineteenth-century Italian romantic criticism (notably Francesco De Sanctis) occasionally criticized Giraldi’s style as theatrical and melodramatic, modern scholarship has re-evaluated him as a central figure in the transition from High Renaissance humanism to Mannerist and Baroque sensibilities. His theatrical innovations established the Senecan aesthetic of horror and psychological excess that directly influenced European drama, while his novellas provided the primary plot structures for major works of world literature. Gabriel Chappuys’s French translation of the Hecatommithi (Paris, 1583) and various English adaptations disseminated Giraldi’s narratives across northern Europe, providing William Shakespeare with the plot for Othello (derived from Decica III, Novella 7, telling the tragedy of Disdemona and the Moorish Captain) and Measure for Measure (derived from Decica VIII, Novella 5, recounting the story of Epitia and Juriste). Today, Giraldi Cinzio is recognized as a master architect of early modern dramatic theory, narrative fiction, and theatrical practice whose works continue to define the intellectual landscape of the Italian sixteenth century.

academic_description: 4to (217x155 mm). 353 [recte 335], [17, of which 2 are blank]. Collation: A-V8 X-Y4 *4 †4. Leaves Y4v and †4v are blank. Full-page woodcut portrait of the author on title-page verso. Woodcut historiated initials. Text printed in two columns. Roman and italic types. Colophon and register at l. †3v. Errata at ll. †1v-4r. Late 17th-/early 18th-century stiff vellum, inked title on spine, sprinkled edges (slightly stained). Title page slightly soiled, outer blank margin of title-page verso reinforced with a slip of paper, occasional light staining and foxing, a good, genuine copy with a few old annotations in the index at the end.Provenance. Front pastedown with the armorial bookplate of Alexander von Hübner (1811-1892), Austrian diplomat, born as Josef Hafenbredl and an illegitimate child of the chancellor K. von Metternich (1773-1859) with the niece of the Viennese glass merchant Rohrweck. From the year 1833 he assumed the name Alexander von Hübner and served on several missions in Italy. During the 1848 Revolution he was taken hostage in Milano and later in the 1860s served as Austrian ambassador in Rome. On the title page stamp of Cardinal Giuseppe Renato Imperiali (1651-1737). Elevated to the Sacred College of Cardinals in 1690, Imperiali exerted a great influence over the temporal administration, diplomatic posture, and intellectual life of the Papal States for nearly half a century. As Prefect of the Sacra Congregazione del Buon Governo for over four decades, he oversaw the municipal finances, public works, and fiscal administration of the entire pontifical territory, operating at the very center of Roman administrative statecraft. Simultaneously, Cardinal Imperiali achieved international renown within the European Republic of Letters (Res publica literaria) as a bibliophile and cultural patron. His private library, housed in the Palazzo Imperiali at Piazza Santi Apostoli in Rome and cataloged by the eminent scholar Giusto Fontanini in 1711, served as a vital institutional nexus for European humanists, antiquarians, theologians, and natural philosophers, embodying the ideal of the open, public-facing aristocratic library. Imperiali’s library was sold in 1793.Rare first and only edition. This verse novel, which Giraldi had extensively discussed theoretically in his Discorsi (1554), was intended to be the practical realization of his ideas. Conceived in fifty cantos, it was published incomplete in Modena in 1557, with only twenty-six cantos, and was never republished. The Ercole is dedicated to the Duke of Ferrara and Giraldi's patron, Ercole II d'Este, who passed away in 1559 and was succeeded by his son Alfonso II, often mentioned as a child in the poem, indicating a complex, layered compositional process.Ercole is a poem overtly pro-French and pro-papal (in line with the Este foreign policy) and is closely linked to the tumultuous events of contemporary history. With this poem, Giraldi seeks to offer an alternative model to Ariosto's Orlando Furioso: moving from the substantial unity of action with a myriad of characters to the unity of the protagonist with a multiplicity of actions. In this sense, Giraldi's novel is an objectively experimental work compared to the codified grammar of the verse poem in the 16th century. Classical mythology, also criticized by Tasso in both practical realizations and theoretical pronouncements in the Discorsi dell’arte poetica (1564), becomes an alternative option not only to the chivalric material of Carolingian descent but also to the historical material that guided another significant mid-16th-century epic experiment, Giovan Giorgio Trissino's Italia liberata dai Goti. The centrality of classical mythology in Ercole allows for a coherent discussion of an "Ovidian antecedent," identifying in the Metamorphoses the only narrative poem that presents, due to the choice of mythological material and the "gratuitousness" of many episodes, structural and thematic analogies with Giraldi's poem. This work is constructed additively, without a criterion in the selection of episodes (beyond their plausibility) and without a true focal point, apart from the protagonist's figure.Giraldi, like all those who wrote narrative poems in the 16th century after Ariosto's masterpiece, intended to propose with Ercole an integral alternative model to the Furioso: this is demonstrated by his use of topical modules of "war poems" (the reviews and catalogues: some incredibly extensive) and moral allegories, typical of the modern poem (above all, Hercules at the crossroads, of probable Ariostean and Trissinian ancestry). Thus, alongside the overall experimentalism of the project, there are also explicit structural homages to tradition, indicative of an ambition, inevitably destined to be frustrated, to rewrite the coordinates of the genre in which his work is placed. Perhaps the most significant aspect of Ercole is the use of the prophecy module (already used by Ariosto and earlier by Virgil), which, in a poem with fluid material and essentially paratactic development, serves to construct a semblance of framework, creating overlaps of temporal registers and thus compensating for the sequential structure of the work. It is curious to note that when Giraldi makes historical prophecies, he is almost systematically contradicted by the actual development of the events to which he alludes. Consider the inevitable prophecy of a new anti-Muslim crusade, with Pope Paul IV invoked as the natural political and military leader: historical fate had it that Pope Carafa died in 1559, unable to materially pursue any such political and religious project. Another element of interest (also linked to a consolidated epic tradition) is the description of the exploits of a specific character (with a clear distinction between war exploits and amorous exploits). Those of Hercules, in the poem, are expanded and amplified to excess. On the other hand, it is only on a level of eloquent elaboration that one can express the creative freedom of an author who deliberately renounces, from the outset, to create an original poem in terms of inventio: almost all the episodes of the work are in fact codified by a robust literary and mythological tradition (with some significant exceptions, such as the Argonautic expedition, in which not Jason, but, understandably, from the encomiastic perspective that partly accompanies Giraldi's work, Hercules himself is the captain of the expedition).Beyond its objective limitations, Giraldi's poem represents an important chapter in the development, far from linear, of chivalric and narrative poetry of the 16th century (especially in Ferrara) and testifies, well beyond the intentions of its author, to the crisis and unrest in which the Este duchy found itself around the mid-century, on the historical plane. To unravel these knots (but not entirely, perhaps, and not without an acute personal crisis), we must await a non-Ferrarese poet, Torquato Tasso, who, by recovering the Ariostean model, but bent to his own needs and intentions, and certainly also keeping in mind the nearby Giraldian Ercole, will propose a new, formidable declination of the verse novel with the Gerusalemme Liberata (cf. D. Rasi, Tra epica classica e tradizione romanzesca: introduzione all’«Ercole» di G. B. Giraldi Cinzio, in: “Schifanoia”, 4, 1987, pp. 73-83; also R. Bruscagli, Vita d’eroe: l’Ercole, in: “Schifanoia”, 11, 1991, pp. 9-19).In the Biblioteca Ariostea, there is an autograph manuscript by Giraldi Cinzio (Classe I 406), containing three unpublished cantos of Ercole, along with numerous corrections and revisions (cf. C. Molinari, 'Correctio et rescritto in forma grande': note sul codice Classe I 406 della Biblioteca Comunale Ariostea (I Canti Undici dell’ “Ercole” di G.B. Giraldi Cinzio), in: “Studi italiani”, 2005, nr. 2, July-December, pp. 139-198). In it, the author states that the tenth canto was composed at the home of Ludovico Castelvetro (on the relationship between Giraldi and Castelvetro, see S. Jossa, Rappresentazione e scrittura. La crisi delle forme poetiche rinascimentali (1540-1560), Naples, 1996, pp. 139-252).G.B. Cinzio initially studied medicine and philosophy, then human letters, succeeding his master C. Calcagnini in the chair in 1541. During the duchy of Ercole II d'Este and in the years of Renata of France's circle, he was the undisputed protagonist of the Ferrarese cultural scene. In 1561, following a conflict with the dukes of his city, he went into voluntary exile first to Mondovì, then to Turin, and finally to Pavia. Among his students, we particularly remember G.B. Pigna, with whom Giraldi had a violent clash regarding the discourse on novels that Pigna published in 1554, arousing the ire and accusations of plagiarism from the old master (cf. G.B. Giraldi Cinzio, Discorso dei romanzi, edited by L. Benedetti, G. Monorchio, and E. Musacchio, Bologna, 1999, passim).The fame and influence of Giraldi were not limited to the Ferrarese environment but had a European resonance. He is credited with the European revival of Senecan theatre with its dark tones and cruelties, in open opposition to the Trissinian formula. The Orbecche, in particular, performed at the author's home in the presence of the duke in 1541, enjoyed considerable public success and constitutes one of the most successful Italian examples of Senecan tragedy (cf. P.R. Horne, The Tragedies of Giambattista Cinthio Giraldi, London, 1962, passim). In 1563, Giraldi published a collection of novellas, the Hecatommithi, which were widely disseminated throughout Europe and provided Shakespeare with material for Othello and Measure for Measure (cf. P. Cherchi, M. Rinaldi, and M. Tempera, eds., Giovan Battista Giraldi Cinzio gentiluomo ferrarese, Florence, 2008, passim).

authors.name: Weigel Christoph
authors.biography: Christoph Weigel the Elder (9 November 1654 – 5 February 1726) stands as one of the most prolific, erudite, and aesthetically influential copperplate engravers, art publishers, cartographers, and art dealers of the German High Baroque. Operating at the vibrant intersection of visual art, craft technology, and early Enlightenment encyclopedism, Weigel transformed the traditional print workshop into an expansive publishing empire centered in the Imperial Free City of Nuremberg. His monumental visual documentation of early modern society—most notably his seminal 1698 publication Abbildung der Gemein-Nützlichen Haupt-Stände (commonly known as the Ständebuch)—represents an unparalleled zenith in the historical cataloging of human labor, mechanical arts, and social hierarchy. Beyond his contribution to the representation of trades, Weigel produced massive illustrative cycles for sacred Scripture, heraldic compendia, architectural treatises, and cartographic atlases. In doing so, he synthesized the refined craftsmanship of the Augsburg printmaking school, the opulent courtly aesthetic of Imperial Vienna, and the sophisticated commercial distribution networks of Nuremberg and Frankfurt am Main. His career embodies the transition of the early modern printmaker from an anonymous artisan to an authoritative intellectual entrepreneur whose visual inventories shaped the empirical worldview of early eighteenth-century Europe.Born in Redwitz (now Marktredwitz in Upper Franconia), Weigel was raised in an environment shaped by Lutheran piety and regional craft traditions. Recognizing his innate talent for precise draughtsmanship and mechanical arts, his family arranged for his early apprenticeship in goldsmithing and copperplate engraving. To refine his technical mastery, the young Weigel traveled to Augsburg, which was then the premier capital of German line engraving, print manufacture, and goldsmithing. In Augsburg, Weigel immersed himself in the rigorous techniques of burin engraving, etching, and the newly developing medium of mezzotint (Schabkunst), learning to manipulate tonal values, light, and texture with exceptional delicacy. Seeking further professional advancement, Weigel traveled to Vienna, the imperial seat of the Habsburg Monarchy. There he gained direct exposure to imperial court art, worked alongside prestigious court goldsmiths and engravers, and absorbed the dramatic visual rhetoric of the Counter-Reformation and Habsburg triumph. Subsequent residences in Frankfurt am Main and Regensburg—the seat of the Perpetual Imperial Diet (Immerwährender Reichstag)—expanded his contact with foreign diplomats, scholars, humanists, and publishing houses. This period of itinerant training not only perfected his skills as an engraver (sculptor) and draftsman (delineator) but also embedded him within an extraordinary network of European intellectuals, political patrons, and book-trade agents.The pivotal epoch of Weigel’s artistic maturity began in 1698 when he gained citizenship (Bürgerrecht) in the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg, establishing his independent workshop, print shop, and art commerce store (Kunst- und Buchhandlung). That same year witnessed the publication of his masterpiece, the Abbildung der Gemein-Nützlichen Haupt-Stände. Spanning over two hundred meticulously detailed copperplate engravings accompanied by moralizing poetic verses and prose descriptions—many composed in collaboration with the famed Augustinian preacher Abraham a Sancta Clara—the Ständebuch reorganized the medieval genre of the "Dance of Death" or "Estate Book" into a progressive, secularized encyclopedia of early modern professions. Weigel visually cataloged every stratum of contemporary society, from sovereign princes, scholars, and theologians down to paper-makers, type-founders, bookbinders, lens-grinders, compass-makers, and street vendors. What set Weigel’s work apart from earlier predecessors like Jost Amman was his obsessive technological accuracy: each plate depicted the exact tools, machinery, spatial layouts, and physical gestures intrinsic to the craft. His depiction of the printing arts, in particular, remains one of the primary historical visual sources for early modern typographic mechanics, press construction, and ink application. In addition to this socio-technical survey, Weigel achieved international renown for his devotional and biblical works, such as the Biblia Ectypa (1695) and the Passio Domini Nostri Jesu Christi (1693), which utilized intricate copper engravings to render biblical narratives with theatrical Baroque chiaroscuro, serving both as private devotional aids and artistic exemplar books.The operational scale of Weigel’s establishment in Nuremberg reflected the highest sophistication of early eighteenth-century print enterprise. Functioning simultaneously as engraver, editor, printer, and international distributor, Weigel constructed an integrated publishing house capable of handling large-scale visual production. He invested heavily in rolling presses (Kupferdruckpressen), imported high-grade paper from European mills, and employed a team of journeymen engravers, colorists (Illuministen), and letterpress typographers. His firm pioneered the commercialization of pocket atlases and cartographic collections, most notably the Atlas Portatilis (published in collaboration with his brother Johann Christoph Weigel and cartographers such as Johann David Köhler), which democratized geographical knowledge for the merchant class and grand tourists. Weigel actively competed and collaborated with Nuremberg’s cartographic titan, Johann Baptist Homann, securing imperial printing privileges (Privilegia Impressoria) from the Holy Roman Emperor to protect his copperplates from unauthorized pirating across imperial territories. His publishing catalog expanded to encompass architectural treatises by scholars like Leonhard Christoph Sturm and Paul Decker, heraldic compendia (Weigelsches Wappenbuch), and vast historical line-engraving series illustrating European wars, coronation ceremonies, and city views. Through his sophisticated commercial agents at the Frankfurt and Leipzig book fairs, Weigel’s engraved plates circulated throughout the Holy Roman Empire, the Dutch Republic, France, Britain, and the Italian peninsula.Upon his death on 5 February 1726 in Nuremberg, Christoph Weigel left behind an enduring intellectual and artistic legacy that fundamentally shaped the visual culture of the Enlightenment. His widow, Elisabeth Cecilia Weigel, along with his heirs and descendants, continued the operations of the Weigel publishing house for decades, republishing his famous copperplates and expanding his cartographic catalog under the family name. In the history of art and typography, Weigel is recognized as a master strategist who elevated copperplate engraving from a decorative secondary art into a primary engine of scientific, technical, and religious communication. His visual encyclopedism laid the conceptual groundwork for the mid-eighteenth-century projects of Diderot and D'Alembert, while his extraordinary technical precision provided an invaluable visual archive for modern historians of technology, material culture, and social history. Today, Weigel’s prints, emblematic volumes, and atlases are preserved as prized treasures in major national libraries, print cabinets, and antiquarian collections worldwide, standing as monumental testimonies to the intellectual brilliance and mechanical mastery of the German Baroque book arts.

title: Les Comptes du Monde adventureux par A.D.S.D.

authors.name: Saint-Denis Antoine
authors.biography: Very few is known about this Author: probably a priest from the diocese of Mans, who seems to have been in close relationship with Marguerite de Navarre.

publisher_data: Paris, Estienne Groulleau [for Jean Longis and Vincent Sertenas booksellers], 1555
academic_description: 8vo (169x104 mm). [11], 245, [1] leaves. Collation: ã8 ē4 A-Hh8. Lacking the blank leaves ē4, Hh7 and Hh8. Groulleau’s device on title page. Woodcut initials. Colophon on l. Hh5r, Privilège du Roi on ll. Hh5v-6v. Roman and italic types. 19th-century gilt hazelnut calf, spine in compartments with lettering piece, gilt edges, marbled endleaves, blue silk bookmark (part of the spine and hinges skillfully repaired). On the front flyleaf bookplate with the monogram “AMB”, on the title page barely readable ownership entry “Le marquis De P[…]” and library stamp “Ex bibliotheca J. Richard M.D.” (repeated on l. A1r). Contemporary manuscript notes on ll. Q2r and Q6r in a French hand. Worm tracks repaired on the lower blank margin of most of the volume only occasionally minimally affecting the text, title page slightly soiled, some occasional light browning, all in all a good copy. Extremely rare first edition of this collection of fifty-four moralizing stories, often rather coarse and spicy, nevertheless dedicated “Aux sages et vertueuses Dames de France”. The work is traditionally attributed to Antoine de Saint-Denis, a priest from the diocese of Mans, who seems to have been in close relationship with Marguerite de Navarre. “Par ses tendances come par sa forme littéraire, ce recueil appartient bien au petit cercle des contes de la reine de Navarre, et la personalité d’Antoine de Saint-Denis [curé de Champfleury] s’y encadre sans difficulté […] Il faut reconnaître que, en effet, si Marguerite d’Angoulême étendit largement sa protection sur le monde entier des lettres et des arts, elle se fit tout près d’elle un cenacle choisi de poëtes et de conteurs, et que sa personalité fut, pour ceux-ci, una cause vivante démulation autant qu’un centre d’attraction […] Par ces points de contact fréquents entre le livre de la reine de Navarre et le recueil de Comptes du monde adventureux se trouve corroborée l’opinion que j’ai déjà émise au sujet de la priorité des ces Comptes, priorité d’allieurs publiquement affirmée par les amis de l’auteur au moment de l’impression du recueil in 1555, et qui ne souleva de la part des contemporaines aucune réclamation” (F. Frank, Notice, in: “Les comptes du monde adventureux”, Paris, 1878, pp. XIV, XXIV and CXXVII; see also V.-L. Saulnier, Martin Pontus et Marguerite de Navarre, la Réforme lyonaise et les sources de l’Héptameron, in: “Bibliothèque d’Humanisme et Renaissance”, XXI, 1959, pp. 577-594). At the beginning of each story the author gives his short general moral lesson and at the end he addresses specifically to women to tell them what lesson they have to draw from the story. As in Boccaccio’s Decameron, the stories are told within a narrative frame, which is in itself a short story. The author is traveling from Provence to Savoy through the Dauphiné. Along the way he meets a gentleman who is accompanying his recovering wife to a thermal center. He joins them and their group, and during the journey - on horseback, during and after meals - they tell each others short stories to entertain themselves. Investigations about the sources of the stories were made by G.-A. Pérouse in his Nouvelles françaises du 16me siècle (Genève, 1977, pp. 139-155). Thus the main source of the stories is Masuccio Salernitano (c. 1410-1475), as at least thirty stories are drawn from him. Some single stories are adaptations from the Pecorone of Giovanni Fiorentino (fl. mid 14th cent.), from Heinrich Bebel (1472-1518), from Matteo Bandello (1485-1561) (cf. V.-L. Saulnier, Sur une nouvelle de Bandello et l’un des Comptes du Monde adventureux, in: “Bibliothèque d’Humanisme et Renaissance”, XXIII, 1961, pp. 347-350), from Le petit Jehan de Saintré by Antoine de La Sale (c. 1388-1461) (cf. G.-A. Pérouse, Les Comptes du Monde adventureux et le roman de Jehan de Saintré, in: “Bibliothèque d’Humanisme et Renaissance”, XXX, 1968, pp. 457-469), and from the Cent Nouvelles nouvelles (c. 1450s). The remaining stories, however, are original and “constituent un ensemble de récits inspirés par des anecdotes françaises et contamporaines, dont la note est très distincte de celle que rend le reste du recueil; ce sont des nouvelles, au sens propre du terme” (Pérouse, op. cit., p. 144). “[…] A.D.S.D. est écrivain et, de plus d’une manière, y fait preuve d’originalité. Tout d’abord, ses ‘histoires’ sont loin d’être tout “traduites”; et, lorsque traduction il y a, celle-ci est rarement simple traduction. Mais notre auteur se distingue encore par son recours à un récit liminaire (alors que les collections commerciales en sont depourvues, on l’a constaté), ou par le fait que ses emprunts s’addressent à la ‘deuxième génération’ des modèles italiens, enfin et surtout par sa constante volonté d’enseigner […] Tout cela étant, les Comptes du Monde adventureux ont bien une place entre Taillemont et Tahureau. Mais ils sont aussi liés de près à l’Heptameron […] Malgré la date tardive de leur publication, au bord des années de crise, les Comptes du Monde adventureux se rattachent assurément, pour une part, à la grande époque du genre. Les quinze récits realists qui s’y détachent ont leur place à côté des Nouvelles Récreations et surtout de l’Heptaméron: narrations ‘ancrées’ dans la réalité sociale quotidienne de ce côté-ci des Alpes, et exprimant ces réalités françaises dans des intrigues souvent fort reussies, ce sont proprement des ‘nouvelles’ au sens que nous avons voulu dégager au début de cette étude – éléments épars d’un authentique ‘Decameron françois’ ”(Pèrouse, op. cit., pp. 140 and 154). “La répartition des délits et du personnel criminel entre histoires comiques et histoires tragiques dans l’Heptaméron et Les Comptes du monde adventureux délivre un premier enseignement: les crimes les plus graves sont associés aux histoires tragiques tandis que les crimes bénins sont majoritaires dans les histoires comiques – ce qui n’exclut néanmoins pas la présence de délits majeurs. Dans ces deux recueils, les histoires tragiques accordent une place prépondérante aux crimes les plus graves tels que le meurtre, le viol ou encore l’adultère – ce dernier délit étant lui-même considéré comme le plus criminogène de tous, dans la mesure où il entraîne dans son sillage une multiplication des crimes les plus graves, de l’homicide au crime de lèse-majesté […] [D]ans la trente-quatrième histoire des Comptes du monde adventureux, l’adultère monnayé d’une dame avec un étudiant mène le mari trompé à assassiner son épouse et dans la cinquantième histoire, l’adultère d’une dame avec un écuyer la conduit à commettre un homicide, celui d’un enfant innocent. De manière générale, les pulsions sexuelles et les malheurs liés à l’amour et au désir sont au cœur des histoires tragiques où désir et violence sont étroitement associés […] (dans Les Comptes du monde adventureux, sur onze histoires criminelles trois tragiques, un mariage clandestin, cinq relations sexuelles illicites et quatre adultères peuvent être comptabilisés): l’amour est mortifère et malheureux dans la peinture tragique […] Cependant, contrairement à ce qui se passe dans l’Heptaméron, les histoires comiques réservent dans Les Comptes du monde adventureux une place importante aux délits mineurs, vols, duperies et autres bons tours, dont les victimes provoquent le rire, et non la compassion. Ce personnel criminel professionnel est représentatif de la perspective facétieuse et satirique, tandis qu’il est le plus souvent absent des histoires tragiques ou y apparaît au second plan. La satire des milieux marchands et artisans, dans la tradition des fabliaux, est présente dans la onzième histoire où un couturier voleur se fait meunier et apprend à être un peu larron pour éviter d’être réduit à la mendicité ; les moines malhonnêtes sont mis en scène dans la dixneuvième histoire et dans la vingt-deuxième, alors que les membres du clergé apparaissent au contraire comme des proies faciles pour les voleurs du fait même de leur cupidité et de leur soif d’argent dans les trente-troisième et quarante-sixième histoires. Ces figures criminelles sont héritières de la tradition satirique et se caractérisent par la ruse, la finesse, la duplicité dont elles font preuve pour mystifier leurs victimes. La vingt-quatrième histoire est très représentative, puisque le menu larcin accompli par les protagonistes est assimilé à une plaisanterie, une raillerie permettant de rire aux dépens d’un personnage respecté, un docteur ès lois de la ville de Boulogne: l’identité de la victime, un notable, représentant de la justice ou membre du clergé, contribue beaucoup à faire ressortir le sel des bons tours accomplis par des personnages mi-voleurs mi-plaisantins” (E. Ziercher, Représentations du sujet criminel, entre facétie et pathétique, in: “Juges et criminels dans la narration brève du XVIe siècle, J.-C. Arnould, ed., 2010, pp. 2-3 and 8; see also W.K. Pietrzak, Le Tragique dans les nouvelles exemplaires en France au XVIe siècle, Lódź, 2006, ad indicem; and L. Dion, Histoires de mariage. Le mariage dans la fiction narrative française (1515-1559), Paris, 2017, ad indicem). The present edition was shared between four Parisian publishers: Estienne Groulleau, Jean Longis, Robert Le Mangnier and Vincent Sertenas, and is extant with three variant title pages bearing the name of one or the other publishers. The work was very successful and was reprinted seven times until the end of the century. The 1582 edition contains an addition of five “discours modernes et facetieux”, that do not appear in the latest known 16th-century edition printed in 1595. The first modern edition is the one edited and commented by F. Frank cited above, that was reprinted at Geneva in 1969 (cf. Pérouse, op. cit., p. 502).

title: Arbaʻa avne haǧ-ǧilionim mehat-tora ha-ḥadaša ašer neʻettaqu melišon romi lelišon ʻivri [hebraice] Quatuor Evangelia Novi Testamenti ex Latino in Hebraicum sermonem versa

authors.name: Iona Giovanni Battista
authors.biography: Giovanni Battista Iona (also recorded as Giovanni Battista Jona, born Judah Jona; c. 1588 – 1668) was an Eastern European Jewish scholar, Christian Hebraist, and lecturer who served the Roman Curia and the Papal See during the seventeenth century. Originating from Lemberg (Lviv) in the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth, Iona converted from Judaism to Roman Catholicism, subsequently becoming a prominent figure in the institutionalization of Hebraic studies within the Catholic Counter-Reformation apparatus. His intellectual career illustrates the intersection of early modern Jewish rabbinic erudition and Catholic polemical philology in post-Tridentine Rome.Born into a Jewish family in the late sixteenth century, Iona received a traditional Talmudic and rabbinic education in Poland. He subsequently traveled through the Ottoman Empire, spending time in Palestine and Constantinople. During his travels in the Italian peninsula during the early seventeenth century, he established contact with Catholic ecclesiastical authorities. He formally converted to Catholicism in Tuscany around 1625, adopting the baptismal name Giovanni Battista Iona. His knowledge of Hebrew, Aramaic, and rabbinic literature facilitated his integration into Roman academic and missionary institutions.Following his conversion, Iona relocated to Rome under papal patronage. He was appointed reader and professor of Hebrew at the Archiginnasio della Sapienza (the University of Rome) and taught language courses at the Collegio Urbano de Propaganda Fide. In this institutional role, Iona produced pedagogical and polemical works designed for missionary activities targeting Jewish communities. His scholarship focused on comparative biblical analysis, emphasizing messianic prophecies in the Old Testament and rabbinic commentaries that Catholic exegesis interpreted as prefigurations of Christian theology.The central work associated with Iona's career was a translation of the Four Gospels into Hebrew, titled Evangelia quadrupla Hebraice, printed at Rome in 1668 by the press of the Sacra Congregatio de Propaganda Fide. The typographical execution relied on specialized Hebrew metal type fonts maintained by the Polyglot Press of Propaganda Fide, conforming to seventeenth-century ecclesiastical standards for oriental typography. Prior to this, Iona authored the polemical treatise Discorso sopra la venuta del Messia (Rome, 1663), printed by the press of the Camera Apostolica. He also served as a scriptor and cataloger of Hebrew manuscripts for the Biblioteca Apostolica Vaticana.Iona's output was integrated into the broader framework of seventeenth-century Catholic missionary strategy and Hebraic philology. While contemporary papal authorities utilized his translations and teaching as functional tools for conversionary strategies, modern historical scholarship evaluates his work within the context of Jewish-Christian intellectual transmission, scriptural translation methodologies, and state-sponsored Oriental typography in early modern Rome.

academic_description: Folio (350x235 mm). [28], 395, [1 blank] pp. Collation: [π]4 ++-+++4 ++++2 A-Bbb4 Ccc6. Parallel text in Hebrew and Latin arranged in two columns. Half title, title within a typographic frame with the woodcut device of the Congretatio de Propaganda fide in the center. With four large woodcut vignettes at the beginning of each Gospel showing the Evangelists with their symbols, taken from the Arabic Gospels printed in Rome in 1590-‘91 by the Typographia Medicea. Woodcut initials and ornaments. Contemporary grey cardboards, inked title on spine (endleaves renewed). Some marginal worm tracks partly skillfully repaired, lower inner corner of the first quire repaired not affecting the text, some scattered browning due to the paper, all in all a very good, genuine copy. Uncut with deckle edges.First edition of the Gospels in the Hebrew translation from the Vulgate by the converted Jew Giovanni Battista Iona, who completed his version before 1639. The preliminary matter includes a dedication to Pope Clement IX, a twenty-two-page introduction printed in parallel columns in Latin and Hebrew, and the approbations. Jehudas Jona was born in a Jewish Sephardic family in Safed in 1588 and renamed Giovanni Battista in Warsaw in 1625. After travelling around various cultural centres in Europe, he settled in Rome, where he lectured at La Sapienza University from 1649 to 1664, and subsequently at the Collegio dei Neofiti until his death in 1668. Among his students was Giulio Bartolocci. Like other teachers of the discipline, he was also a Hebrew scriptor in the Vatican and an interpreter of other Eastern languages. In addition to teaching, he was intensely involved in apologetics. We know of his Hebrew and Latin sermons on the true Messiah and the descent of the Holy Spirit, as well as his translations of Bellarmine’s catechism, the Gospels and St Thomas’s Summa contra Gentiles. He died before completing the Hebrew version of the Acts of the Apostles, as well as various dialogues and polemical pamphlets against the Jews, which he left as manuscripts (cf. G. Rita, Le discipline umanistiche da Sisto V a Clemente XII (1587-1740), in: “Storia della Facoltà di Lettere e Filosofia de ‘La Sapienza’”, L. Capo-M.R. Di Simone, eds., Rome, 2000, p. 280).“Three main points may be adduced from [the introduction]. First, one particular reason for which Iona wished to read the Gospels in Hebrew was his belief – a widespread one – that the Gospel of Matthew was originally written in Hebrew. Iona was therefore hoping to find this original version of Matthew or, at least, an approximation to it. Second, the Hebrew versions of the Gospel of Matthew that Iona actually found – the translation included in Shem-Tov ibn Shaprut’s fourteenthcentury polemical treatise ʾEben Bōḥan (The Touch Stone) and the translation published in Paris in 1555 by Jean du Tillet and Jean Mercier – disappointed him greatly, since he deemed that they were written in poor Hebrew, or in what he calls ‘stammered language’ […] Iona believed that the rendering of the Gospel into ‘bad’ Hebrew was a polemical technique used by the authors of these translations in order to make the Gospel ‘despicable’ to Jews […] Third, Iona hoped that his own translation was written in such ‘pure’ Hebrew that may enable it to be perceived as being ‘like the rest of the Holy Scriptures’, that is, as being similar to the books of the Hebrew Bible […] Iona hopes that the reading of his translation will be convincing to some Jews and therefore bring about their conversion. It may be noted that Iona’s translation is one of the earliest Hebrew translations of the New Testament in which such a missionary aim is mentioned. Only in the eighteenth and nineteenth century did the mission to the Jews become a main motivation for producing Hebrew translations of the New Testament […] Regarding the Hebrew used by Iona in the translation, it may first be observed that it has some clear ‘biblicizing’ features […] Last but not least, it is not rare to find in Iona’s translation renderings of undeniable quality, that is, cases in which Iona manages to find a translation that both faithfully renders the meaning of the Latin expression or phrase and is idiomatic in Hebrew and resonates with Jewish culture” (E. Shuali, Giovanni Battista Iona’s Hebrew translation of the four Gospels, in: “Journal of Jewish Studies”, 2023, 74.2, pp. 408-428). In 1626, Urban VIII established the Polyglot Printing House of the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith with the aim of producing publications for missionary work. The press soon amassed a considerable amount of typographical material (23 alphabets), which was augmented by oriental characters donated by the Vatican and Medici printing houses. The creation of new typefaces was entrusted to the punchcutter S. Paolini. The press mainly printed religious books, grammars and lexicons.

authors.name: Descartes René
authors.biography: René Descartes (1596–1650), known across the early modern Latinate Respublica Literaria by his Latinized name Renatus Cartesius, stands as the pivotal architect of Western modern philosophy and a foundational figure of the Scientific Revolution. Operating at the turbulent intersection of late Renaissance Scholasticism, early modern natural philosophy, and modern mathematical synthesis, Descartes systematically dismantled the teleological Aristotelian worldview that dominated European universities. In its place, he erected an unapologetically rationalist, mechanistic, and dualist philosophical paradigm. His philosophical project—characterized by the methodological deployment of radical doubt, the foundational formulation of the cogito, ergo sum, the defense of innate ideas, and the division of reality into thinking substance (res cogitans) and extended substance (res extensa)—reconstructed the parameters of epistemology, metaphysics, optics, and physiology. Simultaneously, his invention of analytic geometry synthesized algebra and geometry, providing the indispensable mathematical framework for early modern physics.Born on March 31, 1596, at La Haye en Touraine (a town subsequently renamed Descartes in his honor), he was the son of Joachim Descartes, a magistrate and councillor in the Parlement of Brittany at Rennes, and Jeanne Brochard, who died shortly after his birth. Raised by his maternal grandmother and a nurse, young René belonged to the noblesse de robe, an elite social stratum of legal administrators and royal bureaucrats. In 1607, at the age of eleven, he was sent to the newly founded Jesuit college of La Flèche in Anjou, established by King Henri IV and directed by Father Étienne Charlet. For eight years, Descartes underwent a rigorous humanistic and philosophical education. The curriculum at La Flèche combined classical grammar, rhetoric, and literature with a deep immersion in the Scholastic-Aristotelian curriculum, studying logic, natural philosophy, mathematics, and metaphysics via the commentaries of the School of Coimbra (Conimbricenses), Francisco Toledo, Pedro da Fonseca, and Francisco Suárez. While Descartes praised the institution for its intellectual rigor, he subsequently reflected in his Discours de la méthode that book-learning had saddled him with doubt and uncertainty rather than clear, demonstrable truth. Leaving La Flèche in 1614, he matriculated at the University of Poitiers, where he earned a baccalaureate and licentiate in civil and canon law in 1616, satisfying his family's judicial ambitions before embarking on an independent intellectual quest.Driven by a desire to study "the great book of the world," Descartes traveled to the Netherlands in 1618 to join the Protestant army of Prince Maurice of Nassau as a gentleman volunteer (soldat à la suite). This period marked a crucial intellectual catalyst through his friendship with the Dutch physician and natural philosopher Isaac Beeckman. Beeckman introduced Descartes to a brand of physical-mathematics that sought to explain physical phenomena through micro-mechanical models of matter and motion, sparking Descartes's early work on hydrostatics, acoustics, and falling bodies (the Compendium Musicae, dedicated to Beeckman in 1618). Following the outbreak of the Thirty Years' War, Descartes traveled to Bavaria in 1619, serving under Maximilian I, Elector of Bavaria. It was during the winter of 1619, while stove-heated in a room near Neuburg an der Donau, that Descartes experienced a series of intense intellectual epiphanies and three vivid dreams on the night of November 10–11. He interpreted these visions as a divine mandate to unify all human knowledge under a singular, universal mathematical method (the mirabilis scientiae fundamenta). This methodological vision culminated in his unfinished treatise Regulae ad directionem ingenii (Rules for the Direction of the Mind), written between 1619 and 1628, which laid the groundwork for his intuitive-deductive method.During the 1620s, Descartes traversed Europe, visiting Italy and residing periodically in Paris. In the French capital, he entered the vibrant intellectual circle surrounding the Minim friar Marin Mersenne, who served as the central clearinghouse for European scientific and philosophical correspondence. Mersenne's network exposed Descartes to the debates surrounding libertinism, Pyrrhonian skepticism (popularized by Michel de Montaigne and Pierre Charron), and the emerging new physics of Galileo Galilei and Pierre Gassendi. Seeking total solitude and liberation from social obligations to systematically construct his system, Descartes relocated permanently to the Dutch Republic in late 1628. Over the next twenty years, he moved frequently between various Dutch towns and country estates—including Franeker, Leiden, Amsterdam, Deventer, Utrecht, and Endegeest—benefiting from the religious tolerance and intellectual dynamism of the Dutch Golden Age.Descartes's first major publication project was the ambitious natural-philosophical treatise Le Monde (The World) or Traité de la lumière, accompanied by L'Homme (Man). In these works, he constructed a fully mechanistic universe composed of a continuous fluid matter divided into three element types, operating solely via motion, impact, and spatial rearrangement under God's conserved laws of nature, completely eschewing Aristotelian substantial forms and occult qualities. However, upon learning in 1633 of the condemnation of Galileo by the Roman Inquisition for defending Copernican heliocentrism, Descartes prudently withdrew Le Monde from publication, as his own physics relied upon a moving Earth. Instead, he presented his natural philosophy implicitly in 1637 through a French masterwork published anonymously at Leyden by the printer Jan Maire: Discours de la méthode pour bien conduire sa raison, et chercher la vérité dans les sciences. This work served as a preface to three scientific essays demonstrating his method: La Dioptrique (explaining the law of refraction/Snell's law and eye anatomy), Les Météores (a mechanical account of weather phenomena and the rainbow), and La Géométrie. In La Géométrie, Descartes introduced the method of representing geometric curves through algebraic equations using a coordinate system, thereby inventing analytic geometry and revolutionizing early modern mathematics.The publishing history of Descartes's works reflects the burgeoning international book trade centered in the Low Countries and Paris. Jan Maire's 1637 quarto edition of the Discours was printed in the vernacular French rather than Latin to reach an educated lay audience beyond the university faculties, featuring elegant typography and woodcut diagrams personally supervised by Descartes. Moving to secure his philosophical foundation, Descartes authored his metaphysical masterpiece in Latin: Meditationes de prima philosophia (Meditations on First Philosophy). First published in Paris in 1641 by the publisher Michel Soly, the work featured six set objections gathered by Mersenne from leading intellectuals—including the theologian Johan de Kater (Caterus), Thomas Hobbes, Antoine Arnauld, and Pierre Gassendi—alongside Descartes's exhaustive replies. A second, revised edition was published in Amsterdam in 1642 by the famed printing house of Louis Elzevir (Elsevier), incorporating a seventh set of objections by the Jesuit Pierre Bourdin and Descartes's letter to Father Dinet. The Elzevir press became Descartes's primary publisher, producing elegant, widely circulated octavo and duodecimo editions that reached university professors, theologians, and scholars across Europe.In 1644, Elzevir published Descartes's Principia philosophiae (Principles of Philosophy), dedicated to Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia. Designed to replace traditional Scholastic textbooks in university curricula, the Principia synthesized Cartesian metaphysics, mechanistic vortex physics (explaining planetary motion through rotating celestial matter), and physical cosmology into a rigorous four-part system.Descartes's intellectual life in the 1640s was deeply shaped by his intensive correspondence with Princess Elisabeth of Bohemia (1618–1680), daughter of Frederick V, Elector Palatine. Elisabeth posed penetrating critiques regarding Cartesian dualism, specifically questioning how an unextended, immaterial soul could causally act upon a material, extended physical body (the mind-body interaction problem).Their dialogue pushed Descartes to refine his psychological and ethical theories, culminating in his final published treatise, Les Passions de l'âme (The Passions of the Soul), printed concurrently in Paris by Henry Le Gras and in Amsterdam by Louis Elzevir in 1649. In this work, Descartes analyzed human emotions as physiological processes mediated by the movement of animal spirits flowing through the nervous system, identifying the pineal gland (conarium) as the principal seat of the soul where mind and body interact.The dissemination of Cartesianism triggered fierce theological and academic battles. In the Dutch Republic, Descartes became embroiled in the "Utrecht Crisis" (1639–1643), where Gisbertus Voetius, rector of the University of Utrecht and a staunch Calvinist theologian, accused Descartes of atheist tendencies and subversive skepticism. A similar theological assault erupted at the University of Leiden led by Martinus Schoock and Reinerus Regius. Seeking refuge from these polemics, Descartes accepted an invitation from Queen Christina of Sweden in 1649 to join her court in Stockholm as a royal tutor and philosopher-in-residence. The harsh Scandinavian winter, combined with the Queen's demanding schedule requiring tutorials at five o'clock in the morning in an unheated library, severely compromised Descartes's frail health. In early February 1650, he contracted severe pneumonia and died in Stockholm on February 11, 1650, at the age of fifty-three.Following his death, Descartes's remains underwent a complex journey; his body was buried in Sweden, exhumed in 1666, and transported to France, where it was eventually reinterred in the Church of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris. In 1663, despite the efforts of French Cartesian scholars like Claude Clerselier (who published Descartes's voluminous posthumous correspondence between 1657 and 1667), the Roman Catholic Church placed Descartes's works on the Index Librorum Prohibitorum donec corrigantur (until corrected), perceiving his mechanistic physics as incompatible with the Eucharistic doctrine of transubstantiation. Nevertheless, Cartesianism swept through European intellectual life, fundamentally reshaping European philosophy. His dualist framework directly inspired the rationalist metaphysics of Baruch Spinoza, Nicolas Malebranche, and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, while provoking the empirical critiques of John Locke, George Berkeley, and David Hume. In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, Descartes was elevated as the foundational symbol of the Enlightenment and the modern philosophical subject, securing his legacy as the indispensable initiator of modern epistemological inquiry.

authors.name: Barbapiccola Giuseppa Eleonora
authors.biography: Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola (c. 1700 – c. 1740) was an important figure in early 18th century Naples and a groundbreaking champion for the inclusion of women in natural philosophy and the physical sciences, achieved international scholarly renown through her 1722 translation into Italian of René Descartes’ Principia Philosophiae, which was prefaced by an original feminist manifesto “A’ Lettori” (‘To the Readers’). In this prefatory discourse, Barbapiccola articulated a harsh critique of contemporary educational disparities, arguing that women’s intellectual perceived inferiority was not a consequence of biological or ontological deficiency, but rather the artificial product of systemic educational deprivation. By deploying Cartesian epistemology itself - specifically the doctrine of clear and distinct ideas and the radical dualism of mind and body - Barbapiccola demonstrated that the faculty of reason is fundamentally ungendered, thereby establishing a philosophical foundation for female intellectual emancipation.Born in Salerno around the turn of the eighteenth century, Barbapiccola belonged to an educated, socially prominent family with deep clerical, legal, and intellectual ties across the Kingdom of Naples. Her upbringing was profoundly shaped by her uncle, Agostino Barbapiccola, a learned ecclesiastic, canonist, and active participant in Neapolitan literary circles. Recognizing his niece’s exceptional aptitude, Agostino facilitated her rigorous domestic education, exposing her to classical Latin, modern French, geometry, natural history, and metaphysics. Unlike many of her female contemporaries whose education was confined to devotional literature and domestic arts within convent walls or noble households, Barbapiccola gained direct access to the private libraries and private academies of Naples. During this era, Naples was experiencing a dramatic philosophical shift: the traditional Aristotelian-Scholastic paradigm, long enforced by ecclesiastical authorities, was being vigorously challenged by the jusnaturalism, atomism, and mechanical philosophy promoted by the Accademia degli Investiganti - a vanguard institution founded by Tommaso Cornelio, Leonardo Di Capua, and Lucantonio Porzio. It was within this intellectually charged atmosphere of Neapolitan Cartesianism that Barbapiccola acquired her deep mastery of modern physics and mechanical philosophy.Barbapiccola’s magnum opus, her Italian translation of Descartes’ Principia, was a masterpiece of philosophical translation and linguistic adaptation. Translating Descartes’ original Latin text (first published in Amsterdam in 1644) alongside Claude Clerselier’s authoritative French version (1647), Barbapiccola aimed to make modern mechanical philosophy accessible to an Italian readership, particularly to women who were routinely denied instruction in academic Latin. In her self-assured preface, she boldly situated her work within the long history of female intellectual achievement, evoking classical and modern precedents such as Hypatia of Alexandria, Diotima, Veronica Gambara, Vittoria Colonna, Cassandra Fedele, Anna Maria van Schurmann and Anne Dacier among others. Barbapiccola explicitly challenged the misogynistic assertions of philosophers such as Claude Fleury, who argued in his Traité du choix et de la méthode des études (1686) that female physiology was too delicate or soft to comprehend abstract scientific principles. Barbapiccola contended that if female nerves were indeed more delicate, women were uniquely endowed with superior perceptual sensitivity and cognitive agility, making them exceptionally suited for scientific inquiry. Her translation was not merely a passive linguistic exercise, but an active intervention in European philosophical discourse, seeking to dismantle the gendered barriers surrounding the res publica literaria.Barbapiccola was an active member of the prestigious Accademia degli Arcadi (the Arcadian Academy), adopting the pastoral pseudonym Mirista, under which she composed erudite poetry and exchanged philosophical verses with leading scholars of the realm. Chief among her allies and admirers were the eminent philosopher and historian Giambattista Vico (who is quoted in the preface) and Gherardo degli Angeli. Gherardo was so profoundly impressed by Barbapiccola’s erudition and translation project that he composed an encomiastic sonnet, titled In lode della signora Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola, che ha tradotto da’ francesi ne’ nostri favellari i Principi della Filosofia di Renato Des-Cartes (Rime Scelte, Florence, 1730, vol. 3, p. 104). In this poem, Gherardo celebrated her as a shining beacon of Neapolitan genius who had surpassed the achievements of foreign scholars. Barbapiccola was very close to Vico’s favourite daughter Luisa, also a highly educated woman and a poetress (the two exchanged poems), and cultivated close ties with prominent Neapolitan natural philosophers, including Pietro Antonio de Martino, Bernardo De Dominici, and the literary patron Antonio Niccolini.The publishing history of Barbapiccola’s I Principi della Filosofia di Renato Des-Cartes reflects the complex geopolitical and censorial realities of early eighteenth-century Naples. Printed in 1722, the title page bears the false or strategic imprint of Turin, a common typographical maneuver utilized by Neapolitan publishers to bypass local ecclesiastical censorship and political scrutiny regarding Cartesian mechanical philosophy, which remained controversial due to its implications for Eucharistic theology and scholastic physics. The edition included comprehensive diagrams of Cartesian vortices, planetary orbits, and atomic structures, meticulously reproduced to ensure that Italian readers could fully grasp Descartes’ physical cosmology.

academic_description: 4to (220x155 mm). [40], 350, [18] pp. and the portrait of Giuseppa Barbapiccola engraved by Francesco de Grado. Collation: [†]-†††4 **-***4 A-Zz4. With several woodcut illustrations and diagrams in text (some full page). Lavishly bound in contemporary stiff vellum gilt, on the panels gilt coat-of-arms of Cardinal Niccolò Coscia (1682-1755, a much discussed cardinal who during his life time lived also in Naples and may have personally met Barbapiccola, see below), marbled pastedowns, red marbled edges (slightly soiled and worn). Small hole to l. K4 slightly affecting the text, small tear to the lower blank margin of l. S4, some occasional pale staining, a very good, genuine copy with wide margins. Rare first edition. “In 1722 Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola (ca. 1700-ca. 1740) translated René Descartes’s Principles of Philosophy (1644), working primarily from the 1647 French edition rather than the Latin original. Allegedly published in Turin by Giovan Francesco Mairesse, it was in all likelihood one of many books published in Naples under false imprimatur in the late seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. The fact that a Neapolitan artist, F. De Grado, engraved Barbapiccola’s portrait for the translation makes it even more probable that it was both written and published there. Like many philosophical works published in Naples, including a number of books that Barbapiccola cited in her preface, it may have been part of the semiclandestine circulation of books in the capital city of the Kingdom of Naples […] More than simply a translation of Descartes’s important work, Barbapiccola’s Italian edition was also a manifesto of women’s right to learn. In her preface, entitled ‘The Translator to the Reader’, she presented Descartes as the creator of a philosophy that celebrated the female mind […] Barbapiccola demonstrated that one did not need to be of royal blood to understand Descartes or, more generally, to reflect on important philosophical questions. But she did far more than this, since her preface was simultaneously a history of women’s learning, a history of philosophy, and an autobiography. She self-consciously presented herself as an heir to the seventeenth-century tradition of Cartesian women and celebrated its arrival in the city of Naples, where she was one of several women known for their philosophical crudition by the early eighteenth century. Another leading female Cartesian, the duchess of Limatola, Aurelia d’Este (1683-1719), had recently died , making it possible for a younger, less noble woman to claim the place that d’Este had occupied as the preeminent Cartesian woman in the city. Barbapiccola offered her own tribute to d’Este when she praised Paolo Mattia Doria for writing his Dialogues in Which It Is Demonstrated That Woman, in Almost All the Important Virtues, Is Not Inferior to Man (1716), a work he addressed to his famous aristocratic pupil, Aurelia d’Este, while he was still enamored with Cartesian philosophy […] Barbapiccola’s preface brought together several different strands of intellectual debate then preoccupying scholars in Naples. On the one hand, it responded to the growing anti-Cartesianism of important philosophers such as Vico and Doria, who increasingly felt that a modern metaphysics that emphasized the mathematical certainty of reason limited the possibilities for other kinds of discussions about the nature of knowledge. On the other hand, it sought to integrate some of the new philosophical insights of Neapolitan scholars into a fresh reading of Descartes. Her preface, for example, invoked Vico’s On the Most Ancient Wisdom of the Italians (1710), a controversial book dedicated to Doria that presented his new historical consciousness about the origins of knowledge as an implicit alternative to Cartesian epistemology. Within a decade, both philosophers would tum away from Descartes, leaving others to defend his philosophy: Barbapiccola, for example, would argue that these different approaches to knowledge were not incompatible […] So much of Barbapiccola’s text is concerned with these philosophical issues that it is easy to forget that she also intended her work as a defense of women’s right to philosophize. History gave her inspiration for her pursuit of learning with its numerous examples of learned women. Knowledge of languages such as Latin gave her the tools for reading and understanding the kind of learning that lay beyond the traditional scope of women’s studies. But it was Cartesian philosophy that gave her the tools to think critically about knowledge […] Through the early 1730s, Neapolitan scholars continued to celebrate Barbapiccola as the woman who had made Descartes glorious in Italy, even as the fascination with Descartes was eclipsed by a new passion for the writings of English philosophers such as John Locke and Isaac Newton.The printer-bookseller Bernardino Gessari advertised Barbapiccola’s translation in 1734 as one of the books to be purchased at his shop on Via San Biagio del Libra. Her book also circulated in other parts of the italian peninsula. In 1740 , for example, when the Sienese cleric Giovan Nicolò Bandiera published his important and controversial treatise on women’s education, he knew enough about Barbapiccola’s work to include her name in his list of contemporary women engaged in philosophical and scientific pursuits in Naples” (P. Findlen, Giuseppa Eleonora Barbapiccola, in: “The Contest for Knowledge: Debates over Women’s Education in Eighteenth-Century Venice”, R. Messbarger and P. He studied at La Sapienza University in Rome, obtaining a doctorate in utroque iure (both canon and civil law) on 30 March 1715. He met Cardinal Vincenzo Maria Orsini, the Archbishop of Benevento and future Pope Benedict XIII, while still young. During one of the cardinal's pastoral visits, he encouraged Coscia to enter the ecclesiastical state and conferred the first tonsure in May 1696. Niccolò studied under the cardinal’s auspices and learned about the affairs of the archiepiscopal curia. In October 1703, the cardinal granted him a canonry in the collegiate church of San Bartolomeo in Benevento. In April 1708, he exchanged this for another in the chapter of the metropolitan cathedral, at the same time being named chancellor of the curia. He was ordained on 28 March 1705 and was appointed secretary to Cardinal Orsini, Archbishop of Benevento. In the archdiocese of Benevento, he served as master of the chamber, treasurer, apostolic visitor, archpriest, and abbot mitered of S. Lorenzo d'Aprice.He accompanied Cardinal Orsini to the conclaves of 1721 and 1724 as conclavist. When Cardinal Orsini was elected pope, Coscia followed him to Rome. On 7 June 1724, he was appointed secretary of Memorials. On 26 June 1724, Coscia was elected titular archbishop of Traianopoli and was created cardinal in the consistory of 11 June 1725. Coscia was also appointed Protector of the Sovereign Order of Malta and the Order of the Friars Minor Conventual in 1725, and Protector of the city of Avignon and Prefect of the Congregation of Avignon in 1726.Cardinal Coscia’s conduct had created a great deal of animosity among the other members of the Sacred College of Cardinals. When Pope Benedict XIII died, Cardinal Coscia hid in Rome before fleeing to Cisterna in the fiefdom of Prince Michelangelo Gaetani, Duke of Caserta. Despite the cardinal’s behaviour, the duke gave him refuge and protection. Cardinal Coscia warned the Sacred College that the election of the new pontiff would be invalid without his vote, and he was given assurances that he would be allowed to participate in the conclave. It took him forty days to arrive in Rome with the Duke of Caserta, who accompanied him into the city until the Cardinal had securely entered the conclave. He resigned from the government of the archdiocese on 8 January 1731, not without protest, and sought refuge in Naples the following March, which resulted in the confiscation of all his possessions. He was imprisoned in Castel SantìAngelo, but was treated fairly.On 23 February 1734, the same pope lifted the major excommunication penalty and restored his active voice in the July 1738 conclave.From 1735 onwards, he was permitted to visit various thermal baths to treat his gout. Following the death of Pope Clement XII, he was released and permitted to participate in the 1740 conclave, which elected Pope Benedict XIV. He retired to private life in Naples in 1741. The new pope ordered a review of the case, and on 8 January 1742 he pardoned the remaining time of his ten-year sentence, reinstated his cardinalate, and absolved him of all charges. Coscia died in Naples on 8 February 1755 (cf. F. Petrucci, Coscia, Niccolò, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 30, Rome, 1984, s.v.).
