authors.name: Bourbon Louis-Auguste
authors.biography: Louis-Auguste de Bourbon, Prince de Dombes (4 March 1700 – 1 October 1755), was a high-ranking French prince, military commander, and sovereign ruler whose life bridged the late reign of Louis XIV, the turbulent Regency of Philippe d'Orléans, and the mature reign of Louis XV. Born into the extraordinary and politically precarious lineage of the legitimised royal bastards (princes légitimés), he was the eldest surviving son of Louis-Auguste de Bourbon, Duc du Maine—himself the favorite natural son of King Louis XIV and Françoise-Athénaïs de Rochechouart de Mortemart, Marquise de Montespan—and Anne-Louise-Bénédicte de Bourbon-Condé, a princess of the royal blood (princesse du sang). As the sovereign ruler of the Principality of Dombes, Comte d'Eu, Grand Master of the Royal Artillery of France (Grand maître de l'artillerie), Colonel General of the Swiss and Grisons, and Governor of Languedoc, Louis-Auguste represented the institutional convergence of royal military aristocracy, sovereign provincial autonomy, and elite cultural patronage in Enlightenment France. His historical significance extends beyond his battlefield accomplishments into the realm of intellectual history and typography: under his sovereign aegis, the independent enclave of Dombes and its capital, Trévoux, remained a crucial hub for independent printing, most notably sustaining the production of the famed Journal de Trévoux and the Dictionnaire de Trévoux, which served as powerful intellectual counterweights to both Jansenist theology and the radical encyclopedism of the mid-eighteenth century.The early years of Louis-Auguste de Bourbon were profoundly shaped by the elevated status and eventual political downfall of the House of Bourbon-Maine. Raised amidst the opulent splendor of the Château de Sceaux—where his mother, the Duchesse du Maine, held legendary literary salons known as the Grandes Nuits de Sceaux—the young prince was immersed from infancy in an atmosphere of intense artistic patronage, theatrical pageantry, and high dynastic ambition. King Louis XIV, seeking to secure the future of his legitimised sons, had elevated the Duc du Maine and his male descendants to the rank of Princes of the Blood in July 1714 and designated Maine in his royal testament as regent and guardian of the infant Louis XV. However, following the Grand Roi's death in September 1715, the Parlement of Paris annulled these testamentary dispositions, bestowing full regency power upon Philippe, Duc d'Orléans. The young Louis-Auguste thus grew up under the shadow of his family's dramatic political disenfranchisement, exacerbated by the failed Cellamare Conspiracy of 1718, in which his parents attempted to strip Orléans of the regency in favor of King Philip V of Spain. While his parents suffered imprisonment and temporary exile, the young Prince de Dombes was carefully shielded from direct treason charges, undergoing a rigorous martial and classical education supervised by elite military tutors and humanists at Court. This education emphasized classical historiography, siegecraft, mathematics, cartography, and foreign languages, instilling in him a lifelong commitment to technical military science and statecraft.Demonstrating a remarkable dedication to martial service, Louis-Auguste embarked on an active military career that served to rehabilitate the public standing of the House of Maine. In 1717, at the tender age of seventeen, he received permission to join the Imperial army commanded by Prince Eugene of Savoy in Hungary during the Austro-Turkish War (1716–1718). He distinguished himself through conspicuous bravery during the siege and capture of Belgrade, earning high praise from Prince Eugene and establishing a formidable reputation among European military elites. Upon his return to France, he assumed command of the Regiment of Dombes and was appointed Colonel General of the Swiss and Grisons in 1726. During the War of the Polish Succession (1733–1735), the Prince de Dombes served with distinction in the French campaigns along the Rhine, participating actively in the Siege of Kehl (1733) and the costly Siege of Philippsburg (1734) under the command of the Duke of Berwick. Following the death of his father in 1736, Louis-Auguste inherited the historic office of Grand maître de l'artillerie de France, a supreme military rank that granted him total administrative and tactical authority over the realm's ordnance, foundries, and artillery corps. In this capacity, he worked diligently to modernize artillery technical specifications, standardize gun foundries, and expand the royal arsenals. His strategic expertise was further called upon during the War of the Austrian Succession (1740–1748), where he participated in the campaigns in Germany and the Low Countries, including the Battle of Dettingen (1743) and the Flanders campaigns under Marshal de Saxe.Beyond his high military commands, Louis-Auguste's most enduring historical legacy lies in his role as the sovereign Prince of Dombes, an independent enclave situated on the left bank of the Saône River between Bresse and Lyonnais. Inheriting the principality upon his father's death, Louis-Auguste governed Dombes as an absolute sovereign, exempt from French royal taxation, salt monopolies (gabelle), and royal censorship decrees. The capital of his sovereign principality, Trévoux, had been transformed by his father into a major typographical sanctuary, a legacy that Louis-Auguste zealously protected and financially underwrote throughout his reign. Free from the restrictive oversight of the Paris Guild of Booksellers and Royal Censors, the sovereign press at Trévoux—the Imprimerie Prince de Dombes—flourished as one of Northern Europe's primary centers for classical, legal, and theological printing. Louis-Auguste actively protected the Jesuit scholars who edited the Mémoires pour l'Histoire des Sciences & des Beaux-Arts (widely known as the Journal de Trévoux), a monthly periodical that stood as one of the most authoritative intellectual journals of the eighteenth century, offering rigorous reviews of scientific, literary, and philosophical treatises across Europe. Furthermore, under his patronage, successive editions of the monumental Dictionnaire de Trévoux (Dictionnaire universel françois et latin) were expanded and printed, serving as a masterwork of French lexicography that directly challenged the anti-clerical momentum of Voltaire and the French Philosophes. The revenue, international prestige, and legal immunity generated by these printing activities turned Trévoux into an extraordinary anomaly: a micro-sovereignty sponsoring high Enlightenment erudition and polemics.In addition to his sovereignty in Dombes, Louis-Auguste was appointed Governor of Languedoc in 1737, a crucial administrative post in one of France's largest and most fiercely autonomous frontier provinces. Managing the provincial Estates of Languedoc with diplomatic tact and administrative efficiency, he successfully mediated between royal tax demands and local aristocratic privileges, overseeing major public works, civil engineering projects, and canal maintenance throughout the region. Despite his immense wealth, vast estates—including the Duchy of Gisors, the County of Eu, and the Castle of Anet—and prominent standing at the court of Versailles, the Prince de Dombes never married and left no legitimate issue. His private life was marked by a passion for hunting, arms manufacturing, and architectural embellishments at his estates in Anet and Sceaux. On 1 October 1755, Louis-Auguste died unexpectedly at the Château de Fontainebleau at the age of fifty-five, following injuries sustained during a private duel or a fatal accident during a royal hunt, as recorded by contemporary court chroniclers such as the Duc de Luynes and the Marquis d'Argenson. His titles, vast fortune, and the sovereignty of Dombes passed to his younger brother, Louis-Charles de Bourbon, Comte d'Eu (1701–1775). Following Louis-Charles's eventual cession of Dombes to King Louis XV in 1762, the sovereign status of Trévoux was formally dissolved and integrated into the French Crown. Historiographically, Louis-Auguste de Bourbon stands as a striking exemplar of the late-feudal sovereign prince in early modern France, whose institutional authority seamlessly blended high military office with significant contributions to the Republic of Letters through the press of Trévoux.

academic_description: 8vo (185x110 mm). [10], 244 pp. Slightly later green cardboards (worn and rubbed). On the front pastedown ownership entry ‘Vendier' and bookplate ‘Jacques et Hélène Bon'. On title-page verso double stamp ‘Au Preal de Soissons'. Slightly uniformly browned. Uncut with deckle edges.Rare second enlarged edition (first 1740), in which the important Lettre du Patissier Anglois, attributed to Mr. Desalleurs the Elder, son of the French ambassador to Constantinople, appears for the first time.The anonymous work is prefaced by a witty dedicatory epistle “To His Most Serene Highness, His Lordship the Prince of Dombes,” signed by the Gascon Cook, who is none other than the prince of royal blood, whose anonymity fooled very few people: “The work I take the liberty of presenting to You is nothing other than the fruit of my reflections on Your practice,” writes the pseudo-Gascon, who does not hesitate to identify himself as “one of the best chefs in France.” Louis-Auguste de Bourbon, grandson of Louis XIV and Madame de Montespan, was appointed Grand Hunt Master to Louis XV in 1738. After the hunt, the monarch's dining companion at suppers in the private apartments would take charge of the kitchen alongside a few high-ranking lords of the court, sending away kitchen boys and servants to prepare their favorite dishes.Le Cuisinier Gascon, one of the most peculiar French cookbooks, contains 217 recipes, suited to both stately tables and more modest tastes. So much so that “Sausages in Champagne Wine” appear alongside “Peasant-Style Fruit Salad,” “Pig's Tails,” stews, and soups. There is a marked inclination toward Italian cuisine: ravioli, macaroni, gnocchi, lasagna, veal à la Piémontaise - and a few surprising dishes, such as breaded and grilled veal teats, veal eyes stuffed and baked au gratin, frogs in green sauce, green monkey sauce, eggs without malice, veal cooked to resemble donkey droppings, bat-shaped chicken, etc. More than two centuries later, certain chefs continued to draw inspiration from this manual without revealing their source.

authors.name: Ptolemaeus Claudius
authors.biography: Claudius Ptolemaeus (ca. 100 – ca. 170 CE), known universally to history as Ptolemy, stands as one of the most monumental polymaths of classical antiquity. Operating in the vibrant intellectual matrix of Roman Alexandria during the second century of the Common Era—specifically under the Antonine emperors Hadrian, Antoninus Pius, and Marcus Aurelius—Ptolemy synthesized, codified, and mathematically transformed ancient Greek astronomy, geography, cartography, optics, harmonic music theory, and astrological doctrine into unified, axiomatic systems. His massive written treatises served as the undisputed, authoritative scientific paradigms across the Byzantine Empire, the medieval Islamic Caliphates, and Western Latin Christendom for over a millennium and a half. In the history of ideas, few figures possess a historical legacy so expansive that their name becomes synonymous with an entire cosmological framework: the Ptolemaic System—a geocentric model of the universe that governed human spatial and cosmological understanding until the epistemological ruptures of the Copernican Revolution in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.Biographical details concerning Ptolemy’s early life, family lineage, and personal circumstances remain remarkably sparse, preserved almost exclusively through internal textual markers within his own surviving writings and brief late-antique historical notices. His binomial name offers important sociopolitical clues regarding his identity: the Roman gentilicium Claudius indicates that he or an ancestor held Roman citizenship, likely granted by the Julio-Claudian emperors Claudius or Nero, while the Greek cognomen Ptolemaeus underscores his Greek cultural identity and deep connection to Egypt, the former kingdom of the Hellenistic Ptolemaic Dynasty. From precise observational logs recorded within his astronomical masterwork, the Mathematikē Syntaxis (later known to posterity through its Arabic title as the Almagest), historians have established that Ptolemy conducted systematic astronomical observations in Alexandria between 127 and 141 CE. Alexandria in the Antonine era remained the supreme scientific hub of the Mediterranean basin, home to the celebrated Library and Museum of Alexandria. Ptolemy worked within a long, prestigious Alexandrian tradition, drawing directly upon the theoretical foundations, empirical logs, and mathematical methods of predecessors such as Euclid, Eratosthenes, Apollonius of Perga, Posidonius, and above all Hipparchus of Nicaea, whose second-century BCE observational records and trigonometric chord tables provided the indispensable raw material for Ptolemy’s theoretical constructs.Ptolemy’s crowning achievement in mathematical astronomy is the Mathematikē Syntaxis (Mathematical Syntaxis), a monumental thirteen-book treatise designed to 'save the appearances' (sōzein ta phainomena) of planetary motion within a strictly geocentric framework. To explain the complex non-uniform motion of celestial bodies—including retrograde loops, brightness fluctuations, and variable orbital velocities—without abandoning the fundamental Aristotelian axiom of uniform circular motion, Ptolemy refined and engineered three brilliant geometric constructs: the eccentric circle, the deferent-and-epicycle system, and his most original, controversial mathematical innovation, the equant point (punctum aequans). By placing the equant point offset from the physical center of the deferent circle, Ptolemy mandated that a planet’s epicycle center swept out equal angles in equal times relative to the equant, thereby achieving extraordinary empirical predictive accuracy for planetary positions. Beyond planetary mechanics, the Almagest contained a comprehensive star catalog enumerating 1,022 stars categorized into forty-eight distinct constellations, complete with precise ecliptic coordinates and visual magnitudes, as well as foundational contributions to spherical trigonometry, most famously Ptolemy’s Theorem concerning cyclic quadrilaterals.Parallel to his astronomical endeavors, Ptolemy revolutionized the scientific conceptualization of space and cartography through his eight-book treatise, the Geōgraphikē Hyphēgēsis (Theoretical Geography or Geography). Ptolemy defined geography as 'a representation in picture of the whole known world, together with the phenomena contained therein,' explicitly distinguishing it from regional chorography. Moving away from qualitative descriptive geography, he established a rigorous mathematical architecture based on a grid of latitude and longitude coordinates. The Geography provided precise coordinates for over 8,000 specific locations across the known inhabited world (the oikoumenē), stretching from the Canary Islands (the Fortunate Isles) in the far west to China (Sera and Cattigara) in the east, and from Scandinavia down to sub-Saharan Africa. To transfer the spherical surface of the Earth onto a two-dimensional plane, Ptolemy invented sophisticated map projections, including a simple conic projection and a modified pseudoconical projection. Although his adopted estimate for the Earth's circumference (borrowed from Posidonius rather than the more accurate calculation of Eratosthenes) resulted in a significant overestimation of the east-west terrestrial span—an error that famously emboldened Christopher Columbus late in the fifteenth century—the Geography established the scientific foundation for modern quantitative cartography.Ptolemy’s intellectual inquiries encompassed the entire spectrum of imperial natural philosophy. In the Apotelesmatika, traditionally designated as the Tetrabiblos (Four Books), Ptolemy attempted to systemize astrology into an empirical, physical natural science rooted in Aristotelian physics. Unlike mystical celestial divination, Ptolemaic astrology interpreted planetary influences as physical mechanisms operating through primary qualities—heat, dryness, moisture, and cold—that exerted continuous material forces upon the sublunary sphere and human physiology. In his Optics, surviving largely through a medieval Latin rendition of a lost Arabic translation, Ptolemy conducted pioneering experimental studies on visual perception, mirror reflection (catoptrics), and atmospheric light refraction, compiling quantitative measurement tables for angles of refraction between air, water, and glass. In the Harmonics, he developed a sophisticated mathematical theory of musical scales, seeking a philosophical synthesis between strict Pythagorean numerical abstraction and Aristoxenian empirical auditory validation. Finally, in his late physical cosmological work, the Planetary Hypotheses, Ptolemy transitioned from abstract geometric models to a concrete physical universe, conceiving the heavens as a series of nested physical crystalline spheres that completely filled celestial space without vacua.The manuscript transmission and early modern printing history of Ptolemy’s corpus constitute a crucial chapter in European typographical culture and humanistic scholarship. While Ptolemaic texts were preserved, expanded, and critiqued in the Islamic world during the Middle Ages by scholars such as al-Battani, Ibn al-Haytham, and Nasir al-Din al-Tusi, and translated into Latin by Gerard of Cremona in Toledo in 1175, the advent of Renaissance printing elevated Ptolemy to the center of European print culture. The Geography enjoyed immediate typographic popularity: translated into Latin by Jacopo d'Angelo, it was first printed at Vicenza in 1475 (without maps), followed by the historical 1477 Bologna edition featuring the world's first engraved copperplate maps, and the celebrated 1478 Rome edition printed by Arnoldus Buckinck using plates prepared under Conrad Sweynheym. The magnificent 1513 Strasbourg edition by Johann Schott, edited by Martin Waldseemüller, integrated Ptolemaic maps with twenty modern woodcut maps (tabulae novae). The Almagest saw its princeps Latin publication in Venice in 1515 by Johannes Liechtenstein (Gerard of Cremona's medieval text), followed by the elegant Renaissance Latin translation by George of Trebizond, edited by Luca Gaurico and published by Lucantonio Giunti in Venice in 1528. The editio princeps of the original Greek text of the Almagest was printed in Basel in 1538 by Johann Walder, edited by Simon Grynaeus and accompanied by the fourth-century commentaries of Theon of Alexandria. The Tetrabiblos had already been printed by Erhard Ratdolt in Venice in 1484, while its original Greek text was issued by Johann Oporinus in Basel in 1553.The historiographical reception and scientific assessment of Ptolemy have undergone dramatic shifts over the centuries. For over thirteen hundred years, Ptolemaic astronomy was accepted as the definitive account of physical reality. However, the sixteenth-century scientific revolution initiated a process of relentless critique. Nicolaus Copernicus, in his De revolutionibus orbium coelestium (1543), while admiring Ptolemy's genius, rejected the equant point as a violation of uniform circular motion, ultimately replacing the geocentric framework with a heliocentric arrangement. Subsequently, Johannes Kepler utilized Tycho Brahe’s high-precision observational data to replace circular planetary orbits with ellipses, dissolving the Ptolemaic machinery entirely. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, historiographical debate turned toward Ptolemy’s observational integrity. Astronomers such as Jean-Baptiste Joseph Delambre, and later Robert R. Newton in his polemical monograph The Crime of Claudius Ptolemy (1977), alleged that Ptolemy had fabricated observational data or unethically plagiarized the star catalog of Hipparchus. However, contemporary scholarship led by historians of science such as Otto Neugebauer, Gerald J. Toomer, Noel Swerdlow, Bernard R. Goldstein, and Alexander Jones has contextualized Ptolemy's methodology within ancient scientific norms, demonstrating that his parameter selections and mathematical smoothing were intended to reconcile discrete empirical observations into coherent, predictive theoretical models. Today, Claudius Ptolemaeus is recognized not as a fabricator, but as the supreme architect of classical mathematical science whose systematic vision framed human understanding of the cosmos for millennia.

authors.name: Ruscelli Girolamo
authors.biography: Girolamo Ruscelli (ca. 1504/1518 – 1566) stands as one of the most quintessential and versatile representatives of sixteenth-century Venetian vernacular humanism, embodied in the historical archetype of the poligrafo—the professional editor, translator, literary critic, and cultural mediator who operated at the epicenter of the early modern European print industry. Operating during the golden age of Venetian typography, Ruscelli navigated the intersecting currents of literary theory, experimental natural philosophy, emblemology, and cartography. His career transformed the vernacular press from a vehicle of mere textual reproduction into an dynamic engine of intellectual dissemination, codifying the Italian language, introducing groundbreaking cartographic standards, and pioneering empirical scientific methodologies through pseudonymous publications that achieved European-wide bestseller status. Far from being a mere mercenary scribe compiling commercial miscellanies, Ruscelli actively shaped the intellectual architecture of Late Renaissance Europe, maintaining sprawling scholarly networks that connected humanistic academies in Rome, Naples, and Venice with the major print shops of Central and Western Europe.Born in Viterbo during the first two decades of the sixteenth century—likely between 1504 and 1518—Ruscelli spent his early formative years in relative obscurity, though his later writings indicate a rigorous classical education grounded in Latin humanities, rhetoric, and natural philosophy. Seeking career advancement within the turbulent network of Italian courtly and academic patronage, Ruscelli migrated to Rome around 1540. There, he quickly integrated himself into the vibrant literary debates of the papal capital, founding the short-lived but influential Accademia dello Sdegno in 1541 under the patronage of Roberto Strozzi. This Roman period was marked by fierce polemical disputes; Ruscelli positioned himself as a militant defender of vernacular literary standards, engaging in passionate public controversies over tragic poetics (notably regarding Sperone Speroni's controversial play Canace) and the stylistic authority of Giovanni Boccaccio and Francesco Petrarca. By the mid-1540s, economic necessity and political instability prompted his relocation to Naples, where he entered the household of Ferrante Sanseverino, Prince of Salerno, and associated with Alfonso d'Avalos, Marquis of Pescara. In Naples, Ruscelli catalyzed an extraordinary intellectual experiment by founding the Accademia dei Secreti (Academy of Secrets)—a pioneering brotherhood of scholars, artisans, and herbalists dedicated to the systematic empirical testing of physical, medical, chemical, and metallurgical recipes. This academy served as a crucial precursor to the formal scientific societies of the seventeenth century, prioritizing direct sensory experimentation and repeatable practical demonstration over scholastic dogma.Driven by the printing revolution and the unmatched commercial infrastructure of the Republic of Venice, Ruscelli permanently relocated to the Serenissima in late 1548 or early 1549. Venice provided the ideal crucible for his intellectual ambitions, allowing him to establish himself as a paramount editorial director and authorial partner for premier Venetian publishing houses. Ruscelli's textual output during his Venetian period was staggering in breadth and depth. In 1555, under the pseudonym Alessio Piemontese (Alexius Pedemontanus), he published the Secreti del recondito donno Alessio Piemontese, an monumental compendium of empirical recipes, medical treatments, alchemical procedures, and technical instructions. The work became an unprecedented international publishing phenomenon, undergoing dozens of editions and translations into Latin, English, French, German, Dutch, and Spanish across Europe. It was only in his posthumously published I Secreti (1567) that Ruscelli's authorship and the operational framework of his Neapolitan academy were fully disclosed to the public. Concurrently, Ruscelli exerted a profound influence on Italian linguistics and poetics. In 1559, he released Del modo di comporre in versi nella lingua italiana, a seminal rhyming dictionary and theoretical manual that provided exhaustive instructions on poetic meter, stanzaic structures, and stylistic decorum, substantially contributing to the standardization of literary Tuscan across the Italian peninsula.Ruscelli's intellectual versatility reached its graphic and visual zenith through his monumental contributions to cartography and emblemology. In 1561, working in close collaboration with the renowned printer Vincenzo Valgrisi, Ruscelli published La Geografia di Claudio Tolomeo Alessandrino. Translating Ptolemy's ancient geographical treatise into the vernacular, Ruscelli expanded and modernized the text by introducing sixty-four double-page copperplate maps engraved by master artisans such as Giulio Sanuto and Girolamo Porro. This atlas combined classical Ptolemaic geography with newly engraved maps (*tavole nuove*) representing contemporary European explorations, the routes to the East Indies, and detailed cartographic depictions of the Americas, establishing a benchmark for early modern cartographic publishing. In 1566, the final year of his life, Ruscelli published Le imprese illustri through the press of Francesco Rampazetto. This masterwork of emblem literature featured intricate copperplate engravings illustrating the personal devices (*imprese*), heraldic emblems, and mottoes of European monarchs, popes, commanders, and intellectuals. Ruscelli provided deeply erudite iconographic, historical, and philosophical commentaries for each entry, turning the volume into a foundational reference for Renaissance iconology and courtly symbolism.The operational mechanics of Ruscelli's career reveal a master strategist of the early modern typography economy. Rather than binding himself exclusively to a single press, Ruscelli established dynamic commercial and editorial partnerships with the most sophisticated Venetian printers of his day, including Vincenzo Valgrisi, Francesco Rampazetto, Giordano Ziletti, Plinio Pietrasanta, and Giovanni Griffio. Ruscelli acted as a modern series editor, copy editor, indexer, and marketing innovator. He was instrumental in popularizing the shift from traditional woodcut illustrations to fine copperplate engraving (*calcografia*) for technical, cartographic, and emblematic texts, recognizing that copperplate offered superior detail for geographical coordinates and complex symbolic imagery. Furthermore, Ruscelli was a central figure in intense intellectual feuds, most notably his famous literary war with his rival Venetian *poligrafo*, Lodovico Dolce. Their public squabbles over the textual accuracy of Ariosto's Orlando Furioso, Boccaccio's Decameron, and Petrarca's Canzoniere highlighted the fierce competition among publishers to claim scholarly authority and capture market share in vernacular classics. Ruscelli died in Venice in 1566, leaving behind an colossal archive of published works and unpublished manuscripts that continued to be issued by his literary executors and publishers well into the seventeenth century.In modern historiography, Girolamo Ruscelli has undergone a complete critical re-evaluation. While nineteenth-century literary historians occasionally dismissed the 16th-century *poligrafi* as mere opportunistic popularizers, contemporary scholarship—led by historians of the book such as Brian Richardson and historians of science such as William Eamon—recognizes Ruscelli as a pivotal figure in the early modern knowledge revolution. His work as 'Alessio Piemontese' is now studied as a crucial milestone in the democratization of scientific knowledge and the emergence of the 'Professor of Secrets' phenomenon, bridging the gap between medieval occultism and the experimental methodologies of Baconian science. His cartographic editions remain essential milestones in the history of Renaissance geography, while his critical editions and linguistic treatises remain foundational to the history of the Italian book and linguistic codification. Today, Ruscelli stands acknowledged as an extraordinary nexus where humanistic philology, empirical science, visual arts, and print technology harmoniously converged.

academic_description: Three parts (each with a separate title page) in one volume, 4to (mm 212x152). Geografia: [8], 358, [2] pp.; Espositioni et introduttioni universali di Girolamo Ruscelli sopra tutta la Geografia di Tolomeo: [28] leaves, [4: Tavola universale, con la descrittione di tutto il mondo] pp., 27 and XXXVI engraved numbered double plates; Discorso universale di M. Giuseppe Moleto matematico: 47, [49] pp. Signatures: *4 A-YY4; α-η4 +2 1-272 (2A-2Z2 A1-D42) I-XXXVI2 (3A-Nn2); 4A-4F4 5A-5F4. The edition contains several woodcut diagrams and illustrations in the text (including two portraits of Ptolemy), and overall 64 engraved double-page maps, of which 27 are Ptolemaic and 37 are new. Ziletti's device on title pages, Valgrisi's device after plate XXXVI (l. Nn4v). Later vellum with inked title on spine (endleaves renewed). Tear anciently repaired to l. η4 with no loss, slightly uniformly browned, some light occasional marginal foxing and staining, short margins, but overall a good copy. Second Ruscelli edition of Ptolemy's Geography, a reprint of the first issued by Vincenzo Valgrisi in 1561. A third edition, revised and corrected by Giovanni Malombra and with the addition of a map (Territoria di Roma), was printed by Ziletti in 1574. Ruscelli was responsible for the Italian translation of the text and for the maps, which he drew reproducing on a larger scale those published by Gastaldi in his 8vo edition of Ptolemy's Geography appeared in 1548. The most important innovation introduced by Ruscelli is the division of the modern globe into two circular hemispheres depicting the New World and the Old World; a feature previously used only by François de Malines in 1528 and later become popular with the famous Mercator globe of 1587. Particularly innovative is also the map of the Arctic regions, in which Ruscelli correctly separates Greenland from Norway, usually depicted as forming a single land. When in 1559 Pius IV commissioned Pirro Ligorio to have a gallery in the Vatican painted with geographical maps, Ruscelli's modern maps were chosen as models for the frescoes. Girolamo Ruscelli, of humble origins, was born in Viterbo and became one of the leading editors of the Cinquecento.He was first active in Rome, where he founded the Accademia dello Sdegno together with Tommaso Spica and Giovanni Andrea dell'Anguillara. He later settled in Venice working for such publishers as Sessa and Valgrisi. He was a friend of Bernardo and Torquato Tasso, Lodovico Dolce and Pietro Aretino. The last two were to become his rivals in several bitter controversies. He edited the works of Boccaccio, Petrarch and Ariosto and translated Ptolemaeus' treatise on geography. While in Venice he had contact with other academies (della Fratta, dei Dubbiosi, della Veniera and della Fama), and was interested in issues such as the systematization of the Italian language (cf. P. Procaccioli, ‘Costui chi e' si sia'. Appunti per la biografia, il profilo professionale, la fortuna di Girolamo Ruscelli, in: “Girolamo Ruscelli. Dall'accademia alla corte alla tipografia. Atti del Convegno internazionale di studi, Viterbo, 6-8 ottobre 2011, Roma, 2012”, pp. 13-76; and C. Di Filippo Bareggi, Il mestiere di scrivere: lavoro intellettuale e mercato librario a Venezia nel Cinquecento, Rome, 1988, pp. 78-80; 296-301). Giuseppe Moleti, born in Messina, Sicily, was an Italian mathematician who held the chair of mathematics at the University of Padua before Galileo (cf. A. Carugo, Giuseppe Moleti: mathematics and the Aristotelian theory of science at Padua in the second half of the 16th-century Italy, in: “Aristotelismo veneto e scienza moderna. Atti del 25° anno accademico del Centro per la storia della tradizione aristotelica nel Veneto”, L. Olivieri, ed., Padua, 1983, I, pp. 509-517). He also played a key role in the reform of the calendar promoted by Pope Gregory XIII. Moleti also wrote an important dialogue on mechanics and in 1562 (Venice, Valgrisi) published his own edition of Ptolemy's Geography, mainly based on Ruscelli's 1561 edition.
bibliography: Edit 16, CNCE41068; N. Broc, La geografia del Rinascimento, Modena, 1986, pp. 114 and 130; Sabin, 66504.

title: Il ritratto del vero governo del prencipe dall'essempio vivo del gran Cosimo de' Medici

authors.name: Rosello Lucio Paolo
authors.biography: The Venetian humanist, dialogist, and editorial editor Lucio Paolo Rosello (ca. 1485 – 1552)—frequently recorded in archival and typographical sources under the variants Roselli or Rossello—occupies a singular, if historically contentious, position within the intellectual ecosystem of mid-sixteenth-century Renaissance Italy. Operating in Venice during the golden age of vernacular publishing, Rosello belonged to that dynamic cadre of men of letters known to modern historiography as the poligrafi. These independent scholars, working at the intersection of humanist philology, commercial print, and social critique, transformed the literary marketplace of the Serenissima into a vibrant crucible of popular philosophy, political speculation, and vernacular translation. Rosello’s historical significance rests principally on his function as a crucial conduit for the reception, adaptation, and vernacular dissemination of Northern European humanist political thought—most notably Sir Thomas More’s foundational work Utopia—within the framework of Italian civic humanism, courtly advice literature, and post-Machiavellian statecraft.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative EducationBorn in the late fifteenth century, approximately around 1485, in the mainland territories of the Republic of Venice (with archival indications pointing toward Padua or the immediate Venetian hinterland), Lucio Paolo Rosello received an extensive education rooted in classical Latin rhetoric, Aristotelian dialectic, and moral philosophy. Though precise biographical records regarding his familial lineage remain sparse, his early epistolary exchanges and literary dedications demonstrate a deep familiarization with both classical antiquity—particularly Cicero, Seneca, and Quintilian—and the early Italian humanism of Petrarch, Coluccio Salutati, and Leonardo Bruni. Like many ambitious scholars of his generation, Rosello migrated to Venice in the early decades of the sixteenth century, drawn by the unparalleled economic and intellectual vitality of the lagoon city under the dogeships of Andrea Gritti and Francesco Donà. In Venice, Rosello inserted himself into private literary academies, informal salon gatherings, and the burgeoning workshops of Venetian printer-publishers, where classical learning was systematically harnessed to meet the demands of an expanding vernacular readership.Major Works, Philosophical/Literary Analysis, and Intellectual NetworksRosello’s magnum opus, titled Due Dialoghi di M. Lucio Paolo Rosello, l'uno della vita civile, la qual contiene il vero reggimento de l'isola de Eutopia, et d'altre cose no lesso utili che facete. L'altro della vera virtu, da cui nasce la vera felicita de gli huomini & de principi..., was published in Venice in 1552. This two-part vernacular dialogue represents a complex synthesis of utopian vision, civic humanism, and ethical philosophy. The first dialogue, focused on civil life and the governance of the hypothetical island of Eutopia, directly adapted the vernacular Italian translation of Thomas More’s Utopia published just four years earlier (in 1548) by the heterodox scholar Ortensio Lando and printed by Anton Francesco Doni. Rather than offering a literal translation, Rosello ingeniously refashioned More’s text into a lively vernacular conversation between fictional interlocutors, stripping away certain raw radicalisms while amplifying its practical application to Italian political realities. In the second dialogue, Rosello shifted his focus to the moral foundation of political power, analyzing true virtue (vera virtù) as the indispensable prerequisite for personal and civic happiness (vera felicità). Through this bipartite structure, Rosello aligned himself with the broader intellectual networks of mid-century Venice, maintaining close ties with fellow literary innovators such as Pietro Aretino, Ludovico Domenichi, Bernardo Tasso, and the members of the Accademia degli Infiammati and Accademia dei Pellegrini.Printing History, Typographical Context, and Publishing CirculationThe publication history of Rosello's works reflects the sophisticated material culture of the mid-sixteenth-century Venetian print industry. The 1552 edition of his Due Dialoghi issued from the printing house of Comin da Trino di Monferrato, an influential printer operating in the Venetian neighborhood of San Zulian, known for producing high-quality vernacular literature, theatrical works, and political treatises. Set in elegant chancery italic types (corsivo) accompanied by historiated woodcut initials and featuring Comin da Trino's distinctive printer's device—often depicting the allegorical figure of Prudence or Hercules—the volume was meticulously engineered for aesthetic appeal and commercial viability. The physical distribution of Rosello’s book extended beyond the borders of the Venetian Republic, finding readership across the duchies of Lombardy, Tuscany, and Emilia, as well as entering international diplomatic circles. However, the rapidly tightening censorial apparatus following the early sessions of the Council of Trent and the subsequent promulgation of the Roman Index of Prohibited Books created a precarious environment for vernacular dialogues dealing with ideal societies and socio-political critique. Despite these mounting pressures, Rosello’s text circulated widely, serving as a vital bridge between mid-century Italian humanism and late Renaissance political theory.Critical Reception, Historical Controversies, and Enduring LegacyIn the centuries following his death in 1552, Rosello became the subject of intense historiographical debate. Early modern literary chroniclers and nineteenth-century bibliographers frequently dismissed him as a mere compiler or plagiarist due to his heavy reliance on Ortensio Lando’s rendering of Thomas More. However, modern twentieth-century scholarship—pioneered by eminent historians such as Luigi Firpo, Delio Cantimori, Eugenio Garin, and Paul F. Grendler—has radically re-evaluated Rosello’s legacy. Far from being an uncritical copyist, Rosello is now recognized as a sophisticated practitioner of early modern imitatio and inventio. He deliberately mediated northern European utopianism for an Italian public accustomed to the genre of the dialogue and the discourse on princehood (speculum principis). By embedding More’s radical communal vision within an Aristotelian and civic humanist framework, Rosello demystified political theory and contributed directly to the development of early modern political science. Today, his work stands as an indispensable milestone in the history of European utopian literature, highlighting the creative vitality, commercial adaptability, and philosophical audacity of the Venetian poligrafi.

publisher_data: Venice, Al Segno del Pozzo (per Giovanni Maria Bonelli), 1552
academic_description: 4to (153x105 mm). 107, [3] pp. Collation: A- N⁸ O⁴. Contemporary limp vellum, signs of ties, partially faded inked title on spine (slightly stained and soiled). Bonelli's woodcut device on title page (Minerva riding a lion) with the latin motto "Virtuti omnia parent" ('Everything leads to virtue'). Woodcut historiated initials and, on title-page verso, large woodcut illustration of a man holding a rock and pointing to a dove and a crown within clouds, with the Greek motto "God is with me". Some occasional light foxing and staining, but a very good, genuine copy.First and only edition, dedicated by the author to Cosimo the Medici's firstborn, Francesco, with an obvious pedagogical aim. Rosello's work is divided into two “Ragionamenti” followed by two Isocrates' Orationes translated from the Greek by the author himself and already translated from the Latin by Erasmus and published as an appendix to many editions of his Institutio principis christiani.Il ritratto is structured as a dialogue, a literary style much appreciated in the 16th century which permits a certain neutrality. The interlcutors of the first “Ragionamento”, which takes place in Naples (the city where Juan de Valdès lived for a period), are Girolamo Muzio (Italian humanist, courtier, and literary theorist closely associated with Counter-Reformation culture), Ferrante Carafa (a Neapolitan nobleman, soldier, and man of letters active in the cultural and political life of Spanish Naples), and the Marquis of Laterza Giambattista d'Azzia (a Neapolitan nobleman and intellectual associated with the aristocratic and literary circles of the Kingdom of Naples under Spanish rule). Choosing historical relevant people instead of fictional characters, shows Rosello's intention of disclosing his own political position: Muzio, for instance, is the leading character in the conversation (“princeps sermonis”), but he was also a controversial personality who publicly joined the Counter-Reformation: he therefore represents an ideological position that Rosello needed to put forward after his conviction for heresy.Muzio begins the dialogue by recalling his experience at Henry II of France's court: while drawing inspiration from Machiavelli's The Prince, Rosello significantly modifies the meaning of his example, which considered the institution of the French Parliament as a means for the king to combat the “great” and favor the “lesser”; here, instead, its institution is seen as a guarantee for the sovereign, who thus manages to maintain equidistance from the warring classes. Muzio also recalls as well his time spent at Cosimo the Medici's court in Florence: the Grand Duke was legitimately elected by incorruptible free men and he always had been tolerant towards his enemies. Carafa, embracing Machiavelli's philosophy more closely, replies that a prince should instead “exstinguish” his opponents, while Muzio, who represents the author's and Erasmus' perspective, considers it a dangerous behaviour especially in case of conflicts. Other topics addressed include the cruelty of the prince, whether he should be loved or feared, and his qualities and education, as well as that of his sons. Several examples are taken from Erasmus's Apophthegmata, Declamatio de pueris instituendis, Adagia, and Institutio principis christiani. However, as with Machiavelli, Rosello never mentions Erasmus as a source.The second “Ragionamento” deals with the usefullness of weapons and literature as a mean to preserve the State. It has two new interlocutors: Girolamo Ruscelli (a sixteenth-century Venetian humanist, editor, and cartographer whose works contributed significantly to Renaissance geography and scientific dissemination) and Bernardino Bonifacio (an Italian humanist, and bibliophile renowned for his extensive intellectual networks and his commitment to the preservation of books and learning. His personal library, later donated to the city of Ljubljana, became one of the most important humanist collections in Central Europe). Rosello is inspired by a debate which just took place in Florence between Lelio Torelli and Duke Cosimo himself. Torelli, an Italian jurist and humanist renowned for his expertise in Roman and civil law during the Medicean period, argues that literature should be preferred to weapons, while Cosimo claimes the opposite. Benedetto Varchi (Florentine humanist, historian, and man of letters closely associated with the Medici cultural politics, renowned for his Storia fiorentina and his lectures on Dante and Petrarch) and Stefano Colonna (member of the influential Roman family, connected with prominent intellectuals and figures of the papal and imperial courts) also join the debate, arguing that if you can rely on brave captains, it makes little difference whether you have foreign soldiers or your own. Colonna, exactly like Machiavelli (The Prince, chapters XII-XIV), differentiates between the various types of soldiers (mercenary, auxiliary, mixed), and harshly criticizes the less courageous mercenary troops, while praising the native militias.There is a clear contrast between the two parts of the work: while the first portrays the Duke as an ‘Erasmian' prince, the second reveals his bellicose nature. In Erasmus's Institutio principis christiani, there is a section dedicated to war, which the author believes should be avoided among Christians. Rosello also considers Machiavelli's arguments on this topic and quotes several examples from The Prince, particularly from chapters VIII, XII-XIV, XIX, XX, XXI and XXII. However, he censored Machiavelli's writing extensively, removing anything that contradicted the Christian charity that inspired Erasmus's political and religious work.Following the conclusion of the dialogue, Rosello inserts his translation of two of Isocrates' Orations: Ad Nicoclem and Nicocles. The texts address the concept of the wise courtier or philosopher educating the prince, known as the "paideia" in Isocrates' works. Greece in the 4th century BC and Europe in the 15th and 16th centuries have some things in common. Firstly, there was a need for a new type of communication: the former shifted from an oral to a written tradition, while the latter shifted from manuscripts to print. In both cases, we see a significant increase in the number of people who benefitted from culture. This lead to an elite who had the cultural and linguistic means to educate their leaders, just as Erasmus did for Charles V of the House of Habsburg, the future emperor who was destined to partially unite Europe.Lucio Paolo Rosello (or Roselli) was a cleric, editor, and intellectual connected to the humanist circles and heterodox religious movements of the Republic of Venice. He came from a well-know family of jurists based in Arezzo and he was related to Antonio Roselli, Venetian nobleman and professor at the Padua's University from 1438 to 1468, a fierce anti-papal polemicist. Trained in legal and theological studies, he carried out an intense editorial activity, distinguishing himself by publishing and revising classical, legal, and religious texts according to the philological criteria of humanism, in collaboration with Pietro Bembo, the printer Pietro Perna and with Cornelio and Girolamo Donzellini. His literary activity appears to have begun in 1510 when he became the editor, for an unknown Venetian printer, of Masuccio Salernitano's Novellino, which was reprinted in Venice in 1522. Venice indeed was a very important publishing centre, but also a place where new religious ideas developed, also due to its importance in trade and its well-known greater tolerance: Italian historian Giuliano Procacci affirmed that, at least in the first period of Rosello's life, “All roads leads to Venice” (Machiavelli in European culture during Modern Age, Rome-Bari 1995, p.92). Having come into contact with the Erasmian thought and the Reformed circle centered around the figure of Pier Paolo Vergerio and the German humanist Friedrich Nausea, Rosello concentrated himself on writing works characterized by demands for spiritual renewal close to Protestant sensibility. Around 1531 Rosello began an epistolary correspondence with the theologians Philipp Melanchthon and Agostino Terzi, showing that he had adhered to the Reformation but with its typical traits of simulation and dissimulation also visible in the Ritratto. Appointed priest of the province of Pordenone in 1532, where Lutheran ideas were widely spread, he nevertheless maintained close ties with the Venetian publishing circles, participating in the circulation of texts suspected of heresy. Between June 22 and 23 1551, he was tried by the Venetian Inquisition following the discovery of prohibited books in his home; after his abjuration, he received a relatively moderate sentence.His best-known work, The Portrait of the True Government of the Prince (1552), represents an attempt to reconcile Machiavellian political realism and Erasmian moral idealism, outlining a model of government founded both on political prudence and the ethical discipline of the prince. The choice of such a topic derives from the tumultuous development of the sixteenth century in Italy, which led men of culture to ask themselves what an excellent prince should have been, like Machiavelli did a few years before. The choice of Cosimo de Medici as well was not accidental: the Grand Duke in fact had several conflicts going on with the then Pope Paul III, who had aims of control over Florence and was enraged by Cosimo's refusal to take the hand of his niece Vittoria Farnese. Moreover, Cosimo's confessor, Raffaele Sannini, was accused of being Lutheran and close to Juan de Valdès. Comparing the autograph manuscript of the work, today preserved at the Ambrosian Library in Milan, with the printed edition, Rosello's uncertainty can be easily seen: he modified the structure of the text until its final publication. In the first place the manuscript is lacking a title and the dedication, but moreover it does not contain any historical and geographical reference, beside Cosimo himself, therefore the author's hidden intentions are less clear. In conclusion, if the manuscript appears more like a flat apologia of the Grand Duke, the Ritratto is instead a much more structured and political work.An analysis of the book has been made by L. Perini (Gli eretici italiani del Cinquecento e Machiavelli, in: "Studi storici", X, 1969, pp. 880-902), showing how themes and concepts taken from Machiavelli's The Prince are woven into a fundamentally Erasmian idea of the figure of the prince, sometimes with almost literal borrowings (cf. A. Del Col, Rosello, Lucio Paolo, in: “Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani”, vol. 88, Rome, 2017, s.v., see also A. Del Col, Lucio Paolo Rosello e la vita religiosa veneziana verso la metà del secolo XVI, in: “Rivista di storia della Chiesa in Italia”, XXXII, 1978, pp. 422-459).
bibliography: Edit 16, CNCE29529; L.P. Rosello, Il ritratto del vero governo del prencipe (1552), M. Salvetti, ed., Milan, 2008.

title: La tariffa delle puttane di Venegia (XVIe siècle). Text Italien et traduction littérale
academic_description: First modern and first available edition, on which all subsequent editions are based. It opens with an ‘avertissement' and reprints the famous short poem on Venetian prostitutes, written in tercets and published in Venice in 1535 (the original of which is now lost), alongside a French translation. The author of the poem is unknown, but it has been attributed to various people, including Aretino, Franco and Venier, and more recently to the Paduan jurist Antonio Cavallino (cf. D. Romei, Nota al testo, in: “La tariffa delle puttane di Venegia”, Nuovo Rinascimento, 2020, pp. 64-66).
bibliography: Brunet, V, 659 and Supplement 728; Graesse, VI, 2, 29; Italian Union Catalogue, IT\ICCU\TO0\1427013.

title: Avventure di Angelina Chigi cominciando dal 1° Gen. 1854. Manuscript on paper in Italian.

authors.name: Chigi Albani Della Rovere Angela
authors.biography: Donna Angela Chigi Albani Della Rovere (1837–1901) represents a pivotal figure within the high patrician social fabric of nineteenth-century Rome, standing at the complex juncture where ancient papal aristocracy confronted the modern secularization of the Italian nation-state. Born into the illustrious Chigi Albani della Rovere line—a family that held the prestigious hereditary title of Maresciallo di Santa Romana Chiesa e Custode del Conclave (Marshal of the Holy Roman Church and Guardian of the Conclave)—Donna Angela embodied the aristocratic ethos, cultural patronage, and strict religious devotion characteristic of the Roman elite during the twilight of the Papal States and the consolidation of the Kingdom of Italy. Her life, spanning from the pontificate of Pope Gregory XVI through the tumultuous reign of Pius IX and into the post-Unification era under Humbert I, offers a profound case study in the resilience, adaptational strategies, and social functions of the Roman high nobility during a period of profound socio-political transformation.Born in Rome in 1837, Donna Angela was the daughter of Prince Sigismondo Chigi Albani della Rovere (1798–1877), 8th Prince of Farnese, Prince of the Holy Roman Empire, and hereditary Marshal of the Church, and Princess Leopoldina Doria Pamphili Landi (1811–1843). Through this union, Angela was embedded within an intricate web of European high aristocracy, directly tied to the grandest papal dynasties, including the Doria Pamphili, the Barberini, the Colonna, and the Borghese. Her early years were spent between the imposing family residence of Palazzo Chigi in Piazza Colonna—the monumental urban palace originally designed by Matteo Bartolottini and expanded by Gian Lorenzo Bernini—and the magnificent suburban estates of Palazzo Chigi in Ariccia and the coastal villa at Castel Fusano. Her formative education was governed by the rigorous religious and domestic protocols standard for noblewomen of the Roman patriciate, emphasizing classical languages, French epistolary style, sacred music, genealogical history, and the management of extensive household economy and pious foundations.The central decade of Donna Angela’s youth coincided with the catastrophic political ruptures of the mid-nineteenth century. The revolutionary outbursts of 1848 and the subsequent establishment of the short-lived Roman Republic of 1849 forced the papal court into exile in Gaeta and severely disrupted the traditional pattern of patrician life in Rome. Following the French military intervention and the restoration of Pope Pius IX, the Chigi household reassumed its paramount position within the Papal Court. As the daughter of the Marshal of the Holy Roman Church, Angela was raised in the immediate shadow of the Papal throne, participating in the elaborate ritual calendar of the Vatican Court and witnessing firsthand the administrative and diplomatic maneuvering that characterized the final decades of temporal papal rule. Her family’s heritage combined three distinct testamentary and heraldic traditions: the Sienese banking and artistic legacy of Agostino Chigi "il Magnifico" and Pope Alexander VII (Fabio Chigi); the testamentary succession of the Albani family (instigated by Pope Clement XI); and the ancient feudal titles of the Della Rovere line, inherited through complex matriarchal transmission.The definitive geopolitical catastrophe for Donna Angela’s social order arrived on September 20, 1870, with the Breach of Porta Pia and the annexation of Rome to the Kingdom of Italy. In the wake of this traumatic transformation, the Roman nobility divided into two distinct ideological factions: the "White Nobility" (Nobiltà Bianca), who accepted positions at the Savoyard Royal Court and integrated into the institutions of the new Italian Kingdom, and the "Black Nobility" (Nobiltà Nera), who remained fiercely loyal to the Holy See, closed the formal reception rooms of their palaces, and refused official recognition of the Italian state. The Chigi Albani della Rovere family was among the cornerstone families of this Black Nobility. Donna Angela’s adult life after 1870 was profoundly conditioned by this stance of internal exile and spiritual resistance. Deprived of their traditional political prerogatives within the Papal government, elite Roman women like Angela redirected their energies toward intensive religious philanthropy, the sponsorship of conservative Catholic educational institutions, and the stewardship of family archives and art collections.Throughout the late nineteenth century, Donna Angela Chigi Albani della Rovere occupied a key role within the private social networks of Roman patrician charity. She served as a director and benefactor for numerous confraternities, Marian sodalities, and charitable organizations, such as the Dame di Carità di San Vincenzo de' Paoli and local Roman pious houses (*conservatori*) dedicated to the protection and vocational training of orphaned young women. Her correspondence, meticulously preserved within the vast Archivio Chigi (now primarily divided between the Vatican Apostolic Library and the Vatican Apostolic Archives), reveals an extensive network of epistolary contacts across the Catholic nobility of Europe, encompassing letters on domestic administration, spiritual guidance, family inheritances, and diplomatic updates on the status of the Catholic Church. Her archival legacy provides invaluable insight into the day-to-day operations of an elite Roman household navigating the economic transitions of late nineteenth-century urban expansion, including the management of agricultural estates in the Lazio region, agricultural leasehold agreements, and the preservation of dynastic heirlooms.Donna Angela died in Rome in 1901, at the dawn of the twentieth century, marking the closing chapter of the traditional nineteenth-century Roman patriciate. Her historical legacy lives on not only through her genealogical footprint within the grand lineage of the Chigi Albani della Rovere family, but also through the extraordinary historical and material record preserved in the family’s architectural and archival monuments. Modern historical scholarship on nineteenth-century Rome, the Risorgimento, and the history of noblewomen has increasingly turned to figures like Donna Angela Chigi Albani della Rovere to illuminate the crucial, often understated role played by aristocratic women in maintaining dynastic continuity, managing extensive patrimonial wealth, and preserving religious and cultural identity during an era of sweeping socio-political modernisation.

academic_description: 178x118 mm. 35 unnumbered leaves plus one final blank. It features two small drawings of Angelina's siblings, Mario and Teresa (called Teta), dressed in carnival costumes. Original marbled cardboards. Very well preserved.The original title of the diary, Viaggio da Roma a Venezia 1853 (‘Journey from Rome to Venice, 1853'), has been crossed out and replaced with ‘The Adventures of Angelina Chigi, beginning on 1 January 1854'.The diary provides a detailed account of Angelina Chigi's daily activities in 1854, just before her marriage to Flavio Buonaccorsi (1826-1908), a nobleman from Macerata, on 30 November of that year. The couple had nine children.Angelina was born on 28 May 1837 in Rome. Her father was Sigismondo Chigi Albani della Rovere, the 6th Prince of Farnese (1798-1877), and her mother was the Roman princess Leopoldina Doria Pamphilj Landi (1811-1843). She had two siblings: Mario and Teresa. She died of a heart attack on 12 January 1901 at Villa Bonaccorsi in Potenza Picena.The diary vividly depicts the everyday life of a young Roman princess who attended all the balls and public events in the papal capital. Her social life was particularly active, and it is hard not to wonder whether her impending marriage added a certain excitement to her life. There are also frequent references to minor and major events happening around her, such as the first gas illumination of Via del Corso that went on without disruption or the killing of a carabiniere by mistake by a killer who was being chased by the crowd. At p. 32 begins the description of a journey that took Angelina to Viterbo, Siena, Livorno (by train and visit to the steam boat Capri), Florence (evening at La Pergola Theater), Bologna, Ferrara and the river Po, Padua, Venice (description of the Pala d'oro), Vicenza, Verona, before returning home. At the end of the booklet is a short section called Ricordi d'Angelina (‘Memories of Angelina'), in which she recounts her earliest memories (the oldest of which date back to 1844, when she was seven) and records important dates in her family's history, such as her siblings' and relatives' birthdays and confirmation dates.Some excerpts from the diary:Sabato 11. Molto freddo, vi è stato del gelo nella notte. Ballo da Lady Best […] Mercoledì 14. Tempo buono, ho scritto a Bepi per San Giuseppe che è il santo del suo nome. E ho ricevuto una lettera d'Emilia. Il principe di Prussia è partito per Napoli. Vi è a Roma il Duca di Wellington, Nonno lo conosce, e il D Principe di Sassonia. Le truppe francesi e inglesi sono in viaggio per Costantinopoli per combattere i Russi, insieme ai Turchi. Il ministro dei lavori pubblici cioè Jacobini sta molto male. Si parla di un matrimonio fra Maria Cini e Don Francesco Delgallo […] Domenica 28. Oggi essendo il mio compleanno terminando anni 17 Buonaccorsi mi ha donato una magnifica spilletta, ed è venuto a pranzo. Bonfigli mi sta facendo il ritratto in miniatura da dare a Buonaccorsi […] (‘Saturday 11. Very cold, there was frost during the night. Dance at Lady Best's […] Wednesday 14. Good weather, I wrote to Bepi for St. Joseph's Day, which is his name day. And I received a letter from Emilia. The Prince of Prussia has left for Naples. The Duke of Wellington is in Rome, Granpa knows him, and the D Prince of Saxony. French and English troops are on their way to Constantinople to fight the Russians, together with the Turks. The Minister of Public Works, Jacobini, is very ill. There is talk of a marriage between Maria Cini and Don Francesco Delgallo […] Sunday 28. Today is my birthday, I am turning 17, and Buonaccorsi gave me a magnificent brooch and came to lunch. Bonfigli is painting my portrait in miniature to give to Buonaccorsi […]').

title: Archaeological and historical researches of Peking and its environs by E. Bretschneider, M.D., Physician to the Russian Legation at Peking

authors.name: Bretschneider Emil Vasilievich
authors.biography: Emil Vasilievich Bretschneider (July 4 [O.S. June 22] 1833 – May 12 [O.S. April 29] 1901) stands as one of the most remarkable intellectual figures of nineteenth-century European sinology, botanical taxonomy, and historical geography. Born into the Baltic German gentry in Bankau (present-day Latvia), within the Livonian Governorate of the Russian Empire, Bretschneider embodied the unique cultural and scientific synthesis characteristic of the Baltic German intelligentsia who served the Tsarist state.Operating at the boundary where classical Western scientific methodology met the vast, uncodified philological traditions of Imperial China, Bretschneider transformed the European understanding of East Asian flora, historical geography, and medieval trade routes. His dual capacity as an official physician to the Imperial Russian Legation in Peking (Beijing) and a self-taught polymath permitted him unprecedented access to Chinese literary sources, native scholars, and living botanical specimens during the late Qing dynasty, a period when Western knowledge of the interior of China was often fragmentary and tainted by colonial misunderstanding.Early Life, Lineage, and Formative Academic BackgroundBretschneider received his early education in the rigorous classical gymnasia of Livonia, where he mastered Latin, Greek, French, and German, while acquiring fluency in Russian. In 1853, he matriculated at the renowned Imperial University of Dorpat (modern Tartu, Estonia), which served as the premier Baltic German seat of higher learning and a primary conduit for German scientific idealism into the Russian Empire. At Dorpat, Bretschneider pursued medicine, studying under leading scholars of anatomy, chemistry, and natural history. He graduated with his Medical Doctorate (M.D.) in 1858, having defended a dissertation grounded in clinical physiology. Far from limiting his intellectual horizons to clinical practice, his university years instilling in him a deep devotion to systematic empirical observation, comparative linguistics, and natural history. Shortly after graduation, Bretschneider entered the medical service of the Imperial Russian Ministry of Foreign Affairs—a career choice that would determine the trajectory of his life's work. His initial overseas posting took him to Tehran, Persia, where he served as physician to the Russian Embassy from 1862 to 1865. This Persian tenure served as his apprenticeship in Oriental diplomacy and linguistic immersion, preparing him for his seminal appointment to China.The Peking Years: Synthesis of Sinology, Medicine, and BotanyIn 1866, Bretschneider was appointed Chief Physician to the Russian Legation in Peking, a position he retained for nearly two decades until 1883. The Russian Legation, housed within the historic EIFan Guan (Russian House) established by the Treaty of Kyakhta, enjoyed a unique institutional status in Peking compared to Western European diplomatic missions. This position granted Bretschneider extraordinary stability and access. Upon his arrival in the Qing capital, Bretschneider recognized that European botanical and geographical science suffered from a profound defect: Western scholars were utterly incapable of identifying the botanical taxa and geographic locations described in thousands of years of classical Chinese literature, while Chinese scholars possessed no systematic understanding of Linnaean nomenclature. Determined to bridge this intellectual chasm, Bretschneider engaged native scholars and tutors, acquiring an exceptional mastery of literary and classical Chinese (wenyan).Bretschneider’s intellectual work in Peking proceeded along two interconnected tracks: botanical translation and historical-geographical reconstruction. He began collecting plant specimens systematically in the Western Hills (Xishan) surrounding Peking, as well as in the broader province of Zhili (modern Hebei) and the mountains of Shandong. Rather than operating as an isolated collector, Bretschneider established a formidable network with Chinese Buddhist monks, herbalists, and peasant gatherers, purchasing living plants, seeds, and dried herbarium specimens. Simultaneously, he applied his philological prowess to the monumental corpus of traditional Chinese materia medica and agricultural treatises. He scrutinized foundational texts such as the Shennong Bencao Jing (Divine Farmer's Materia Medica), the Nanfang Caomu Zhuang (Plants of the Southern Regions), and above all, Li Shizhen’s masterpiece of the Ming Dynasty, the Bencao Gangmu (Compendium of Materia Medica). By critically comparing the vernacular Chinese plant names, morphologic descriptions, and historical uses with his own field specimens, Bretschneider established precise botanical identifications for hundreds of plants that had previously confounded European sinologists and naturalists.Major Works and Scientific ContributionsBretschneider’s publication record represents an unprecedented monument of nineteenth-century scholarship. His first major publication in East Asia, On the Study and Value of Chinese Botanical Works (Shanghai, 1870), laid out his methodology for extracting scientific taxonomy from traditional Chinese texts. This was followed by a series of foundational monographs that redefined European sinology. In 1881, he published Early European Researches into the Flora of China in the Journal of the North-China Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society, tracing every recorded Western interaction with Chinese flora from the Jesuits to early nineteenth-century naturalists.Between 1882 and 1895, Bretschneider produced his crowning Sinological-botanical achievement: the three-part Botanicon Sinicum: Notes on Chinese Botany from Native and Western Sources. Published sequentially in the Journal of the North-China Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society and as separate volumes in London and Shanghai, Botanicon Sinicum provided the global scientific community with a definitive dictionary of Chinese plant names, identification of classical Chinese agricultural crops, and detailed cross-references between traditional Chinese economic botany and modern scientific taxonomy. The work remained the indispensable authority on the subject for nearly a century.Parallel to his botanical endeavors, Bretschneider made groundbreaking contributions to historical geography. In his masterwork Mediaeval Researches from Eastern Asiatic Sources (2 volumes, London: Trübner & Co., 1888), he translated, annotated, and analyzed a vast collection of thirteenth- to seventeenth-century Chinese travelogues, diplomatic records, and military narratives regarding Central and Western Asia. Key among these were the travels of the Daoist master Changchun (Qiu Chuji) to the court of Genghis Khan, the itineraries of Yelü Chucai, and Chinese accounts of the Mongol conquests and the Timurid Empire. Bretschneider utilized his profound knowledge of Central Asian geography and Eurasian languages to identify long-lost medieval cities, mountain passes, and river systems, providing Western historians with their first reliable Chinese perspective on the history of the Mongol Empire and the Silk Road.Typographical Context, Print Networks, and Botanical CirculationThe dissemination of Bretschneider’s scholarship illustrates the globalized nature of nineteenth-century scientific publishing. His works were printed across multiple continents: in Shanghai by the press of the North-China Branch of the Royal Asiatic Society and the Presbyterian Mission Press; in London by the legendary Orientalist publisher Nicholas Trübner; and in St. Petersburg by the Imperial Academy of Sciences. Bretschneider was meticulous regarding typographical layout, often insistence on parallel columns of Chinese characters alongside English, Latin, and French transliterations, requiring highly specialized typography and master compositors capable of cutting and setting Chinese lead characters alongside Roman types.Beyond the printed page, Bretschneider’s primary medium of exchange was material: dried herbarium sheets, living seeds, and detailed geographic maps. During his seventeen years in Peking, he dispatched thousands of meticulously labeled dried plant specimens to the principal botanical gardens of Europe: the Imperial Botanical Garden of St. Petersburg (where he collaborated closely with its director, Eduard August von Regel, and the Chief Botanist, Carl Johann Maximowicz), the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew (directed by Sir Joseph Dalton Hooker), and the Muséum National d'Histoire Naturelle in Paris. Many of the most iconic East Asian plant species introduced to Western horticulture during the late nineteenth century—including various species of lilacs (such as Syringa bretschneideri), crabapples, pears, and ornamental shrubs—were first raised from seeds collected by Bretschneider or procured through his local networks in northern China.Return to St. Petersburg, Late Works, and LegacyRetiring from diplomatic and medical service in 1883, Bretschneider returned to St. Petersburg, where he spent his final eighteen years as an independent scholar. Unburdened by administrative duties, he devoted himself to synthesized historical works and cartography. In 1896, he published his magnificent Map of China and the Surrounding Regions, accompanied by a detailed geographical handbook, which was recognized immediately as the most accurate European map of the Qing Empire ever produced.In 1898, he published his monumental, 1,300-page opus magnum: History of European Botanical Discoveries in China (2 volumes, London and St. Petersburg). This monumental treatise remains an unmatched masterpiece of bio-bibliographical scholarship, providing a exhaustive, chronologically arranged history of every European physician, missionary, diplomat, traveller, and professional collector who had observed or gathered plants in China from the sixteenth century down to the end of the nineteenth century. The work stands as a monument to Victorian erudition, synthesizing archival research from across Europe with deep botanical authority.Bretschneider’s intellectual contributions were recognized globally during his lifetime. He was awarded the prestigious Stanislas Gold Medal, elected a corresponding member of the Académie des Inscriptions et Belles-Lettres in Paris (winning its coveted Prix Stanislas Julien twice for his Sinological contributions), and honored by the Royal Geographical Society of London and the Berlin Geographical Society (receiving the Karl Ritter Medal). He died in St. Petersburg on May 12, 1901. His taxonomic legacy is immortalized in the monotypic plant genus Bretschneidera (family Bretschneideraceae / Akaniaceae), named in his honor by the botanist Hermann Harms, as well as dozens of plant species bearing the specific epithet bretschneideri. As a bridge between Chinese erudition and Western empirical science, Emil Bretschneider remains an unexcelled colossus of late nineteenth-century scholarship.

publisher_data: Shangai-London, American Presbyterian Mission Press-Trübner & Co., 1876
academic_description: 8vo (246x160 mm). [2], 63, [1 blank] pp. Illustrated with a map of Beijing and surroundings at p. 56 and IV folding plates with Chinese plans printed on thinner rice paper. Editor's printed wrappers (only front cover preserved). Ownership entry “Herr Profess. L. Müller in Wien […]” on the front cover. Bookplate John and Margareth Mackail on the title page. A good copy.Rare first edition of this very important historical and geographical study on Beijing, first published in “The Chinese Recorder” the year before (1875, vol. VI, nos. 3, 5, and 6).“His research on Beijing, which has been honored with a French translation by a young scholar, Mr. Collin de Plancy -now the French Minister in Seoul- is a model of local history; this excellent monograph is drawn from a large number of works written on the capital of China, and in particular from the Ji hia kiu wen, published in the 17th century in 42 chapters by Tchou I-tsoun” (H. Cordier, Le Docteur Emile Vasilievitch Bretschneider, in: “T'oung Pao”, second series, vol. 2, no. 3, 1901, pp. 193 and 196).“Emil Bretschneider, ‘physician at the Russian Embassy in Peking', as he calls himself, published an interesting booklet in 1876: Archaeological and Historical Researches on Peking and its Environs. Originally published in Shanghai by the American Presbyterian Mission, the work has recently been reprinted in an anastatic edition by Elibron Classics, s.d., Boston. In the enjoyable introduction, the author states how he had the chance to examine ancient Chinese texts in Peking, quoting from them with an archivist's precision. The works referred to include the Rixia jiuwen, by Zhu Yijun (1629-1709), which is a sort of anthology of texts from different periods referring to the city of Peking. The Qing emperor Qianlong set up a committee of literati to update the work and the new version was published under the title of Rixia jiuwen kao (1744, 160 chapters). The information gathered on the city in the past and in the present, on roads, temples, parks and suburbs, was mentioned in part by Bretschneider” (S. Cammelli, Storia di Pechino, Bologna, 2004, p. 27).After earning his doctorate in medicine from the University of Dorpat, Bretschneider was appointed to the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in 1862 as physician to the Russian legation in Tehran. He was then appointed physician to the legation in Beijing in 1866. He resided there from 1866 to 1883, taking two leaves of absence, one in 1871 and the other in 1878. He was granted retirement in February 1884 with the rank of current State Councilor. After retiring, he moved to St. Petersburg, where he continued to write and publish the works that established his reputation. In 1886, he was appointed a corresponding member of the Institut de France. He was also a corresponding member of the Paris Geographical Society.

title: Titi Livii Historiarum Libri ex recensione Heinsiana

authors.name: Livius Titus
authors.biography: Titus Livius (59 B.C. – A.D. 17), known universally in the Anglophone tradition as Livy, stands alongside Sallust and Tacitus as one of the three canonical historians of ancient Rome. Operating at the profound epochal threshold where the battered Roman Republic dissolved into the monarchical architecture of the Augustan Principate, Livy devoted the greater part of his adult life to the creation of a prose monument: the Ab Urbe Condita Libri ('Books from the Founding of the City'). This colossal historiographical enterprise, spanning 142 books, sought to chronicle the entire trajectory of the Roman people from the mythic arrival of Aeneas and the foundation of the city by Romulus down to the contemporary deaths of Drusus in 9 B.C. and Augustus himself. Beyond his primary historical function, Livy served as a crucial ideological and literary pillar of the Augustan cultural restoration, synthesizing moral philosophy, civic rhetoric, and providential nationalism into a prose style characterized by Quintilian as a lactea ubertas—a rich, milky abundance—that defined Latin historical composition for centuries.Born in Patavium (modern Padua) in Northern Italy—a prosperous Cisalpine city renowned for its staunch Republican traditions, strict moral conservativism, and immense wealth—Livy retained an indelible imprint of his provincial origin throughout his life. This geographic and cultural provenance gave rise to the famous literary enigma of patavinitas, a stylistic or moral quality attributed to Livy by his contemporary, the acerbic critic and historian Gaius Asinius Pollio. While modern scholars debate whether Pollio meant to disparage subtle regionalisms in Livy's Latin syntax or to mock the provincial, old-fashioned moralism that permeated his narrative, the concept of patavinitas came to signify the historian's unwavering devotion to traditional Roman virtus, pietas, and gravitas. Unlike his predecessors Cato the Censor, Sallust, or Pollio, Livy never pursued a senatorial career, nor did he hold military command or public magistracies. His life was that of a dedicated man of letters, educated thoroughly in philosophy and rhetoric, who arrived in Rome during the 30s B.C., shortly after the defeat of Mark Antony and Cleopatra at Actium had established Gaius Julius Caesar Octavianus (Augustus) as sole master of the Mediterranean world.Despite his lack of political office, Livy established a close personal rapport with Augustus.
